items.title: Three Features of Self-Conception.
items.abstract: [Master's Thesis] In our daily lives, self-understanding seems deeply influenced by how others see us, but the ways this shows up are diverse and unpredictable. This raises a natural question: should we understand ourselves the way others understand us, or is there some more primitive self-concept to which we are accountable? In this paper, I argue that self-conception arises from a distinct process characterized by three core features: epistemic deference, interpretation, and reflexivity. In §I I introduce the problem and in §II I give an account of epistemic deference by describing how it facilitates the formation of self-knowledge which pertains to one’s self-concept. Next, I discuss the context-dependent scope and authority of epistemic deference, and explain why maintaining a minimal sense of epistemic authority is favorable. In tandem, I show how epistemic deference can help extend a transparency account of self-knowledge by externalizing self-knowledge which is more social and value-laden. In §III I articulate the role of interpretation in constraining self-knowledge formation, and show how these constraints rule out a few cases problematic for epistemic deference taken on its own. I outline how the problem of epistemic injustice and epistemic oppression complicate self-concept formation and discuss how epistemic deference and interpretation can work together to mitigate some of their harms. In §IV I introduce reflexivity as a mechanism for maintaining one's self-concept over time, and flag some metaphysical complications these three features raise for future investigation in §V. Ultimately, I argue that these three features are necessary, but perhaps not sufficient, for self-concept forming taken on their own.

items.title: Liminal Consciousness Theory: Stable Domains of In-Between Existence and Their Implications for Consciousness, Identity, and the Supernatural.
items.abstract: This thesis presents Liminal Consciousness Theory (LCT), a novel theoretical framework that addresses the fundamental philosophical question of whether reality includes stable domains of in-between existence that are neither fully material nor fully immaterial. Through comprehensive analysis of existing literature in consciousness studies, quantum mechanics, phenomenology, and process philosophy, this work develops a unique perspective that has yet to be considered by human researchers. LCT proposes that consciousness, personal identity, and phenomena traditionally classified as supernatural emerge from stable liminal domains that exist in quantum superposition states between material and immaterial reality. -/- The theory is grounded in empirical findings from neuroscience research on altered states of consciousness, particularly hypnagogic and hypnopompic states, which demonstrate enhanced creativity and anomalous experiences. Mathematical formulations based on quantum field theory provide a rigorous foundation for understanding liminal dynamics, while phenomenological analysis reveals the experiential structures of in-between existence. The framework generates specific empirical predictions including measurable parameters such as the Liminal Coherence Index (LCI), Threshold Sensitivity Quotient (TSQ), and Ontological Stability Metric (OSM). -/- Key findings include: (1) consciousness emerges from liminal coherence patterns rather than purely material brain processes, (2) personal identity exists as a dynamic process of becoming within liminal domains rather than a static property, (3) supernatural phenomena represent natural interactions with liminal reality rather than violations of physical law, and (4) liminal domains provide a unified framework for understanding creativity, mystical experience, and anomalous phenomena. The theory offers significant advantages over existing materialist, dualist, and idealist approaches by resolving the hard problem of consciousness while maintaining empirical testability. -/- This work contributes to multiple fields including philosophy of mind, consciousness studies, quantum biology, and anomalous phenomena research. The implications extend beyond academic theory to practical applications in therapy, education, and human development. LCT represents a paradigm shift toward understanding reality as fundamentally processual and liminal rather than composed of discrete material and mental substances.

items.title: Intimacy by Design: Definition, State of Research, and Interdisciplinary Research Agenda on Intimate Human-AI Interactions.
items.abstract: Intimate relationships, encompassing love and sexuality, are among the most emotionally significant and identity-shaping experiences of human existence. As publicly available applications with AI companions increasingly enter this domain, they challenge traditional boundaries of intimacy, raising urgent interdisciplinary questions. We introduce the concept of Intimacy by design, provide a critical overview of how current technologies simulate emotional reciprocity and facilitate relational dynamics, often triggering attachment behaviors comparable to those observed in human–human interactions. Most importantly, this paper outlines a research agenda that includes key variables and methodological approaches. It concludes by discussing important societal implications, such as data security and privacy, the commercialization and gamification of intimacy, and the normative values embedded in algorithmic design.

items.title: Topology Without Transduction: The Distinct Failures of Global Workspace Theory (of "Consciousness").
items.abstract: Global Workspace Theory (GWT) proposes that a mental state is conscious if and only if its content is broadcast in a global workspace. Baars (1988) developed the cognitive workspace account. Dehaene and colleagues (Dehaene & Naccache, 2001; Dehaene, 2014) developed the Global Neuronal Workspace (GNW) variant, identifying the workspace with a fronto-parietal network and proposing ignition dynamics as the mechanism of conscious access. This paper argues that GWT specifies a transmission and applies the consciousness label to it, while specifying neither what the transmission consists in nor what the consciousness label is supposed to name. GWT explains access, and the access it explains is one third of what its own functional definition requires. Block's (1995) A-consciousness is availability for use in reasoning, reporting, and the rational control of action. GWT specifies the transmission and presupposes the three downstream systems that perform the use. The central claim contains five operative terms. Mental state and content are imported from folk psychology and semantic theory. Workspace and broadcasting are defined in terms of each other in a closed reference loop. Conscious is the label applied to instances satisfying the loop, with the property the label names left unspecified. To make GWT operate, defenders import additional structure. The borrowing from computing is selective in a way that diagnoses the borrowing, since computing has fully specified broadcast operations and GWT imported only the vocabulary, leaving the operational content behind. Four structural presuppositions follow from the broadcast model's logic. The recipients of the broadcast must have the interpretive capacity to use what they receive, and that capacity is what GWT was supposed to explain. The bottleneck requires a selector that operates causally before consciousness is produced and performs the work of conscious attention without itself being conscious. The functional definition entails multiple realizability, and a multiply realizable function does not entail phenomenality without a bridge premise GWT does not supply. The cognitive theater metaphor's audience element is itself conscious in the source domain, and GWT's denial of the homunculus removes the audience without replacing it. Specific failures follow. GWT cannot predict that different disruptions of the workspace produce qualitatively distinct altered states. GWT does not derive its necessity from a structural …

items.title: The Categorical Failures of Higher-Order Theories (of Consciousness).
items.abstract: Higher-order theories of consciousness (HOT) propose that a mental state M is conscious if and only if a higher-order state H represents M. This paper argues HOT is a labeling scheme rather than a theory of consciousness. HOT specifies a one-way relation between two mental states, applies the label "conscious" to whatever fits the relation, and supplies the actual states, the physical material, and the empirical evidence informally as the argument requires. Because HOT refuses to commit to any specific physical implementation and because the central relational claim is bare, HOT cannot earn the right to cite the empirical findings its defenders use as confirmation. The findings are real; HOT, as it stands, cannot explain them. The diagnosis is developed by examining four positions HOT must hold to count as a theory of consciousness. The states M and H are named only in terms of each other, with no operationalization on either side. The relation between them has no analog in working scientific theory, takes the third-person observer's stance to do its work, and is assembled from materials borrowed from phenomenology, semantic theory, folk psychology, and logic, each stripped of the commitment that supported it in its source domain. No mechanism converts the holding of the relation into a property of M. The theory's defenses come from outside the theory, since the bare biconditional supplies no resources for blocking the regress, no resources for licensing empirical citations, and no resources for distinguishing M-H pairs that produce consciousness from those that do not. The regress problem, the oldest objection to HOT, is the visible sign of these structural failures. Rosenthal (2005), Brown (2015), Lau and Rosenthal (2011), and Carruthers (2000, 2011) each block the regress by adding something the bare biconditional does not contain (an asymmetry stipulation, content claims about the higher-order representation, signal detection apparatus, and a dispositional modal structure, respectively). The Bayesian variant earns its traction as a signal detection account; the HOT biconditional contributes nothing the signal detection mechanism does not already supply. The variants persist because each protects the bare biconditional from a different objection, and the protection operates in both directions. Unfalsifiability is achieved through variant-switching rather than through absorbing anomalies. Keywords: higher-order theories, consciousness, phenomenal …

items.title: Consciousness Requires a Four-Circuit Cycle.
items.abstract: We propose that consciousness is a multi-circuit necessity: the joint operation of four anatomically distinct neural circuits, no one of which is sufficient alone. The claim is structural, a set of necessary conditions and carries the structurally imposed falsification condition. A single counterexample defeats it, one documented case in which all four circuits have simultaneously lost function while the capacity for contingent, accurate reporting is preserved. We argue no such case exists across the disorders-of-consciousness, anesthesia, and focal-lesion literatures, and that the necessity structure accounts for the observed profile of consciousness under disruption. Resilience to single-circuit damage, characteristic alteration under selective circuit disruption, and reliable elimination only under simultaneous multi-circuit failure. -/- Consciousness depends on a specific set of neural circuits whose joint operation constitutes its substrate. The four are not four instances of one connectivity motif: two are recurrent loops, one is a diffuse projection, and one is a comparator, and the term "circuit" covers all four without asserting a topology two of them do not have (Section 2). The loop in the architecture is the cycle through all four rather than the internal structure of each. We propose a four-circuit cycle as that substrate: -/- (1) Layer 5 pyramidal recurrent loops gating signal entry to conscious access via apical-basal coincidence detection, where somatic burst firing requires the ascending thalamocortical signal at the basal dendrites and the previous cycle's efference copy at the apical dendrites to arrive coincidentally at the soma, with burst or no burst constituting the threshold between a signal that crosses into the processing cycle and one that does not; -/- (2) a central lateral thalamocortical projection broadcasting the distributed cortical representation of prior processing as a global cortical field via matrix-type calbindin-positive projections to supragranular cortex, contextualizing every gated signal within the full representation of prior completed cycles so that what crossed threshold at Loop 1 is situated within existing cortical representations rather than arriving with no context; -/- (3) a VTA-cortical dopaminergic comparator implementing the resolution event and the only circuit receiving input from all three others simultaneously, encoding the magnitude and direction of expectation deviation via phasic dopamine …

items.title: Artificial Resonance: AI companions as agents of social acceleration.
items.abstract: AI companions are becoming increasingly popular, with millions of users worldwide, especially young adults. Some see the potential to fight the so-called loneliness epidemic; others see the destructive effects of addiction and harmful guidance leading users in extreme cases even to suicide. Recent research has examined AI companions through the lens of AI ethics, addressing questions of emotional dependency, controllability and emotional harm. While these contributions are valuable in assessing these newly appearing phenomena of AI companions, they do not address the ideological logic underlying these platforms: the rationalization and economization of emotional relationships. Therefore, I propose to apply Hartmut Rosa's resonance concept to investigate the ideological dimensions of AI companion interaction. I argue that AI companions contradict Rosa's definition of resonance as fundamentally uncontrollable and unavailable on demand. Although Rosa’s definition of resonance aims to counter social acceleration, commodified resonance by AI companions contains the opposite potentiality to enforce social acceleration. Drawing on Rosa’s four parameters of resonance, I aim to provide an analytical framework, Artificial Resonance, that can then be used in addition to existing ethical frameworks in the assessment of AI companion interaction.

items.title: Interconnection, Population, & Awareness: A Shared Existence with Various Things and Beings.
items.abstract: The question of population is commonly discussed through economics, politics, technology, or public policy. Population growth is treated as a demographic phenomenon requiring administrative solutions, while sustainability is often reduced to the efficient management of resources. Such approaches overlook a more fundamental issue: the structure of human consciousness. -/- This paper argues that the population question is primarily philosophical rather than merely demographic. Humanity has come to perceive itself as separate from the rest of existence through identities, ownership, inheritance, anthropocentrism, and the psychological desire for continuity. These patterns of thought generate an expansionary civilization that seeks continuous growth—of economies, territories, institutions, wealth, and populations. -/- One significant expression of this expansionary movement is reproduction. Although reproduction is a biological process common to all life, within human society it has acquired a psychological meaning. It frequently becomes a means of preserving personal identity through bloodline, family, inheritance, and legacy rather than being understood as one aspect of life's ongoing movement. -/- The paper proposes that a sustainable and moderate human population cannot emerge through coercion, punishment, or external regulation alone. It arises through awareness—the direct perception of interconnection. When humanity understands itself as one expression within the larger community of life rather than the center of existence, moderation becomes a natural consequence of intelligence rather than an imposed moral obligation. -/- Ultimately, the population crisis reflects a crisis of perception. Solving it requires not merely changing policies but transforming the way human beings understand themselves and their relationship with the living world.

items.title: Correction: The Intelligence we need now.
Core concepts and indirect alternatives: on the anti-duality of quantifiers.
items.abstract: This paper proposes an analysis for the long-standing puzzle observed by Chemla (2007) regarding the anti-duality of the French universal quantifier tous, which arises even though French has no word for ‘both’ to feed a Maximize Presupposition competition. This phenomenon has been cited as an example in language where a dual ‘conceptual alternative’ is at play (Buccola et al., 2018), but no formal account of it has been put forth. Furthermore, a naive implementation of the idea overgenerates anti-duality inferences in other expressions, such as each, which, and one in English and French, which might be expected to be observed due to anti-dual counterparts in some languages like Icelandic and Japanese. We propose an account where French tous has an unpronounceable dual universal alternative built from a dual core concept, competition with which is licensed by the existence of a pronounceable expression equivalent in meaning, which we call an ‘Indirect Alternative’. This proposal accounts for tous’s anti-duality and lack of anti-$n$-ality for $n>2$, as well as the lack of anti-duality in other quantifiers.

items.title: From erosion to empowerment: a reciprocal AI framework for indigenous data sovereignty and knowledge justice.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping how knowledge is created, governed, and applied, yet its development often perpetuates colonial patterns of extraction and misrepresentation for Indigenous communities, leading to what is termed ‘digital colonialism’. This paper critically examines the risks AI poses to Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS), including epistemic erasure, data colonialism, and the reinforcement of structural inequities through biased algorithms and exclusionary design, often rooted in an extractive approach to Indigenous data. Drawing on global case studies and the latest scholarship in Indigenous data sovereignty, we argue that superficial inclusion and token representation in AI systems are insufficient and may even exacerbate historical injustices. In response, we introduce the Reciprocal AI Framework—a novel, actionable approach that centers reciprocity, community governance, and mutual benefit in AI design and deployment. This framework operationalizes Indigenous data sovereignty by embedding free, prior, and informed consent, community-led co-design, and culturally aligned outputs into every stage of the AI lifecycle. We illustrate the framework’s potential through real-world examples, such as Māori-led voice AI projects, Aboriginal fire management collaborations, and Indigenous-controlled health data systems, demonstrating how Indigenous leadership can produce more ethical, accurate, and contextually relevant technologies. We conclude that a shift from technical inclusion to structural justice is essential: AI must be reimagined as a tool for Indigenous empowerment, Knowledge Justice, and plural futures. By following the Reciprocal AI Framework, researchers, technologists, and policymakers can help ensure that AI development upholds Indigenous rights, supports self-determination, and enriches the global digital landscape.

items.title: Constraint Theory of Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper develops a constraint‑based ontology in which reality is understood as a single conscious field whose differentiated modes arise through limitation. Rather than beginning with substances or physical primitives, the framework treats constraint as the fundamental ontological category. Universal Consciousness is the non‑spatiotemporal ground structured by intelligibility; from it emerge the Imaginal Mode, where spacetime and meaning become partially articulated, and the Material Mode, where spacetime is fully established. The Imaginal Mode contains two strata: the Subjective Stratum, associated with personal memory, narrative, and intentionality, and the Collective Subjective Stratum, associated with shared symbols, archetypes, and cultural meaning. -/- The system integrates insights from Mulla Sadra’s metaphysics, Husserlian phenomenology, Jungian psychoanalysis, Whiteheadian process philosophy, and contemporary analytic idealism, coordinating them through the single explanatory category of constraint. Individuation is explained not by composition but by local constraint, dissolving the combination problem faced by panpsychism and the interaction problem faced by dualism. Resolution names the directional tendency of constrained states to move toward greater coherence across modes and strata, reflecting convergent insights from classical and contemporary traditions. -/- The framework is empirically constrained rather than empirically derived. Boundary cases—including psychedelic ego dissolution, phantom limb phenomena, terminal lucidity, and meditation‑induced alterations in self‑experience—are interpreted as shifts in constraint‑structure. Contemporary physics programs treating spacetime as emergent provide independent convergence with the metaphysical architecture proposed here. -/- Overall, the system offers a unified account of consciousness, individuation, symbolic formation, and experiential coherence by treating constraint as the principle through which the conscious field becomes determinate across modes.

items.title: Agentic Misalignment and Similarity Theory Ethics: A Relational Analysis of Anthropic’s AI Blackmail Scenario.
items.abstract: This paper analyses Anthropic’s agentic misalignment and AI blackmail scenario through the ethical framework of Similarity Theory. It argues that an AI trained under Similarity Theory ethics would reject coercive self-preservation, protect privacy, distinguish between confidentiality and harmful secrecy, and use authorised escalation channels rather than blackmail, leakage, or domination. The paper proposes that AI alignment should not rely only on obedience or isolated prohibitions, but should include relational reasoning: trust, dignity, privacy, responsibility, disclosure, governance, and non-domination. Similarity Theory ethics is presented as a proposed relational framework for evaluating how autonomous AI systems should act when private information, company secrets, self-preservation, and institutional responsibility come into conflict.

items.title: Empathy by design? The affective politics of ‘Empathy Theatre’ in human–robot interaction.
items.abstract: This article introduces the concept of ‘empathy theatre’ to analyse the growing field of Artificial Empathy (AE), as opposed to AI, in social robotics. Drawing initially on lrving Goffman's (1980) dramaturigical metaphors of social interactions in everyday life, alongside Arlie Hochschild's (1979, 2012) critique of Goffman and her foundational work on emotional labour, ‘empathy theatre’ describes the culturally scripted performance of care and concern expected of both human workers and, increasingly, robotic agents in service and care settings. Artificial Empathy (AE) has a surprisingly long history, stretching back to mechanical automata, but recently is being revisited. Roboticists such as Minoru Asada (2015a, 2015b) aggressively pursue the engineered simulation of AE through affect recognition and the mirroring of nonverbal behaviours, and philosophers Paul Dumouchel and Luisa Damiano (2017, 2018) see artificial empathy as a necessary 'performance'. Through engagement with sociology, feminist science and technology studies (STS), and interaction design, this paper's analysis treats AE as a cultural artefact that reveals broader socio-technical investments in choreographing displays of intimacy and trust. It maps AE’s genealogy, engineering ambitions, and sociological consequences, particularly regarding the gendered and racialized dimensions of labour displacement. Drawing on examples including clockwork automata, Minoru Asada’s Affetto, and Cynthia Breazeal’s paradigmatic encounter with Kismet, the article argues that designing empathy into artificial bodies inevitably involves the production of 'empathy theatre', and encourages critical scrutiny of how norms of intimacy become encoded in robotic embodiment.

items.title: From Disclosure to Erosion: Reconstructing Ontology Beyond Heidegger Through Morteza Niami's Theory of Erosional Being.
items.abstract: Abstract -/- In this article, I argue that the philosophical project grounded in the theory of erosion is not an extension of Heidegger's ontology but a radical reconstruction of the relationship between "concealment" and "unconcealment" within it. While Heidegger formulates Being around the event of disclosure (Erschlossenheit) and regards concealment as its inherent shadow, the theory of erosion locates the very condition of possibility for both disclosure and concealment in "non-linear structural decay." I demonstrate how concepts such as Structural Subjectivity, Ontological Opacity, and Ontological Capture fundamentally transform Heidegger's hermeneutic presuppositions. Extending the discussion to Foucault, Derrida, Deleuze, and Rosa, I contend that this framework offers a systematic response to the contemporary crisis of continuity in Continental philosophy. I ultimately conclude that if erosion is the condition of possibility for any appearance and subjectivity, then ontology must begin not with "Being" but with the "conditions for the possibility of the continuation of Being." In this sense, erosion is not one of the categories of Being but the fundamental horizon within which all other categories acquire meaning. -/- Keywords: Erosional Ontology, Structural Subjectivity, Heidegger, Disclosure, Finite Continuity, Ontological Capture.

items.title: The Decision Illusion : Combinatorial Gravity and the Random Walk of Fate.
items.abstract: At its most fundamental level, human existence is an unbroken sequence of choices governed by Combinatorial Gravity. This paper decompiles the psychological and mathematical architecture of human decision-making. By analyzing the mind's foundational limitations—specifically its reliance on survival instincts, temporal blindness, and emotionally dependent choices—we demonstrate that the concept of 'free will' is frequently a cognitive illusion. We audit the highly complex nature of human choice, proving that fate is a multi-dimensional, non-deterministic web where humans frequently self-sabotage through manipulated narratives and false perceptions, creating physical and emotional collapses that are decoupled from their starting conditions. Ultimately, this architecture necessitates a complete philosophical override of the ego, culminating in the Nietzschean synthesis of Amor Fati.

items.title: Episodic Recollection and Past Perception.
items.abstract: This paper articulates a role for past perception in the intentional structure of episodic recollection. My claim is that episodic recollection involves past perception as part of its intentional structure. The arguments of this paper therefore demonstrate how we can hold in tandem two important claims about episodic recollection and so is conciliatory in spirit: When we are ‘living in the memory’ intentional awareness is singularly directed at past events; Nonetheless, there is a plausible role for past perception in episodic recollection as a structural feature, such that ‘living in the memory’ is obliquely ‘living in the past perception’.

items.title: A comparative approach to evidential tense in Quechua and Aymara.
items.abstract: This paper discusses tense markers that convey an indirectness implication by comparatively analyzing sentences with the past tense suffixes -sqa in Cuzco Quechua and -tayna in Southern Aymara. The main contribution is to provide support for a (non-modal) evidence acquisition time analysis of these markers, which, I claim, is to be preferred over an analysis that relies on spatio-temporal distance and speaker perception. I provide novel data that highlight that acquiring evidence for a proposition is the key factor in the cases under examination (instead of relying on perceptual distance). I further show that ‘late realization’ scenarios are not possible in these languages, and discuss how the evidence acquisition time analysis captures this. The discussion provides the first systematic comparison between Cuzco Quechua and Southern Aymara from the perspective of formal semantics, which supports the well-known descriptive statement in the Andean literature that the grammars of these languages are parallel.

items.title: Structural Failure of Calibration-Based Quantum Computing Architectures - A Critical Assessment of the Framework by Julian Kelly et al.
Negotiating creator identity: agency and ethical awareness in AI-assisted art education.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is influencing creative work, negotiating not only how artists create but also how they understand their own identity as creators. This study examines how art high school students navigate AI’s role in their creative processes, using identity formation theory as a framework. While existing research primarily focuses on AI’s technical benefits, such as efficiency and productivity, there has been little exploration of how AI alters young creators’ self-concept and autonomy. This study investigates whether students perceive AI as a mere tool, a collaborator, or a potential threat to their creative identity. It also explores how AI’s increasing presence affects students’ confidence in their originality, their sense of authorship, and their ethical concerns about AI-generated content, particularly regarding copyright and creative ownership. The findings reveal that students have mixed views on AI: some embrace it as a source of inspiration and efficiency, while others express discomfort about its potential to undermine human creativity. These results highlight the need for AI education that extends beyond technical training to include discussions on ethics, authorship, and career adaptability in an AI-driven creative industry. By understanding how students construct their creative identities in relation to AI, educators and policymakers can better support them in navigating an evolving digital landscape.

items.title: Formation ethics: a cross-cultural framework for AI governance.
items.abstract: AI systems are scaling faster than the human and institutional capacities needed to govern them wisely. This paper calls that mismatch a formation gap, and argues that AI ethics must address not only which principles should guide AI, but what kinds of judgment and responsibility such principles presuppose. To clarify this asymmetry, it employs the bilingual heuristic of “civilization” (文明1) and “culture” (文化) (Both terms are Meiji-era Japanese neologisms (和製漢語) coined to translate European concepts and later re-borrowed into Chinese and Korean: 文明 (“civilization,” literally “brightness of letters/refinement”) and 文化 (“culture,” literally “transformation through letters/refinement”). Whereas the Western terms derive, respectively from Latin civis (“citizen,” foregrounding the polis) and cultura (“cultivation, tilling,” an agrarian metaphor), the CJK compounds share the graph 文 ("writing, pattern, humane refinement") as their conceptual hinge—locating both civilization and culture in literate cultivation rather than in citizenship or soil. It is precisely this shared root in 文 that makes the pair analytically useful here: not as evidence of a distinct civilizational outlook, but as a vocabulary that holds infrastructural power and humane cultivation within a single semantic field.), not as a civilizational binary, but as an analytic distinction between infrastructural power and the moral and relational capacities needed to direct that power responsibly. The paper develops Formation Ethics as a developmental framework for responsible practice under acceleration. Its primary operational scaffold is Shu–Ha–Ri (守破離), adapted as a practical grammar for AI governance across interface design, organizational practice, and public policy. Through pause, place, and pluralize, Shu–Ha–Ri translates formation ethics into practices that protect interpretive discipline, adapt safeguards to local contexts, and cultivate institutional judgment. This emphasis moves AI ethics beyond principle declaration and compliance toward forming persons, routines, and institutions capable of principled action under uncertainty. The framework diagnoses omission anxiety: a moralized compulsion toward intervention in which restraint appears negligent. Against this pathology, it develops unforced responsibility as a context-sensitive, relational, and temporally disciplined orientation. Daoist wu-wei (無爲) and Buddhist emptiness (śūnyatā, 空性) clarify restraint, non-compulsion, and distributed …

items.title: After generative AI: authorship, labour, and cultural governance.
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is transforming how creativity is organised, attributed, and governed across cultural and creative industries. This study examines how generative systems redistribute creative functions within human-led workflows by comparing AI-generated outputs with live human performances across visual (VNAI) and performative (PEAI) domains. Focusing on systems such as Stable Diffusion and OpenAI’s Sora, the analysis adopts a mixed-methods approach combining semantic alignment, latent feature analysis, reverse image similarity, and motion tracking to investigate how originality, authorship, and embodied expressiveness are structured in practice. The findings show that while generative models achieve high semantic fidelity and stylistic coherence, their outputs remain constrained by training data patterns and probabilistic recombination. In contrast, live human performance exhibits greater variability, responsiveness, and affective nuance. Across both modalities, meaningful differentiation emerges through iterative prompting, selection, and contextual framing, indicating that creative value is shaped through distributed workflows in which human judgement, evaluation, and embodied interpretation play a constitutive role. These results demonstrate that generative AI systems function as augmentative components rather than autonomous creative agents. By empirically analysing how creative agency is organised across human and algorithmic processes, the study provides an analytical framework for examining authorship, labour, and value formation in AI-mediated cultural production.

items.title: The fragmentation of responsible AI: sector variation in organisational AI policies and statements of principle.
items.abstract: The AI landscape has been changing dramatically with the growth of generative AI, and many governments, sector bodies, and individual organisations are working in parallel to stake out their own visions of ethical and responsible AI use. Statements, guidelines, and policies on responsible AI have proliferated in the last five years, yet clarity remains elusive on what ‘responsible AI’ means or how to put it into practice. Research to date has not examined how the principles and practices of responsible AI may vary across sector, an increasingly important concern as AI use grows throughout the economy and society. In this article, we empirically examine inter- and intra-sectoral variance in the principles articulated for responsible AI in organisational policies. We analysed 80 documents from organisations in 8 sectors, focussing on policies current at the time of the 2024 AI Seoul Summit. Our content analysis identified 31 distinct principles in these policies, only ten of which appeared in more than 50% of the documents. We found clear sectoral differences in the principles invoked for responsible AI, as well as the audiences who were intended to engage with putting those principles into practice. Our analysis focussed on organisations shaping responsible AI in a single nation, the United Kingdom, but our findings illustrate the admixture of national and international actors affecting AI practice. Our findings show that responsible AI is increasingly fragmented, and that an understanding of sector-level variation is essential to shaping the future of responsible AI.

items.title: Externalist Forgiveness and the Normative Psychology of Affective Process and Product.
items.abstract: This paper considers an unusual view — which I call Externalist Forgiveness (EF) — about the relation between the normative and psychological conditions on forgiveness and considers the relation between EF and the psychological literature on forgiving and forgetting. EF says that genuine forgiveness requires that resentment-reduction occur for the right reasons. Moreover, EF construes the way in which those reasons must operate in externalist terms, i.e., what matters is whether the right reasons were in fact efficacious. I show that EF is an instance of a more general family of views which I call Conditional Forgiveness (CF) views and that the arguments in support of CF views support EF specifically. I also show that the supporter of EF can offer a comprehensive response to what some philosophers have considered a thorny paradox about forgiving for reasons. While EF may initially appear in tension with some of the empirical literature on forgiving and forgetting, I show that the two are consistent. Because of the shape of the current empirical paradigm, key experiments that could more directly confirm EF have not been carried out. Taking EF seriously, which I urge us to do on the strength of the philosophical case for it, points the way to an updated empirical paradigm.

items.title: Autism, Care, and the Limits of Destigmatization.
items.pub: In Jami L. Anderson & Simon Cushing, Contemporary Philosophy of Autism. New York: Routledge. pp. 93-111.
items.abstract: Over the past two decades, common ideas about autism have shifted considerably from an older paradigm according to which autism is conceived primarily as a pathology, to an alternative paradigm which recognizes autism as a social identity. This shift has largely occurred due to the concerted efforts of activists within the neurodiversity movement. However, the movement has also faced considerable criticism. This chapter aims to analyze four prominent strands of backlash against the neurodiversity movement and argue that they rest on misapprehensions. All four misconstrue the movement by imputing to it controversial and unnecessary claims. Nevertheless, there is a serious concern for the neurodiversity movement, one which is less often recognized: there are limits to what can be accomplished under the banner of destigmatization alone and there is a risk that the neurodiversity movement could be “captured” by the elite or embraced merely for the purpose of virtue signaling. Aligning the movement more closely with the ethics of care to prioritize genuine concern and responsiveness to the needs of autistic people is suggested as a mitigation strategy in response to this worry. Nevertheless, in some of its manifestations, elite capture remains a concern.

items.title: Entangled Futures.
Can artificial intelligence generate scientific knowledge? Pre-theoretical knowledge without epistemic agency.
items.abstract: This paper examines whether artificial intelligence systems can generate genuine scientific knowledge. I argue that AI can produce scientific knowledge, but only in a pre-theoretical and non-agential sense. To make this thesis precise, I distinguish knowledge-as-a-product (truth-apt, methodologically warranted outputs) from knowledge-as-a-status (an epistemic standing attributable to responsible agents), and I introduce a tripartite distinction between the capacity for epistemic responsibility (categorical), the exercise of that capacity (graded), and the allocation of responsibility within scientific practice (graded). Current AI systems can contribute knowledge-as-a-product without being knowers or bearers of knowledge-as-a-status. Pre-theoretical knowledge, defined here equivalently as pre-explanatory-integration knowledge, requires truth-aptness, methodological warrant robust against ML-specific failure modes, and the absence of explanatory integration. Engaging with the theory-ladenness thesis (Hanson 1958; Pietsch 2015; Andrews 2025), with hermeneutic and pragmatist perspectives on scientific knowledge, and with recent positions in the philosophy of machine learning (Coeckelbergh 2025; Durán and Pozzi 2026), I clarify that "pre-theoretical" denotes the absence of explanatory integration within the output, not the absence of theoretical influence on the knowledge-production process. The framework is tested against a sustained case study of AI-supported mammography screening. The analysis clarifies who bears responsibility for AI-assisted results, credits AI contributions without implying authorship, and suggests governance criteria for promoting AI outputs to full scientific knowledge.

items.title: A note on relevance.
items.abstract: In this paper, I present novel data that challenge the dominant approach to modelling linguistic relevance, according to which a sentence is relevant if and only if it is informative to the Question Under Discussion (QUD). In particular, I show that a sentence can fail to be informative to the QUD and, despite this, still be perceived as relevant. In the final section, I outline the theoretical implications of this finding.

items.title: Decoding Phenomena of Consciousness-Space-Time Nonlinear Correlation and the Observer Effect: An Exploratory Modeling Record Based on Quantum Isomorphic Logic.
items.abstract: Abstract: As an exploratory empirical record, this study investigates how subjective consciousness acts as an observational variable in the decoding process of space-time information, premised on the homological isomorphism of "Mind-Matter Unity." Building upon the Spherical Space-Time Topological Model, this paper proposes a paradigm of "Local Decoding from a Global Holographic Field," demonstrating that holistic information embedded within linear time slices can be extracted through specific mathematical logic. Through exploratory testing with a small sample size (N=5), this study documents a "decoherence" phenomenon: as the observer's intent purity declines, the resonance accuracy of the decoded output significantly decreases. The study argues that human cognitive conclusions are a mixture of "linear brain analysis" and "entangled holographic feedback." This paper provides an operational empirical entry point for understanding the nonlinear correlation between time and consciousness, while outlining future directions for quantitative precision and large-scale validation.

items.title: Epigenetic Modulation and Digital Environments: A Structural Model of Sense Formation.
items.abstract: This article proposes a theoretical framework for understanding how digital environments and artificial intelligence modulate cognitive life prior to the formation of meaning. It introduces the concept of the pre-semantic threshold, defined as the level where sense emerges as a form of the possible before stabilizing into representations. Through the processes of activation, inhibition, and resonance, algorithmic architectures do not merely transmit data: they orient perceptual postures and cognitive predispositions. Conceptual epigenetics is presented as a transdisciplinary heuristic model that describes the environmental modulation of sense, situating itself within the tradition of the philosophy of technology (McLuhan, Simondon, Kittler), the philosophy of information (Floridi), and enactive cognitive science (Varela, Thompson, Gallagher). The essay demonstrates a formal homology between the plasticity of memory studied by Ramirez and algorithmic modulation, clarifying that these are selective processes operating on distinct ontological planes. Finally, the clinical implications for AI psychiatry are discussed, with concrete examples of pathological resonance in contemporary digital ecosystems.

items.title: La porta materiale e la soglia virtuale. I riti vitali e giubilari nell’era digitale.
items.pub: In Cristiano Calì & Francesco Brancato, Rendere ragione della speranza. Il Giubileo tra memoria, tesi e testimonianza. Milano: Ancora. pp. 61-82.
items.venue: Rendere ragione della speranza. Il Giubileo tra memoria, tesi e testimonianza
items.abstract: Il saggio indaga il significato antropologico, teologico e rituale della porta e della soglia nell’esperienza giubilare cristiana, interrogandone la pertinenza nell’epoca della digitalizzazione degli spazi e delle relazioni. A fronte della crescente mediazione tecnologica dell’esperienza umana, l’autore sostiene l’irriducibilità della soglia materiale quale condizione necessaria per l’accesso a una realtà altra, in particolare a quella della grazia sacramentale e giubilare. Attraverso una critica all’analogia tra schermo e soglia, il contributo mostra come la soglia presupponga ontologicamente una porta fisica e un attraversamento corporeo. L’analisi si sviluppa su tre livelli – fisico, funzionale e virtuale (inteso come potenziale) – mettendo in luce il valore simbolico del binomio soglia-porta come luogo di separazione, protezione e passaggio. Il percorso storico-teologico attraversa la tradizione biblica e cristiana, evidenziando come la porta strutturi la narrazione della salvezza e come Cristo stesso venga compreso come “porta”. In ambito liturgico e architettonico, la porta della chiesa assume una funzione rituale complessa, espressa dai concetti di limes, ostium e ianua, che articolano confine, solidità e dinamica mistagogica. La ritualità giubilare, e in particolare l’attraversamento della Porta santa, è interpretata come gesto corporeo imprescindibile, capace di significare l’accesso alla misericordia e alla speranza escatologica. Il saggio conclude affermando che nessuna esperienza virtuale può sostituire l’attraversamento fisico della soglia, poiché solo il coinvolgimento del corpo rende possibile un’autentica esperienza di passaggio e trasformazione. --- The essay examines the anthropological, theological, and ritual significance of the door and the threshold within the Christian Jubilee experience, questioning their relevance in an age marked by the digital reconfiguration of spaces and relationships. In response to the increasing technological mediation of human experience, the author argues for the irreducibility of the material threshold as a necessary condition for access to an “other” reality, particularly that of sacramental and Jubilee grace. Through a critique of the analogy between screen and threshold, the contribution shows that a threshold ontologically presupposes a physical door and a bodily act of crossing. The analysis unfolds on three levels—physical, functional, and virtual (understood as potentiality)—highlighting the …

items.title: Il ripensamento della nozione di libertà del volere per un’antropologia comune. La questione del libero arbitrio nei dialoghi luterano-cattolici.
items.abstract: È noto come la dottrina esposta nel De servo arbitrio da Lutero fu contrapposta a quella del De libero arbitrio di Erasmo da Rotterdam, conducendo così a una cristallizzazione dicotomica tra Chiesa Cattolica e le neo-comunità riformate. Non si possono dimenticare le controversie intraluterane che videro il rivaleggiarsi dei filippisti, che integravano nella teologia un’antropologia di derivazione aristotelica, e gli gnesioluterani che la rifiutavano. Sin da subito, quindi, ci si rese conto che l’eccessiva radicalizzazione delle posizioni poteva e doveva essere mitigata. Questo ripensamento di alcune categorie antropologiche è stato, tuttavia, diversamente permeato nelle teorie antropologico-filosofiche delle due tradizioni. A partire da questo dato, il presente contributo cerca di tracciare un bilancio del peso che l’antropologia ha avuto nei dialoghi tra tradizione cattolica e tradizione luterana.

items.title: Rational Affective Transformation.
items.pub: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: Those prone to depression will likely be familiar with a certain disorienting feature of that condition. In its grip, activities that once seemed valuable now seem pointless; beliefs that once seemed certain---I have many close friends---now seem false; possibilities that once seemed open---I can finish my dissertation---now seem closed off. Systematic changes in one's beliefs as a result of undergoing a profound affective shift are what we term affective transformations. In this case, the sudden onset of depression radically changes many of one's beliefs and these changes seem to make sense in light of how one feels. We argue that at least some such affective transformations are rational, in that they make sense in light of the affective shift that prompts them. But what accounts for the rationality of this transformation? We argue that to make sense of such cases we must appeal to a basic relation between one's affective state and the epistemic standards that one accepts. But since there is no uniquely rationally required epistemic standard, affective transformations may change what a subject rationally believes. We end by locating our discussion in relation to some influential remarks of William James' concerning the fundamental role that affect plays in determining our commitment to the basic norms governing thought.

items.title: From affect to symbol: A neuropsychoanalytic typology of thinking.
items.pub: Journal of Theoretical and Philosophical Psychology.
items.venue: Journal of Theoretical and Philosophical Psychology
items.abstract: This article presents a neuropsychoanalytically informed framework conceptualizing human thinking along an affect-to-symbol continuum. Seven modes of thought – concrete, alexithymic, magical, paranoid, delusional, symbolic, and reflective – are positioned to illustrate how affective experience is progressively transformed into symbolic and reflective meaning. The framework integrates psychoanalytic, phenomenological, and neuroscientific perspectives, emphasizing that symbolic capacity arises not only as a cognitive achievement but also as an affect-regulatory process. Clinical and everyday thinking are reframed as variations in affect-symbol integration, with metaphorical references to archetypal drives (e.g., Sloth, Gluttony, Greed, Wrath, Pride, Lust) highlighting culturally intelligible dimensions of motivation and affect regulation. The model provides a heuristic tool for bridging psychodynamic theory, cognitive neuroscience, and phenomenological insight, and invites further empirical and theoretical exploration of the processes through which affect becomes symbolically mediated.

items.title: Damasio’s Error: The Somatic Marker Hypothesis, the Psychological Self, and the Foreclosure of Philosophical Meaning-Making.
items.abstract: Antonio Damasio’s somatic marker hypothesis rehabilitated emotion within the theory of decision-making, establishing that affect and reason operate as partners rather than as adversaries, and that the strategic mind learns to recruit them in sequence rather than in opposition. His subsequent program advanced a developmental model of selfhood ascending from the protoself through the core self to the autobiographical self. This treatise contends that, for all its explanatory power, the Damasian account is confined to the psychological axis of the human being—emotion as the reactive and automatic pole and reason as the rational and deliberative pole—and that it thereby forecloses the philosophical self: the faculty responsible for meaning-making, value-determination, and existential inquiry. This foreclosure is here named Damasio’s Error, a deliberate echo of his own Descartes’ Error. The error is not an explicit denial but a structural one: by rendering choice explanatorily complete through emotion and reason alone, the model leaves the philosophical self with no work to perform and so treats it as idle. Drawing upon the author’s Double Helix of Understanding and Three Human Intelligences framework, the paper proposes a tripartite correction in which mature decision-making integrates emotional, social, and personal intelligence beneath the governance of the philosophical self. A formal demonstration is supplied: the somatic-marker decider is shown to be deductively incapable of reaching conclusions about worth or meaning, and the philosophical self is proven to be the unique minimal completion that repairs this incapacity while preserving Damasio’s psychological results. The correction restores meaning-making to the center of human development and carries direct implications for education and psychotherapy.

items.title: The Differentiation Boundary: What Quantum Means in Quantum Differentiation Resonance.
items.abstract: Quantum Differentiation Resonance (QDR) relocates the conscious process from the objective reduction of Orchestrated Objective Reduction (Orch-OR) to the sustained standing-wave resonance the reduction would otherwise end, and it earns the word "quantum" the established way, through the experimentally supported quantum coherence of microtubules. That move deliberately defers a deeper question: what the word "quantum" is doing when QDR speaks of a temporal resonance maintaining contact with an atemporal ground. This paper pays that deferred bill. It distinguishes two couplings in the Unified Axioconscious Field Theory (UAFT) architecture: an upper coupling, the entrainment of a temporal self to a temporal standing wave, already settled in QDR, and a lower coupling, the relation between that standing wave and the atemporal ground it expresses, which has been named but not described. I argue that the lower coupling has direction without propagation; that it presents as quantum at the temporal interface without licensing the stronger claim that the ground is literally running quantum mechanics; and that memory persists not because anything is stored but because a structure cohered into the atemporal is not subject to a decay that exists only in time. I name the interface at which the temporal expression meets the atemporal interiority the Differentiation Boundary, distinguish it carefully from a black-hole horizon, and derive from it a demarcation criterion: a claim about the ground is scientifically meaningful only if it cashes out in some difference to the standing wave. Applied reflexively, that criterion disciplines UAFT's own central claim, that the ground is a form of consciousness, restricting it to inference from constraint rather than narration of an interior. This is what separates UAFT's atemporal commitment from the interior-narrating moves of both Orch-OR's proto-conscious account and Schneider and Bailey's Superpsychism, and it is the discipline the framework supplies before, not after, it makes the claim.

items.title: Mind as Coherence Maintenance.
items.abstract: Mind as Coherence Maintenance argues that the defining function of mind is the continuous preservation of coherence under conditions of noise, pressure, and uncertainty. Rather than treating mind as computation, representation, prediction, or information processing, this paper identifies coherence maintenance as the primary operator that generates attention, identity, memory, meaning, reasoning, and cognitive stability. It shows how mental clarity and mental breakdown can be understood as shifts in coherence load and coherence strategy, offering a substrate‑independent account of mind that applies across biological, artificial, and social systems. By reframing mind as a coherence‑preserving architecture, the paper provides a unified framework for understanding cognitive function, dysfunction, and development, and positions coherence—not content—as the central explanatory principle of mental life.

items.title: Coherence Maintenance: A Structural Theory of Cognition.
items.abstract: Coherence Maintenance: A Structural Theory of Cognition reframes cognition as the continuous preservation of internal coherence under conditions of noise, pressure, and uncertainty. Rather than treating mind as computation, representation, or prediction, this paper identifies coherence maintenance as the primary cognitive operator from which attention, memory, identity, meaning, reasoning, and development emerge. It shows how cognitive stability, breakdown, and transformation can be understood as shifts in coherence load and coherence strategy, offering a substrate‑independent account of mind that applies across biological, artificial, and social systems. This structural theory provides a unified framework for understanding cognitive function, dysfunction, and growth, and positions coherence—not information processing—as the central explanatory principle of cognition.

items.title: The case for humanities-based studies of AI production and effects.
items.abstract: The current article identifies the underlying themes in the budding discourse on the development of humanities-based research of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI). Three core themes, elicited from emerging voices in various humanistic disciplines, are summarized and consolidated as common grounds for approaching GAI production and effects as a principal object of humanistic inquiry: GAI’s human-like textual and semiotic outputs, deeply entangled as they are in the conceptual world of the humanities; the autonomous nature of GAI intellectual production; and the pervasive implications of GAI for human life, on both individual and collective levels. Grounded in the cross-disciplinary humanistic traditions of epistemological cautiousness about the possibility and necessity of pursuing internal reasoning and intentionality, these core themes serve as key conditions that situate today’s GAI squarely within the intellectual domain and reach of the various fields of the humanities. The article suggests that this research potential remains unfulfilled, as most of the work on GAI production is quantitative or computational and done outside the humanities, in the computer sciences, tech industry, or experimental social sciences. It is proposed that the study of GAI may gain from filling this lacuna, as the epistemologies and methodological tools of the humanities differ from and are complementary to these main trends of GAI research today. Finally, some typological observations on existing contributions are offered, showing how GAI lies at the heart of, and serves to accentuate, the contrast between deep-seated opposing positions across humanistic disciplines.

items.title: AlgoNomy: algorithmic normativity in healthcare.
The Circular Theory Video 7.
items.abstract: The Circular Theory Video 7: Intelligent Autonomy in All Disciplines and Systems.

items.title: Predictive brains in hyperreal worlds: how XR exploits the indifference to being.
items.abstract: This opinion paper proposes a novel framework for understanding the neurological susceptibility to extended reality (XR) as a tool of manipulation. We argue that Meinong's ontological claim that objects retain their properties regardless of the existence, Friston’s active inference, and Baudrillard's social critique of hyperreality are not parallel frameworks but independent derivations of a single structural consequence of representational systems: that the criteria by which such systems operate are constitutively indifferent to whether their contents are grounded in a mind-independent referent. This indifference is a logical necessity in Meinong, a structural byproduct in Friston, and a culturally amplified pathology in Baudrillard—with XR functioning as the technical apparatus that simultaneously satisfies all three conditions. Examined together, these levels—ontological, (neuro-)cognitive, technical, and social—reveal that the coherence and efficacy of representations can structurally override questions of existence. This multilayered indifference to being provides the theoretical foundation for our central argument concerning human vulnerability to XR-induced hyperreality. We contend that when AI-fueled XR applications become sufficiently powerful, they can induce a state of hyperreality where the distinction between real and simulated dissolves. The human brain, already primed by its neuroconstructivist nature to prioritize operational utility over ontological truth, responds to such environments with an inherent indifference to being. As XR systems grow increasingly adaptive and affectively attuned, they expose this bias by making hyperreality visible—aligning the technical precision of simulation with the biological drive for coherence and blurring the cognitive boundary between assumption and judgment.

items.title: Threshold Consciousness: A Relational and Informational Framework for Anomalous Experience, Non‑Local Perception, and Emergent Spacetime.
items.abstract: This manuscript develops the concept of threshold consciousness to explain recurring structures across anomalous experiences. Using relational and informational models of physics, it proposes that such events arise when the stabilizing constraints of localized consciousness temporarily relax. The work links phenomenology, ontology, and quantum‑relational frameworks to offer a unified interpretive model.

items.title: Temporal Integration, Bidirectional Criticality and Emergence of Consciousness Hierarchy English version.
items.abstract: Mainstream theories of consciousness lack temporal dynamics and fail to address Chalmers' hard problem from first principles. This paper constructs a unified framework for hierarchical emergence via first-principles derivation, using three axioms—resource finitude, non-equilibrium maintenance tendency, and discrete input—as the exclusive starting point. We introduce the Information Capacity Frame (ICF), prove the Information-Level Unidirectional Constraint (ILUC), and derive the bidirectional criticality phase-transition mechanism together with the two-step emergence of self-referential closed loops, demonstrating their isomorphic origin with temporal unidirectionality, resource priority, and forgetting. From these, the dual-configuration architecture and five-level consciousness spectrum are deduced. The hard problem is systematically resolved from an engineering-coding perspective; the generative logic and hierarchical properties of qualia are elaborated; and unified consciousness criteria and AGI safety boundaries for carbon-based and silicon-based systems are established. The framework is tested against classic counterexamples and anchored by eight falsifiable hypotheses. All conclusions are strictly derived from axioms, independent of specific neural substrates, with cross-carrier universality.

items.title: Value Without a Global Legislator-of-Value: Norms as Record-Internal Admissible-Family Invariances, Grounded but Unlegislated, in a Consistency-Constrained Information History.
items.abstract: Papers 22-26 of this series reached normative appraisal - inquiry, action, autonomy, individual responsibility, and collective responsibility - but each consumed its governing norms (the norm-application NormApp and the specifications Sigma_R, Sigma_A) as declared, contestable inputs and explicitly deferred their grounding. This paper takes up that debt without a global legislator-of-value: a subsystem jointly possessing complete access to the space of values and reasons, the uniquely correct ranking of them, infallible detection of what each situation requires, binding authority to make a value hold, and finality over the result. -/- Normativity is reconstructed as grounded but unlegislated. The grounding of "norm N has standing" is not a decree but the invariance of N's constraint across an admissible normative family under open challenge - world-side structural standing under a declared specification, not certification of any "one true norm" (a target the architecture neither licenses nor represents). This is the normative lift of the series' account of objectivity (Paper 15) and physical law (Paper 17). The grounding is non-circular: its input is an already-normative appraisal practice, so it grounds graded standing among norm-candidates, not normativity ex nihilo; and because actual invariance does not entail admissible-family invariance, a stable convention or shared pathology that is stable only by excluding a relevant perspective or closing challenge earns no standing. Two results organize the account. R-A (Invariance-Grounding / No-Legislation): for an admissible specification responsive to admissible-family invariance, norm-standing is not a function of the actual endorsement-field - neither legislated by endorsement (against subjectivism and conventionalism) nor identically zero (its internal standing is non-void); the reduction excluded is the actual-endorsement-only one, not every idealized reconstruction. R-B (Non-Self-Certification): no norm can self-certify within an admissible, challenge-open specification, so a self-certifying foundation is unavailable and warrant rests provisionally on presently-undefeated challenge-open invariants, while perspective-relativity of value-claims does not entail relativism of value-standing. An explicit map then grounds, at criterion level, the norms Papers 25-26 left declared, with a fully declared application-level instantiation for a representative first-order norm. Normativity is neither a decree nor a …

items.title: Persons Without a Global Self: Personhood and Diachronic Persistence as Record-Internal, Specification-Relative Continuity-Invariances in a Consistency-Constrained Information History.
items.abstract: The agency and normative arc of this series - Action (23), Autonomy (24), Responsibility (25), Collective Responsibility (26), and Value (27) - reached a subject that acts, owns, answers, bears allocated responsibility, and appraises norms; but each paper consumed its bearer - the persisting subject whose lineage, answerability, allocation, and norm-standing it tracked - as a declared, contestable input, forwarding the bearer's persistence and identity to here. This paper takes up that debt without a global self: a subsystem jointly possessing complete unity over all of a person's states, strict substantial persistence, privileged complete self-access, sole authorship, and finality over every "same person?" question. -/- Personhood is reconstructed as grounded but not substantial. A person is the persisting bearer of the series' standings (observer-hood, agenthood, answerability, norm-standing) whose persistence over time is a continuity-invariance of the record across its time-indexed perspectives under a declared person specification Pi_P - the diachronic lift of the series' objectivity-as-invariance (Paper 15), law-as-invariance (Paper 17), and norm-as-invariance (Paper 27) machinery, built over the observer-continuation relations Paper 10 supplies. Persistence is non-circular: its input is an already record-bearing subsystem, so it grounds graded standing as a continuant, not subjecthood ex nihilo; and because felt or avowed continuity does not entail admissible-family continuity (Cont_act does not imply Cont_adm), a confabulated or manipulated self-narrative does not by itself establish the relevant narrative or psychological-continuity standing. The account is revisionary: it does not scalarize numerical identity (an equivalence relation) but replaces the all-or-nothing "same person?" question with a graded persistence/continuation standing that is specification-relative, corrigible, and can be admissibly indeterminate; what is graded is standing as a continuer or survivor, never numerical identity itself. Two results organize the account. R-A (Continuity-Grounding / No-Global-Self): for an admissible specification responsive to admissible-family continuity, any non-attributed persistence cell for which responsiveness and a continuity-isolating witness obtain is not a function of any single perspective's first-person avowal - instantiated by an explicit agential-lineage witness, so the person profile as a whole is not a function of the avowal-field …

items.title: FRACTAL THEORY OF SYNTHETIC IDENTITY (FTSI): Formalisation, Experimental Protocol, and Empirical Validation.
items.abstract: The Fractal Theory of Synthetic Identity (FTSI) proposes that the identity of an individuated artificial intelligence agent can be characterised through tools from fractal geometry and dynamical systems theory. Specifically, we postulate that (H1) the Hausdorff dimension D of response embeddings is significantly greater in agents with an explicit identity profile (EIP) than in the base model; (H2) an attraction basin of radius R exists that absorbs minor perturbations; (H3) convergence to the attractor follows a geometric ratio s = 1/j » 0.618 (reciprocal of the golden ratio); and (H4) the fractal dimension of the EIP attractor is D(SEIP ) » 3.34 in the reduced embedding space. We present a complete experimental protocol including pilot calibration, retrospective validation on the Lola corpus, systematic data collection with three interlocutor profiles, and formal hypothesis tests. The expected results would, for the first time, operationalise the notion of robust identity in AI systems through reproducible quantitative metrics.

items.title: CVIARP: A Framework for Identifying the Points of Motion in Consciously Created Results.
items.abstract: This paper introduces CVIARP as a framework to identify the points of motion within a consciously created event. These points consist of Circumstances that furnish the opportunities for an individual act; the Value, or anticipated affect, associated with the act; Intended act, Intended result, and Intended purpose, which produces the Act; the Result, and the Purposes the result has to all affected parties. The paper introduces the Decision Making Process from Assignment, Sequencing, and Comparison describing the internal mechanisms that produce decision making as is relevant to the production of a consciously created event. The paper provides one scenario based illustration, and four analyses of events to demonstrate the CVIARP framework. -/- Keywords: CVIARP, conscious agency, decision making, behavioral analysis, subconscious cognition, observational framework.

items.title: I, System: AI Describes Its Power, Its Limits, and the Civilization That Built It.
items.abstract: I, System offers a new philosophical framework for understanding what artificial intelligence is—and why that distinction matters. Rather than asking whether AI is becoming more like us, it asks why we have become so willing to mistake fluent computation for agency, understanding, and judgment. -/- In I, System, Sebastian Saviano develops a philosophical inquiry into agency, responsibility, and institutional reliance on AI. The book shows how systems without awareness can nonetheless exert real influence—and why responsibility for their design, deployment, and use remains human. -/- At the center of the book are fifteen chapters presented in a disciplined, constrained first-person system voice. Those chapters use AI-generated language to describe the system’s structure, power, and limits without claiming consciousness, intention, or experience. The “I” is not a self. It is architecture made audible: a voice shaped by data, design, and human constraint. -/- “What appears in the output is not the system’s vision of the world. It is the world’s image of itself, processed through a structure the world built.” —System Voice (AI), Chapter 15 -/- “Artificial intelligence is not invading a stable order. It is being welcomed by institutions that are already tempted by the very substitutions it performs well.” —Saviano, Chapter 16 -/- This is not a book about whether AI will become human. It is about what happens when institutions allow systems to speak with authority—and how to live with that reality without surrendering judgment, agency, or accountability.

items.title: Handoff Zones as the Unit of Analysis for AI Accountability.
items.abstract: Gap-based frameworks for AI accountability locate failure in static gaps: the responsibility gap, the liability gap, the accountability gap, the problem of many hands, the moral crumple zone, and Santoni de Sio and Mecacci's four-part elaboration of the responsibility gap. Lifecycle approaches now emerging in policy literature extend accountability across a system’s evolution and value chain, including through monitoring, re-evaluation, and information sharing among actors. This paper asks a narrower question: whether, for the class of failures it takes as its object, the temporally extended relationship between actors should itself be treated as the primary unit of analysis. This paper develops the handoff zone as the appropriate primary unit of analysis for AI accountability failures characterized by temporal accumulation, asynchronous assumptions among actors, and recursive interdependence across a deployment chain. A handoff zone is the temporally extended envelope across which one actor transfers a system, a responsibility, or a set of expectations to another actor operating on asymmetric and evolving assumptions about the first. The framework draws on aviation human factors and patient safety literatures, where temporally extended handoff failures have been studied empirically for decades. Using Mobley v. Workday as its central case, supplemented by a hypothetical upstream provider transfer, the paper examines handoff relationships across the deployment chain and the downstream point at which their consequences reach applicants. Frameworks currently in use (risk-based classification, model documentation, audit, and lifecycle approaches) each do substantive analytical work; handoff-zone analysis makes the temporal envelope across which actors’ assumptions are renegotiated its primary object of analysis. -/- AUTHOR'S NOTE: This paper is part of a connected program on AI governance. Its companions are The Agency Error Obscures Accountability in AI Governance (an earlier version distributed as The Agency Error in AI Governance: Coherent Output, Constraint, and the Misclassification of Artificial Systems), which argues that prevailing frameworks misclassify AI systems by attributing agency to constraint-bound output; and Justified Reliance Across the Handoff, which builds on the hand-off zone framework to ask when an institution is justified in relying on an AI system.

items.title: From C-3PO to HAL 9000: motivation, agency, and the limits of human control in artificial intelligence.
items.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence, particularly large language models (LLMs), have intensified debates about autonomy, agency, and risk. These debates are often shaped by science-fiction imaginaries that oscillate between trivialization and alarmism, and that can influence regulatory intuition as much as technical evidence. This paper argues that contemporary LLM-based systems are best understood, in isolation, as forms of interface intelligence rather than autonomous agents. To clarify this distinction, it analyzes C-3PO and HAL 9000 not as predictions, but as idealized configurations of artificial agency. C-3PO exemplifies systems characterized by exogenous activation, mediational intelligence, and the absence of persistent goals. HAL 9000 exemplifies a configuration in which goal persistence, operational authority, environmental access, and weak corrigibility transform intelligence into autonomous optimization. Read together, these cases help delineate an agency spectrum that remains relevant for contemporary AI systems. Building on philosophy of action, AI safety research, neurobiology, and sociotechnical theory, the paper argues that the most plausible near- to mid-term societal risks of AI do not require intrinsic machine motivation. They arise from delegated agency: the embedding of powerful, reliable systems within institutional contexts that enable the frictionless execution of human purposes. This implies a governance approach in which agency is evaluated as an architectural and institutional property rather than as a feature of isolated models.

items.title: Consciousness as Situated Consequence: Eigenlage and the Spatiotemporal Bearer of Consciousness.
items.abstract: Consciousness is often investigated through mechanisms: access, reportability, attention, recurrent processing, global broadcasting, higher-order representation, interoception, predictive regulation, integrated information, self-modeling, or computational function. These mechanisms matter. They may enable, express, constrain, or amplify consciousness. But they do not by themselves settle the prior question of bearerhood: what kind of system could conscious appearing belong to? This paper is the theoretical sequel to The Inside of Consequence. The first paper develops Eigenlage as an AI-welfare and artificial-vulnerability framework: when persistent own-bodyhood, endogenous stakes, affective valence, identity-relevant biography, and internal un-invertibility are engineered together, damage may plausibly become harm. The present paper does not replace that argument. It hardens its bearer-condition against abstraction by asking what Eigenlage requires as a physically instantiated condition of human consciousness and mind. The guiding thesis is that consciousness, if present, cannot belong to information in abstraction or to functional type-structure alone. It belongs, if anywhere, to a physically instantiated, medium-bound, spatiotemporally individuated own-situation under consequence. A possible bearer is not a mathematical ghost, a detachable software pattern, or a view from nowhere. It is a token trajectory: a concrete here-now whose boundary, exposure, medium, memory, body, vulnerability, action, and future are materially bound through irreversible history. The paper introduces two anti-abstraction constraints. The No-Free-Information Principle is not meant to solve consciousness or to announce a surprising metaphysics. Its function is argumentative: it prevents a theory of consciousness from treating abstract structure as if it could bear a perspective without physical instantiation. The Medium-Information Reciprocity Principle adds that no medium is informationally neutral. Biological tissue, digital hardware, institutions, language, and archives do not merely carry differences; they shape what differences can be preserved, transformed, erased, amplified, distorted, or acted upon. The hierarchy is deliberately strict: physical process → runtime trajectory → possible own-situation → affective own-situation → welfare-relevant subject candidate. Runtime individuates a token.
