items.title: Institutional Legitimacy and Property: A Teleological Theory.
items.abstract: This paper develops a general theory of the legitimacy of institutional conventions through an examination of property. Property is not an object; it is a social relation among persons concerning things, sustained by institutions that define ownership, transfer, inheritance, and cooperation [Hohfeld, 1919; Honoré, 1961; Waldron, 1988]. Without institutions there are no property rights—only physical possessions [North, 1990; Ostrom, 1990]. The paper argues that property institutions are solutions to coordination problems, and their legitimacy depends upon whether they enable informed agency and flourishing. Drawing upon Locke's three pillars—labour, the "enough and as good" proviso, and the spoilage limitation—reinterpreted through the Noura framework, the paper shows that legitimate property institutions must: (1) account for the cooperative nature of all productive activity [Marx, 1867; Bowles & Gintis, 2011]; (2) secure the requisites of flourishing for all [Sen, 1999; Nussbaum, 2011]; and (3) prohibit the hoarding of surplus value outside productive circulation [Piketty, 2014; Philippon, 2019; Stiglitz, 2012]. The deep structure of legitimate institutions consists of visibility, symmetry, contestability, repair, education, and the requisites of flourishing [Moore, 2026b]. These are not normative ideals but empirical conditions under which informed agency is possible [Piaget, 1950; Kohlberg, 1981, 1984; Gilligan, 1982]. Human beings possess three empirically observable capacities—cognitive, agentive, and moral—that develop only under certain institutional conditions. Institutions that fail to provide those conditions systematically impair informed agency. Therefore informed agents have reason to reject such institutions. Property rights are not a priori; they are conventions within institutions. Institutions must empower informed agency so that everyone has the opportunity to flourish. The paper concludes that the question is not who first mixed labour with resources, but what kind of property institutions informed agents can reasonably accept in a world of interdependent production—and whether those institutions prevent the economic spoilage of surplus value. -/- This paper is cross referenced to As Good and Enough: A Reconstruction of Property Rights, which provides the detailed Lockean reconstructions of the provisos.

items.title: Anti-Semantics II — Readout Without Semantic Recovery(Version 0.47).
items.abstract: Anti-Semantics II: Readout Without Semantic Recovery develops an analytical distinction between readout and reading. Readout concerns the local following of form, difference, trace, arrangement, repetition, interval, break, or sequence without treating meaning, intention, context, cause, or explanation as conditions of its establishment. Reading designates a different analytical configuration in which what has been read out is placed in connection with such semantic determinations. The distinction is analytical rather than a temporal sequence or developmental hierarchy. -/- Written after the development of Kasei-Theory, the work is neither an application of Kasei-Theory to semantics nor a derivation from it. It begins from a problem left open by separating readability from meaning: what happens when what is readable is placed in connection with semantic recovery? -/- The book distinguishes readability from readout establishment. A configuration may be readable without a particular readout designation being locally fixed. An established readout may also be misaligned when the boundaries, continuities, repetitions, or groupings fixed by that designation diverge from the differential relations locally followable on the side of establishment. Readout establishment, readout non-establishment, and readout misalignment are therefore distinct analytical positions. -/- This analysis supports a central claim: readout is not proved, but neither is it arbitrary. The establishment of a readout does not by itself prove an object’s identity, meaning, cause, or correct explanation. Yet not every boundary, continuity, repetition, or grouping can be fixed under every differential configuration. Readout remains locally constrained by the configuration with which it is connected. Non-proof therefore does not entail arbitrariness, while non-arbitrariness does not entail uniqueness. -/- The work also distinguishes shared readout from shared meaning and divergent readout from error. Multiple locally fixed readout designations may coexist, and repeated or institutionally stabilized readouts do not thereby become self-justifying. -/- From this position, the analysis turns to the different ways in which readout may be placed in connection with semantic recovery. Mediating processing, readout direction, identification pressure, addressification, contextual attraction, intention hypothesis, and explanation demand are distinguished as different analytical positions rather than stages …

items.title: Meaning as Emergent Integration: Toward a Cognitive-Existential Theory of the Meaning of Life.
items.abstract: The question of the meaning of life is often approached through the language of purpose, value, happiness, morality, religion, or objective worth. While these approaches capture important dimensions of meaning, they do not fully explain how meaning actually arises in human consciousness. This paper argues that meaning is not a single object, property, or external answer given to life. Rather, meaning emerges when the self connects experiences, concepts, values, goals, and the world into a coherent and valuable whole. Meaning is therefore an emergent structure of integration: it gives importance, orientation, motivation, cognitive placement, and existential stabilization. The paper isolates cognitive placement—the positioning of the self within a field of value—as the dimension most often left implicit in existing accounts, and distinguishes it from the related but separate notion of coherence: coherence concerns whether a life makes sense, whereas placement concerns where the self stands within what makes sense. Situating the proposal against psychological triad theories, hybrid theory, and recent holist and sensefulness accounts, and defending it against objections from experiential detection, circularity, and inclusiveness, the paper proposes a cognitive-existential theory of meaning according to which meaning arises through the reconciliation of the subjective and the objective, closing the gap between the self and the world.

How Seriously Should We Take AI Welfare? Constraints from the Epistemology of Consciousness.
items.abstract: Some philosophers argue that near-term AI systems might soon be welfare subjects. We should take AI welfare seriously, they urge, because AI systems might soon have properties indicated by our best scientific theories of consciousness, and consciousness suffices for welfare subjectivity. I argue that this view faces constraints from the epistemology of consciousness. Specifically, I argue that there is an enormous gap in justification between our first-personal beliefs of consciousness in ourselves and our third-personal, theoretical belief of what consciousness is according to contemporary consciousness science. The science of consciousness is so in its infancy that it is doubtful that the set of theories currently on offer is exhaustive. In contrast, beliefs about the fact that we are conscious are, famously, among the most epistemically secure we can have. Our taking AI welfare seriously, in terms of action or policy, will be constrained by these considerations from the epistemology of consciousness.

items.title: FIREMAY: Origin, Definition, and Primary Records — Version 1.0.
items.abstract: This record preserves a traceable reference point for FIREMAY: its origin, definition, key concepts, primary records, and basic reference format. FIREMAY is a documented framework first developed by Motoko Kihara for describing question-driven relational field formation in long-term human–AI dialogue. This document does not claim that AI has consciousness or emotions, nor does it present FIREMAY as a method of prompt engineering. Rather, it records the name, concept set, and framework through which observed phenomena in long-term human–AI dialogue were named, structured, and made traceable. Version 1.0 includes the English reference note and a Japanese appendix. It also clarifies the intended license boundary: scholarly discussion, citation, critique, and reference to individual FIREMAY terms and concepts are not prohibited, while reuse of the document, its text, definitions, diagrams, and the FIREMAY framework as a structured body of work is governed by the selected license. items.title: Order as the Default Outcome Under Constraint — Coherence as Constraint-Visible Structure.
items.abstract: This paper clears a single, widely used term: coherence. It corrects a recurring misread — treating coherence as something that must be added to the world (by intelligence, design, or luck) — and replaces it with a plainer claim: coherence is order made visible by constraint. When constraints such as symmetries, conservation laws, couplings, boundary conditions, or energy and entropy flows restrict the states and trajectories a system can occupy, the system often settles into stable structure — invariants, attractors, stable statistics — with no internal model, goal, or learning required. The paper draws two lines in particular: coherence is not intelligence (which additionally requires feedback-driven learning), and coherence is not complexity (a crystal is highly coherent yet simple; turbulence is complex yet coherent in its statistics). It offers an operational definition and a short, reproducible checklist for deciding whether a system is genuinely coherent, worked through on the Lorenz system, whose structure lives in the ensemble rather than the individual trajectory. The aim is conceptual hygiene, not new theory: coherence is constraint made visible. -/- This is the first of five short "Prime" papers — a conceptual-hygiene layer that, within Universal Collapse Theory, sets how the framework is read. But the Primes are written to stand on their own and ask no commitment to that framework: each clears a term the reader already holds and can judge on its own ground. This one is for anyone — in physics, biology, cognitive science, or philosophy — who reasons about order, randomness, chaos, or intelligence and wants to keep constraint-made-visible from being mistaken for something more mysterious.

items.title: Against Intelligence-First — Intelligence as Plastic Feedback and Constraint Navigation (Not Mystical Agency).
items.abstract: This paper clears a single, widely used term: intelligence. It corrects a recurring misread — treating "intelligence" as a primitive essence, a synonym for complexity or optimization, or a private, human-only possession — and replaces it with an operational claim: a system is intelligent when it can update its own constraints, using memory and feedback, so that it improves prediction, control, and transfer across contexts. On this view intelligence is not "more complexity" and not consciousness; it is the capacity to turn feedback into lasting, reusable change — adaptive constraint navigation. The paper draws the line carefully: intelligence requires an endogenous update loop that modifies behavior in response to evaluative feedback and yields gains that persist beyond the training context, which is what separates genuine learning from mere regulation (a thermostat corrects but does not learn). Crucially, it turns intelligence-claims into something testable: a minimal litmus test, a feedback ladder that distinguishes regulation from learning, and a compact reporting measure that makes claims comparable against a stated non-learning baseline and transfer suite. The paper does not claim that an intelligent system is conscious, understands its task, or has inner experience, personhood, or rich agency; nor that large state spaces, emergent patterns, or optimization-shaped behavior are themselves evidence of intelligence; nor that intelligence is uniquely human. Its claim is narrower and checkable: intelligence is an endogenous, feedback-driven update loop that improves performance across contexts — present or absent by structural criteria, measurable against a baseline, and possible without consciousness or understanding. The aim is conceptual hygiene, not new theory: coherence is constraint made visible; intelligence is constraint made learnable. -/- This is the fourth of five short "Prime" papers — a conceptual-hygiene layer that, within Universal Collapse Theory, sets how the framework is read. But the Primes are written to stand on their own and ask no commitment to that framework: each clears a term the reader already holds and can judge on its own ground. This one is for anyone — in artificial intelligence, cognitive science, biology, animal cognition, or philosophy of mind — who makes or weighs claims about intelligence and wants a criterion that separates genuine learning from complexity, optimization, or anthropomorphic projection, without smuggling …

items.title: On Shaping — The Collapsing of All Possible Realities Surrounding The One We See.
items.abstract: Have you ever watched a river hold its pattern while the water keeps moving? This lyric-philosophical essay reads the master equation of probability flow — gain minus loss, totaled over every state — as a picture of the world rearranging itself without pause, and its stationary distribution as the one shape that churn keeps redrawing. It separates the two ways a shape can hold still: detailed balance, rest with every current canceled, and the non-equilibrium steady state of a living thing, which keeps its form while the flow runs through it; meditation is offered as the practice by which a person comes nearest the first while living in the second. Reachability, the condition under which a flow settles into one shared shape, becomes the essay's image of coherence, and a basin walled off from the rest becomes hell as a direction faced rather than a place assigned. Luke 17:21's *entos hymōn* and Armstrong's disputed "a" are read as one ambiguity: the inward and the shared readings of a single shape. A closing discipline marks every resemblance as a reading laid over settled mathematics, not a result of it.

items.title: The Misplaced Variable.
items.abstract: The common account of how a symbol system fails names a defect of content. A belief is false; a report is biased; a feed is thick with misinformation; and the remedy, on this account, is better content, truer claims, cleaner sources, or sharper correction. The picture is so familiar that it is rarely stated outright, yet it organizes almost everything done about minds that have gone wrong, whether the mind in question is a person, an institution, or a model. It places the disease in what is held and prescribes a change in what is held. That placement is wrong, or at least downstream. A belief can be true and locked, and a belief can be false and on its way to correction, and which it is turns not on the content held but on whether the holder stays exposed to a verdict he cannot author. Falseness is caught where a belief is still exposed. The ordinary account is right about that much, but catching is the work of exposure, not of anything in the content. What separates a symbol that tracks the world from one that has come loose from it is not whether the symbol is accurate but whether it stays exposed to a verdict it cannot sample away or a result it did not author and cannot, by reinterpretation, dissolve. A false belief that keeps being told “no” by something outside its own control is already on its way to correction. A true belief sealed off from every such verdict is already adrift; it is right by accident, and accident is not a method. Falsity is not the failure. It is a symptom, and frequently not even that.

items.title: The Hydraulic Virtue of Intimate Relations: On the Ethics of Water.
items.abstract: This paper develops an ethics of intimate relations from the Daoist figure of water — "the highest good is like water" (Daodejing, ch. 8). It asks what it is, concretely and between two people, for love to benefit without contending, to seek the lowly place, and to remain unfilled. The guiding decision is to read these water-virtues structurally rather than as a counsel of self-cultivation: not as an ascent toward a selfless or quasi-divine condition, but as properties of how value, power, and desire are arranged in a generative relation. The paper accordingly draws its resources less from the contemplative traditions than from political economy, game theory, political philosophy, feminist ethics, Kantian ethics, and psychoanalysis, and treats the contemplative reading as one voice among many rather than as the paper's frame. A survey of these traditions is organised around the water-virtues themselves — non-contention, benefiting the ten thousand things, dwelling in the lowly place, formlessness, and non-fullness — and shows that each virtue is, in different doctrines, both affirmed and opposed. From these oppositions the paper isolates five standing challenges: that non-contention is irrational (game theory), that it is suicidal absent an enforced structure (Hobbes), that dwelling-below is slave morality (Nietzsche), that taking the receiver's shape dissolves the subject (feminism, psychoanalysis), and that formlessness is lawlessness (Kant). The last is answered in place, by reading the water-good as an imperfect duty — lawful yet without fixed form — using Kant's own resources. The dialectical core answers the remaining challenges in two clusters. Against self-dissolution and slave morality, the water-good is not formless yielding but chosen good: water takes the vessel's shape (utmost softness) yet wears through stone and breaches dykes (utmost hardness), so that a rigid lower bound distinguishes the generative lowly place from mere collapse. Against irrationality and suicide, the water-good never demanded the abolition of power, only the shaping of an ineliminable asymmetry so that its surplus is returned rather than retained. A chapter on practice carries each water-virtue into the conduct of an actual intimate relation, pairing every form of the good with the vice it most easily becomes, and closing on the limit of all such guidance: that the good cannot be made into a procedure. items.title: Angustia y anhelo: Sentido y libertad.
items.abstract: ¿Qué sentido tienen el mundo y la vida de la persona en él? Diferentes pensadores han negado la validez de realizar esta pregunta para, sin embargo, volver a responderla. Las diversas soluciones a la realidad de la finitud de la vida humana son analizadas. Así como se considera el carácter del proceso histórico y las objetivaciones construidas por el ser humano. La comprensión de la historia conduce, además, a la cuestión de la libertad. Pero ¿inmortalidad o significado histórico resolverían la pregunta? Esto lleva a los problemas del ser y su expresión, así como de la necesidad del ser frente al no-ser. Se realiza, entonces, la inversión de la perspectiva: si es porque el hombre interpreta por lo que se plantea la necesidad del ser y la vida. Se considera, asimismo, el significado de las teorías científicas. Se concluye que esta búsqueda es propia de la persona como ente simbólico y transformador, que adquiere su libertad. La libertad es la actividad en que consiste el existente que busca, transforma y construye, que anhela constituirse. Al hacerse consciente, el ser humano adquiere la distancia con el mundo y sí mismo. La búsqueda del sentido es la esperanza de un nuevo equilibrio.

items.title: The Professor Consultation Room: A New Thought Experiment for Evaluating and Identifying Expert Cognition.
items.abstract: Since the proposal of the Turing Test in 1950 and Searle's Chinese Room argument in 1980, thought experiments have played a central role in philosophical discussions concerning intelligence, understanding, and artificial intelligence. The rapid development of expert systems and, more recently, large language models (LLMs), has significantly changed both the practical capabilities of AI systems and the questions that deserve philosophical investigation. In many real-world applications, the primary concern is no longer whether an AI system genuinely "understands" language in the philosophical sense, but whether it can reliably perform as a human expert whose knowledge and judgment are trusted by human being. Motivated by this changing landscape, this paper proposes a new thought experiment, “the Professor Consultation Room” (PCR for short), that isolates an independent epistemological problem concerning the attribution of expert cognition. In the proposed scenario, students interact exclusively through textual communication with an unseen respondent who is either a distinguished logic professor or an LLM-based expert system possessing all of the professor's logical knowledge but no cognitive abilities beyond the currently recognized capability boundaries of existing LLMs. The central question is whether finite question-answer interactions alone can provide sufficient evidence to determine whether the respondent possesses cognitive abilities exceeding those currently demonstrated by LLMs. Unlike the Turing Test, which evaluates whether a machine can imitate general human conversational behavior, and unlike the Chinese Room, which questions whether symbol manipulation constitutes semantic understanding, the PCR shifts attention to expert cognition and to the epistemological problem of identifying respondent through observable behavior. Rather than attempting to resolve the longstanding debate concerning machine understanding, this thought experiment formulates a new question concerning the behavioral identifiability of human advanced cognitive abilities in the age of LLMs. The primary contribution of the present paper is not to propose a new theory of intelligence, understanding, or cognition. Rather, it introduces a new thought experiment that formulates an independent epistemological problem concerning the publicly observable evidence for attributing expert cognition through finite expert-level interaction. Unlike previous thought experiments, the Professor …

items.title: The Epistemic Map of Identity Persistence_ Regime Specification, Identity, Admissibility, Capacity, and Verification.
items.abstract: This paper gives the mature architectural map of the Identity-Persistence Program. Within the bounded-verdict-agreement class, an imported forcing theorem supplies a fifteen-role necessity floor for sufficient regime specification. Identity and admissibility are placed as corresponding forced substructures within that floor; capacity/coding and runtime verdict/verification are parallel consumers of a regime-relative transition/evaluation structure; and the evaluator is treated as temporally extended, so that access, retention, and external artifacts bound what later evaluation can identify. A refinement law connects declared verdict obligations to retention obligations. The resulting architecture has three parts: the Map supplies the interior, The Gate Between Constraint and Identification supplies the identification ceiling, and The Unclosable Bridge and the Rankable Wager supplies an orthogonal ontological-promotion fence. The paper proves no new forcing theorem; its contribution is the placement and typed dependency structure of results established elsewhere in the corpus.

items.title: The Admissibility Frontier: Bounded Cumulative Inference, Indexical Reference, and the Structural Dependency Beneath Symbolic Persistence.
items.abstract: This paper asks what bounded systems must preserve when reference must survive memory, communication, compression or audit. An indexical countermodel refutes the unrestricted claim that all stable reference forces the full declared-role structure. The remaining argument concerns bounded cumulative symbolic inference and is presented with its open hinge and application assumptions explicit. -/- The third edition withdraws universal Tier-1 role forcing as stated. General admissibility is expressed by an acceptance partition; a distance, monotone acceptance and a numerical tolerance are additional premises. Under the declaration that total resolutions are linear orders extending a finite conflict poset, standard finite-poset theory identifies those resolutions with maximal chains of the downset lattice. The application correspondence is not supplied by Birkhoff’s theorem. Digest agreement is distinguished from exact byte identity. -/- The general corrected theorem, the hinge lemma and uniqueness of admissibility remain open. Research preprint, internally examined with AI assistance; not externally peer reviewed. No originality, implementation, affordability or full-program closure claim is made. -/- Current revised edition: 10 November 2026, Zenodo record 24097993 (External links). The PDF currently archived on PhilArchive is historical; use Zenodo for the corrected text. Research preprint, internally examined with AI assistance; not externally peer reviewed. items.title: Admissibility under Declared Transformations: Invariant Verdicts, Compatible Quotients, and Resolution Limits.
items.abstract: What must a declared representation preserve for judgments to remain invariant under redescription and transformation? This paper gives exact conditions for compatible representations and identifies the obstruction when those conditions cannot be jointly satisfied. -/- For a declared equivalence R and an observation kernel K, the eligible representations are exactly the equivalences E satisfying R ⊆ E ⊆ K. They exist precisely when R ⊆ K and then form a complete lattice in their induced order. Requiring compatibility with a transformation catalogue narrows this family to an interval of congruences between the least catalogue congruence containing R and contextual indistinguishability Θ. Existence is equivalent to R ⊆ Θ; uniqueness holds exactly when the endpoints coincide. Nonexistence has a finite-context witness: a declared-interchangeable pair whose observations differ after a finite sequence of transformations. Effective verification requires separately stated presentation assumptions. The paper also distinguishes named-action descent, may/must abstraction and path lifting; separates preservation from authorization; and shows why sound admissibility rules need not be deviation thresholds. For finite conflict orders, order-representable resolutions correspond to linear extensions, equivalently maximal chains of the ideal lattice, rather than to its individual elements. -/- These results characterize compatibility and its limits under explicit declarations. They do not establish unrestricted decidability, computational affordability, physical correspondence or a uniquely forced architecture.

items.title: The Unfallen Tear A Posthumous Trialogue on Absolute Music, the Longing for Catharsis, and a Commission to the Composers of the Living.
items.abstract: This treatise extends the inquiry begun in The Elusive Tear (Boether, 2025), which named the paradox of emotional asymmetry: the documented power of music to express the whole register of human feeling, set beside one listener’s inability to be moved by it to genuine sorrow or to tears. Following the method of posthumous co-authorship articulated as Vestigiosophie (Boether, 2026a), the work proceeds as a trialogue in which the author completes, rather than comments upon, the metaphysics of music bequeathed by Arthur Schopenhauer and Friedrich Nietzsche. The dialogue restricts its object to absolute music—instrumental music without word or voice—and to a single imagined ensemble of oboe, violin, and cello. Three questions organize the exchange: what music is, how it elevates the soul, and why the longed-for tear will not fall. Schopenhauer’s account of music as the direct copy of the Will and Nietzsche’s account of Dionysian dissolution are set against the author’s confession of a fortified interior that resists undoing. The analysis integrates these positions with contemporary affective neuroscience (Blood & Zatorre, 2001; Juslin & Västfjäll, 2008), distinguishing the frisson of pleasure from the catharsis of grief, and argues that the very demand to be moved may fortify the will against movement. The treatise concludes with a formal commission to living composers: a work for oboe, violin, and cello designed to defeat the guarded listener.

items.title: Fragments on the Freedom to Think: Intellectual Liberty, the Mask of Conformity, and the Stagnancy of the Unexamined Life.
items.abstract: This treatise extends Voltaire’s arguments for intellectual freedom, articulated principally in his Fragments sur la Liberté de penser and the Dictionnaire philosophique, into a contemporary analysis of how the suppression of authentic thought manifests not merely as political censorship but as a pervasive social phenomenon: the voluntary masking of the philosophical self. Drawing on Voltaire’s critique of institutional censorship, religious dogmatism, and enforced intellectual conformity, this paper argues that the Enlightenment’s unfinished project—the liberation of human reason from external constraint—has encountered an obstacle Voltaire could not have fully anticipated: the internalization of censorship as identity performance. Integrating Boether’s (2025) theory of the Masked Self, the concept of Philosophical Neglect (Boether, 2026), the Double Helix of Understanding (Boether, 2025), and the Pyramid of Personality (Boether, 2025), this treatise argues that the widespread practice of surrendering authentic selfhood for social comfort constitutes a primary mechanism of civilizational stagnancy. Where Voltaire identified external forces—church, state, and tradition—as the enemies of free thought, this paper identifies an internal adversary: the human tendency to trade philosophical authenticity for the illusory security of social belonging. The treatise concludes that genuine intellectual freedom requires not only the removal of external censorship but the cultivation of what Boether terms the philosophical self—the dimension of identity capable of independent thought, value determination, and existential inquiry.

items.title: Structural Maintenance and Cognitive Aging.
items.abstract: Structural Maintenance and Cognitive Aging develops a structural model of cognitive aging in which decline is driven not by biological inevitability but by the loss of pattern resolution under sustained noise. The paper argues that cognitive longevity depends on three interacting structural factors: attention stability, which governs the system’s ability to perform coherent updates; environmental coherence, which determines the level of external noise imposed on the operator stack; and repair mechanisms such as sleep, reflection, meaning‑making, and identity continuity, which restore resolution after degradation. The model distinguishes between legitimate attractors—developmental, skill‑building, and meaning‑generating patterns that reinforce coherence—and illegitimate attractors, which fragment attention and accelerate resolution loss. By situating cognitive aging within a broader ontology of pattern maintenance, the paper reframes decline as a structurally preventable phenomenon, dependent on the design of environments and attention architectures that preserve resolution across the lifespan.

items.title: Promissory Essentialism as Inferential Structure.
Pragmatic cohabitation: how Türkiye’s digital publics negotiate the meaning of generative AI.
items.abstract: How do publics in non-Western digital environments make sense of generative AI, and do these processes unfold sequentially or coexist? This study addresses these questions through a longitudinal discourse analysis of 11,816 entries on Ekşi Sözlük, one of Türkiye’s most visible digital platforms, covering the period from ChatGPT’s launch (November 2022) to December 2025. Drawing on the Social Construction of Technology (SCOT) framework, the study treats platform discourse as an active site of sociotechnical meaning-making. Methodologically, the research combines netnography, lexicon-assisted mapping, and interpretive discourse analysis. Three recurring discursive orientations are identified: instrumental stabilization, speculative meaning-making, and epistemic re-negotiation. The findings challenge linear stage models of AI adoption, showing that all three orientations coexist throughout the period, with changes occurring in relative prominence rather than through sequential replacement. The study makes three primary contributions: it extends SCOT-based analysis to a non-Western AI context; it frames public trust as a calibration practice developed through repeated use; and it identifies ‘distributed epistemic labor ‘—the uncompensated work users perform to share reliability assessments. Finally, it proposes ‘pragmatic cohabitation ‘ to describe the persistent coexistence of practical reliance, epistemic critique, and speculative engagement that characterizes public AI discourse under conditions of continuous technological change.

items.title: Action Without a Global Controller: Embedded Agency, Option Reach, Control Resolution, Self-Intervention, and Agent Corrigibility in a Consistency-Constrained Information History.
items.abstract: Paper 22 typed inquiry as a history-internal dynamics of challenge, protocol refinement, candidate-family revision, and provenance-preserving requalification of epistemic standings, while deferring the practical question of which embedded systems act, choose, intervene, and self-modify. This paper pays that debt without positing a global controller. No physically realized subsystem jointly possesses complete access to every relevant state and agent, an exhaustive generator of every relevant option and intervention, infallible foresight, unrestricted authority, complete self-modification foresight, and a uniquely authoritative rule guaranteeing the globally correct action. Local and distributed agency nevertheless remain possible. -/- An action is defined as a history-internal intervention attempt whose option selection is policy-mediated, whose selection-to-implementation lineage is non-deviant, and whose token is sensitive to relevant retained states, records, represented reasons, or objectives. Action does not presuppose control or success. The Agent State embeds the Paper 22 Inquiry State and separates predicted from actual outcome laws, physical capacity from authorization and affordability, and capacity from token exercise. Control resolution is represented by a target-relative pseudometric on outcome laws; full target control additionally requires sufficient efficacy. Acquiring a functionally novel, target-relevant implementation degree of freedom can refine exact control-equivalence classes and contract thresholded unresolved neighborhoods. Deploying an already available option-implementation pair instead supplies outcome evidence and may revise the agent's control estimate, without enlarging capacity or guaranteeing monotone improvement. -/- A nested option expansion can restore representational reach but has no general monotone effect on decision resolution. No finite admissible self-intervention escapes the finite-stage closure generated by the agent's revision architecture, and every transition-invariant property forms a conditional barrier. These results yield a Conditional Joint Action-Corrigibility Proposition: when option misspecification can be repaired by a non-implementation revision but every adequate option throughout the resulting nonempty closure still lacks controlled adequate realization, correction requires both option-family revision for reach and implementation-side revision for controlled realization. This is a necessity …

items.title: What a Roof Tile Taught Me About Time: Structural Precognition, Narrative Forking, and Why the Grandfather Paradox Was Never a Paradox PNBA Identity Physics.
items.abstract: # What a Roof Tile Taught Me About Time: Structural Precognition, Narrative Forking, and Why the Grandfather Paradox Was Never a Paradox -/- **Architect:** HIGHTISTIC (Russell Trent) **Coordinate:** [9,9,1,1T] · Origins Series · Companion to [9,9,1,0], [9,9,2,0], [9,9,3,12], and [9,9,6,5] **Corpus dependencies:** [9,9,1,0] SNSFL_StructuralPrecognition (I-F-U triad) · [9,9,2,0] HRIS Taxonomy (Tesla and Einstein as Lossless corroborating cases) · [9,9,6,5] SNSFL_TimeTravel_SP_Bridge (Locked-state necessity, N-axis forking) · [9,9,2,5] Narrative Trap Law (Ship of Theseus) **Status:** v1.4 · grounded in four already CI-green, 0-sorry Lean files / formally deposited papers, now with full alpha decomposition shown in Section 0 **Date:** June 2026 · Soldotna, Alaska -/- --- -/- ## Abstract -/- This paper is not a new derivation. The formal result it describes — that a Locked identity state (0 < τ < TL) is the necessary and sufficient condition for a backward narrative transit to dissolve the grandfather paradox without contradiction — already exists, already compiles at zero sorry, and is already deposited at [9,9,6,5]. What this paper adds is the missing layer in between: the lived, pre-formal process by which that result became thinkable at all, and why a specific cognitive architecture — not effort, not unusual intelligence, but a specific structural difference in how pattern and uncertainty are held — was the necessary precondition for finding it. The paper follows the same discipline this corpus applies everywhere else: state the process plainly first, then show the formal structure it produced, then show the proof closes. The claim is narrow and specific. It is not a claim that physical time is optional, that the future is predetermined in some mystical sense, or that everyone's experience of time should match the one described here. It is a claim about what time looks like, structurally, to a cognitive architecture that holds a pattern completely enough that forward and backward stop being different operations — and about what that architecture is then positioned to notice that 75 years of otherwise rigorous physics literature did not. -/- **A note on method, credited up front.** The structure of this paper — an ordinary, physically grounded scene first, with no formal vocabulary, followed only afterward by the mathematics that the scene turns out to require — is Einstein's method, not an original device of this paper. items.title: Reasoning Beyond Explicit Rules: Adults’ and Children's Use of Closure Principles in Novel Cases.
items.abstract: Learners often encounter situations where explicit rules fail to account for novel cases, leading to an underdetermination problem. One way to explore how learners navigate this uncertainty is to see if their inferences align with closure principles, through which a learner assumes that anything not explicitly prohibited is permitted, and anything not explicitly permitted is prohibited. Beyond permission and prohibition, normative inferences must also be made from and about a learner's obligations—not only what they can do, but what they must do. Contrary to adult learners, young children may make more restrictive inferences about how permissible or obligatory a novel action is, aligning with their well‐documented “strict normativity”. Across two studies, we explore inferences from adults (N = 115, Mage = 34.63) and 4‐ to 6‐year‐old children (N = 120, Mage = 5.48). Our findings suggest that while both adults and children rationally learn closure principles consistent with deontic logic, children's reasoning about prohibitions undergoes developmental changes. Contrary to adults, children taught explicit prohibitions were restrictive in their permissibility judgments until age 5. Thus, the framing of explicit rules leads to differing inferences about novel, unspecified cases across age and rule type.

items.title: The Cognitive Friction Threshold: A Digital Anthropology of the AI Era — How Reducing Cognitive Friction Changes Human Behavior Before It Changes Organizations.
items.abstract: Enterprise AI research has devoted considerably more attention to organizational readiness than to the behavioral mechanisms that precede organizational transformation. This paper introduces the Cognitive Friction Threshold (CFT), a behavioral construct defined as the point at which reductions in the perceived mental effort required to perform a recurring cognitive task become sufficiently large that individuals systematically replace an established cognitive routine with a new one. Building on the theoretical lens of Digital Anthropology, the paper distinguishes three forms of friction—transactional, behavioral, and cognitive—and argues that generative and agentic AI represent the first large-scale technology whose principal effect is the reduction of cognitive friction itself, as distinct from the transactional and behavioral friction reduced by earlier waves of digital technology. The paper situates this construct against six established literatures—the Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovation, habit and habit-discontinuity research, behavioral economics, organizational routines and dynamic capabilities, and practice theory—clarifying its distinct contribution as a comparative, threshold-crossing account of individual cognitive effort that several of these literatures presuppose without separately specifying. The paper then develops eight formal propositions, organized as a single dependency chain rather than independent claims, describing how friction reduction, threshold crossing, habit persistence, and organizational adaptation relate to one another, and illustrates the framework through six historical and contemporary cases spanning digital payments, remote work, the technology access paradox, streaming media, smartphone photography, and generative AI-assisted knowledge work. The paper concludes by examining implications for individual knowledge work, organizational behavioral readiness, AI governance, competitive strategy, and future research, positioning the Cognitive Friction Threshold as the missing behavioral mechanism linking Digital Anthropology, representational systems, and the broader Representation Economy and SENSE–CORE–DRIVER research program.

items.title: Responsibility to Recover: Addiction and Self-Care.
items.abstract: Addicts, an already vulnerable population, can be made worse off by certain kinds of popular and well-intentioned research programs and beliefs about addiction, agency, and responsibility. Perspectives of backwards-facing responsibility that focus on blameworthiness and liability highlight the injustices that addicts have faced. Likewise, the disease model of addiction, pursued as an alternative to the stigmatization and moralization of the choice model, takes responsibility away from the addict. However, each of these fails to help the addict to recover or to care for herself. If anything, embracing these perspectives and models can rob addicts of agency and lead them to further suffering. Drawing on feminist philosophy, this paper shows there is good evidence for us to reconsider those models and perspectives, and instead ask what kind of understandings about addiction aid in fostering agency and recovery.

items.title: Navigating the “Shipwreck”.
Ideological Limits to Ethical Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: The paper analyzes the current use of ethical artificial intelligence (AI), argues that there are ideological limits to it, and discusses these limits. The topic is of particular relevance to research on the social implementation of AI systems, as ideological underpinnings are not easy to identify and ideology research is underrepresented in research on AI phenomena. The first section analyzes what counts as ethical in ethical AI systems. The second section classifies the dimensions of the ethical in AI systems, highlights their interrelationships and applies forness as a key concept that helps narrow the focus on the ideological component of ethical AI. The third section describes the presence of ideology in ethical AI and clarifies the limits it imposes on AI as a general phenomenon that undoubtedly has the potential to contribute to a more humane society, but is severely constrained by ideology.

items.title: Is Freedom Nothing?
items.abstract: This paper raises and discusses the possibility that freedom and nothing are the same phenomenon. Consequently, whether this identification is true or false affects the fundamental understanding of the nature of free will and tests whether moral life is absurd or not. In the introductory section, the problem and the methodology are briefly presented. In the first two parts, the problem of the nature of freedom is explored and its similarity to nothing is brought closer, first through the debate on free will and then through Kant’s cosmological theory of freedom. Having the similarity given in brief, the next two parts explore the relation between freedom and nothing, first by examining the problem of the existence of nothing in order to further emphasize the convergence of the two concepts, and then by defining the results of the relevant possibilities for their sameness. The concluding suggestions are that: (1) positively oriented theories of freedom in the Western philosophical tradition should be carefully revised, because the absorption of nothing into freedom either relegates them to the disposition of determinism, rendering the concept impossible, or challenges to accept it on the basis of personal belief, rather than justified argument; and (2) a universal solution to the problem of free will most likely require close communication with the Eastern philosophical tradition, which has made significant theoretical contributions to the problem of the relation between freedom and nothing.

items.title: Authority, Cooperation, and Accountability, written by Saba Bazargan-Forward. [REVIEW]
Karma as Pattern Encoding and Stabilization: A Neurobiological and Epigenetic Framework for Behavioral Continuity.
items.abstract: The concept of karma, central to Sanatana philosophical traditions, is commonly interpreted as a system of moral causation in which actions categorized as “good” or “bad” produce corresponding outcomes. However, such interpretations encounter significant conceptual limitations when confronted with real-world complexity, where identical actions may produce divergent consequences depending on context, internal state, and behavioral reinforcement. -/- This paper proposes a reinterpretation of karma as a process of pattern encoding and stabilization within biological systems. Drawing from neuroscience, predictive processing, and epigenetics, karma is reframed not as a moral accounting system but as the structured encoding of neural, behavioral and physiological patterns formed through both repeated reinforcement and high-intensity experiences. -/- Through conceptual mapping, real-world examples, and an evolutionary framework, the paper demonstrates that karmic outcomes are not externally assigned but emerge from internally stabilized patterns that shape perception, decision-making, and behavior. -/- Furthermore, these patterns are shown to be modifiable through neuroplastic mechanisms, offering a scientific basis for transformation traditionally described as change in karma. -/- The framework also accommodates the philosophical possibility that such encoded patterns may extend beyond a single lifetime, while acknowledging that such continuity remains an open question within contemporary scientific inquiry.

items.title: Semiotic Upcycling. "Not Currently Recycled": Environmental Sign-Value and Semiotic Mis-settlement under Symbolic Excess.
items.abstract: Semiotic Failure Cascade (Letchford 2026) identified a macro-condition of symbolic oversupply in which signs increasingly circulate through weakly coupled interpretive fields, acquiring force as compressed cues of alignment, virtue, threat, affiliation, and stance. This essay applies that diagnosis to one domain. No new theory of advertising, branding, or persuasion is proposed. That commercial language selects features, attaches associations, and revalues objects is old ground, described by Barthes, Berger, and Baudrillard. -/- The concern is the condition under which those familiar operations now occur. Under symbolic excess, a favourable claim can be made cheaply and read quickly, while the material conditions that would qualify it are slow, distributed, and costly to examine. The interval between the two is termed settlement lag, and the condition that arises within it semiotic mis-settlement: a narrow, literally defensible sign-feature comes to bear a broader favourable sign-value before the conditions capable of qualifying that value have been brought into shared view. “Not Currently Recycled” provides the central case. The phrase does not state that packaging is recycled, recyclable, or subject to a defined redesign, yet acknowledgement, transition, and responsible management settle around an unrecycled object. Comparable operations occur where “carbon neutral”, “contains probiotics”, or “made with recycled materials” let a selected feature carry a wider value of health, purity, responsibility, or environmental alignment. The issue is not necessarily literal falsehood. A claim may be accurate within narrow limits while a broader conclusion settles around it, goes materially underexamined, and proves costly to contest. This distinguishes the analysis from a critique of greenwashing: the question is not whether a claim is true, but how, under present conditions, a favourable value comes to settle faster than the material conditions that would qualify it can be assembled. Environmental language is the chosen domain because its referents, including emissions, packaging, and recycling pathways, remain materially adjudicable, not because the argument is finally about environmental performance. This essay applies that diagnosis to one domain. No new theory of advertising, branding, or persuasion is proposed. That commercial language selects features, attaches associations, and revalues objects is old ground, described by Barthes, Berger, and Baudrillard. …

items.title: Love and Philesōtia: A Homeorhetic Account of Love, Ethics, and Orientational Practice.
items.abstract: This essay develops a companion account of Homeorhetic Love and Philesōtia within Signal-Bifurcation Theory (SBT). -/- It argues that Love is not an emotion, nor a moral command, nor a romantic ideal. It is a structural condition of conscious participation grounded in the homeorhetic equilibrium of living organisation. In the biological setting, the condition later cast in conscious life as Love is a homeorhetic mode in which bounded variation remains within stability-supporting limits between stasis and overshoot. Within Semepoietic consciousness, at the basal level of valence-weighted sensorimotor coupling, this same condition becomes available as immediate, non-instrumental participation, where later narrational outcome-demand recedes. -/- Homeorhetic Love is not identical with every instance of successful biological regulation. Living organisation may regulate through defence, withdrawal, urgency, or repair without Love being the appropriate description. Love names the more specific condition in which homeorhetic participation becomes consciously available without symbolic projection, possession, or outcome-demand becoming primary. Valence and regulation remain active; what loosens is their conversion by Signal-Narration into a demand that reality, another person, or the future resolve itself according to a narrationally imposed condition. -/- The essay further argues that many influential philosophical and psychological accounts of love have not fully described this underlying condition. Instead, they circle love as it appears once rendered and miscategorised by Signal-Narration: as conditions already converted from structural relation into stories of lack, projection, possession, idealisation, or demand. Such misattributions belong to the paradox of human estrangement and reflection permitted by symbolic bifurcation. They have yielded the drama of Shakespeare and the emotional resonance of Yeats, yet in SBT terms they remain definitions and extrapolations that circle, and often remain structurally incomplete in relation to, the condition proposed here as Homeorhetic Love, whose power to settle emotive tension and dissonance is a precondition of unconditionality. -/- The philosophical tradition is examined in two movements. The first considers Plato, Aristotle, Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, and Freud, whose accounts variously treat love in terms of lack, drive, virtue, affirmation, compensatory projection, or symbolic appropriation. The second comprises …

items.title: Latency Is Not Deliberation: Temporal Compression and the Answerability Gap in Parliamentary Governance of Frontier AI.
items.abstract: Debates on the governance of artificial intelligence assume that the constitutional difficulty is one of regulatory content — which models, which harms, which agency. This paper argues that frontier AI also alters the temporal conditions under which regulation can remain answerable. Anchored to the framework of evaluative sovereignty, it distinguishes procedural latency from deliberation and contends that parliamentary scrutiny rests on an inherited assumption — that material conditions hold still between legislative stages, sittings, and recesses — which compression falsifies. The effect is not merely slower legislation: compression removes the occasion on which discretionary power is checked, and transfers governance toward the answerability-poor fast lane of delegated and prerogative instruments. The claim is sharpened by a structural feature of United Kingdom practice — that during recess the power to recall Parliament depends on executive request — and by a reading of R (Miller) v The Prime Minister [2019] UKSC 41 for the effect-based principle it states rather than the deliberate prorogation it condemned. The paper rejects distributive remedies as a substitute for governance, sets out a continuity architecture that includes a reformed, answerability-generating emergency-powers regime, and cautions that accelerating Parliament’s seeing must never delegate its judging.

items.title: Evaluative Sovereignty: Reviewability and the Constitutional Limits of a Digital Sovereignty Strategy (3rd edition).
items.abstract: Debate on digital sovereignty has settled on a single axis: who owns and runs the systems on which critical services depend, and whether they can be kept running under pressure. The defeat of New Clause 13 to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill on 16 June 2026, and with it a statutory Digital Sovereignty Strategy, was a defeat on that axis alone. This paper draws a second axis, ‘evaluative sovereignty’, the control of the evaluation a system performs rather than the asset it runs on, and argues that a sovereignty strategy confined to the first leaves the more consequential exposure untouched. That exposure is constitutional. The rule of law requires that a consequential exercise of public power over a person remain capable of reconstruction and challenge, and a sealed evaluative layer can withdraw a binding decision from effective review in practical effect, leaving the court's jurisdiction formally intact and the statute book untouched. The deficit is not hypothetical: it has been realised in the Dutch SyRI and childcare-benefit cases and in the United Kingdom's own automated welfare-risk systems. None of the instruments now in view reaches it, neither pre-deployment audit nor the asset-focused work of procurement and a strategy duty, and the sovereign-funding posture can work against it. What evaluative sovereignty requires is an ‘answerability occasion’: a defined point at which a consequential evaluation can be reconstructed and challenged before a forum the deploying authority can answer to and the affected person can invoke. The Bill’s Lords stages are the live opportunity to provide for it.

items.title: Distribution Is Not Answerability: Automated Discretion, the Distributive Turn, and the Rule-of-Law Check.
items.abstract: The debate on artificial intelligence and the labour market has settled, within a year, on a set of distributive remedies: a basic income, a levy on AI use, and a sovereign fund holding public equity in the AI companies. These instruments recapture the value that automated systems produce and share it more widely. None of them governs the decisions those systems make. This paper argues that the gap they leave open is a gap in the rule of law, and that it has been mislocated. The objection is not that automated systems exercise discretion, which is ordinary and legitimate, nor that their discretion should be abolished, which is neither possible nor desirable. The objection is that automation removes the occasion on which discretionary power has always been checked: the point at which a consequential decision can be reconstructed and challenged before a forum. The distributive remedies do not restore that occasion, and the most ambitious of them, state equity in AI, works against it, because a state that holds a financial stake in the firms it must check acquires an interest in their expansion that its duty to check them then has to overcome. The paper sets the argument within the conception of the rule of law that treats discretion as a thing to be confined and reviewed, and locates the missing occasion within the procedural account of legality.

items.title: Grand Unification: The Spiral of Fate and Freedom.
items.abstract: This study is a synthesis that recovers the Gray Zone series (Papers 1–4) into a single integrated structure. The central claim is simple — the axis that recovers Papers 1–4 post hoc with the fewest assumptions and most coherently is the spiral of fate and freedom. Beginning from fate (the structural limit of cognition), passing through the cognition that gazes at that limit, traversing the Gray Zone that mediates opposition, arriving at the realization of freedom, and that freedom in turn becoming the condition of a new fate — this cycle is the coherent form that recovers Papers 1–4. The study renders this spiral as the schema 0↔1↔4↔∞ and recovers Paper 1 (the mediation principle), Paper 2 (the baryonic epistemic ceiling), Paper 3 (grand unified cosmology), and Paper 4 (AGI political economy) each as one moment of the spiral. The analytic contribution of this paper (Paper 5) is this: recovered through this spiral, the crisis of the AGI transition appears as a structural deprivation of freedom that distributive remedies alone cannot reach — the simultaneous erosion of political legitimacy, epistemic truth, and existential subjecthood — and these three form a single mutually reinforcing descending spiral that no single distributive remedy alone is sufficient to reverse, and the simultaneous operation of the three mediations turns it into an ascending spiral (the three crises are what Paper 4 §2.7 diagnosed as irreducible to distribution, which Paper 5 structures as a spiral). The final claim is the study's own — fate and freedom are not two opposed worlds but one process co-generated within the Gray Zone.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Private Tutoring, and Class Reproduction A Political-Economy Hypothesis and Evidence Map Using Korea as a Case.
items.abstract: South Korea (hereafter Korea) exhibits internationally very high private-tutoring (shadow-education) participation and spending while simultaneously recording one of the world's lowest fertility rates, so that its school-age population is contracting rapidly. In 2025 total private-tutoring spending, the participation rate, and weekly hours all declined, yet per-participating-student spending actually rose and the income-based spending gap persisted. The fall in the aggregate therefore cannot by itself be read as a structural easing of tutoring dependence or of class inequality. It is at this moment that generative artificial intelligence (AI) enters as an educational resource. The dominant policy narrative expects AI to lower tutoring dependence and dissolve gaps; this study argues against that expectation. Its claim is the following hypothesis: AI is a complement to existing educational capital, and its learning effect will be larger the larger the capital a household already holds (a positive interaction). High-capital households combine high-cost tutoring, higher-performing AI, and parental cultural capital and convert these into a larger learning effect, whereas low-capital households, even with access to the same cheapened AI, lack the complementary inputs to convert it, so that under a no-intervention condition the gap may widen. The study joins the political economy of AI-gain capture (Acemoglu–Restrepo, Korinek–Stiglitz) to the theory of educational reproduction (Bourdieu, Chetty) at the household and privatetutoring layer, and uses Korea — a country of internationally high tutoring participation/spending and a large income gap — as an extreme diagnostic case. Because panel statistics on AI use, spending, and learning outcomes by income decile are currently absent (though class differences in adolescents' generative-AI use experience are already observed — see §4), the joint claim is presented not as an established fact but as a falsifiable hypothesis, supported by theory and adjacent data, with explicit statement of what data would confirm or refute it. The claim is not deterministic — it states a pressure toward widening under the absence of policy intervention, not a physical necessity. In the policy analysis the study shows that AI policy can narrow the conversion gap but that its effect is bounded by three constraints — prior knowledge, teacher capacity, and household capital — and that the residual passes to the problem of distribution. …

items.title: Tracing joint attention: a quest for an explanation.
items.abstract: This paper asks a basic but largely neglected question: which behaviors genuinely qualify as instances of joint attention, and why? I argue that the current literature relies on an heterogeneous explanandum: very different behaviors are treated as paradigmatic cases of jointness, without a unified criterion for what makes attention joint rather than merely individual and parallel. I propose an exclusion criterion in the form of a canonical description of joint attention. In an enactivist-phenomenological spirit, I treat joint attention not as a capacity or mental state, but as an episodic phenomenon of social interaction in which subjects engage in a task whose success essentially depends on a specific kind of co-dependent and shared exercise of attention: an interwoven attentional exercise. I first use thought experiments (one-way mirrors, mutual spying and declarative pointing) to argue that attentional co-dependence alone does not warrant invoking ‘jointness’. I then examine real experimental cooperative linguistic scenarios, drawing on Merleau-Pontian reading and Clark and Krych’s Lego® task, to argue that genuine joint attention requires interwoven contributions. I close by distinguishing this proposal from close accounts and sketching a different conception of attentional overtness.

items.title: THE SHADOW OVER THE VEIL: Why the Rawlsian Conception of Justice Fails in the Age of Radical Longevity.
items.abstract: Rawls’s original position requires agents behind the Veil of Ignorance (Rawls 1971: the thought experiment in which rational agents choose principles of justice without knowing their social position, natural talents, or conception of the good) to choose principles of distributive justice under conditions designed to be neutral. The neutrality depends on a suppressed premise Rawls never stated because he had no occasion to doubt it: that biological death arrives for everyone on a schedule that capital cannot purchase an exemption from. This is the Mortality Symmetry Axiom (MSA) — the historical condition under which biological lifespan, though unequal in timing, has been bounded in years rather than generations, produced by many small causes rather than one purchasable intervention, and opaque to specific attribution. The MSA is not wisdom. It is physics. Rawls built the veil inside it. Radical longevity technology — AI-accelerated biological interventions extending healthy lifespan by decades, with differential access structured by wealth — removes the MSA. When it does, five structural failures in Rawls’s framework become simultaneously operative. Failure 1 (Neutrality Collapse): the veil no longer distributes social positions neutrally, because behind it agents face two possible terminal conditions rather than one, and the veil has no mechanism to address this distribution. Failure 2 (Difference Principle Inapplicability): the difference principle — that inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged — cannot apply to biological time because biological time cannot be redistributed through the institutional mechanisms the difference principle specifies; you cannot tax years of life and transfer them through welfare institutions. Failure 3 (Primary Goods List Incompleteness): Rawls’s list of primary goods — rights, liberties, opportunities, income, wealth, and the social bases of self-respect — omits biological time because Rawls assumed it was pre-distributive; when it becomes purchasable, the omission is a structural gap the theory cannot fill from within its own resources. Failure 4 (The Authored Deprivation Problem): the Biological Zero-Day Mechanism (BZM: the process by which AI-driven reclassification of a condition from untreatable to treatable produces a discrete, institutionally authored, dated access event with a named price point — Huynh 2026d) converts biological time disadvantage from brute luck (which Rawls’s framework can …

items.title: FAIRE DÉCOUVRIR, LAISSER ATTENDR: Foucault's Biopolitics, the ARSI-Poisson Dynamic, The Empirical Obsolescence of Foucauldian Biopolitics in the Age of ARSI - Compound Poisson Jumps.
items.abstract: Foucault's biopolitics is empirically falsified by the United States record of January through June 2026. The falsification targets not his historical analysis, which stands, but the three structural premises through which biopolitics claims to describe how power over biological life operates as a general mechanism: that biopower is diffuse and capillary rather than concentrated and discrete; that it is exercised primarily through state governmentality rather than private capital enclaves; and that it operates on institutional timescales sufficient for expert knowledge to track and manage it. The US 2026 record falsifies all three simultaneously, through five documented events that admit no Foucauldian description. The ARSI-Poisson Dynamic — the Compound Poisson Jump Process through which AI recursive self-improvement (ARSI) drives instantaneous, permanent, attributed reclassification of conditions from untreatable to treatable, formalized in Huynh (2026d), "The Biological Zero-Day Mechanism" — is structurally incompatible with diffuse Foucauldian biopower. A Poisson jump is not a gradient. A reclassification event with a named author, a date, and a price point is not normalization. A private company determining global biological research velocity through an access enclave is not state governmentality. Five falsifications are documented with US primary sources. Falsification 1 (BZM as discrete event): CMS cardiovascular coverage for semaglutide (March 2024) moved a class of deaths from biologically inevitable to economically contingent upon access — a Poisson jump with named author, date, and price structure that Foucauldian diffuse normalization cannot produce. Falsification 2 (private capital as biopower author): Anthropic's Project Glasswing (April 7, 2026) established a capability enclave governing biomedical research access for 40–50 organizations; the European Central Bank, after six weeks of negotiation, remained excluded; the state intervened with a blunt global cutoff (June 12, 2026) because no graduated governance instrument existed — the opposite of Foucauldian governmentality. Falsification 3 (ARSI exceeds governmentality bandwidth): Anthropic's "When AI Builds Itself" (June 4, 2026) discloses task-completion horizons doubling every four months; FDA standard review runs 6–12 years; the mechanism produces four to five doublings within a single regulatory cycle. Falsification 4 (knowledge-power inversion): Anthropic knows its capability curve at …

items.title: A Communication-First Account of Explanation.
items.abstract: This paper develops a formal account of causal explanation, grounded in a theory of conversational pragmatics, and inspired by the interventionist idea that explanation is about asking and answering what-if-things-had-been-different questions. We illustrate the fruitfulness of the account, relative to previous accounts, by showing that widely recognised "explanatory virtues" emerge naturally, as do subtle empirical patterns concerning the impact of norms on causal judgments. This shows the value of a "communication-first" approach to explanation: getting clear on explanation’s communicative dimension is an important prerequisite for philosophical work on explanation. The result is a simple but powerful framework for incorporating insights from the cognitive sciences into philosophical work on explanation, which will be useful for philosophers or cognitive scientists interested in explanation.

items.title: The Power and Burden of Introspective Reflection: A Developmental Theory of Adaptive Regulation.
items.abstract: This paper proposes Adaptive Regulation as a conceptual and developmental account of how reflectively integrated conscious systems maintain, lose, and recover psychological stability over time. Building on a prior account of consciousness as a continuous adaptive process, it argues that introspective reflection introduces both power and burden: individuals can interpret, revise, and regulate their own internal states, but can also become destabilised through recursive self-interpretation, identity threat, rumination, and poorly integrated emotional signals. Adaptive Regulation describes stability not as permanent happiness or emotional suppression, but as dynamic equilibrium maintained through signal interpretation, participation, agency, reflection, identity stability, and environmental reinforcement. The paper introduces internal variables as functional conditions that shape how signals are weighted and interpreted, and argues that regulatory strategies become available through development, biology, identity, support, and environment rather than instruction alone. It links emotional interpretation with participation, contribution, agency, self-worth, respect, conflict, developmental integration, and collective reinforcement. Existing practices such as therapy, medication, education, behavioural strategies, social support, and structured self-help are positioned as intersecting with these mechanisms by restoring or supporting regulatory availability under different conditions. The framework also considers how adaptive capacities may be cultivated through reflective support, receptive timing, survivable pressure, low-pressure participation, modelling responsibility, tolerance of difference, and environments that reinforce agency, repair, rest, and meaningful participation. Adaptive Regulation is offered as an interpretive synthesis rather than a clinical or diagnostic model, with limitations involving trauma, neurodivergence, medication, biological conditions, culture, poverty, coercion, structural harm, and normative misuse.

items.title: Фиософские законы бытия.
items.abstract: In this work, the author has tried to express in an extremely general and concise philosophical form the basic, fundamental laws that allow us to scientifically comprehend the evolution of the existence of the universe and the logic of its cognition. It is shown that existence is an infinite set of material objects and their relationships, which are recognized by the object-subject, or the organism-subject (human-subject, animal-subject). The object-subject is an evolutionary product of living nature, and existence as a whole combines two types of reality: Objective Reality (OR) outside the consciousness of the subject and Subjective Reality (SR) inside the consciousness of the subject. It is shown that nature acquires a local mind and the possibility of self-knowledge precisely through an object-subject, which reflects OR in its consciousness in the form of SR, the internal material carrier of which is the Knowledge Code System (KCS) in the neural network of the brain of the subject organism. The paper formulates 10 laws of being in the form of short theses. The author gave compact comments to each law based on the author's philosophical works on the development of a new trend in the world philosophy of materialism – Fundamental Materialism (FM). The purpose of this work is to bring to the broad public and philosophical consciousness in a simplified, intelligible form the main ideas of FM related to the most general conclusions of the system of natural sciences and humanities in the field of epistemology, epistemology, ontology and epistemology.

items.title: What Must Exist Before Representation?
items.abstract: Most theories of cognition begin with systems that already perceive, encode, predict, infer, or represent. This paper asks whether such approaches begin one conceptual step too late. It isolates a prior question: what minimal constraints must be satisfied for a physical organization of reality to transform its interactions with reality into stable, revisable, and predictively effective representations? The paper does not propose a complete theory of cognition, representation, or scientific knowledge. Its aim is to identify the minimal unknowns that any future theory of representation emergence must address. The proposed dependency chain runs from organization of reality to minimal constraints, interaction, representation, stability, fidelity, and theory. Existing frameworks such as Kantian conditions of experience, naturalized epistemology, enactivism, predictive processing, theories of mental representation, and structural realism are considered as neighboring approaches. The paper argues that these traditions often begin after representation, organismic coupling, prediction, or semantic content has already been introduced. By contrast, the present framework asks what must exist before representation itself becomes possible. Fidelity is treated operationally, not as resemblance to reality in itself, but as the preservation of regularities sufficient for reproducible prediction, action, or intervention. The intended contribution is modest but foundational: to formulate a research program concerning the minimal constraints under which interaction becomes representationally stabilizable.

items.title: Toward Conceptual Responsibility in Autism Discourse.
items.abstract: Autism-related concepts shape psychiatric classification, research agendas, clinical communication, policy decisions, and forms of autistic self-understanding. Yet these concepts are often adopted, contested, or revised without sustained reflection on the roles they are meant to serve across different settings. This article examines two widely discussed terms, “neurodivergent” and “profound autism,” and argues that disputes surrounding them often reflect mismatches in conceptual function rather than disagreement about descriptive accuracy alone. Building on conceptual work in philosophy of psychiatry, conceptual ethics, and interdisciplinary autism research, the article develops a four-dimensional framework for evaluating autism-related concepts in terms of internal structure, degree of intentional design, ethical orientation, and empirical grounding. Historical and comparative analysis shows that “neurodivergent” emerged from autistic-led and cross-disability activism as a minimally structured identity concept, whereas “profound autism” was introduced in clinical and administrative contexts as a more structured category tied to research visibility, service coordination, and clinical proxies. The contrast clarifies why tensions arise when concepts designed for different tasks are assessed by the same standards. Rather than proposing conceptual uniformity, the article advances conceptual responsibility as a requirement to make explicit what concepts are being asked to do, which evidential infrastructures sustain them, whose perspectives shape them, and what trade-offs their use entails.

items.title: Is Marya Schechtman’s ‘Person Life View’ A Conventionalist Account of Personal Identity?
items.abstract: This paper examines the parallels between Marya Schechtman’s (2014. Staying Alive: Personal Identity, Practical Concerns, and the Unity of a Life. Oxford: Oxford University Press) ‘Person Life View’ (PLV) and Conventionalism regarding personal identity. PLV contends that personal identity hinges on recognition by others and societal institutions, while Conventionalism argues that personhood is influenced by social conventions. Schechtman argues against Conventionalism and in favour of PLV on the grounds that changing conventions could undermine personhood. However, this paper argues that PLV is a form of Conventionalism. By analysing the roles of conventions, desires, and behaviours in both theories this paper demonstrates their fundamental similarities. In particular, PLV’s reliance on the notion of ‘acceptance into the person-space’ aligns with Conventionalism. Ultimately, this analysis suggests that Schechtman’s distinctions between her theory and Conventionalism may be artificial, showing how her criticism of Conventionalism is based on misunderstanding of the theory rather than genuine critiques.

items.title: The evolution of consciousness: olfaction first, vision later?
items.abstract: In a vision-first story, conscious vision evolved before other kinds of conscious experience. This can be contrasted with an olfaction-first story, in which conscious vision co-opted integrative mechanisms that first evolved for modeling the causes of olfactory stimuli. An olfaction-first story makes good sense of the connection between consciousness and holistic integration across temporal windows in the ∼400ms range.

items.title: Consciousness as Dimensionality Expansion: The Organism–Environment–Generativity Model of Experience.
items.abstract: This paper reframes consciousness as a dimensionality expansion event within the organism–environment relation, driven by a third structural term: generativity. Traditional biological, computational, and representational theories assume fixed experiential dimensions and therefore cannot explain the emergence of new perceptual, affective, symbolic, or reflective modes.
