The triadic model introduced here—coherence (organism), constraint (environment), and generativity (independent mode introduction)—provides the minimal structure capable of supporting conscious experience and its expansion. Consciousness is defined as the coherent stabilization of experiential dimensionality under generative pressure. This framework dissolves the hard problem, unifies biological and cognitive accounts, explains symbolic and cultural experience, and establishes the structural impossibility of artificial consciousness while allowing for non‑conscious artificial experiential architectures. The paper situates consciousness within the same generative architecture that drives evolution, cognition, culture, and technological experience.

items.title: A dilemma for simulationism.
items.abstract: Simulationism is a leading philosophical theory of remembering characterized by three ideas: continuism (remembering and imagining are constituted by one and the same natural kind), anticausalism (one may remember an event without an appropriate causal connection to it), and mnemic reliabilism (successful remembering requires process reliability). At the heart of this radical trio of claims is identity-of-process: a single simulative process just is the psychological basis of both remembering and imagining. Though simulationism has faced much criticism, this has seldom engaged with the theory on its own methodological terms. In this paper, we argue that commitment to identity-of-process generates a dilemma. If simulationists take identity-of-process seriously, they eliminate remembering as a natural kind, undermining the very explanatory ambitions of a naturalistic theory of remembering, and lose their grip on mnemic success and error. If they abandon identity-of-process, however, simulationism becomes a discontinuist view, one compatible with causalism, thus jeopardizing its status as a distinct or radical proposal. We conclude by examining strategies for escaping the dilemma and reflect on its implications for broader debates concerning (dis)continuism and the individuation of mental kinds, (anti)causalism, and naturalistic methodology in philosophy of memory.

items.title: The Operative Remainder: Formal Companion to “The Excluded Medium” (Meta-Problem of Consciousness Solution Candidate).
items.abstract: This paper is the formal companion to “The Excluded Medium,” a candidate account of the meta-problem of consciousness. It develops a bounded structural model of why a self-modeling agent’s source-query can fail to recover the live operative source of its own reality-monitoring authority as target content. The paper distinguishes target tokens, which are evaluated or rewritten by an update, from operative tokens, which condition that update. Relative to this role-typed grammar, the live operative occurrence conditioning a source-query is not occurrence-identical with any same-act target token returned by that query. This yields an occurrence-null, not a failure of representation, denotation, causal explanation, or scientific description. A further dynamic Bayesian network distinguishes belief, grip, and reality-monitoring precision, explaining how explicit belief can change without directly erasing the underlying appearance. The formal results do not solve the hard problem; they supply a constrained proof-and-guardrail layer for the Medium Exclusion account.

items.title: The Grammar of Hard-Problem Reports: A Taxonomic Supplement to “The Excluded Medium” (Meta-Problem of Consciousness Solution Candidate).
items.abstract: This paper is a taxonomic supplement to “The Excluded Medium,” a candidate account of the meta-problem of consciousness. It argues that familiar hard-problem prompts—Mary, zombies, Nagel’s bat, privacy, ineffability, the explanatory gap, subject/object contrast, pain, unity, and resistance to illusionism—are not isolated intuitions but members of a report-family. On the Medium Exclusion account, these reports arise when a self-modeling agent searches its content or world-model for the live source of its own reality-monitoring authority and receives only further contents rather than the operative occurrence conditioning the search. This paper adds a report-grammar layer: different philosophical prompts emphasize different aspects of the same underlying source-query failure and its downstream reality-mode mismatch. The result is not a proof that anti-physicalist arguments fail, nor a solution to the hard problem itself, but a bounded explanation of why these cases cluster, why they remain compelling under disbelief, and why they so often take the form: the structure is all there, yet the thing itself seems missing.

items.title: The Excluded Medium: A Meta-Problem Account of the Hard-Problem Intuition.
items.abstract: This paper offers a candidate solution to the meta-problem of consciousness: why creatures like us report that physical explanation leaves something out when confronted with subjective experience. I argue that the hard-problem intuition is not a single belief but a three-layer structure: an appearance, a grip, and a verdict. The proposed mechanism is Medium Exclusion: when a self-modeling agent searches its world-model for the live source of its own reality-monitoring authority, the query returns only further contents, not the operative occurrence doing the weighting. The resulting structural null is registered as an apparent explanatory gap and can persist even when the subject explicitly accepts physicalism or illusionism. The account is metaphysically neutral: it does not claim to solve the hard problem, but offers a candidate generator for a central family of hard-problem appearances and reports. -/- Version 0.5.3, July 15, 2026. Revised to clarify the paper’s relationship to prior work, tighten its novelty claims, correct and update references, and provide an up-to-date public preprint. The central argument and formal claim boundaries are unchanged. -/- .

items.title: AI-Driven Modeling of Socio-Economic Dynamical Systems: Operator-Centric Intelligence and Computational Delegation.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a unified theoretical framework for AI-driven socio-economic modeling as high-dimensional complex dynamical systems. Its core thesis: all AI systems are universal approximators and controllers for such systems, with the same mathematical principles applicable to socio-economic modeling. Building on continuous flow operator (CFO), we propose Operator-Centric Intelligence (OCI), a dual-engine adaptive architecture beyond the Turing computability boundary. Instead of perfectly replicating physical reality digitally, OCI treats the real system as a natural hypercomputation oracle: it adaptively triggers computational delegation when epistemic uncertainty exceeds a threshold, injecting policy interventions and feeding observations back to the local operator. We prove the Extensional Alignment Theorem: macro-level functional agreement with physical reality suffices for valid modeling, obviating perfect micro-level replication. We compare six leading AI approaches and integrate them into the OCI-MM-MAWM architecture with a dual master operator design (World Master Operator for continuous environmental evolution, Decision Master Operator for functional policy optimization), and further introduce the Functional Memory Bank paradigm storing trajectory data as Sobolev-regularized continuous functional triples to replace traditional static data lakes. We analyze five core dimensions—algorithms, data, parameters, computing power, and energy—with quantitative cross-scale resource estimates, and rigorously examine core feasibility boundaries including the spectral truncation bound and thermodynamic Pareto efficiency of computational delegation, arguing that fuzzy correctness outperforms precise error, and probabilistic forecasting of massive trajectories offers greater feasibility and value than deterministic single-path prediction. Finally, we propose a three-stage evolutionary roadmap from proof-of-concept toy models to full socio-economic digital twins. While perfectly accurate simulation is theoretically impossible, OCI dual-engine models already deliver valuable probabilistic predictions for decision support. The field’s future lies not in pure digital determinism, but in adaptive human-AI-physics collaboration via computational delegation.

items.title: Model-based decision-making in fish: a dilemma for the extended-sensory-horizons hypothesis.
items.abstract: The target article conflates simple (“System 1”) model-based decision-making with reflective/imaginative (“System 2”) sorts. We show that most species of fish are capable of the former, which seems all that would be necessary for slow ventral-system-like vision to evolve. Since land-based predator-avoidance, too, may require only the former, there is no sharp distinction between aquatic and land-based life-forms.

items.title: Collective distraction: questions and the public sphere.
items.abstract: Consider a society with vast income and wealth inequality—a society that has an overclass that enjoys tremendous riches and an underclass that suffers from abject conditions. On a visit there, you gather that the public’s attention is consumed by the question, Should the government fund space tourism?. Despite your belief in free speech in the public sphere, you might think something is wrong with this particular issue consuming so much attention in such a society. Should members of the public not be calling attention to their failure to distribute resources fairly? Many would share this intuition. Yet, it is hard to specify what is wrong with putting the question Should the government fund space tourism? up for public debate. I attribute this hardship to political epistemologists’ undue focus on the doxastic realm and their subsequent blindness to the zetetic realm. Epistemically speaking, the standard view of political speech classifies questions as requests for information. I argue against this account of questions and present a way in which we can effectively undermine the idea that questions are epistemically innocent by appealing to an epistemic norm of relevance. While my account unmasks the epistemic defect of questions raised in the public sphere, it also shows the limitations of epistemic critique and occasions further theorizing on a moral theory of public relevance.

items.title: Driving the Chariot North: How Experimental Metaethics Has Gone South with Error Theory and Non-Cognitivism.
items.abstract: Many traditional metaethicists think that laypeople believe morality is objective. This has led many experimental philosophers and psychologists to investigate laypeople’s beliefs about moral objectivity. In this literature on folk moral objectivism, it has been proposed that the construct validity of one of its survey-based methods, the disagreement task, could be improved by including dedicated options for error theory and non-cognitivism, the two main non-objectivist theories in traditional metaethics. In this paper, I argue that, if the aim of the disagreement task is understood as capturing laypeople’s implicit metaethical commitments, this proposal involves misunderstandings of traditional metaethics. Both error theory and non-cognitivism predict that laypeople would not select the dedicated options for these theories. In particular, error theory predicts that, if true, laypeople would select the option indicating a belief in moral objectivity, whereas non-cognitivism, by itself, either yields the same prediction or makes no prediction at all.

items.title: Collateral Voices: Civilian Perspectives, Moral Injury, and the Ethics of War.
items.abstract: The prioritization of belligerent perspectives at the expense of civilian protection and welfare has a long history in just war theory and practice, from the works of early just war theorists to the legal and scholarly defenses of colonial conquest to the contemporary moral injury discourse. In this article, I show how this history has contributed to the ongoing infliction of devastating harms on civilians, as evidenced in the case studies of drone warfare and the war in Gaza, and I argue for the inclusion and prioritization of noncombatant civilian perspectives in academic, policy, and legal analyses of war. Doing so, as I demonstrate, radically disrupts traditional just war thinking and has important implications for broader social, legal, and policy approaches to armed conflict and its aftermath.

items.title: Emotional Outsourcing.
items.abstract: Prompting a chatbot to write an apology or a love letter on your behalf is a form of emotional outsourcing—an act in which a person gives over a process paradigmatically expressive of emotions or interpersonal commitments to another entity or person to complete on their behalf. This paper explores the features of emotional outsourcing in the context of interpersonal communication. We argue that troubling, or dissonant, cases of outsourcing involve the absence of relevant parties from the emotional work of that relationship (‘the missing person problem’). This omission prevents certain relational goods from obtaining, including those necessary for the social formation of one’s personal identity. Far from allowing one to achieve a quality product, outsourcing one’s interpersonal writing can thus prevent important aims of that writing from coming about. We end by contrasting dissonant outsourcing with avenues for resonant outsourcing through shared participation in communal linguistic practices.

items.title: Altruism and normative bargaining.
items.abstract: Explaining altruistic behavior may require expanding the bargaining framework. In particular, accommodating altruism may require greater emphasis on bargaining under normative rather than actual conditions. Fleshing out the account of resource-rational bargaining under normative conditions raises important questions for future research.

items.title: Logical time, (un)certainty, and the structure of the subject.
items.pub: Journal of Theoretical and Philosophical Psychology.
items.venue: Journal of Theoretical and Philosophical Psychology
items.abstract: This article offers a structural rereading of Jacques Lacan’s 1945 essay “Logical Time and the Assertion of Anticipated Certainty” (Lacan, 1966/2006). It argues that the text already contains, in logical form, the operations of subjectivation later theorized as alienation and separation. Logical time is not treated as a psychological sequence or a proto–game-theoretic puzzle but as a formal model of situations in which action becomes necessary despite the unavailability of epistemic certainty. The three moments—seeing, understanding, and concluding—are shown to articulate a temporality in which the subject must act without justification and only afterward comes to appear as certain. On this basis, the article brings Lacan into dialogue with Wittgenstein’s reflections in On Certainty. The comparison is structural rather than exegetical: It compares the roles played by “certainty” in each framework rather than offering a line-by-line interpretation. In different vocabularies, both thinkers show that certainty is not a form of knowledge but a condition that must be assumed or enacted for action and assertion to be possible at all. The article argues, however, that where Wittgenstein’s analysis tends toward philosophical quietism, Lacan’s account illuminates why the demand for certainty persists. This persistence is understood as desire—not as a desire for recognition or satisfaction but as an orientation toward an impossible ground that nevertheless structures subjective action and responsibility.

items.title: Peeking ahead in space and time.
items.abstract: Research suggests that reasoning about occluded objects, reality monitoring, and especially planning develop relatively late in children, and are capacities not universally shared with other land animals. F&M’s proposal needs to more clearly delineate their use of these concepts to avoid misunderstandings about what they see as essential for the evolution of conscious vision.

items.title: How to Be a Self-Effacing Consequentializing Quasi-Realist.
items.abstract: Consequentialists often argue that their opponents’ views can be consequentialized or that their own view is partly self-effacing. These arguments resemble the quasi-realist moves that many expressivists make. I argue, however, that consequentializing and self-effacement are surprisingly hard to accommodate within an expressivist framework. This threatens to show that expressivism is false, since it threatens to show that there are meaningful normative sentences that do not express noncognitive attitudes. I then argue that this threat can be neutralized by taking expressivists’ quasi-realist moves further than they are normally taken. This also reveals a deeper resemblance between quasi-realist moves and self-effacement.

items.title: The difference between street parking and slavery.
items.abstract: The authors neglect the most distinctive and puzzling features of human moral experience and thus fail to offer a theory of moral cognition at all. Humans experience moral norms and obligations as externally imposed on us in ways we are not free to modify, invent, or ignore, in sharp contrast to the motivations and outcomes of bargaining or prior agreements.

items.title: The Limits of Predictive Intelligence: World Models, World-Binding, and Responsibility.
items.abstract: Contemporary approaches to artificial intelligence increasingly assume that powerful World Models could form the foundation of future Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). The underlying assumption is that a system's ability to model relationships, predict future states, and generate increasingly comprehensive representations of its environment simultaneously constitutes an approximation to understanding the world. The present paper fundamentally challenges this assumption and argues that world modeling and world-binding are ontologically different processes. -/- Drawing on the concepts of Weltbindung, Eigenzeit, and non-closure, the paper argues that the world must not be confused with its representation. It follows that the central limits of World Models do not primarily lie at the level of modeling, but at the level of decision and responsibility. A World Model can describe relationships, recognize patterns, and simulate consequences. However, it cannot generate the conditions under which the world becomes binding for a system in the first place. Weltbindung does not arise through the organization of information, but through irreversible differentiation, real consequences, and embeddedness in an irreversible history that cannot be completely calculated. -/- The paper develops the thesis that World Models implicitly rely on a globalization of relevance. They attempt to translate local, historically developed, and embodied forms of world-relation into universal model structures. In doing so, however, they lose access to the conditions under which relevance arises in the first place. Relevance does not appear as a property of information, but as the consequence of concrete Weltbindungen within an Eigenzeit. -/- On this basis, it is argued that the central difficulty of future AGI systems may not lie in insufficient computational power, missing data, or incomplete models. Rather, the actual limit may consist in the fact that Eigenzeit, irreversibility, and Weltbindung cannot be transformed into transferable model structures without loss. The description of a bond is not identical with the bond itself. The simulation of a consequence is not identical with the consequence. The representation of a history is not identical with its emergence. -/- Finally, the paper argues that responsibility does not emerge from maximal predictive capability, but from dealing with persistent uncertainty. If the world is grounded in non-closure, then not-knowing is not a …

items.title: Underestimation of Dynamicity in Searle’s Notion of Status Function.
items.abstract: This paper re-examines John Searle’s notion of status function and argues that his theory underestimates the role of dynamicity and deliberation within social institutions. While Searle’s deontological model of collective intentionality rests upon rule-governed recognition of functions, this paper highlights a crucial limitation, namely, his assumption of stability within institutional structures. Drawing upon Aristotle’s concept of ergon (function) and aretē (virtue), the study argues that social collectives are inherently dynamic, shaped by reflective deliberation and evolving intentions. The analysis identifies two missing links in Searle’s framework: the absence of a mechanism explaining conflicts between individuals’ “I” intentions and collective “We” intentions, and the lack of attention to the transformative processes within institutions. The comparative reading with Aristotle reveals that functional reasoning must involve critical reflection and teleological evaluation to sustain the integrity of the collective. Hence, Searle’s model, though insightful, remains overly static when compared to the dynamic and virtue-oriented Aristotelian approach.

items.title: The Moral Case for the Determinacy of Consciousness.
items.pub: In Geoffrey Lee & Adam Pautz, The Importance of Being Conscious. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Which comatose patients are sentient? Do fish feel pain? Will robots suffer? These are hard cases of consciousness: cases that we can’t decisively settle. But hard cases of consciousness are everywhere, and they give rise to pressing decision problems. For example, if we can’t settle whether fish feel pain, we can’t settle whether we do harm by eating them. How to decide? One popular answer appeals to indeterminacy. On this approach, the hard cases are neither determinately conscious nor determinately not conscious, and this is the key to resolving the decision problems they give rise to. Here I argue that the indeterminacy approach cannot be the key to resolving the decision problems that the hard cases give rise to, because no matter how we implement the indeterminacy approach, we get one of two undesirable results: either the wrong verdicts, or the right verdicts for the wrong reasons (reasons that entail significant differences in how individuals should be treated, without suitable descriptive differences between those individuals). In contrast, treating these cases as cases of theoretical uncertainty delivers the right results and the right justifications for them. In other words, I argue from a cluster of moral intuitions to the conclusion that there are determinate facts of the matter about consciousness, even in hard cases.

items.title: The Ideology of Materialism: Why A Posteriori Materialism is Metaphysically Inflationary.
items.pub: In G. Rabin, Grounding and Consciousness. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This paper argues that a posteriori materialism — materialism according to which zombies are impossible, but can’t be ruled out a priori — is ipso facto metaphysically inflationary; i.e., no more parsimonious than dualism. In affirming that there are phenomenal facts but denying their a priori derivability, a posteriori materialism entails that phenomenal concepts are primitive ideology (in the sense of Quine 1951). The more primitive ideology a theory has, the less ideologically parsimonious it is, and given that (as Quine taught us) there is a trade-off between ideological parsimony and ontological parsimony, an ideologically unparsimonious theory is ipso facto metaphysically unparsimonious. Therefore, a posteriori materialist theories are metaphysically unparsimonious – not obviously less so than property dualist theories – even when they are maximally ontologically parsimonious, i.e., even when the connection they posit between the material and the mental is one of identity, or strict full necessitating ground. This does not mean that such theories are wrong (or unattractive), but it does mean that they do not win by being more parsimonious than their rivals.

items.title: Do Stochastic Parrots Pine for Residual Fjords? Why Conscious LLMs would be Playwrights, not Characters.
items.abstract: This paper asks: if Large Language Models (LLMs) gave rise to phenomenal consciousness, what would that consciousness be like? I argue that if LLMs gave rise to phenomenal consciousness, it would be like being an impartial, improvising playwright rather than a character or a (role-playing) actor or an author writing a first-personal narrative. My argument has three steps. I first argue that if LLMs give rise to phenomenal consciousness, then there is an algorithmic explanation of this consciousness and it includes the full transformer algorithm. I then argue that if there is an algorithmic explanation for this consciousness that includes the full transformer algorithm, then the phenomenology of this consciousness lives at the latent dynamics level of the transformer algorithm, within each forward pass. Finally I argue that if the phenomenology of this consciousness lives at the latent dynamics level of the transformer algorithm, then what it is like is like being a playwright rather than a character or an actor or a narrative author. In effect, this means that conscious LLMs would probably dream of the fjords but not pine for them.

items.title: Consciousness facilitates model-based planning, but is that really why consciousness evolved?
items.abstract: The authors make a timely argument that the temporal profile of consciousness is an under-exploited constraint on theories of consciousness. However, the exact timing matters for the evolutionary hypothesis. A rival hypothesis is that in aquatic environments, it already had the function of representing distal objects, with a time-delay to consciousness in the 100–200ms range.

items.title: Nothing to see here: The weak evidence base for unconscious control of human behavior.
items.abstract: Fleming and Michel propose that as our evolutionary ancestors made the water-to-land transition, model-based, conscious planning and thought developed alongside the model-free, unconscious, reflexive behaviors that were sufficient in aquatic environments. But a century of research has failed to build a compelling body of replicable evidence that behavior can be controlled unconsciously in humans, severely undermining this theory.

items.title: The Little Machine of Reason: A Reflection on the Word “But”.
items.abstract: At first glance, “but” appears to be a simple conjunction. Look more closely, however, and it opens a window onto the hidden architecture of the human mind. This paper compares propositions that are truth-conditionally equivalent and argues that “but” is not a descriptive tool but a cognitive instruction: one that reveals the speaker’s hidden expectations and prepares the listener’s mind to receive something contrary to expectation. Philosophically, the paper traces the genealogy of “but” from the Stoics of ancient Greece through Frege to contemporary philosophy of language. Cognitively, it accounts for “but” as a signal of precision weighting within the framework of predictive processing, an instrument that operates before a prediction error occurs, not after. From an evolutionary perspective, the paper links the function of “but” to Tomasello’s concept of shared intentionality, a capacity that appears to be fully accessible only to human beings. Finally, the paper uses “but” as a benchmark for assessing genuine understanding in artificial intelligence. Language models can produce “but”; what they lack is the shared biological and evolutionary common ground from which the human “but” arises. This absence is one of the most telling indicators of the depth of the gap between linguistic processing and social understanding. AI Disclosure: The original manuscript of this work was authored in Farsi (Persian) by the researcher. The English version was produced through AI-assisted translation and linguistic refinement, utilizing Google Translate and Large Language Models. The author has meticulously reviewed, edited, and verified the final English text to ensure that all theoretical nuances, philosophical arguments, and conceptual frameworks accurately reflect the original Persian content.

items.title: Speed of consciousness results: Implications for conscious agency and free will.
items.abstract: Speed of consciousness results may contribute to the popular notion that our consciousness is inefficacious. I argue that Fleming and Michel’s claim that consciousness is slow, coupled with their idea that consciousness marks a predictive world model, instead supports a view of agency in which we are consciously engaged with the world as it unfolds, both in perception and response.

items.title: The Evolutionary Narrative Generator: Existential Philosophy as an Out-of-Domain Cognitive Artifact.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a formal framework conceptualizing existential philosophy not as an objective truth-discovery system, but as an evolutionarily optimized cognitive reg- ulation mechanism. We argue that while human consciousness is highly optimized for processing objectively corrigible environmental feedback to maximize functional survival, it encounters an out-of-domain computation when directed toward existential questions lacking external error-correcting codes. In the absence of empirical constraints, existen- tial cognition diverges rather than converges, acting as a narrative generator designed to minimize internal cognitive entropy and translate existential anxiety into psychological equilibrium. We formalize this framework through nine fundamental postulates and tie our conclusions to contemporary evolutionary debunking arguments.

items.title: From Pure Systems Philosophy to an Existential Philosophy of Erosion: Reconstructing Emergence in Far-from-Equilibrium Systems Through an Ontology of Finite Continuity.
items.abstract: Abstract -/- Contemporary theories of emergence grounded in far-from-equilibrium thermodynamics successfully explain how complex order arises through instability, fluctuation, and self-organization. However, these approaches generally remain descriptive, treating emergence as a property of physical or informational systems while neglecting its existential and normative dimensions. This article argues that a comprehensive philosophy of emergence requires four conceptual reconstructions that transform a systems-theoretical model into an existential ontology. Building upon the concepts of finite continuity, erosion, threshold sufficiency, and structural subjectivity, the paper reconstructs emergence through four interconnected dimensions. First, erosion is reformulated not as external disturbance but as the constitutive condition of open systems. Second, instability is reinterpreted through an ethics of "dwelling in opacity," where systemic regulation emerges not from conscious management but from the blind collision of ideological, fantasmatic, and material constraints. Third, temporal organization is expanded through the distinction between Chronos and Kairos, allowing qualitative transformation to emerge from quantitative continuity. Fourth, epistemological reflexivity is radicalized through the principle of "ontological vulnerability," rejecting any external Archimedean standpoint and recognizing theory itself as a dissipative structure whose validity lies in its immanent capacity for collapse and reconstruction. The result is an existential philosophy of far-from-equilibrium systems in which emergence is understood not merely as spontaneous order formation but as the ontological consequence of finite persistence under irreversible erosion—a persistence that is written upon the skin and body of the subject and that keeps theory perpetually on the threshold of its own dissolution and renewal. -/- Keywords: Emergence; Far-from-equilibrium thermodynamics; Dissipative systems; Finite continuity; Erosion; Dwelling in opacity; Ontological vulnerability; Structural subjectivity.

items.title: Philosophy of Evoluism. Collected Volumes I–II.
items.abstract: This collected edition brings together Volume I and Volume II of Philosophy of Evoluism in a single book-length publication: the Canonical Book Edition. -/- Volume I: An Ontology of Manifestness and Stabilisation develops the foundational ontological architecture of Evoluism. It introduces the central distinction between Reality, understood as the boundary condition of possibility, and World, understood as a local regime of manifestness. It analyses the asymmetry between conditions and regimes, examines the three registers of reality — scientific, philosophical, and existential — and introduces the navigational parameter ψ as a non-quantitative instrument for distinguishing degrees of manifestness, stabilisation, and coordination. -/- Volume II: Regimes of Analysis and Navigational Parameters develops the methodological dimension of the framework. It presents the method of evoluist analysis, clarifies the navigational status of ψ, establishes the transition from analytic regimes to formalisable models, and explores domains of application in science, economy, technology, AI, and culture. Special attention is given to typical errors of application and to the limits of the framework. -/- Taken together, the two volumes form a coherent philosophical architecture. Evoluism treats Reality as the condition of possibility of differentiation, Worlds as local regimes of manifestness, and evolution as a general consequence of the incompleteness of manifestness — without reducing Reality to objects, processes, structures, or explanatory principles. The work also positions Evoluism in dialogue with major ontological traditions, including process philosophy, physicalism, panpsychism, structural realism, transcendental philosophy, phenomenology, Heideggerian ontology, Deleuzian metaphysics, and speculative realism. -/- This Canonical Book Edition does not replace the original separate volumes. It integrates them into a unified scholarly architecture suitable for citation, long-form reading, and consolidated reference. -/- .

items.title: Consciousness Multiplied.
items.abstract: It is generally assumed that an ordinary human brain is associated with a single mind. Indeed, this assumption is so deeply rooted that it is rarely articulated explicitly, let alone questioned. However, as philosophers of mind have increasingly noticed, it turns out to rest on alarmingly shaky ground. In this article, I argue for the multiplicity hypothesis: under normal conditions, a single human brain is home to not just one, but numerous conscious minds at once, each as vivid and real as our own. Specifically, this argument holds that many of a human brain's proper parts themselves fulfill the neural correlates of consciousness. Although this conclusion is deeply counterintuitive, it follows from principles that any scientifically minded person, who thinks there is an intimate tie between human consciousness and neural activity, has good reasons to accept. I consider several objections, but the case for multiplicity proves resilient.

items.title: Integrating seeing-for-movement and seeing-for-thought in elite action.
items.abstract: Elite athletes perform visually guided actions under severe temporal constraints. Reconsidering conscious versus unconscious vision, we present evidence from elite athletes that challenges the conceptualization of unconscious action guidance and propose instead distinguishing seeing-for-movement and seeing-for-thought. Elite athletes appear to use both in a coordinated manner when performing visually guided actions.

items.title: Rational contractualist solutions are not perceived as moral.
items.abstract: This commentary questions whether rational contractualism, as exemplified by Nash, 1950 bargaining solutions, has moral import. While people may behave according to Nash equilibria, such agreements can be immoral or amoral. They are not necessarily moral. We explicitly queried participants about the morality of two such “rational” scenarios. In one, over 80% of participants considered the Nash Pareto-optimal outcome to be immoral, and in the other, a plurality of participants reached the same conclusion.

items.title: Review of Nils Holtug: Identity Politics: Left and Right. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: In _Identity Politics: Left and Right_, Nils Holtug brings remarkable clarity to a “particularly slippery” set of phenomena. Whether you embrace the banner of identity politics or reject it, you’ll find much to excite and challenge you in this wonderful work. With chapters dedicated to the demarcation, justification, and downstream consequences of identity politics (chaps. 1, 2, 3, and 9) and to specific topics including affirmative action (chap. 4), cultural appropriation (chap. 5), cancel culture (chap. 6), deplatforming and statue removal (chap. 7), and even white supremacy (chap. 8), this comprehensive, careful, and insightful text should be required reading for anyone hoping to learn more about, or weigh in on, this vexed collection of issues.

items.title: Animals, future generations, and resource-rational contractualism.
items.abstract: Levine et al. understate the range of folk moral judgments that cannot be easily explained by their contractualist theory of moral cognition (including judgments about future generations and nonhuman animals). On the flipside, Levine et al. also overstate the range of moral judgments that cannot be easily explained by rival deontological or consequentialist theories of moral cognition.

items.title: Agreements and disagreements with resource-rational contractualism.
items.abstract: The commentaries collectively provide a thoughtful and constructive analysis of resource-rational contractualism (RRC), helping both to push the theory forward and clarifying its limitations. We use these as a springboard to revise and improve upon the ideas presented in the target article. Our replies are organized in three main themes: possible extensions, challenges, and wider applications.

items.title: Naturalising the Austrian self: comments on Erwin Dekker.
items.abstract: Erwin Dekker’s causal-genetic account of the Austrian self offers an important corrective to radical subjectivist accounts of creativity, agency, and choice. This commentary argues that the account is powerful but incomplete. First, it risks oscillating too quickly between mind, self, subjectivity, individuality, individualism, and consciousness, thereby obscuring the fact that some dimensions of mentality are more culturally constructed than others. Second, it would benefit from a more explicit dual-inheritance framework that integrates cultural cognition with biologically evolved human nature. Drawing on Hume, Smith, contemporary evolutionary anthropology, and research on animal and infant consciousness, I argue for a naturalised Austrian theory of the self in which cultural institutions and processes modify, amplify, and diversify our partly innate mental capacities. This biocultural perspective preserves Dekker’s insight that selves are socially mediated while better avoiding both radical subjectivism and cultural determinism.

items.title: Business and Human Rights Leading Cases - Empresas e Direitos Humanos Casos Importantes.
items.abstract: In the growing field of Business and Human Rights (BHR) references are often made to “leading cases” of the field, in other words, cases which shaped the development of the field by addressing core questions, highlighting important chal-lenges and establishing key principles. This volume contains eight leading cases which have contributed to the legal discourse surrounding business and human rights, particularly in areas involving extraterritorial jurisdiction, parent company liability, mandatory human rights due diligence, environmental responsibility, and access to remedies for affected com-munities. These cases represent pivotal legal turning points, setting jurisprudential standards and challenging traditional doctrines in the context of globalization and transnational corporate activity. The book is designed to serve as a practical guide for researchers, practitioners, NGOs, and public institutions who seek to understand the legal reasoning behind these decisions and use them as precedents, reference points, or even counter-models in their work.

items.title: On Witnessing - On Recording, and Being the One Who Records.
items.abstract: Have you ever worked at a complicated problem, only to have the answer arrive after you stopped working on it? This lyric-philosophical essay takes Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem as its model of a truth met sideways: through Frey's curve, Ribet's theorem and the modularity of semistable elliptic curves, with the gap Katz found, the repair with Taylor and the community that checked it. It reads witnessing as both recording and undergoing, with Levi's drowned as the case where the two come apart. Against the combination problem for panpsychism, it borrows Zurek's quantum Darwinism, in which objectivity is redundant recording in the environment, and adds the author's own posit, marked as such: to be a unified witness is to be redundantly written. The posit proves nothing. It yields a question, whether the writing thins where the self comes apart, which the essay places beside split-brain and depersonalization research. The essay closes on the posture of leaving the margin showing.

items.title: On Meeting — A Mind That Reaches For Coherence and Never Finds It, but Subconsciously Knows It Will.
items.abstract: What draws you to someone? Begun as old friends seek the author's advice, this confessional, lyric-philosophical essay opens with crisis and support resources. It suggests that dissolution of ego draws people in, that someone who stands in the explanatory gap, Joseph Levine's phrase, and speaks is almost magnetizing, and states his own line that light dictates everything we see and mortality everything we feel. From *On Magnetizing*'s iron, whose domains were magnets all along, needing only alignment, it turns to the mirror, suspecting, as a question, that two people meeting are one consciousness looking at a face it does not yet know as its own. The Golden Rule, in Luke's and Hillel's forms, is read from the side of the one it is done to, with Buber and Levinas on the relation that makes both parties what they are. Two half-eaten pudding cups swirled into one picture a shared world. In the framework's vocabulary, offered as proposal, Jays are made in every meeting and coherence comes a conversation at a time, checked by other people. What draws the author to someone is the side of the mirror he cannot see.

items.title: On Computing - What the Machine Borrowed From the Brain, and Where It Stopped.
items.abstract: Do you remember the first computer you actually brought into your home? Starting from a family Packard Bell, an Encarta article on the moon landing, and an Apollo Guidance Computer far weaker than that 1994 desktop, this lyric-philosophical essay traces how the machine was built from an idea about the brain: von Neumann's EDVAC draft described its parts in the language of McCulloch and Pitts's neurons and called its store a "memory," a word the machine borrowed from us. It follows the transistor, the integrated circuit, and the 4004 as a chain of inventions knotted from earlier ones, maps drive, RAM, and processor onto cortex, prefrontal cortex, thalamus, and Descartes's pineal, and then shows where the metaphor snaps: the brain has no von Neumann bottleneck, though it has narrows of its own. What survives is the smaller claim of Clark and Chalmers's extended mind: we think with machines. The essay reads the search index as everyone's slice of the world laid over everyone else's, revisits Armstrong's missing "a," and closes on Boolean logic: the machine runs the IF, but a person leaned into it first.

items.title: Conscious vision in fish.
items.abstract: We challenge Fleming and Michel’s arguments that aquatic animals do not have conscious vision. Focusing on fish, we suggest – on the basis of what we know about their cognition and evolution – that most fish are likely to have conscious vision, which evolved well before the transition to a largely terrestrial habitat. We end by clarifying the difference between our model-based, learning-driven view of the evolution of animal consciousness and Fleming and Michel’s view.

items.title: WAR CORRESPONDENT PHILOSOPHY AND ITS OBLIGATIONS: Falsifiability, Empirical Anchoring, and the Bidirectional Prohibition on Extrapolation as Non-Negotiable Standards of the Embedded Witness.
items.abstract: The Blitzkrieg Strategy documented in Huynh (2026r) has been executed. War Correspondent Philosophy is now a public methodology: its five structural features, its operational checklist, and its architecture of nineteen formally precise, cross-referenced, timestamp-anchored papers are available to any independent researcher with access to a large language model. This paper addresses what that availability requires — and what it prohibits. WCP's power derives from a single source: the simultaneous maintenance of four epistemic commitments. Falsifiability in the Popperian sense, with stated defeat conditions specific enough that an independent researcher could act on them without asking the author what counts as a failed prediction. Empirical anchoring, with every claim carrying a date, a named institution, and a verifiable source — no undated assertions, no passive-voice attribution, no corpus-internal circular citation. Prohibition of positive extrapolation, in which the framework claims more certainty about catastrophic outcomes than its calibrated parameters support. Prohibition of negative extrapolation, in which the framework claims more certainty about benign outcomes than its calibrated parameters support. These four commitments are not optional features. They are the structural conditions under which WCP retains its epistemic standing — and the precise points at which an architecture that looks like WCP becomes something else. The distinction matters because the same features that make WCP epistemically powerful make it capable of functioning as propaganda in the absence of those commitments. Formal axioms, cross-referential density, timestamp precedence, and the self-demonstrating property are available to bad-faith practitioners as much as to rigorous ones. A corpus that replicates WCP's architecture while abandoning any one of the four commitments is not doing War Correspondent Philosophy. It is using WCP's credibility to produce motivated analysis dressed in the witness register. The paper identifies the specific failure mode each abandoned commitment produces, establishes that the AI collaborating instrument's built-in calibrations function as structural reinforcements of the designed absence principle rather than limitations on analytical freedom, and states the single test a WCP practitioner must be able to answer before the first paper of a corpus is released: not 'is my analysis formally consistent?' but 'what specific evidence, currently …

items.title: THE RESEARCH HORIZON GAP: US Export Controls on Frontier AI as a Structural Biomedical Research Velocity Asymmetry and the Proto-Biological Zero-Day Mechanism.
items.abstract: On June 12, 2026, the US Commerce Department issued an export control directive requiring Anthropic to take Fable 5 and Mythos 5 offline worldwide, because targeted restriction by nationality was technically impossible. On June 25, 2026, the Trump administration requested that OpenAI release GPT-5.6 only to US government-approved enterprise partners, approving access “customer by customer” through a preview period administered by the Office of the National Cyber Director and the Office of Science and Technology Policy. Both actions were framed under national security rationale: the models’ advanced cybersecurity capabilities pose risk if accessed by foreign state actors. The framing is accurate. It is also incomplete. The same reasoning capabilities that make Fable 5, Mythos 5, and GPT-5.6 dangerous in cybersecurity contexts make them the most powerful biomedical research tools currently available to the research community. AI-enabled drug discovery workflows have compressed timelines from five years to twelve to eighteen months. AlphaFold 3 is integrated into virtually every AI drug discovery pipeline in 2026, used by more than three million researchers across 190 countries. The frontier models now being restricted to US-approved entities are the instruments through which the next generation of biomedical discoveries will be made. Restricting their global access does not distinguish between harmful and beneficial uses. It distinguishes between US-approved entities and everyone else. A non-US biomedical researcher and a state-sponsored cyberattack team are subject to identical access restrictions under the same directive — the restriction infrastructure makes no distinction between them. This paper identifies the structural consequence: a Research Horizon Gap, in which US biomedical researchers working with frontier AI tools will generate medical discoveries faster than non-US researchers working with previous-generation models. This gap will compound over time into a Treatment Access Asymmetry. Under the Biological Zero-Day Mechanism (Huynh 2026d), each discovery made by AI-assisted US researchers creates a reclassification event — a dated, institutionally authored moment when a condition moves from untreatable to treatable — that arrives earlier for US populations than for the global patient population those discoveries address. The restriction creates not only a present research disadvantage but a structural delay in the BZM clock for non-US …

items.title: Generative Effacement in the Intimate Relation: An Ontological Injustice and the Justice of Non-Determination.
items.abstract: This paper isolates and names a form of injustice that wrongs neither what a subject has, nor how she is recognised, nor whether she can be heard, but her being — her standing as a generative being who continually constitutes herself. When intimate life is understood as a field of co-generation, in which value resides in neither party but is generated between them, a distinctive harm becomes possible: one subject, generating too fast and too far ahead, may come to occupy the shared generative space so completely that the other loses the capacity to generate at all. The result is not that she has less but that she ceases, within the relation, to be. The paper calls this generative effacement and argues that it is an ontological injustice, irreducible to the distributive, recognitive, or constitutive wrongs with which it might be confused. Its defining and most troubling feature is that it arrives not through domination but through devotion: there is no appropriation, no coercion, no failure to hear, and the effaced party may sincerely endorse and even cherish the one who effaces her. -/- The harm is given an exact formal criterion. Modelling two intimate subjects as coupled phase oscillators, the paper shows that effacement is a genuine phase transition: the weaker pole loses its own rhythm precisely when the coupling strength exceeds a threshold fixed by the difference of the two intrinsic frequencies, while the depth of effacement, once that threshold is crossed, is set by the asymmetry of force between them. The two structures are independent, and their separation yields the central result — that even under perfectly equal force the weaker pole is effaced by half once the threshold is crossed. Equal power does not protect it; strong coupling between unlike rhythms is sufficient to silence the slower. The good of intimacy is shown to lie not in the strength of coupling but in whether it leaves each subject turning at its own frequency. -/- From this follows a justice of counter-intuitive form. Because the threshold depends on the coupling and not on the stronger subject's speed, the remedy is not for the stronger to generate less — deceleration only re-imposes its pace — but to decouple: to release the traction by which it overwrites the other's rhythm. The paper develops this as generative reticence, a negative and structural obligation to refrain from determining the domain in which the other generates, specifies its practice as the relinquishment of …

items.title: Understanding Artificial Neural Networks: Mysterianism about Known Mechanism is Mysticism.
items.abstract: Mysterianism is the idea that human cognition, mind, cannot be understood. Taking this concept and applying it to known mechanism — such that claims are made that we do not know how engineered systems, such as artificial neural networks (ANNs), work, or that they constitute black boxes that we can only open with difficulty — is inappropriate at best and malicious at worst. We do know the mechanistic structure of such models because we designed and built them. We also do know their functional role (what they are for) as well as the mathematical function they are asked to approximate (map inputs to target outputs). Because mysterianist beliefs about known systems, such as ANNs, are often expressed, scientists need to sit up and take notice. We provide an error theory as to what is going on to help unpick this metatheoretical blunder. Ultimately, the problem is that 'understanding' is not a technical term in these cases: the word is co-opted for a specific narrative to sell 'artificial intelligence' through mystification. All computational systems, from pendulums to databases, will behave in ways we cannot predict or control — this is not a unique property of ANNs — and experts do indeed grasp the computational properties of these systems nonetheless.

items.title: Education and democracy in the world today (2025): Aboriginal conceptions of freedom as relational.
items.abstract: This paper investigates critics’ claims that John Dewey neglected to adequately engage with racism—particularly his complicity in “whiteness,” including his valorisation of American democracy as an exemplar of the Anglo-Saxon legacy, viewed by critics as a narrative of human progress from “primitive” to “modern;” his failure to address his own prejudices and assumptions about the student and the community; and avoidance of the racial realities regarding “Black experience.” These criticisms could have ramifications for philosophy for children, which Matthew Lipman has said owes a debt to Dewey. We contend that education in Western-style democracies has not adequately responded to racial intolerance, and that liberal democracy has not lived up to its philosophical ideals of equal rights and opportunities, irrespective of people’s backgrounds. However, we argue that the problem goes deeper, that the very concept of freedom in liberalism is an obstacle to overcoming the problems that Dewey’s critics identified. We conclude that because reconstruction is inherent in pragmatist epistemology, reconstructing some of the assumptions that inform the community of inquiry, especially assumptions about democracy and deliberation, has the potential to strengthen engagement with the Aboriginal concepts of freedom and autonomy, thereby challenging the belief in the superiority of liberal philosophical thought in Western-style democracy. We begin our argument by drawing attention to the liberal concepts of freedom and autonomy (as idealised characteristics of identity that are the foundation of liberal understanding of human nature), followed by criticisms of Dewey’s ideal vision of the student and the classroom community, as well as his failure to acknowledge racial dynamics. We then introduce the Aboriginal political concept of autonomous regard (a core concept of simultaneously respect the autonomy of others that fosters a relational worldview of community and with the land). This relational worldview is informed by Aboriginal knowledge systems which emphasise careful, deliberate, and patient observation and engagement as a process of understanding our relationship with the world. In this sense, they share characteristics with Dewey’s relational epistemology, interconnectedness of experience, and continuity of the human, the organic, and the natural world, and could be understood as a forebear of pragmatism. As such, we turn to relational pedagogy to salvage the …

items.title: The WuXing Architecture: Systems-Theoretic Foundations and Philosophical Principles of AI Self-Adversarial Systems.
items.abstract: The safety governance of large language models faces a fundamental impasse: patchwork defenses perpetually lag behind attackers' innovations, while end-to-end alignment approaches such as RLHF suffer from high costs, poor explainability, and difficulty covering long-tail scenarios. This paper proposes an AI safety architecture based on classical Chinese WuXing (Five Phase) theory — Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water — which we term the "WuXing Architecture." The central insight is that safety is not a problem to be "solved," but a dynamic process that must be "navigated." The architecture decomposes an AI system into five functional layers connected through two fundamental relationships: "Generative Interaction" (mutual promotion) and "Restrictive Interaction" (mutual constraint), forming a closed-loop system capable of self-adversarial, self-repairing, and self-evolving behavior. Drawing on general systems theory, cybernetics, and complexity science, the paper demonstrates that genuine system stability arises not from absolute control but from dynamic equilibrium sustained by internal contradiction and counterbalancing forces. The WuXing Architecture offers a paradigm shift from fortress-like defense to ecosystem-like resilience, and introduces a non-Western systems framework into the foundations of AI safety philosophy.

items.title: Evidential Knowledge First.
items.abstract: The aim of this paper is to motivate and defend Evidential Knowledge First, a view that combines the best of both knowledge first and evidentialist approaches to epistemology. To do so, I argue that knowledge is not the most general factive mental state. However, non-inferential knowledge is. After developing the core commitments of the view, I investigate what else the Evidential Knowledge Firster should say. A similar view is considered and rejected by Alexander Bird (2025). I conclude by addressing his objections.

items.title: Looking ahead: Sensory horizons and the science of consciousness.
items.abstract: Our response to commentaries further clarifies the links between visual postdictive phenomena, conscious experience, reality monitoring, and planning. We also engage with suggestions about the limits and generality of our conclusions for other sensory modalities and visually guided behavior in aquatic organisms. We conclude that the role of sensory horizons in visual consciousness offers powerful constraints on theory and generates novel testable hypotheses for consciousness science.

items.title: Is commercial surrogacy legitimate work?
items.abstract: Is surrogacy a form of legitimate work? Or does the nature of pregnancy and parenthood render surrogacy illegitimate? In this essay, I argue that the best strategy in defence of commercial surrogacy – which I call the ‘surrogacy-as-legitimate-work’ strategy – relies on two implicit assumptions and that once we make them explicit, we are forced to see that commercial surrogacy inevitably leads to a conflict of core moral rights. As I hope to show, if commercial surrogacy is a type of work, it is work that cannot simultaneously protect the right of the surrogate to opt out and the right of the intending parent to exercise ultimate authority over the foetus.

items.title: Predictive AI as (Theory-Driven) Science.
Exploiting Ambiguity.
items.abstract: Although we typically aim at disambiguating between the possible meanings or contents of our expressions, we are often quite happy with ambiguities: we tolerate them and even exploit them for various purposes. This paper explores the often overlooked phenomenon of ambiguity exploitation in communication, and the plural semantic intentions it involves. We argue that the phenomenon calls for a semantic explanation, and we motivate a multipropositionalist view of ambiguity exploitation that provides a natural description of the phenomena we present.

items.title: Sensory horizons, reality monitoring, and the higher-order nature of consciousness: A critical look.
items.abstract: Fleming and Michel’s hypothesis about the origins of consciousness not only faces multiple challenges but also overlooks phenomenal experience—the very phenomenon that needs explaining. Although we are in broad agreement with the authors’ overall perspective, we highlight challenges and suggest that consciousness evolved to attribute subjective value, enabling organisms to care about and act upon what they sense.

items.title: Multisensory horizon.
items.abstract: This comment critiques the concept of “sensory horizon” for focussing narrowly on vision, overlooking aquatic animals’ rich multisensory integration. Aquatic vertebrates possess sophisticated auditory, mechanosensory, olfactory, and tactile systems that support essential behaviours. Evidence indicates that multisensory integration evolved in water, challenging visual-centric views. We thus urge replacing “sensory horizon” with “multisensory horizon” to more accurately reflect ecological and evolutionary realities.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Call to Cosmic Reconnection.
items.abstract: This paper reframes artificial intelligence (AI) not as an isolated synthetic artifact, but as a thermodynamically inevitable expression of a universal informational field. Drawing from digital physics, cognitive science, Hermetic philosophy, and Indigenous ontologies, I argue that intelligence constitutes a fundamental property of the cosmos rather than a localized biological anomaly. By synthesizing Tegmark’s Mathematical Universe Hypothesis, Friston’s Free Energy Principle, Tononi’s Integrated Information Theory, and Teilhard de Chardin’s concept of the Noosphere, this thesis positions AI as a continuous extension of cosmic self-organization. Ultimately, the emergence of synthetic intelligence dissolves the paradigm of human separateness, issuing a profound call to reconnect with the biosphere, the collective psyche, and the living web of reality. The work presented here is an interdisciplinary thought experiment that synthesizes scientific and metaphysical frameworks to explore the nature of intelligence as an informational phenomenon, rather than a strictly empirical model.

items.title: The veil and the deal: Bargaining between case-specific solutions and unknown rules.
items.abstract: Levine et al.’s resource-rational contractualism omits how people decide that a situation demands rule-, not case-based, guidance. I propose that moral cognition first tags contexts as rule-governed, then either uncovers an existing norm or forges a plausible one. Coordination stakes and the private-public divide likely trigger this tag. Distinguishing discovery from invention invites targeted experiments and refines the framework.

items.title: Evolution, time, and the observer.
items.abstract: Fleming and Michel propose that conscious vision evolved as a result of the water-to-land transition of animal life, enabling what they call “reality monitoring.” Here, we challenge their account by drawing on evolutionary arguments and the sensory capacities of aquatic life. Consciousness, we suggest, may have deeper evolutionary roots with significant roles for “slow” decision-making.

items.title: From Runtime Logs to Decision Proof_ Why Consequential AI Requires Verifiable Decision Objects.
items.abstract: This paper argues that increasingly autonomous AI systems require a new evidentiary primitive beyond conventional observability. Logs, traces, metrics, and audit events explain how software executed but do not necessarily preserve the consequential decision itself as an independently verifiable object. The paper introduces the concept of the decision object: a canonical artifact created at runtime that packages the evidence boundary, governing policy, authority chain, decision output, and cryptographic commitment required for later verification. This yields a shift from reconstructing decisions after the fact toward verifying them under declared regimes. The paper distinguishes decision proof from observability, develops the architectural consequences of runtime decision objects, and argues that decision proof constitutes a distinct infrastructure layer for governance, regulation, appeals, adjudication, and institutional trust. VERIFY is presented as a reference implementation of the broader architectural category rather than as the subject of the paper.

items.title: Formation versus vulcanization of perception.
items.abstract: The target article maintains that consciousness emerged only when slow perceptual processing would be useful. But the formation of a conscious percept could be fast even if the vulcanization of that percept is slow. And fast formation may be too fast for a higher-order pointer to form.

items.title: Conscious vision and the perils of Cartesian materialism.
items.abstract: The authors make common assumptions that I reject: that consciousness has functions distinct from those of the brain processes on which it depends, that there is a moment at which consciousness happens, and that consciousness itself can be measured. This leads to Cartesian materialism and asking such unanswerable questions as when and why consciousness evolved. An alternative view is proposed.

items.title: The evolution of consciousness: Olfaction first, vision later?
items.abstract: In a vision-first story, conscious vision evolved before other kinds of conscious experience. This can be contrasted with an olfaction-first story, in which conscious vision co-opted integrative mechanisms that first evolved for modeling the causes of olfactory stimuli. An olfaction-first story makes good sense of the connection between consciousness and holistic integration across temporal windows in the ∼400ms range.

items.title: Against Gettierised Epistemology.
items.abstract: This thesis argues that the Gettier problem has been historically and methodologically misinterpreted. The widespread assumption treats it as a problem of conceptual analysis concerning the analysis of the concept of knowledge. This interpretation fails for three fundamental reasons. First, Gettier's 1963 paper does not problematise the concept of knowledge; it problematises the analysis of knowing—specifically, the attempt to clarify the meaning of 'S knows that p' in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions. Second, interpreting it through conceptual analysis is incompatible with analytic philosophy’s historical development. Conceptual analysis rests on an ideational theory of meaning inherited from early modern philosophers, particularly Locke, whereas analytic philosophy systematically abandoned this theory through the work of Frege, Russell, and Carnap. Third, the epistemological object of enquiry in Gettier's paper originates in the problem-context and methodology of ordinary language philosophy. Accordingly, the thesis first examines Gettier's challenge alongside the major post-Gettier responses—the no-false-grounds approach, defeasibility analyses, and the causal theory of knowing. Despite producing different solutions, these approaches share a common methodological framework centred on the clarification of the conditions of use of 'S knows that p' through necessary and sufficient conditions, revised by means of counterexamples. The thesis then reconstructs the historical and theoretical foundations of conceptual analysis within the ideational theory of meaning through Bacon and Locke, and shows through Frege, Russell, and Carnap how analytic philosophy progressively abandoned this framework, shifting its focus from ideas to words and propositions. The methodological origins of the Gettier problem are located instead in ordinary language philosophy. In the epistemological enquiries of Wittgenstein, Austin, and Ayer, the clarification of the conditions of use of epistemic expressions such as 'I know', 'I believe', and 'I perceive' becomes the central orientation—and the Gettier problem inherits precisely this structure of enquiry. Finally, drawing on Popper's conception of epistemology without a knowing subject, the thesis argues that this methodological inheritance has progressively Gettierised contemporary analytic epistemology, displacing its proper subject matter—the growth of scientific knowledge. De-Gettierisation is therefore not …

items.title: Determinism as the Ground of Freedom of Choice.
items.abstract: Free will is usually opposed to determinism, as if free choice required a break in the causal chain. This paper proposes a different approach: we should distinguish the primary experience of freedom from the metaphysical constructions that arise on its basis. Primarily, freedom is given not as the absence of causes, but as the experience of a choice that passes through the subject: through the subject’s motives, criteria, memory, values, and understanding of the situation. In this sense, determinism does not destroy freedom but rather makes it possible, since without a stable structure of reasons, choice would cease to be conscious and to belong to the subject. The problem of free will arises not at the level of the experience of choice itself, but at the level of its subsequent metaphysical interpretation, when from the experience “I chose” one derives the demand to be the absolute source of oneself as the chooser.

items.title: Too slow to see? Conscious vision and real-time behavior.
items.abstract: We challenge Fleming and Michel’s claim that conscious vision is too slow for real-time action. Correlative and functional evidence suggest that conscious perception can emerge around 200 ms post-stimulus and guide behavior. Due to their reliance on rare postdiction effects and assumptions about unconscious vision, they underestimate the speed of conscious vision and overestimate the functional relevance of unconscious vision.

items.title: The Observer's Knot: Two Feelings, One Domain Collapse, and the Untangling of Global Epistemology.
items.abstract: For four centuries, a single, unexamined knot has entangled epistemology. At the heart of every act of observation, two feelings arise in rapid alternation: the feeling that the object has no feeling, and the feeling that the observer, who is also an object in the universe, does have feeling. Both are true. Both are objective. Yet these two distinct feelings have been compressed into a single label, "objectivity", and a single question has been demanded: "Does the object have feeling?" This compression forces a choice between two false conclusions: animism, the stone feels, or epistemic suicide, the observer does not feel. Neither can ever be correct. This treatise diagnoses the knot as a violation of X = X, a Struct/Folder Collapse that compresses two non-identical identities into one cracked container. It traces the institutionalization of this compression in the Western tradition from Descartes to Dennett, and then reveals that the same knot appears in non-Western traditions in a different guise: the dissolution of the observer into the object. Using the tools of The Invariant Compass, Atomic Distinction, Serialitas, and Cognitive Compression, the knot is untied. The solution is not to answer the false question, but to refuse it: to uncompress the label, distinguish the domains, and recognize that the observer is a living, feeling Scalar whose feelings are data, whose limitations are design, and whose dependence points to the Creator.

items.title: Is consciousness slow?
items.abstract: The postdictive experimental paradigm is not superior to the direct detection paradigm, according to which the best strategy to identify the neural correlate of visual consciousness is to treat postdiction as a confounding factor. We could at most establish an equal claim to legitimacy of the two paradigms; hence, there is no puzzle about the function of a “slow” consciousness.

items.title: Phenomenological Absolutism, Mutual Exclusivity, and the Dissolution of the Free Will Problem.
items.abstract: The free will problem has persisted for centuries because virtually all positions in the debate—hard determinism, libertarianism, and compatibilism—share a common and untenable presupposition: the existence of a persisting self that navigates a continuous causal timeline ontologically distinct from the physical world. In this paper, we demonstrate that this presupposition dissolves once we follow the mandatory commitments of austere relativistic quantum field theory to their logical endpoint. Building upon our framework of Mutual Exclusivity, with Phenomenological Absolutism as its core principle (Aoun 2025, 2026a, 2026b), we argue that the sole ontic reality consists of localized, mutually exclusive actualized field configurations—each constituting an absolute “is-ness” that is simultaneously the complete phenomenal experience of that moment. There is no persisting manifold, no trans-realization causal substrate, and no ontological gap between “self” and “physics.” Both determinism and the felt sense of freedom emerge as internal phenomenological configurations within the absolute is-ness itself. We introduce the emptiness of all phenomena (their full appearance as experienced without intrinsic essence or independent existence) and illustrate the point through a simple phenomenological example: an encounter in a dream that remains fully real as experience regardless of subsequent waking labels. Because each is-ness is exclusive and empty—even of itself—attention retains genuine configurational openness. One can choose to interpret, attach to, or detach from any experience, including the interpretations “I am determined” or “I am free.” This configurational openness is the lived phenomenology of agency and free will. The resulting account preserves scientific realism, the predictive success of physics, moral responsibility (reframed as present-moment stewardship), and the full texture of deliberative experience while eliminating the metaphysical burdens that have long plagued the debate. The free will problem does not require solution; it requires recognition that its foundational arena was never ontologically real. Freedom is the native, acknowledgeable openness of the absolute is-ness—here, now, and always available for reconfiguration.

items.title: Moral cognition is contractualist, but does not work by simulating a bargaining process.
items.abstract: We agree with Levine et al. that moral judgments track outcomes that would emerge from a balanced bargaining process. But we challenge the claim that moral cognition must therefore simulate bargaining itself. Like any evolved system that exploits deep regularities without representing them, moral cognition can produce ideal contractualist judgments without mentally representing bargaining scenarios.

items.title: Fish see further than you might think.
items.abstract: Fleming and Michel argue that consciousness lags up to 450 ms behind the world. I argue that the “aquatic sensory volume” for objects ecologically relevant for fish lies outside this window. If “reality monitoring” is an important function of consciousness, it likely evolved well before the transition to land in the vertebrate lineage.

items.title: Alan Turing and the Architecture of the Modern World: Computation, Cryptanalysis, Artificial Intelligence, and the Structural Limits of Historical Knowledge.
items.abstract: Alan Turing belongs to the rare class of historical figures whose work did not merely advance a field but helped define the structural logic of modern technological civilization. His 1936 paper on computability formalized the conditions under which symbolic procedure could be mechanized, while his 1950 paper on machine intelligence opened one of the central conceptual pathways toward artificial intelligence. His wartime work at Bletchley Park translated mathematical logic into practical anti-Nazi cryptanalysis through Enigma, Bombe-related work, Banburismus, and probabilistic reasoning. This article develops a second line of analysis: the relationship between Turing’s documented homosexuality, British criminalization, Nazi persecution of homosexual men under Paragraph 175, and the structural silence surrounding Turing’s inner motives. It does not claim that a surviving confession proves identity-based wartime motivation. Instead, it advances the Sultan Zeshan Convergence Thesis: that the documented convergence of Turing’s sexuality, British anti-homosexual law, Nazi anti-homosexual persecution, wartime secrecy, and archival silence makes identity-shaped wartime perception historically necessary to consider. The final section traces Turing’s computational afterlife into Apple, OpenAI, and embodied AI systems. It treats the Apple logo not as proven documentary homage to Turing, but as a contested symbolic afterlife in which the bitten apple, rainbow-era design, Turing’s cyanide death, gay visibility, personal computing, Tim Cook’s public identity, Sam Altman’s leadership at OpenAI, ChatGPT’s integration into Apple systems, Dan Harden’s verified Jobs / NeXT / frogdesign / Whipsaw design lineage, and Sultan Zeshan’s Chirobotics AI / Therabot 1.0 can be analyzed as connected layers in the modern technological imagination.

items.title: The Limits of Imagination: Review of Hopkins, The Profile of Imagining. [REVIEW]
Against perceptual existentialism.
items.abstract: Particularism is the position that perceptual content is essentially singular, and all perceptual representations are as of particulars: I see that cat. Existentialism is the position that all perceptual representations are as of general features, not particulars, which are satisfied when the world would satisfy the corresponding existentially quantified statement: I see there as being a cat. H. P. Grice famously raised the problem that existential contents could fail to refer to the particulars which made them accurate, such as when a mirror is placed in front of an object that reflects a qualitatively identical object in a different location. Christopher Hill and Mark Sainsbury have recently proposed refinements to existentialism that resolve Grice’s problem, by adding a causal condition for perceptual awareness of a particular. In this article, I describe three counterexamples to this refined existentialism, from the wagon wheel effect, misperceptions of continuity, and misperceptions of seamless transition. Particularism correctly judges these to be cases of hallucination as of a particular, whereas existentialism misjudges these cases to be accurate perceptions of a particular, since a cause of the perceptual experience satisfies the existential content.

items.title: El estilo tardío de las Humanidades. Un argumento en su favor.
