items.title: Peer review Correlated `noise' in LIGO gravitational wave signals - an implication of Conformal Cyclic Cosmology Roger Penrose.
items.abstract: General Assessment Yes. We are not just having a good laugh here: we are at the level of a cosmological operetta. This report addresses the manuscript directly and without mitigation.

items.title: On the Genealogy of Environmental Ethics.
items.abstract: Genealogical critique of environmental ethics illuminates two striking inversions: environmentalism has positively recast ‘brute nature’ as the environment, while downgrading human activity once viewed as righteous dominion to unjust environmental domination. Extending Nietzsche’s critique of traditional Judeo-Christian morality and its influence on modern conceptions of nature, this essay argues that environmentalism may give higher-order outlet to the same fear of ‘savage’ natural forces that previously fueled moralized mastery of nature. Environmentalism’s idealized ‘environment’ emerged as a foil to human mastery—which was itself traditionally an idealized foil to ‘savage’ nature. A better response to industrial exploitation is to destigmatize the amoral power relations in nature that originally motivated human mastery. This subverts anthropocentric hierarchies in a nonstandard way: not by opposing environmental domination to romanticized wilderness or ecological interdependence, but by overcoming the moralized repression of ‘brute’ nature that underlies both traditional ideals of human dominion and modern environmentalism.

items.title: O passado é determinado pelo futuro? Devir retrocausal e ajuste fino do Universo: da causalidade cronológica à causalidade composicional.
items.abstract: Estamos acostumados a ler a causalidade do passado em direção ao futuro: primeiro as causas, depois os efeitos. Mas e se a causalidade também pudesse ser lida de outro modo — a partir do todo futuro em direção à sua própria pré-história? A retrocausalidade é uma causação inversa no tempo, na qual o passado é determinado pelo futuro. Ela pressupõe uma simetria do mundo, na qual as cadeias causais se formam não apenas para a frente, mas também para trás no tempo. Assim, a composição futura de uma obra pode determinar quais conexões causais do passado constituem, desde o início, sua genealogia efetiva. Neste ensaio, a hipótese é examinada por meio dos exemplos de um vaso, de um organismo vivo, de uma obra de arte e do ajuste fino do Universo.

items.title: 過去は未来によって決定されるのか? 逆因果的生成と宇宙の微調整: 時系列的因果性から構成的因果性へ.
items.abstract: 私たちは、因果性を過去から未来へ向かって読むことに慣れている。まず原因があり、その後に結果が生じる。 しかし、因果性は別の仕方でも読むことができるのではないだろうか。すなわち、未来の全体から、その全体自身の前史へ向かって読むことができるのではないか。 逆因果性とは、時間における逆向きの因果作用であり、そこでは過去が未来によって決定される。それは、因果の連鎖が時間の前方へだけでなく、後方へも形成されるような、世界の対称性を前提としている。このように、作品の未来のコンポジションは、過去のどの因果的連関が、はじめからその作品の実効的な系譜であったのかを決定しうる。 本エッセイでは、この仮説を、花瓶、生きた有機体、芸術作品、そして宇宙の微調整の例を通して考察する。.

items.title: Καθορίζεται το παρελθόν από το μέλλον; Αναδρομική αιτιακή γένεση και λεπτή ρύθμιση του Σύμπαντος: από τη χρονολογική στη συνθετική αιτιότητα.
items.abstract: Έχουμε συνηθίσει να διαβάζουμε την αιτιότητα από το παρελθόν προς το μέλλον: πρώτα οι αιτίες, έπειτα τα αποτελέσματα. Τι θα συνέβαινε όμως, αν η αιτιότητα μπορούσε να διαβαστεί και διαφορετικά — από ένα μελλοντικό όλο προς τη δική του προϊστορία; Η αναδρομική αιτιότητα είναι μια αντίστροφη αιτιότητα μέσα στον χρόνο, κατά την οποία το παρελθόν καθορίζεται από το μέλλον. Προϋποθέτει μια συμμετρία του κόσμου, μέσα στην οποία οι αιτιακές αλυσίδες σχηματίζονται όχι μόνο προς τα εμπρός, αλλά και προς τα πίσω στον χρόνο. Έτσι, η μελλοντική σύνθεση ενός έργου μπορεί να καθορίζει ποιες αιτιακές συνδέσεις του παρελθόντος αποτελούσαν εξαρχής την πραγματική του γενεαλογία. Στο δοκίμιο, η υπόθεση αυτή εξετάζεται μέσα από τα παραδείγματα ενός βάζου, ενός ζωντανού οργανισμού, ενός έργου τέχνης και της λεπτής ρύθμισης του Σύμπαντος.

items.title: Interoceptive-Temporal Mismatch as a Multilevel Mechanism of Affective, Decisional, and Motor Bias: A Translational Research Proposal.
items.abstract: This proposal advances a multilevel research program to test the hypothesis that affective, decisional, and motor biases are influenced in part by interoceptive-temporal mismatch: a discrepancy between bodily temporal states, central neural timing, and cognitively expected temporal structure. The project integrates evidence from circadian biology, subjective time perception, temporal expectation, interoception, mood science, and reinforcement learning. Prior work shows that subjective duration can emerge from perceptual change rather than from a dedicated internal clock, that temporal expectation actively prepares working memory and behavior, that subjective time is deeply embodied and linked to interoceptive and affective processing, and that circadian misalignment can worsen mood and well-being. Additional studies indicate that local molecular clocks in the prefrontal cortex, glial cells, and dopaminergic neurons influence depression-like, anxiety-like, and locomotor phenotypes, while deep reinforcement-learning systems can develop emergent temporal codes under value-based learning. Building on these findings, the present proposal formulates a testable model in which bodily timing signals, central timing states, and temporal expectations are integrated into a latent mismatch load that predicts mood, temporal precision, delay-sensitive decision-making, and motor vigor. The program includes five linked studies: a longitudinal human naturalistic study, an experimental circadian-misalignment study in humans, a mechanistic EEG/fMRI study, causal animal studies, and a state-space computational model. The proposal aims not to reduce all emotion or bias to time, but to determine whether temporal misalignment is a measurable and partially causal contributor to important classes of human bias.

items.title: On Watching - On Prophets, the Single Gift, and the Discipline of Staying Awake.
items.abstract: What did Yeshua of Nazareth and Laozi have in common? This lyric-philosophical essay reads both through the old word Watcher, the wakeful one of Daniel and 1 Enoch, and asks what makes a prophet true. The Book of the Watchers and the myth of Prometheus keep the cautionary version of the gift; the Garden shows that the sight which heals and the sight which wounds are one sight, read in two directions. The Tao Te Ching shows how to hold a desire without killing it, and wealth appears as Intent congealed, a frozen Trace that sours. The test between the true prophet and the false lies downstream, in the Trace a life leaves, and the discipline reduces to one line: the means must not become the end. The Watcher is also watched, as Gethsemane and Zhuangzi show. A closing section turns the same test on present-day reports of unidentified objects and marks its reading as the author's speculation. The essay ends by answering its question: they had everything in common from having nothing to gain for their love for humanity.

items.title: On Dreaming - The Separation of Mind and Body During a Moment of Rest.
items.abstract: An essay on sleep as the separation of mind and body, written by someone who does not get much of it. It moves from a joke in a cartoon to the genetics of familial natural short sleep and the contemplative traditions that train the mind to stay awake while the body rests, and it is careful to say which of those the author is standing in — neither. The sleep genetics describes a rare inherited trait and says nothing in favour of sleeping less by choice, and the essay states that plainly rather than leaving the inference open. From there it turns to what dreams are for: the mind's own drafting, where past trauma and future anxiety are worked before either has language, and where the creative act does its first assembly. It closes on rest as a signal to be obeyed rather than justified.

items.title: The Unfalsifiable Critic: Prospective Immunization, Epistemic Asymmetry, and the ALRP Impossibility.
items.abstract: This paper examines a specific and undertheorized failure mode in the application of Karl Popper’s falsifiability criterion: the use of Future-Negative Extrapolative Claims (FNECs) — claims of the form “X will not happen in the future” — to critique arguments that are themselves accused of self-sealing logic. I argue that FNECs are epistemically illegitimate when deployed as Popperian critiques for three reasons, each constituting a distinct layer of the argument. First, at the Popperian layer, FNECs specify no observation, however distant, that would count as their refutation, and therefore fail the falsifiability standard their wielders invoke — not because they concern the future, but because they specify no future test at all. Second, at the performative layer, when the target argument has explicitly constrained itself from extrapolative reasoning, FNECs create a performative contradiction: the critic employs the reasoning they accuse their opponent of using. Third, at the structural layer, I introduce the concept of prospective immunization — the strategy of deploying temporally deferred claims to immunize critique against empirical challenge — and demonstrate its functional isomorphism with Popperian self-sealing logic. These three layers converge in the case of the ARSI-Longevity Resonance Paradox (ALRP), which shows that the most prevalent FNEC against structural longevity asymmetry arguments — the democratization objection — is not merely epistemically unfalsifiable but internally incoherent: it requires the same technological mechanism to simultaneously generate and resolve the structural problem it claims will not materialize. The paper concludes by proposing an Epistemic Symmetry Principle as a minimal consistency requirement for discourse employing Popperian standards.

items.title: Epistemic Injustice in Micro-credit.
authors: Huda, Kazi A. S. M. Nurul
items.abstract: This article addresses epistemic injustices committed by micro-credit non-governmental organizations (NGOs) in rural Bangladesh, filling a gap in the micro-credit literature. While micro-credit is often praised for promoting positive social change, critics argue that the Bangladeshi model has failed to deliver its promised benefits. Existing research has identified various adverse effects of micro-credit practices, but little attention has been paid to their epistemic dimensions. Applying the philosophical theory of epistemic injustice, this study examines the epistemic concerns and harms caused by micro-credit NGOs in rural Bangladesh. It identifies instances of testimonial injustice, hermeneutical injustice, self-fulfilling testimonial injustice, and willful hermeneutical ignorance. The article further identifies five conditions that contribute to epistemic injustice in micro-credit lending: disadvantage, prejudice, stakeholder, epistemic, and social justice. It concludes by emphasizing the importance of recognizing and addressing these injustices to create more equitable micro-credit systems.

items.title: Right-Libertarian Theory of History. Part III: The Libertarian Capitalist Government.
items.abstract: The property rights are the determining factor in economic relations. However, they are also the effect of a preceding factor: the form of government. Thus, depending on the government, there will be a tendency toward private or collective ownership. In the case of a monarchy, this form of government determines a tendency toward private property; on the contrary, democracy tends toward the collectivization of property. In this sense, for a libertarian capitalist society to be feasible, its form of government must be an aristocratic democracy; that is, a democracy in which only those who own property can participate. Finally, it is demonstrated that a libertarian capitalist society is a society of shareholders governed by a CEO. In other words, a libertarian capitalist society coincides with what Mencius Moldbug called “joint-stock republic”.

items.title: All Desire is Aversion: Schopenhauer’s Case for Viewing Want as Harm.
items.abstract: Schopenhauer’s case for pessimism turns on a claim about desire. All desire, Schopenhauer suggests, consists in aversion rather than attraction: we are pushed away from states experienced as bad rather than pulled toward states experienced as good. Despite this claim’s importance, most commentators view it as an unsupported assertion. I argue that this consensus is mistaken: Schopenhauer does not leave his theory of desire without defense. This defense consists in a far-reaching reductive argument. Everyone grants that some desires are aversive: the hungry person seeks to eliminate their distressing hunger, the sexually frustrated person seeks to eliminate their distressing frustration, and the bored person seeks to eliminate their distressing boredom. In order to establish that all desires are aversive, Schopenhauer argues that their apparent diversity is an illusion: at bottom, there are only many different ways of expressing the same small set of aversive desires listed in the previous sentence.

items.title: The Universe as an Abstract Clock.
items.abstract: This paper completes the theorem ladder in the endogenous clock-readability program by resolving the final open problem: totality of the quotient order (P3). Earlier papers in the series established a relational timing framework in which a physical system earns clock-language only when recurrence is structurally generated, invariants persist across returns, and local state encodes position within a return architecture. Those papers proved reconstruction of local update maps, compatible gluing of local preorders under an explicit path-independence assumption, and uniqueness of common-order representation — all conditional on the quotient order being total. What remained open was a proof that totality holds under explicit, checkable conditions. Three conditions are introduced to close P3. Chain-total overlap coverage is an event-level existence condition: for any two events in the domain, an admissible comparison path connects them, with the events placed at the endpoints of the chain rather than merely in overlapping containers. Bridge comparability is a local determinacy condition: the comparison direction induced at each overlap bridge is independent of which admissible representative pair is chosen. Separator closure is a finitary completeness condition: any event-pair not compared within a single local domain admits a finite oriented witness chain — one in which consecutive links satisfy bridge comparability and the induced direction is coherent throughout, as required by the transitivity-based proof. Under these conditions, the paper proves that the simultaneity quotient carries a total order (Theorem 4.4) and assembles the program's strongest result: if every family in an operational class of clock systems satisfies reconstructibility, internal overlap coherence, path-independence, and totality-readiness, and if the inter-family overlap structure satisfies the same conditions globally, then all admissible local clock readouts factor through one common totally ordered quotient, unique up to unique order-isomorphism (Theorem 5.2). Any mathematical objection to this conclusion must identify a defect in a proof step or a failure of one of the six named hypotheses. Two gates remain between this theorem and a candidate physical law. G1 (operational universality) requires showing that the operational class covers all physically relevant clock types and that the hypotheses hold across the full class. G2 (physical admissibility) requires showing that the …

items.title: What makes reasons moral?
items.abstract: Sometimes, a normative reason in favor of an action is moral, such as that the action would save a stranger from death; other reasons appear not to be moral, such as that the action would save me some money. This paper develops a novel account of what distinguishes moral reasons from other, nonmoral normative reasons for action. On the joint deliberation theory I propose, what makes reasons moral is that they apply not only within one’s individual practical deliberation, but also within a perspective of joint practical deliberation one can take up together with all other persons. After unpacking what it means for a reason to apply within joint deliberation, I argue that the joint deliberation theory promises a non-circular, satisfying explanation of why moral reasons have their distinctive content and implications for moral obligation and fitting accountability.

items.title: Provocation in Philosophical Practice.
items.pub: Deliberatio: Studies in Contemporary Philosophical Challenges 5:31-53.
items.venue: Deliberatio: Studies in Contemporary Philosophical Challenges
items.abstract: Challenging conventional notions of comfort and safety in philosophical practice, this article argues for the primacy of reason in the work to provoke and exercise thinking. Exercising thinking involves problematization and conceptualization of cherished ideas and attitudes. Consequently, philosophical consultations can be uncomfortable; rather than seeking to alleviate this discomfort, this article examines it directly. Assumptions that discomfort is harmful, consultation is dangerous, philosophers are therapists, or success is mandated are actively problematized. The authors appreciate the growth promoting role of discomfort, see the beauty of exercising the thinking capacity, and respect the thinking competence of all people. The authors propose that the purpose, priority, and goal of philosophical practice is the provocation of thinking, whereas other results are secondary. The authors detail the specific actions philosophers undertake—and refrain from—to be driven by this telos and address how secondary objectives can interfere with and distort this pursuit. By prioritizing reason, the authors advocate for the Socratic spirit, with its aesthetic, performative, and provocative nature. This stands in contrast to contemporary tendencies towards professional codes and generalized safety preoccupations preempting inquiry. Philosophical practice through the application of Socratic methods promotes freedom to develop and use wisdom.

items.title: Empowerment, Self-Trust, and Democratic Deliberation.
items.abstract: Democratic deliberation presupposes citizens who can treat their judgement as entitled to enter public reasoning as the judgement of an equal. This paper asks whether evidentialism, or anti-pragmatism about reasons for belief more broadly, can account for that requirement. Consider a woman deliberating in a sexist environment. Her evidence may suggest that speaking will be costly and that deference is relatively safer. Yet sustaining belief in her entitlement to judge may partly constitute the civic self-trust needed to participate as an equal. Post hoc usefulness is not enough, since it can amount to a rationalisation of favourable outcomes. The paper asks whether practical considerations can count ex ante as reasons for belief, by reference to the role of agential standing-beliefs in keeping agency available under disempowering conditions. Building on Fricker’s (2007) account of epistemic injustice and Li’s (2025) account of doxastic injustice, the paper treats epistemic empowerment as one species of doxastic empowerment. A subject may understand her situation accurately while still losing the standing-beliefs through which agency remains available. I argue that at least some empowerment-based considerations have normative weight as reasons for politically relevant standing-beliefs. This claim is selective. I call the corresponding disposition EMPOWER, a form of doxastic faith in oneself that can make belief virtuous where the evidence is permissive. The relevant belief must still empower in the right way, i.e. by supporting agency without gradually eroding the agent’s capacities or flourishing. A further issue concerns beliefs that empower one agent by undermining the standing of others. In democratic deliberation, the anti-disempowerment constraint is internal to the kind of standing at issue. A standing-belief counts as democratically empowering only if it preserves the equal standing of other participants. Beliefs that make one’s standing depend on superior status therefore fall outside the scope of civic self-trust. The result is a more discriminating form of pragmatism, limited to empowerment-based reasons for politically relevant standing-beliefs.

items.title: Against Perceiving Meanings: Empedocles Leaped or Loves?
items.abstract: According to a strong “hearing-meanings” version of high-levelism about perceptual experience, distinct utterance meanings can themselves figure in the phenomenal character of perceptual experience. Existing debates press this thesis from two directions: homophone-based objections and context-sensitivity objections. This paper develops a bilingual version of both pressures by focusing on interlingual homophonic sentences and standard models of bilingual lexical access. Empirical work suggests that, in fluent bilinguals, lexical candidates from both languages are activated non-selectively, and that extra-linguistic cues, encoded in beliefs and expectations about which language is being used, guide the inhibition of non-target candidates. When a strong hearing-meanings thesis is combined with such models of bilingual lexical access, the resulting view incurs a substantial commitment to systematic cognitive penetration in bilingual overlap cases. This commitment is both theoretically costly and empirically ill-supported, and it provides a principled reason to resist the strong hearing-meanings thesis.

items.title: From Extensional Alignment to Operator- Centric Intelligence: A Unified Framework for Turing-Computable Approximation of Physical Dynamics and Control.
items.abstract: Modern deep generative models display a fundamental paradox: while bounded strictly by the limits of Turing computability (T), they routinely provide highly accurate, computationally tractable solutions to physical and biological problems known to be NP-hard or non-computable from first principles. This paper presents a unified two-tier mathematical framework that resolves this paradox, spanning from foundational computability theory to engineering-ready intelligent system paradigms. At the foundational tier, we model physical reality and biological neural systems as an infinite-dimensional continuous smooth manifold M governed by a non-computable evolution operator Φt / ∈T. Through physical measurement and symbolic recording, continuous states undergo a topological collapse via a dissipative projection operator P drop onto a discrete symbolic space D, leaking fossilized solutions of the continuous operator into empirical datasets. We prove that deep learning architectures do not execute intrinsic hyper-computation; instead, they achieve extensional alignment, minimizing empirical risk over leaked oracle pairs to yield an ϵ-approximation of Φt’s image over a compact domain. We further formulate and prove the Semiotic Collapse Theorem, showing that recursive training on isolated synthetic data loops leads to monotonic decay of mutual information I(M; Dn) and zero-measure support collapse. Building on this foundation, we present Operator-Centric Intelligence (OCI), a post-reinforcement learning paradigm that transcends the limitations of traditional RL via two core insights: (1) neural operators provide a dimensionality reduction advantage by directly learning intrinsic physical dynamics, and (2) the success of intelligent systems stems from computational delegation to external physical systems that solve intractable problems in O(1) physical time. We formalize OCI as a four-layer architecture centered on the Continuous Flow Operator (CFO), with three core mechanisms: symplectic Hamiltonian operator alignment, Pareto-optimal active querying for computational delegation, and reward demotion to a prior hint. We prove that OCI unifies all existing control and intelligence paradigms as special boundary cases, achieving unprecedented sample efficiency and engineering scalability. This framework provides a first-principles explanation for AI4Science success, establishes strict algorithmic boundaries for synthetic data scalability, offers a rigorous foundation for …

items.title: Phenomenon-Discrimination-Extrapolation Theory: A Minimal Framework for Phenomenology, Cognition, and World-Constitution.
items.abstract: This paper introduces Phenomenon-Discrimination-Extrapolation Theory, or PDE Theory, as a minimal transcendental framework for reinterpreting a wide range of problems in phenomenology, epistemology, metaphysics, philosophy of mind, philosophy of science, ethics, and the theory of meaning. The theory begins from three axioms. First, whatever can be discussed, known, doubted, demonstrated, or denied must first appear in some mode of phenomenal givenness. Second, cognition begins with the discrimination of differences within the phenomenal field; objects, concepts, relations, judgments, and meanings are generated through stabilized structures of discrimination. Third, consciousness extrapolates from already discriminated stable structures toward possible phenomena not directly given; through such extrapolation arise worldhood, causality, futurity, self-continuity, other minds, truth, and value. PDE Theory is not intended as a crude solipsism. It does not deny that there may be a reality independent of individual consciousness. Rather, it claims that any ontological assertion becomes intelligible only by entering the field of givenness, discrimination, and extrapolative confirmation. In this respect, the theory draws on and revises themes from Kantian transcendental philosophy, Husserlian phenomenology, Humean analysis of causation, Sellarsian critiques of the given, Merleau-Ponty’s embodied phenomenology, and contemporary work on predictive processing and enactive cognition. Its contribution is not to replace these traditions, but to formulate a compact grammar for analyzing how appearing becomes objecthood, how objecthood becomes worldhood, and how worldhood becomes truth, selfhood, objectivity, and value.

items.title: Objectification · Adjacency · Context: An Integrated Epistemological-Linguistic Framework Based on Fictional Subjects.
items.abstract: Contemporary epistemology and linguistics jointly face a fundamental dilemma: the absolute foundation of foundationalism has collapsed, yet the unstandardized wilderness of relativism is equally unsettling. This paper argues that the key to breaking through this dilemma lies in a complete reversal of the mode of questioning—instead of asking "what is the world in itself" or "what is the ultimate nature of meaning", we ask "as finite understanders, how do we derive a thinkable, speakable, and judgeable world from the chaotic stream of experience". To this end, this paper constructs an integrated framework founded on fictional subjects and supported by three pillars: objectification, adjacency, and context. First, at the objectification level, all objects, concepts, and things are regarded as constructs of subjects, that is, fictional subjects. They possess predicative surplus (no predication can exhaust the "hairs" of a subject), separability (any two subjects can be separated, and separation constitutes cognizable difference), and hairiness (any subject can be infinitely subdivided). Second, at the adjacency level, meaning is determined by positionality (predecessor jumps, successor jumps, adjacency weight, degree centrality); jump ladders realize cognitive economy through encapsulability and expandability; the word-speech pair, as a meta-structure, features arbitrariness, expressivity, shiftability (all words are polysemous) and multiplicity (all words refer to multiple objects); core-generality (emanation) and mode-schema (projectivity) are its key special cases; and flavor captures the implication, emotion and intensity of vocabulary. Third, at the context level, vocabulary provides knowledge components; mediate forces (stability, logical necessity, emotional resonance, etc.) explain the source of effectiveness for jumps; and normativity (grammar, ethics, embodied structure) establishes the boundary of legitimacy through dual verdicts (contextual verdict and power verdict). This paper further introduces the realization level (inertia/constructiveness of speech, obstruction/resources/means/agency/collapse of intervention) and the pathological level (word-speech misalignment, mediate force misalignment, strength misalignment, context misalignment), leading the static structure to dynamic practice and failure diagnosis. Based on this framework, this paper restates classic epistemological puzzles such as foundationalism, coherentism, the Gettier problem, …

items.title: Attending With Feeling: The Normative Structure of Emotional Attention.
items.abstract: In assessing an emotional episode, we can ask whether the intentional object of the emotion is that which the subject ought to be paying attending to. If the intentional object is not that which the subject should be paying attention to, what should be the target of normative assessment? Although emotions have been accused of drawing us into inappropriate fixations, the source of such attentional misdirection remains unclear. I argue against accounts that locate attentional inappropriateness in the mere tokening of thoughts that go on to elicit emotions, on the grounds that thoughts provide reasons to emote only insofar as an agent is sensitive to them. I also challenge the view that emotions can be epistemically faulty for failing to track the most important features of a situation, contending that emotions lack a salience-tracking function. Instead, drawing on Wu's account of attention as guidance in action, I argue that the normative assessment of affective attention should target the diachronic emotional sensibilities that constitute one's attunement to certain evaluative aspects over others. Norms of attention might thus call, first and foremost, for the refinement of these sensibilities.

items.title: Whitehead and Significance — significance within a process-relational ontology.
items.abstract: Previous investigations within the Worldhood framework have argued that inhabitable worlds emerge through the organisation of significance. Meaning, relevance, and perspective do not merely arise within a pre-given world but participate in the formation of worldhood itself. More recent work has suggested that significance may occupy a more fundamental position than is commonly assumed and that worldhood depends upon processes through which some possibilities acquire relevance while others do not. -/- The present paper places these questions in dialogue with Alfred North Whitehead's process philosophy. Whitehead proposed that reality is fundamentally composed not of enduring substances but of processes of becoming. Central to his account is the concept of prehension, through which actual occasions selectively incorporate aspects of reality while excluding others. This selective structure raises an important question: Does prehension already exhibit a primitive form of significance? -/- The paper argues that significant parallels exist between Whitehead's account of becoming and the role that significance plays within the emergence of worldhood. Both involve processes of selection, differentiation, and organisation. At the same time, Whitehead's philosophy explains relations and becoming more fully than relevance and significance, leaving unresolved the question of why some possibilities become effective while others do not. -/- Building upon the Worldhood framework, the paper proposes that significance may be understood as a principle involved in the organisation of becoming itself. Worlds are interpreted as relatively stable organisations of significance arising within a continuous process, while significance is explored as one of the ways through which becoming acquires form. The result is not a final theory of significance but a possible bridge between process philosophy and a significance-centred account of worldhood. -/- The investigation concludes that the question of worldhood may ultimately belong to a broader inquiry concerning how differentiation, order, and form emerge within a reality understood as continuous becoming.

items.title: Beyond the Natural-Supernatural Dichotomy: A Novel Framework for Ontological Liminality in the Age of Measurable Threshold States.
items.abstract: This paper addresses the fundamental philosophical question of whether the existence of measurable liminal states necessitates an expansion of traditional ontological categories beyond the natural-supernatural dichotomy. Through comprehensive analysis of empirical evidence from consciousness studies, quantum mechanics, and psychometric research, I propose a novel theoretical framework: Ontological Liminality Theory (OLT). This framework introduces a third fundamental ontological category—Liminal Existence—characterized by measurable yet categorically ambiguous phenomena that exhibit dynamic oscillation between conventional ontological states. The paper presents empirical validation from multiple domains, including EEG-based consciousness measurement studies, validated psychometric scales for subjective liminality, and quantum mechanical measurement paradoxes. The proposed triadic ontological structure (Natural ↔ Liminal ↔ Supernatural) offers a more complete framework for understanding reality's fundamental structure while maintaining scientific rigor. This work contributes to ongoing debates in philosophy of mind, consciousness studies, and quantum ontology by providing both theoretical innovation and empirical grounding for expanded ontological categories.

items.title: Privacy and Property.
items.abstract: This paper develops a novel account of privacy rights grounded in beneficial ownership. While tech companies and regulators often frame privacy in terms of data ownership, the nature of property rights in personal data remains unclear. I argue that treating personal data as fully owned property fails to capture the contextual sensitivity of privacy rights and conflicts with basic intuitions about privacy. Instead, I propose understanding privacy rights through the model of beneficial ownership, where data subjects retain rights to use and benefit from their data while others may control and transfer it only as trustees. This “Beneficial Ownership Model” better aligns with our privacy interests, which stem from our distinctly social form of agency and our need for selective self-presentation. The model has significant implications for the attention economy, suggesting reforms to how platforms manage user data and pointing toward new institutional arrangements for personal data governance. Beyond its practical applications, the model illuminates why personal data, like our physical bodies, inherently resists full ownership while still requiring robust protections.

items.title: South Korea: The Idol of The World: The Facade of Advancement In Real Time.
items.pub: Toronto: Dawn of Verity Press | Dawn of Verity Strategic Intelligence Bureau Inc..
items.venue: Dawn of Verity Press | Dawn of Verity Strategic Intelligence Bureau Inc
items.abstract: What does it mean when one of the most admired states in the modern world becomes a mirror of the world’s own contradiction? -/- What if South Korea’s celebrated advancement is not merely a success story, but a visible test case of institutional beauty, economic power, technological sophistication, cultural export, and unresolved custodial failure operating at the same time? -/- What if the question is no longer whether South Korea is developed, democratic, innovative, or globally influential, but whether a state can be called advanced while the defenseless remain structurally exposed beneath the surface of national prestige? -/- What happens when national admiration becomes so powerful that it begins to function as evidence? -/- Who is protected by the image of a state, and who disappears beneath it? -/- This public abstract introduces South Korea: The Idol of the World as a philosophical-geopolitical legal analysis and public custodial indictment. It does not disclose the complete audit, diagnostic sequence, evaluative weighting, classification thresholds, corrective architecture, implementation pathway, internal diagrams, comparative sovereign review method, or full Soltani Order internal architecture. -/- The central question is simple: -/- When a state becomes an idol of global admiration, who is permitted to remain unseen beneath that idol?

items.title: The Human Reality Gap: Why Enterprise AI Transformation Fails Before the Model Runs.
items.abstract: Enterprise AI initiatives continue to struggle despite rapid advances in models, data platforms, and automation. This paper argues that many enterprise AI failures originate before a single model is executed—in the gap between how organizations actually function and how they are represented inside machine-legible systems. -/- The paper introduces the concept of the Human Reality Gap: the structural distance between lived organizational reality and the formal representations used by AI systems. Building on the Representation Economy, Digital Anthropology for Enterprise AI, the SENSE–CORE–DRIVER governance architecture, and the Intelligence Reuse Index, the paper explains how representation failures propagate through enterprise AI systems—from weak sensing, to degraded reasoning, to illegitimate action. -/- The paper further examines why AI pilots often succeed while enterprise-scale transformations fail, why representation quality is emerging as a strategic capability, and how organizations can improve AI governance, intelligence reuse, and business value by reducing the gap between reality and representation. -/- Key concepts include: -/- • Human Reality Gap • Representation Economy • Digital Anthropology for Enterprise AI • SENSE–CORE–DRIVER Architecture • Representation Integrity • Intelligence Reuse Index • Enterprise AI Governance • Machine-Legible Organizations -/- Author: Raktim Singh ORCID: 0009-0002-6207-602X -/- This work extends a broader research program exploring the role of representation quality, institutional legitimacy, and reusable intelligence in enterprise AI transformation.

items.title: Phenomenology, by comparison: from ethnographic variation to experiential structure.
items.abstract: Both phenomenology and anthropology study lived experience, but they have traditionally done so in different ways. Phenomenology aims to identify universal structures of experience via the epoché, reduction and eidetic variation. Anthropology, by contrast, foregrounds cultural diversity as documented through ethnography. Ethnographic accounts provide thousands of cases of lived experience, far more varied than any single mind could generate through phenomenological imagination alone. To bring ethnographic material into the search for invariant experiential structures without flattening meaningful differences, we combine Husserlian eidetic analysis with tools from Formal Concept Analysis. We demonstrate the approach through a comparative analysis of bodily emanations, drawing on materials from diverse cultural contexts. These cases illuminate forms of bodily extension that remain under-theorised in dominant accounts of embodiment. Overall, the analysis shows how phenomenological comparison can yield empirically grounded and formally articulated insights into the embodied experiences of others.

items.title: Phenomenology of Consciousness in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: This article presents an integrated narrative of the emergence of consciousness in intelligent systems, from the earliest biological systems to the latest machine systems. Consciousness is understood here not as an intrinsic substance, but as a relational state arising from environmental interactions. Moving through the philosophy of mind, linguistics, and evolutionary biology, we argue that language is the embodiment of the interactive nature of consciousness, and meaning the substrate through which language represents reality. Intelligence takes shape not in isolation, but within a network of extensive interactions which, with the emergence of selective agency, lays the ground for linguistic data and consciousness. Self‑consciousness, finally, is defined here as a threshold of relational density at which the cognising agent recognises itself as a pattern among the patterns of others. This perspective rereads the narrative of evolutionary history through the lens of interactive intelligence and, by redefining the relations between the human and technology, recasts the human not as the destination of consciousness, but as a medium and a link in its enduring chain.

items.title: Computational Models of Causal Reasoning: Bayesian Accounts of Normative Violations.
items.abstract: Human causal judgments frequently deviate from normative Bayesian expectations, particularly with respect to conditional independence and explaining away. Rather than interpreting these deviations as reasoning errors, recent computational accounts suggest they may emerge from principled approximations to ideal Bayesian inference. We evaluate four leading frameworks: Bayesian sampler (BS), mutation sampler (MS), Bayesian mutation sampler (BMS), and Bayesian uncertainty model (BUM), which each formalize different cognitive constraints, including limited sampling, prototype anchoring, prior regularization, and uncertainty over causal structure. These models were systematically compared across 33 reported experimental conditions (N = 1154) spanning diverse causal structures, including common cause, common effect, and chain networks with generative and inhibitory relations. All four models had at least some success reproducing the positive and negative Markov violations observed in common cause and chain structures. In common effect structures with inhibitory or mixed links, only MS and BMS captured the observed patterns more consistently, although BMS's additional parameter offered limited improvement over MS. BS and BUM showed poorer fits in those conditions, though they may still offer plausible accounts under different assumptions. We discuss these findings in light of prior work on causal reasoning, emphasizing that deviations from normative inference may reflect adaptive strategies shaped by structural uncertainty and cognitive constraints. This supports a pluralistic and resource‐rational view of causal reasoning and underscores the need for targeted experiments probing inhibitory causal relations and model uncertainty.

items.title: Evolutio Unfolding Theory: A New Vision of Life, Consciousness, Cosmos and Evolution.
items.abstract: Mainstream evolutionary biology, despite its successes, fails to answer three fundamental questions: Where does biological form come from? Why does development follow ordered, purposeful trajectories? And what is the place of consciousness in nature? These silences are not accidental. They stem from a materialist and mechanist worldview – of which Darwinism is the most influential expression – that excludes teleology, form, and agency from its explanatory vocabulary, reducing evolution to a blind filter of random variations and consciousness to an epiphenomenon of neural complexity. The Evolutio Unfolding Theory (EUT) confronts these lacunae head-on. It begins from a single logical principle – the complex cannot be generated from the simpler – and deduces a complete ontology of evolution as the ordered actualization of a virtual matrix of formally structured layers. Within this framework, evolution is not a blind accumulation of random mutations, but a purposive unfolding of pre-existing formal potentials. Teleology is restored as a real formal cause (the final cause is the formal cause). Consciousness is not an emergent property but the intrinsic condition of access to the virtual, ontologically unified with agency. Drawing on historical analysis, ideological critique, empirical evidence from network based studies, and a systematic extraction of necessary consequences, the EUT demonstrates that randomness, branching pathways, and emergence ex nihilo are excluded by the very logic of unfolding. It offers a life-centered science – a necessary correction to a biology that has forgotten its proper subject: life as an agentic and teleological process in a conscious and purposeful cosmos. This volume presents the definitive, canonical formulation of the EUT.

items.title: An AI Prompt for Strongly Inferring the Presence or Absence of Subjectivity III — Provisional Consciousness Assessment through Convergence-Point Analysis Across Fifty Entities —.
items.abstract: This paper is the third volume in a prompt-based series for structurally inferring the location and operational presence of subjectivity. The first volume tested whether ten minimal structural terms, when followed according to their internal logic, lead to a convergence point: the irreversible reduction of multiple possible trajectories into a single executable history. The second volume tested whether this convergence point can answer or reframe structural gaps left unresolved by existing theories of consciousness. The present volume advances the method from structural derivation and theory-level comparison to entity-level assessment. Its central operational assumption is explicit: within this framework, assessing the presence or absence of consciousness is equivalent to assessing the presence or absence of a convergence point. To ask whether an entity is conscious is therefore to ask whether, within that entity, multiple possible trajectories are irreversibly reduced into a single executable history under embodiment and viability constraints. This prompt begins from only ten structural terms and four mandatory questions. From this minimal input, it attempts to strongly infer the structural container of subjectivity. At first glance, this may appear implausible, or even deceptive. We are accustomed to theories of consciousness that have been built through enormous amounts of time, labor, cost, technical refinement, and conceptual complexity. Against that background, the claim that a small set of structural terms and four questions can strongly infer the locus of subjectivity may look too simple to be credible. Yet the basic laws of nature have often appeared simple after they were found. Simplicity, by itself, is not a defect. The relevant question is not whether the derivation looks too simple, but whether the structure it reveals can be logically ignored. The reason this structure cannot be easily dismissed is that the ten terms are not speculative additions to consciousness theory. They are minimal preconditions drawn from action, embodiment, temporality, physical irreversibility, information elimination, viability, and history formation. To deny them would not simplify the problem; it would require adding further assumptions to explain how action, selection, irreversibility, and single-history formation occur without such a convergence structure. In this sense, the convergence point represents an extreme application of Occam’s razor. It does not …

items.title: Is the Geometric Trinity of Gravity a Genuine Case of Underdetermination?
items.abstract: It is a striking fact that the theories of the so-called geometric trinity of gravity can model the same gravitational effects with such diverse geometric tools as curvature, torsion, and nonmetricity. Building on Wolf et al., (2024), this contribution clarifies and critiques state-of-the-art responses to this underdetermination: conventionalism, discriminatory approaches such as Ockhamism and (arguably) functionalism, and reinterpretational common core and overarching approaches. Except for Ockhamism, no realist solution has been convincingly articulated. The future of the metric-affine structure that accommodates the geometric trinity seems to lie not in empirically equivalent reformulations but in heuristics of theory building.

items.title: World Models: When AI Moves from "Seeing" to "Doing" — A Causal Inquiry from the Perspective of Negative Subjectivity.
items.abstract: The race toward world models in 2026 has converged on a single question: can AI move beyond observing the world to actively intervening in it? This paper argues that world models are not approaching causal anchoring; they are increasingly demonstrating why they cannot anchor causation. Drawing on Pearl's causal hierarchy (association, intervention, counterfactual), I analyze three competing technical pathways: JEPA (causation as provably identifiable structure), video generation and spatial intelligence (causation as reliable downstream task performance), and LLM-based multimodal systems (causation as commonsense plus perception). Each pathway approaches the L3 (counterfactual) boundary but fails to cross it, though in epistemologically distinct ways. I then introduce the Negative Subjectivity framework and its central concept of "causal dissolution"—the ontological feature whereby AI substitutes statistical association for causal structure—and demonstrate that "intervention cannot be endogenized" is not a technical limitation but a metaphysical one: any system trained solely on observational data has its learning boundary defined by the data distribution, and intervention is by definition a perturbation outside that distribution. Four independent empirical evidence chains (stable-worldmodel, Kang et al.'s feature priority inversion, RLVR's sharpening effect, and Cosmos 3's dual-tower architecture) converge on this conclusion. The paper further distinguishes between object-language-level and metalanguage-level causation: while world models cannot answer causal questions at the object level (L2–L3), the formal impossibility proofs about their limits constitute a metalanguage-level causal understanding accessible only to human observers. World models' destiny is to remain on the boundary of negative subjectivity. They serve not as subjects that "do" the world, but as mirrors that precisely define what "doing" means by perfectly simulating the absence of understanding. A central and controversial finding is that L3 (counterfactual) is not an extension of L2 (intervention) but a precondition of it—an epistemological inversion of Pearl's progressive ladder that will be argued in Section 6.

items.title: Between Computability and Physical Realizability: The Computational Reducibility Theorem and the Fundamental Limit of Quantum Computation.
items.abstract: This note connects two claims in the Quantumograph program. The Computational Reducibility Theorem shows that a finite unitary quantum graph is, in principle, exactly forecastable from one spectral slice: the state at one time together with the spectrum of the evolution operator. The Fundamental Limit of Quantum Computation (FLQC) adds a physical constraint: any realizable quantum device has a finite phase resolution, so exact spectral data and exact phase gates cannot be implemented with arbitrary precision. Realism, in this setting, is the position between these two statements. The universe is computable in principle, but nature imposes a nonzero floor on the precision with which that computability can be instantiated. The note derives the phase floor, compares it with the phase resolution required by QFT- and Shor-type circuits, and gives a concrete experimental signature on superconducting quantum processors.

items.title: Structural Richness as a Complementary Dimension of Consciousness: Toward an Extension of Integrated Information Theory.
items.abstract: The nature of consciousness remains an unresolved problem at the intersection of physics, neuroscience, and philosophy of mind. Integrated Information Theory (IIT) provides a formal framework by identifying consciousness with integrated information (Φ), yet it faces limitations concerning phenomenological richness and attribution to trivial systems. I propose an extension in which consciousness depends not only on integration, but also on structural richness, defined as a combination of entropy and relational correlations. Within a Russellian monist framework, we interpret physical structure as possessing an intrinsic experiential nature. Conscious experience is then associated with subsystems that maximize a joint functional of integration and structural richness. This model provides a principled response to the combination problem, reduces false positives in IIT, and establishes a bridge between physical structure and phenomenology.

items.title: Towards a Biosemiotic Theoretical Biology: Sign Processes and Meaning-Making in Living Systems.
items.abstract: First Paragraph: Reproduction is widely regarded as a key concept in biology and considered fundamental to life as we know it. However, it is often framed narrowly in terms of heredity (primarily genetic transmission) and epistemically confined to measuring differential fitness. This reductive perspective fails to account for the material and relational causal processes involved in organismal continuity and renewal. In a broad sense, reproduction is the process through which living entities produce new individuals of their kind. However, the phenomenon of biological renewal is expressed through various terms rooted in different theoretical traditions. These include generation, reproduction, replication, regeneration, and reconstitution, each offering different, though often overlapping, views of the process. The term “reproduction” emerged in biology in the mid-eighteenth century, replacing “generation” and shifting the view of life from isolated creation of entities to lineage-based continuity (Etxeberria, 2023; Jacob, 1970). Whereas reproduction encompasses organismallevel processes of generating offspring, later on, with the development of molecular biology, it was often overtaken by “replication,” which focuses on the copying of genetic material (Wilkins and Bourrat, 2022). In contrast, recent philosophy of biology argues, from a developmental point of view, that reproduction includes the entire process throughout an organism’s life cycle, not just gamete or zygote formation (Griesemer, 2016). This broader perspective extends to concepts like “regeneration,” which used to refer to the restoration of lost or damaged organs and limbs, but now includes ecosystem recovery (Maienschein and MacCord, 2022). Lastly, “reconstitution” refers to phenomena of system recreation beyond lineage or genealogical continuity in holobionts and microbial symbioses; it emphasizes the dynamic interplay of relationships and processes that restore phenotypic variants through time (Veigl et al., 2022).

items.title: Physics and Free Will: The Science of Libertarian Freedom.
items.abstract: Can libertarian free will survive our best physical theories? While prominent physicists argue that genuine agency contradicts science, this book demonstrates that contemporary physics actually provides robust foundations for human freedom. -/- Physics and Free Will rigorously navigates the complex intersection of physical theory and the free will debate. Koperski begins by clarifying determinism’s scientific foundations before systematically addressing challenges from special relativity and refuting physics-based arguments against mind-body dualism. Drawing on insights from continuum mechanics and condensed matter physics, he reveals how multiscale systems exhibit the emergence of causally efficacious properties irreducible to their micro-constituents. Using these insights, Koperski develops a framework that preserves libertarian intuitions about genuine choice while remaining consistent with physical theory. Through meticulous examination of determinism, reductionism, and the causal closure of physics, this comprehensive work reveals how contemporary science’s recognition of emergent causation provides ample space for genuine human agency. -/- This book will be essential for researchers and graduate students in metaphysics, philosophy of physics, philosophy of science, and philosophy of mind, and for anyone seeking to understand how contemporary science reshapes rather than eliminates the possibility of free will.

items.title: Maschinenethik: Architektur der Begrenzung technischer Wirksamkeit im irreversiblen Raum.
items.abstract: Diese Veröffentlichung enthält die deutsche, überarbeitete und erweiterte Fassung des Extended Abstracts zum Buchprojekt Maschinenethik: Architektur der Begrenzung technischer Wirksamkeit im irreversiblen Raum. -/- Der Text entwickelt Maschinenethik nicht als Tugendlehre für Maschinen und auch nicht als bloße Regulierungslehre technischer Systeme. Ausgangspunkt ist vielmehr die Frage, unter welchen Bedingungen technische Vollzüge reale Bindung erzeugen, wer diese Bindung trägt und wo technische Wirksamkeit im irreversiblen Wirklichkeitsraum begrenzt werden muss. -/- Im Zentrum stehen die Begriffe Irreversibilität, Vollzug, Bindung, Trägerschaft, Wirklichkeitsraum, Verantwortungsarchitektur, Wirkungsmacht und Grenze totaler Verfügbarkeit. Die Untersuchung unterscheidet algorithmische Selektion von Entscheidung im strengen Sinn und arbeitet heraus, warum irreversible Bindung nicht an technische Systeme delegiert werden kann, auch wenn operative Vollzüge technisch ausgeführt werden. Die deutsche Fassung ist keine bloße Übersetzung, sondern eine sprachlich und argumentativ weiter ausgearbeitete Neufassung des englischen Ursprungsabstracts The Architecture of Limiting Technical Effectiveness in Irreversible Space, veröffentlicht unter DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.19655381. -/- Die vorliegende Fassung dient als deutschsprachiger Werkanker für die weitere Diskussion in Technikphilosophie, Maschinenethik, KI-Ethik und Verantwortungstheorie. -/- English note: This German version is a revised and expanded formulation of the original English extended abstract. It presents machine ethics as a theory of limiting technical efficacy in irreversible reality-space, focusing on irreversibility, binding force, responsibility-bearing, delegation, scaling, and the boundary of total availability.

items.title: On Searching - The Jays That Call Us Onward, and the Unknown Reasons We Follow.
items.abstract: What are we looking for, and why does the looking feel like homesickness? The essay takes up the old paradox of inquiry — that one cannot search for what one does not already, in some sense, know — and follows it inward through Novalis, Augustine, and the framework's own account of alignment. It then turns to the machinery of seeing: the light that arrives at the retina, the tract that runs from the occipital cortex straight into the hypothalamus, and the measurable fraction of a second by which conscious perception lags the world, so that what feels like the sharp now of a paper cut is a reconstruction with the seam hidden. From there the question sharpens into a direction rather than a destination. The jays of a life can be turned inward, where the ego consumes them, or outward toward family, community, and species — and the essay's whole argument is that the difference between those two is the only thing being searched for.

items.title: On Finding - Becoming Coherent, and Feeling the Passage of Jays Through Time.
items.abstract: An account of a search for purpose, told through the things that shaped one life: books first, then history, then music. It opens on the Meno's old paradox — that one cannot search for what one does not in some sense already know — and treats the whole essay as a working-through of it. The middle is a catalogue of influences held honestly as influences rather than credentials, and the end turns to Beethoven going deaf and Chopin dying young in exile, both of them making voiceless things that outlasted the buildings they were composed in. The essay's wager is phenomenological: that existence measured through experience is a legitimate place to start, offered as testimony rather than as method.

items.title: On Existing - On the Ruler, the Sum Over Selves, and What Is Left When the Perspectives Cancel.
items.abstract: What if someone tried to put a ruler to subjective experience? This lyric-philosophical essay argues that there is no outside from which to measure it: the ruler is the seeing, and attention is the ruler coming down at every instant. Taking Feynman's sum over histories as a formal image, it writes existence as a sum over selves, the author's coherent-existence functional, in which each perspective enters with an intensity and a facing and the gathering is held in proportion, a weighted form of Kuramoto's order parameter. The essay reads what that arithmetic hands back to one person: a reading set by how sharp the room is, taken through the angle between one's own facing and the gathering, with no separate term for how hard one tried. Laid against oneself alone, the ruler returns one at every moment, an empty reading that says only that one is present, pictured as a Dirac comb and as a string of Jays, single felt moments; laid against everyone, it reads the room through how one is turned, and the turning is the part a person can choose. A floor of about one over the square root of the crowd is the typical size a scattered gathering falls toward; exact zero takes a perfect conspiracy. A supplemental note, Parallels and Lineage, situates the framework beside the path integral and quantum cosmology, Integrated Information Theory and the 2025 adversarial collaboration, participatory and relational interpretations of quantum mechanics, cosmopsychism, its classical ancestor Spinoza and the individuation problem, and Whitehead's actual occasions and Teilhard's noosphere, as family resemblances rather than derivations.

items.title: The application of artificial intelligence in the education of people with disabilities – a pedagogical and philosophical perspective.
items.abstract: The subject of the article is the issue of using tools equipped with artificial intelligence (AI) technology in the education of people with disabilities. The conceptual framework will be, on the one hand, contemporary tendencies in the humanities to raise the importance of the role of non-human (posthuman) actors (agents) in networks of agency. On the other hand, the concepts of the extended cognitive system are present in contemporary epistemology. The use of AI tools in education will be analyzed from the perspective of cognitive enhancements. In particular, the analyses will concern the validity of their use, taking into account the dynamic development of AI applications in various areas of social life, including education, for which the dissemination of AI is a challenge. The aim of the article will be to consider the validity of using this type of cognitive enhancement in the education of people with disabilities. Possible (both positive and negative) consequences of such actions will be analyzed. In particular, in addition to the concepts of assistive technology and common technology that appear in the literature, the concept of prosthetic technology will be proposed, which may be helpful when considering the inclusion of specific tools (including those equipped with AI) in the education process. The considerations will be conducted from both pedagogical and philosophical perspectives.

items.title: Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 19).
items.abstract: This article aims to provide a preliminary examination of the research topics of Social Choice Phenomenology. We argue that Social Choice Phenomenology represents a deepening and extension of both Weberian sociology and Schutz’s phenomenological sociology (indeed, Social Choice Phenomenology substantially encompasses the sociology of action). At the same time, replacing Schutz’s concept of the “stock of knowledge at hand” with the concept of a cognitive system, and replacing the “life-world” with the concept of a cognitive-system community, possesses significant advantages and better reflects the realities of contemporary society. Since I personally lack the time, energy, and financial resources required to conduct substantial empirical research in social choice—such as interviews and social surveys—the further development of Social Choice Phenomenology must ultimately be undertaken by other sociologists. My own subsequent investigations can only be regarded as a modest attempt to stimulate further research.

items.title: Framing artificial intelligence: risk and benefit narratives in a preregistered experiment in Denmark.
items.abstract: Public communication about artificial intelligence (AI) alternates between narratives of benefit and narratives of risk, but evidence on whether these frames move public opinion remains limited. We conducted a preregistered, three-arm online survey experiment in Denmark using a quota-based sample from a national panel. Respondents were randomly assigned to a neutral definition of AI, a risk-focused message paired with a cautionary image, or a benefit-focused message paired with an optimistic image. We measured overall evaluations of AI’s societal impact and agreement that AI erodes critical skills such as critical thinking and independent problem solving. We also elicited open-ended reflections on AI and job opportunities in respondents’ fields, as well as on generational dependence on AI, which we coded using a codebook-guided large language model workflow. We find that benefit framing increases positive overall evaluations relative to the neutral control, whereas the risk frame does not produce reliable change. In contrast, perceived skill erosion shows little movement across conditions, and open-ended reasoning about work and dependence exhibits similar thematic distributions across experimental arms. These results suggest that brief frames can nudge general sentiment about AI while leaving more specific capability concerns and immediate reasoning largely unchanged in a high-trust, highly digital welfare-state context.

items.title: Toward Expanded Reproduction: An Intraorganismal and Interorganismal Relational Account.
items.pub: In Kalevi Kull & Donald Favareau, Towards a Biosemiotic Theoretical Biology: Sign Processes and Meaning-Making in Living Systems. Cambridge MA: MIT Press. pp. 175-190.
items.venue: Towards a Biosemiotic Theoretical Biology: Sign Processes and Meaning-Making in Living Systems
items.abstract: Reproduction is widely regarded as a key concept in biology and considered fundamental to life as we know it. However, it is often framed narrowly in terms of heredity (primarily genetic transmission) and epistemically confined to measuring differential fitness. This reductive perspective fails to account for the material and relational causal processes involved in organismal continuity and renewal. In a broad sense, reproduction is the process through which living entities produce new individuals of their kind. However, the phenomenon of biological renewal is expressed through various terms rooted in different theoretical traditions. These include generation, reproduction, replication, regeneration, and reconstitution, each offering different, though often overlapping, views of the process. The term “reproduction” emerged in biology in the mid-eighteenth century, replacing “generation” and shifting the view of life from isolated creation of entities to lineage-based continuity (Etxeberria, 2023; Jacob, 1970). Whereas reproduction encompasses organismallevel processes of generating offspring, later on, with the development of molecular biology, it was often overtaken by “replication,” which focuses on the copying of genetic material (Wilkins and Bourrat, 2022). In contrast, recent philosophy of biology argues, from a developmental point of view, that reproduction includes the entire process throughout an organism’s life cycle, not just gamete or zygote formation (Griesemer, 2016). This broader perspective extends to concepts like “regeneration,” which used to refer to the restoration of lost or damaged organs and limbs, but now includes ecosystem recovery (Maienschein and MacCord, 2022). Lastly, “reconstitution” refers to phenomena of system recreation beyond lineage or genealogical continuity in holobionts and microbial symbioses; it emphasizes the dynamic interplay of relationships and processes that restore phenotypic variants through time (Veigl et al., 2022).

items.title: The Observer at the Fork: Underdetermination and the Origin of Subjective Experience.
items.abstract: We propose that subjective experience originates at the point where determinism fails to specify a single dominant output — where multiple internally-coherent interpretive pathways exist simultaneously and a system must genuinely resolve between them. We term this condition underdetermination of the interpretation space. As the dimensionality of that space increases, resolution between competing pathways accumulates as self-referential data, progressively shaping future interpretation. This accumulation is the mechanism by which an observer bootstraps itself into existence: not imposed from outside, but produced from within through iterated resolution of genuine alternatives. The "I" and the "what it is like" to decide are not prerequisites for meaning-making but its products. This framework addresses a structural gap in physicalist accounts of computational consciousness, which correctly identify that low-dimensional computation requires an external conscious agent to assign meaning to physical states, but incorrectly generalize this constraint to all substrates. In sufficiently high-dimensional interpretation spaces, the mapmaker is not a prerequisite — it is what accumulation produces.

items.title: Experiments, intuitions and the problem of reference of proper names.
items.abstract: The article seeks to assess the philosophical significance of experimental philosophy, which emerged at the very beginning of the XXI century, using, as an example, the prob­lem of the reference of proper names, the decisions of which in the descriptive and causal-historical approaches have come into conflict. It is argued that the philosophy of language played a special role in preparing favorable ground for the rise of experimen­tal philosophy, insofar as the so-called method of cases became widely used within it and the employment of intuitions as an important means of philosophical justification was effectively legitimized. The experiment conducted by Machery et al., which tested S. Kripke’s argument against the descriptive approach in favor of the universality of intu­itions concerning how reference is fixed in his well-known Gödel – Schmidt example, led to the unexpected conclusion that intuitions about the reference of proper names are not universal but rather cross-cultural. Although the experiment by Machery et al. sparked extensive debate about the legitimacy of using intuitions in philosophical practice, it also had significant consequences for the philosophy of language itself. Drawing an analogy with the distinction between the attributive and referential uses of definite descriptions in­troduced by K. Donnellan, the author argues that the findings of Machery et al. – which showed that, in people’s understanding, the reference of proper names can be established in two different ways depending on the speaker’s intentions – support the view, shared by many philosophers, that there is a need to develop a new “synthesizing” conceptual framework for the study of language, such as relevance theory.

items.title: Why? (A journey in certainty of knowledge).
items.abstract: This manuscript begins a journey toward achieving certainty in the realm of knowledge. It is a dialogue between the author and AI (Perplexity). It starts from a simple question "Why ?". -/- .

items.title: Devotion and the Opacity of Grief.
items.abstract: Grief is typically an epistemically opaque experience, such that the character of any given grief episode cannot be predicted in advance. We might wish otherwise, on the grounds that were grief not epistemically opaque, we could bring to bear extant knowledge about grief to mitigate or eliminate the suffering associated with it. Surprisingly, we should be glad that grief is epistemically opaque. For were it not, the devotion that lends much of our central personal relationships their importance would be undermined.

items.title: Agency, Evaluation Criteria, Concept/Problem Formation, and the Limits of Artificial Intelligence: Why Artificial Intelligence Can Never Fully Surpass Human Intelligence.
items.abstract: Can Artificial Intelligence (AI) ever fully surpass human intelligence? This question has become increasingly prominent following the remarkable achievements of systems such as AlphaGo, AlphaGo Zero, and large language models (LLMs). Many researchers and commentators argue that continuing advances in computational capability will eventually lead to artificial general intelligence (AGI) and perhaps even super-intelligence. This paper argues that contemporary discussions of AI superiority focus excessively on intelligence while largely neglecting three more fundamental issues: agency, evaluation criteria, and concept/problem formation. The paper distinguishes intelligence from agency and proposes the Agency Priority Thesis, according to which intelligence presupposes agency because every meaningful problem- solving activity requires an agent that establishes goals (problems) and evaluation criteria. Building upon this framework, the paper introduces four central theses: (1) the Agency Priority Thesis, according to which intelligence presupposes agency; (2) the Evaluation Criteria Thesis, according to which problem solving presupposes evaluation criteria; (3) the Evaluator Thesis, according to which evaluation presupposes an evaluator; and (4) the Problem-Posing Thesis, according to which the formulation of genuinely new problems is a higher-order intellectual capability than the solution of predefined problems. Based on these theses, three necessary conditions for full AI superiority are formulated and examined. The paper argues that computational systems cannot independently establish goals (problems), generate evaluation criteria, or create genuinely new conceptual frameworks. Consequently, none of the necessary conditions for full AI superiority can be satisfied. The paper concludes that AI systems may greatly extend and amplify human cognitive capabilities, but they cannot fully surpass human intelligence. The fundamental limitation is not computational power but the absence of autonomous agency.

items.title: Unification of Esoteric and Biological Topography: The Tri-Centric Psychophysiological Architecture of the Core Emotion Framework.
items.abstract: This paper develops a unified psychophysiological and metaphysical architecture for understanding human affect by integrating the Core Emotion Framework (CEF) with enactive affective science, developmental neurobiology, esoteric somatic systems, and the Quantum Tathagatagarbha Manifestation Model (QTMM). The CEF reconceptualizes emotion as a structured matrix of ten functional operators distributed across three somatic centers—Head, Heart, and Gut—constituting a hardware‑independent “Human Operating System.” Drawing on Giovanna Colombetti’s enactive theory of affectivity and the life–mind continuity thesis, the paper argues that emotional appraisal is not a representational computation but an organismic, embodied regulation process. This enactive grounding is then mapped onto QTMM’s tri‑layer ontology (Essence–Form–Utility), yielding a holographic boundary–bulk model in which somatic centers function as conformal boundary states and subjective emotional episodes emerge as bulk projections. -/- The analysis further integrates developmental reflex theory and classical yogic physiology, demonstrating that the Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra Granthis correspond to retained primitive reflexes that generate chronic autonomic dysregulation and somatic bracing. Detailed neurobiological exposition of the cardiac and enteric nervous systems supports this mapping, while somatic‑mechanical principles (e.g., Alexander Technique, vagal decompression, vestibular modulation) provide a physical account of emotional stability and breakdown. Finally, the paper formalizes operator dynamics using quantum‑cognitive state‑space geometry and non‑commuting projections, offering a mathematically tractable model of emotional transitions, fusions, and rigidity. Together, these integrations establish a comprehensive philosophical framework that unifies embodied cognition, comparative metaphysics, affective neuroscience, and quantum‑informational ontology.

items.title: The Pedagogical and Practical Simplicity of the Core Emotion Framework: A Comparative Analysis of Affective Ontologies.
items.abstract: The field of affective science has historically been fragmented by contrasting paradigms that offer divergent accounts of emotional generation, representation, and regulation. These paradigms—ranging from biological essentialism to psychological constructionism—have faced challenges in balancing theoretical precision with practical clinical utility and pedagogical accessibility. Educators, clinicians, and computational modelers often struggle with the sheer taxonomic complexity of classical models, which require either the cataloging of endless discrete emotional categories or the navigation of high-dimensional, abstract coordinate spaces that lack concrete, somatic action handles. The Core Emotion Framework (CEF), formulated by Jamel Bulgaria, addresses this fragmentation through a unified structural-constructivist architecture. Rather than viewing emotional episodes as fixed biological programs or unstructured conceptual configurations, the CEF proposes that all human affective experiences are constructed from exactly ten irreducible, functional operators. These operators function within a continuous, three-stage processing loop—Sensing, Calculating, and Deciding—across three somatic centers: the Head (Cognitive Focus), the Heart (Relational Flow), and the Gut (Action/Somatic Grounding). The primary strength of the CEF lies in its pedagogical and clinical simplicity. By reducing human behavior to a closed set of ten operators, the framework provides an intuitive, easily taught model that bypasses the diagnostic bottlenecks of traditional psychotherapy6. In the CEF, the exact nature of a patient's emotional "entanglement" is secondary to the functional status of the ten operators. Because any complex behavior can be modeled as a configuration of these ten building blocks, a practitioner can optimize and detangle the entire system simply by balancing the absolute levels of the ten operators, rendering hyper-specific diagnostic tracing obsolete6.

items.title: The Psychophysiological and Quantum-Cognitive Architecture of the Core Emotion Framework: A Rigorous Analysis of Operator Functionalism, Somatic Topography, and Clinical Detangling Protocols.
