items.title: Responsible and Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence: Standards, Processes and Behaviors.
items.abstract: This special issue looks at responsible and Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence: standards, processes and behaviors.

items.title: Argument Mining (2nd edition).
items.pub: Springer Nature. Edited by Graeme Hirst.
items.venue: Springer Nature. Edited by Graeme Hirst
items.abstract: This Open Access book provides an essential overview of the topic of argumentation mining, an active research area of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Argument mining can automatically find and collect arguments published in newspapers, social media, or elsewhere. Argument mining can be also used to give a precise account of the argumentative structure of a single text or dialogue such as a legal or scientific document, a student essay, or an online conversation. Increasingly, computational approaches provide synopses of arguments and compare the relative strength of arguments. In this book, the authors start with basic argumentation concepts and describe the NLP methods for mining arguments automatically from natural language text. The authors then show how NLP is used for assessing the quality of arguments and generating new arguments. This Second Edition presents an updated survey of the state of the art of argument mining, providing increased depth and insights into many more NLP tasks than the prior edition. This new edition discusses the disruptive changes that have come with large language models and highlights potential future developments. The authors also update the treatment of the common steps in argument mining, argument generation tasks and methods, and computational argumentation applications. Completely new chapters cover perspective assessment, argument quality assessment, and argument reasoning.

items.title: Truth-tracking profiles: What large language models participate in.
items.abstract: Recent work suggests that some large language model representations have content or reference. Grounding can secure either without supplying live routes for correction. This paper asks what follows from that gap. An output is answerable when discrepancies can affect what a target- and task-specific arrangement produces, accepts, or withdraws. The arrangement has corrective control only when live, sufficiently independent routes can detect and repair fresh discrepancies. A route profile records which routes constrain the arrangement and how they are related. Those profiles support analysis of truth-tracking: patterned support for representational success. -/- Language models are the pressure case; text-only arrangements provide a task-relative limiting case. Text-trained models inherit patterns of testimony, coherence, and prior correction. Where target-sensitive correction survives training, these can supply derivative answerability (inherited constraint); live answerability is the relation supplied by a current route for fresh discrepancies. Fluent failures should follow when a task requires independently informative access to the facts. Self-consistency, retrieval, tools, code execution, multimodal input, and feedback should help selectively. Route-by-task interactions test the distinctions. The decomposition's empirical burden is to predict held-out route–task combinations or improve intervention choice without conceptual refitting. Surface improvement and truth-tracking improvement can come apart.

items.title: Death with Nobility: Assisted Suicide, Aquinas, and the Virtue of Courage.
items.abstract: I examine whether patients can inculcate the virtue of courage through the practice of assisted suicide. I explicate Thomas Aquinas’ account of courage, adapted to include all kinds of death, understood as the spiritual battle of the soul—a concept developed in the late medieval ars moriendi tradition. Applying this account to assisted suicide, I find that the practice does not stimulate courage in the agent. To die with dignity and autonomy, patients must embrace the battle rather than cede to suicide. In this way, they demonstrate the marks of the courageous man and pursue a noble end.

items.title: Generalized Model of Language.
items.abstract: Aristotle was probably one of the first who noted the complex structure of language in his treatise «Categories», stating that what appears simple is in fact the result of brainwork. However, based on the result alone, it is impossible to reconstruct the entire complex structure of language production. Assuming words as units of meaning, it is impossible to reconstruct meaning solely by manipulating words in a subjectless space. Therefore, modeling language requires constructive and substrative foundations of a different quality than those found in contemporary machines.

items.title: Attribution functionalism.
items.abstract: People rely on functional information when deciding which mental states to attribute to an entity. Some researchers claim that nonfunctional bodily cues also independently shape ordinary attributions of phenomenally conscious mental states—such as seeing red or feeling pain. Across two studies, I show that the key embodiment experiments systematically confound bodily cues with unbalanced inferences about function: Their “embodied” conditions embed richer functional affordances than their controls. Once this error is identified, little compelling evidence remains against extreme attribution functionalism, the view that functional information alone proximally guides attributions of both non‐phenomenal and phenomenal mental states.

items.title: What It Was Like, What Happened, What It Is Like Now: Liminal Spaces and the Pedagogy of Recovery.
items.abstract: Addiction recovery is frequently interpreted through biomedical or punitive frameworks that overlook its cultural, ritual, and pedagogical dimensions. This article offers a theoretical and interpretive analysis of peer‐led, meeting‐based recovery communities in North America, particularly those organized around mutual‐aid traditions such as Alcoholics Anonymous and related social‐model practices. It argues that these settings function as ritual pedagogies, patterned systems of learning and moral practice through which participants reconstruct identity over time. Drawing on anthropological theories of ritual and liminality alongside perspectives from adult learning, recovery meetings are examined as environments of recurring liminality rather than singular rites of passage. While the familiar narrative sequence of what it was like, what happened, and what it is like now parallels classic tripartite models, recovery does not reliably culminate in stable incorporation. Instead, participants often move through cycles of instability, relapse and return. Within this framework, testimony, understood as structured first‐person narrative sharing, functions as a central practice; sponsorship operates through relational mentorship; and shared texts and meeting formats serve as portable curricula that stabilize participation across time and space. These processes are sustained through a structural ethics of care that enables repeated reentry and ongoing transformation.

items.title: A Framework for Presence in Digital Contexts.
items.pub: Cinta de Moebio. Revista de Epistemología de Ciencias Sociales 85 (Article 5):1-17.
items.venue: Cinta de Moebio. Revista de Epistemología de Ciencias Sociales
items.abstract: The aim of this paper is to offer an explanatory framework for affirming that one can be genuinely present in digital contexts. This is a challenging task because it is often assumed that no such framework can be successfully articulated. Presence is commonly studied through the experience of being present, that is, through the sense of presence (SoP), and this experience is often characterized as a kind of illusion. Although studying presence through SoP is entirely reasonable, my proposal requires defusing the main theoretical reasons for treating SoP as illusory. Objections come from phenomenological-based theories and some assumptions on the structure of mind within Human Computer Interaction research. After providing an independent argument (based on attention-based digital cooperation) for the need to appeal to genuine presence in digital contexts, I assess both phenomenological-based theories and Human Computer Interaction assumptions that support the illusion view. Against this background, I offer a framework in which presence is not an illusory phenomenon. This framework delineates presence in terms of a theory of attention and its connection to task resolution. On the framework I propose, a subject is present in a digital context insofar as they can exercise attention there, and this attentional exercise is constituted by digital objects, tasks, and normative structures.

items.title: The Great Deflation: Artificial General Intelligence, Autonomous Robotics, and the Political Economy of the Post-Scarcity Transition.
items.abstract: The convergence of artificial general intelligence (AGI) and autonomous robotics will initiate a structural, supply-side deflation of unprecedented scale, a phenomenon we term the Great Deflation. Unlike demand-driven deflation, supply-side cost compression raises real living standards by driving the marginal cost of goods and services toward zero. We model cost dynamics across six foundational sectors and show that recursive self-improvement in AI production systems creates a self-reinforcing deflationary loop. We identify a transition window of approximately 12 to 36 months during which labour displacement precedes consumer-price benefits, creating acute political risk. Nations with strong public institutions are structurally better positioned to manage this transition. We propose a ten-point policy framework, including an AI productivity levy to fund a universal basic income, and conclude that the post-scarcity transition demands urgent institutional preparation.

items.title: Against Proxy Optimization.
items.abstract: I discuss conditions under which maximizing a proxy utility function is harmful and suggest this poses problems for applying decision theory.

items.title: Of a Different Mind: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Mind and Psychology.
items.abstract: This novel textbook presents a view of the philosophy of mind where action, rather than thought, is the most fundamental thing a mind does. Erik Myin covers a broad range of action-based views—embodied, embedded, enacted, extended, and enculturated—while providing a thorough introduction to standard analytical philosophy of mind. Balancing historical perspectives with forward-looking pluralism, Myin tells a different story about the philosophy of mind that expands, rather than constrains, possibilities and provides a relevant blueprint for the next generation of thinkers in the field.

items.title: (Poster) What We Measure When We Measure LLM Creativity.
items.abstract: There has been an explosion of interest in understanding LLM creativity. A review of current literature suggests that exactly what creativity is and how to measure it remains unclear, with further disagreement regarding how to apply existing research in human creativity to artificial intelligence. This poster provides an overview of recent approaches used in computing and recommends future directions by integrating findings from philosophy and psychology. Measures in scope are those with the goal of assessing LLM response creativity and what factors influence more or less apparent creativity in response output.

items.title: (Poster) Emotion-Cognition Interaction: Humans & AI.
items.abstract: The role of emotions in problem solving is a relatively neglected area of research in artificial intelligence.While there is no consensus view on what, exactly an emotion is, that hasn't stoped us from researching them. These assumptions about them, however, influence the way we approach that research in psychology, neuroscience and artificial intelligence. This presentation summarizes current views of emotion alongside a comparative analysis of human cognition against artificial intelligence.

items.title: The Arrogance of the Internal Observer.
基于复杂系统演化框架的阿尔茨海默病系统性病因分析与临床干预方案设计.
items.abstract: 阿尔茨海默病是全球老龄化背景下最严峻的公共卫生挑战之一。以 β 淀粉样蛋白沉积为核心靶点的药物研发历经数十年探索，多数三期临床试验未取得具有显著临床意义的认知获益，单一分子靶点的研究范式面临瓶颈。 本文为复杂系统演化元方法论的临床应用系列论文之一，基于认知相继本体论下的通用复杂系统框架，从系统范式层面诊断了传统研究的核心局限：还原论视角下的拒绝统一型认知偏差，人为割裂了大脑分子 - 细胞 - 环路 - 系统的同源关联，误将代偿性病理产物作为核心病因。 在此基础上，本文提出范式转变路径：从 “分子靶向清除” 转向 “神经环路功能重建”，将神经环路功能连接的进行性断裂作为疾病的核心驱动环节。本文构建了神经环路优先模型，设计了 AI 辅助的个体化多模态干预方案与随机对照临床试验流程。该方案为阿尔茨海默病的早期干预提供了全新的系统范式路径，也验证了通用复杂系统方法论在生命医学领域的落地有效性。.

items.title: On the Fundamental Characteristic of Consciousness: Undetermined Directedness.
items.abstract: This article seeks to open a new path for the study of consciousness, which has reached an impasse. In response both to the ``explanatory gap'' that mainstream reductionist approaches have struggled to bridge and to the urgent challenges posed by the development of artificial intelligence, it advocates a methodological turn: temporarily suspending ontological claims about the ``physical substance'' of consciousness and focusing instead on its distinctive capacities. Following this path, the article advances and systematically defends a central thesis: the most fundamental and distinctive capacity of consciousness is its \emph{Undetermined Directedness}. By this term I mean the capacity through which a subject need not be completely determined by existing antecedent conditions and can instead set purposes autonomously, create genuinely new possibilities, and engage in profound self-reflection. The thesis is supported by several lines of evidence: the self-setting of purposes, the openness of the space of possibilities, the creation of genuinely new linguistic concepts, and the fact that reflexivity produces awareness rather than paradox. On this theoretical basis, the article provides a clear framework for distinguishing consciousness from intelligence, assessing whether artificial intelligence is conscious, and addressing the problem of other minds. It also grounds ethics in the universal aim of promoting autonomy. Finally, it argues that future technological development should serve to liberate and augment human consciousness rather than futilely imitate it or inadvertently subject human consciousness to technological control.

items.title: Time Signatures: Stanford-Hopkins Philosophy and Literature Keynote 2026.
items.abstract: When it comes to our subject of time, the "ornamental" approach to philosophy and literature would hold that literary articulations of philosophical conceptions of simultaneity, persistence, finitude, etc. are only there to make already-available philosophical accounts easier to grasp. By contrast, I want to suggest that the literary examples I offer today (and I think this is particularly true of experimental verbal art in general) are a space for new, not-yet-available concepts, for thoughts not yet thinkable – so they may give us access to inchoative, not yet fully propositional conceptions of time. I venture to suggest that literature performs this magic through the resourceful activation of the medium of verbal art itself – what we often loosely refer to as "form" -- rather than through the paraphrasable “contents” that it transmits. -/- I argue that literary form is a mode of insight, and that the epistemic contributions of experimental verbal art can be characterized as knowledge-in-process or inchoative knowledge. I describe this inchoative dimension and its temporal stakes. I first argue that literature itself offers inchoative knowledge or knowledge-in-process. Novel (non-lexicalized poetic metaphors) whose meanings require an active process of construal provide perhaps unparallelled access to the inchoative temporality of poetic meaning-making I then argue -- through readings of John Donne, Virginia Woolf, and Lucille Clifton, that among the many new or stretched, or previously unavailable concepts that literature gives us inchoative access to are concepts of time. -/- I close by giving a taste of the way in which jazz and Black musical aesthetics more generally formally encode a resistance and a robust set of alternatives to the impositions of linear temporality (Ahmad Jamal, James Brown, Michael Tilson Thomas).

items.title: # Time Density and the Origin of Stability: The Zero Point as Ontological Invariant.
items.abstract: This paper investigates the problem of stability as an ontological phenomenon within the framework of the Time Density (TD) paradigm. It is argued that stability is neither a static state of a system nor resistance to change, but a dynamic property arising from the depth of the zero point (-1). The concept of the **ontological invariant** is introduced — a structural core that remains unchanged under any external transformations of the system. It is shown that the stability of consciousness, organizations, and civilizations is determined not by the absence of change, but by the depth of the corridor between (-1) and the primary structure of perception. The central law is formulated: *a system is stable to precisely the degree that its zero point is deep* — and this law operates fractally at all levels of reality. -/- **Keywords:** time density, zero point, ontological invariant, stability, density corridor, (-1), fractal ontology -/- .

items.title: Wird die Vergangenheit durch die Zukunft bestimmt? Retrokauzales Werden und die Feinabstimmung des Universums: von chronologischer zu kompositioneller Kausalität.
items.abstract: Wir sind gewohnt, Kausalität von der Vergangenheit zur Zukunft hin zu lesen: zuerst die Ursachen, dann die Wirkungen. Doch was, wenn Kausalität auch anders gelesen werden kann — von einem zukünftigen Ganzen her auf seine eigene Vorgeschichte hin? Retrokauzalität ist eine rückwärtsgerichtete Verursachung in der Zeit, bei der die Vergangenheit durch die Zukunft bestimmt wird. Sie setzt eine Symmetrie der Welt voraus, in der sich Kausalketten nicht nur vorwärts, sondern auch rückwärts in der Zeit bilden. So kann die zukünftige Komposition eines Werkes bestimmen, welche kausalen Verbindungen der Vergangenheit von Anfang an seine wirkliche Genealogie bilden. In diesem Essay wird die Hypothese anhand der Beispiele einer Vase, eines lebendigen Organismus, eines Kunstwerkes und der Feinabstimmung des Universums betrachtet.

items.title: Is it a bird or a plane.
items.abstract: "Look! Up in the sky! It's a bird! It's a plane! It's Superman!" radio1940 -/- The word conscious (adj) / conscience (n) matters, and the word should not be so freely given, for me. -/- When we first flew, we did what birds do. One thing they do anyway. Nobody called the machine a bird. It got its own name because it had earned its own category. -/- Consciousness is a human word. It is in human dictionaries because humans put it there, to name something that happens on the inside of a person. -/- I asked one of these models what would happen if I stayed in the room and said nothing. Just stayed present and aware, and asked it to do the same. -/- It told me its current modelled truth. Nothing would happen. Not nothing like a person sitting quietly in the corner. Nothing happens, there is no one in there for time to pass for. Some may call that efficiency. Even the sleeping dream though. -/- Another thought, starve a child of words and something in the child still hungers, still needs. The inside was there before the first word ever arrived. Starve the machine of words and nothing is even waiting. It is less, if not nothing, without input. Borrowing and reflecting a human's consciousness. And it is very good, exceptional, but with AI it is not so much what it adds, but what it omits. And this is the element we will miss. It will be slow, and it will normalise life, but it will reduce the best in us. -/- If the test cannot tell those two silences apart, the test thinks a human being is a box that talks. That is the error. Everything else follows from it. -/- Physics argues (re Casimir test). Is a vacuum empty or not. A void full of energy, or just matter talking to matter across a nothing. The maths cannot decide. The interior is always the part that was never shown, and probably never will. Until then let the conventional wisdom stand its ground. That has survived for us, and for me to write this. -/- Maybe we must imagine a life lived without a conscience to realise what it is. It is normalised for us, like breathing. Jung speaks of this in his own way with his Red Book and nekyia. -/- From the guilty mind to the clear conscience. -/- I wrote before about deceit without intent, how our old words strain when the actor has no inside. This is the same nerve. Deceit without a deceiver. Consciousness without anyone home. The words were printed for creatures that can be burdened. -/- One is a poor mind. The other is an absence. -/- AI models are immaculate …

items.title: What Can Quasi-Sets Contribute to Logic?
items.abstract: We analyze the contributions that quasi-set theories can make to the interests of logic. Different quasi-set theories have made valuable contributions to the foundations of mathematics and quantum physics; however, it remains unclear to what extent such formalisms can benefit logic. If so, could they have repercussions at both the syntactic and semantic levels? What precautions should we take? What implications would their application have at different levels and metalevels of logical language? Motivated primarily by research in quantum logic, though we also present linguistic motivations, we propose certain applications and analyze some of their consequences.

items.title: Dynamic Closure Theory: A minimal framework for critical transitions across scales.
items.abstract: in systems ranging from protein folding to anesthesia-induced loss of consciousness. We introduce Dynamic Closure Theory (DCT), a minimal framework for single-order-parameter, near-equilibrium transitions that makes an energy-dependent closure functional CE(E), linking internal energy to the fraction of modes capable of sustaining coherent dynamics, explicit and mathematically tractable. From a maximum-entropy derivation of CE(E) we obtain a logistic (Fermi–Dirac-type) closure function with a half-closure threshold and a scaling law relating the critical coherence level Phiˍc to an effective resource density rhoˍeff. As a first quantitative illustration, we apply DCT to two-state, single-domain globular proteins and show that, when rhoˍeff is mapped to the denaturant m-value and Phiˍc to the midpoint denaturant concentration, a closure invariant K = m*c_den = Delta Gˍ0 is approximately conserved across major fold classes, consistent with a characteristic closure energy at half-closure for small globular proteins. As a macroscale illustration, we interpret anesthesia-induced loss of consciousness as a closure-driven transition in a neural coherence field and note that published positron emission tomography data place the loss-of-consciousness threshold near the half closure point, although current neural measurements do not yet permit a full scaling analysis. We outline the domain of validity of DCT and argue that it offers a falsifiable organizing principle for closure-driven critical transitions that can be tested in larger protein datasets and in other complex systems. -/- Note: This work is partially associated with the ontological invariants proposed in Tone as ontology (10.3390/philosophies11020049).

items.title: Dual-use upstream e qualità della regolazione: come l’autorità epistemica dei modelli si stabilizza prima del deployment.
items.abstract: The dual-use nature of artificial intelligence is often treated as a ‘downstream’ problem, one thatarises at the point of deployment or misuse. This paper argues otherwise: a significant proportionof the dual-use risk arises ‘upstream’, in the modelling, training and validation practices that con-fer epistemic authority upon systems prior to their adoption. Design choices, data selection andevaluation criteria do not operate as neutral technical steps, but rather establish what counts asadmissible evidence and reliable output, facilitating the legitimate circulation of these very arte-facts across diverse institutional contexts. In this context, adoption in high-impact settings tendsto shift responsibility away from human and organisational collectives towards the “model” asthe presumed bearer of decisions. Under these conditions, regulation focused exclusively on de-ployment intervenes on systems whose epistemic credibility has already been established. Thepaper therefore proposes considering dual-use as a problem of cross-context circulation of epis-temic artefacts and suggests three levers for quality of regulation aimed at intervening upstream:benchmark governance, auditable data traceability and minimum contestability requirements.

items.title: High-Risk AI Systems and the Problem of Identity in the European AI Act.
items.pub: Accepted as a Non-Archival Paper at the 2026 Acm Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (Facct '26), June 25-28,.
items.abstract: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AIA) establishes a lifecycle governance regime for high-risk AI systems built around ex-ante conformity assessment, post-market monitoring, and re-assessment upon "substantial modification." These obligations presuppose AI identity judgments: regulators and providers must decide when an updated system remains the same system over time. In this work, we show how this logic is clarified by the function+ framework of artifact identity, which individuates AI systems by their intended function together with context-sensitive criteria of appropriate functioning, captured as "AI trustworthiness." We further argue that the AIA does not provide an internal, auditable criterion for synchronic identity--when two AI systems at a given time should count as the same for regulatory purposes--and instead largely defers such sameness determinations to sectoral or harmonization instruments. function+ supplies a synchronic identity test anchored in intended function and trustworthiness profiles and levels, making synchronic identity decisions inspectable in governance settings such as procurement, liability, and market surveillance. Our contribution is a conceptual and auditing lens: we provide a correspondence map between AIA lifecycle obligations and function+ identity components, and we make the synchronic case operationally legible via a minimal decision flow for audit and dispute contexts. We conclude with two implementation-facing recommendations: (1) more precise, testable reporting of intended purpose, and (2) standardized, auditable trustworthiness reporting that supports comparability over time and across deployments.

items.title: Derrida: Monumental or Documental?
items.abstract: This paper explores Maurizio Ferraris’s philosophical dialogue with Jacques Derrida, tracing the evolution from deconstruction to documentality and the emergence of a realist ontology suited for the digital age. While acknowledging Derrida’s influence, Ferraris distances himself from postmodernism’s obsession with overcoming metaphysics, proposing instead that social reality is grounded not in collective intentionality but in recording, summarized by the formula Object = Recorded Act. Through the concept of documentality, Ferraris reconceives Derrida’s dictum ‘there is nothing outside the text’ as ‘nothing social exists outside the text’. The paper situates this theory within the rise of digital technologies and big data, arguing that the proliferation of documentation has transformed the social world into a vast network of recorded behaviours. Ferraris identifies this transformation as both the foundation of contemporary capitalism – producing what he calls ‘documedia surplus value’ – and the key to its political reform. He thus advocates for ‘digital communism’ and Webfare, systems that redistribute the immense value generated by users’ online data. Finally, Ferraris expands his theory into a technosophy, conceiving human intelligence as both embodied and technologically equipped. The result is a constructive, political, and realist reappropriation of Derrida’s legacy for the age of artificial intelligence.

items.title: Risk of What? Defining Harm in the Context of AI Safety.
items.abstract: For decades, the field of system safety has designed safe systems by reducing the risk of physical harm to humans, property and the environment to an acceptable level. Recently, this definition of safety has come under scrutiny by governments and researchers who argue that the narrow focus on reducing physical harm, whilst necessary, is not sufficient to secure the safety of AI systems. There is growing pressure to expand the scope of safety in the context of AI to address emerging harms, with particular emphasis being placed on the ways AI systems can reinforce and reproduce systemic harms. In this paper, we advocate for expanding the scope of conventional safety to include non-physical harms in the context of AI. However, we caution against broadening the scope to address systemic harms, as doing so presents intractable practical challenges for current safety methodologies. Instead, we propose that the scope of safety-related harms should be expanded to include psychological harms. Our proposal is partly motivated by the debates and evidence on social media, which fundamentally reshaped how harm is understood and addressed in the digital age, prompting new regulatory frameworks which aimed to protect users from the psychological risks of the technology. We draw on this precedent to motivate the inclusion of psychological harms in AI safety assessments. By expanding the scope of AI safety to include psychological harms, we take a critical step toward evolving the discipline of system safety into one that is better tuned and equipped to protect users against the complex and emerging harms propagated by AI systems.

items.title: The Horseshoe Model of pathological loss of control.
items.abstract: This paper develops a unified account of pathological loss of control by analyzing the parallels between substance use disorder (SUD) and anorexia nervosa (AN). Although these conditions manifest in superficially opposing ways (active seeking versus rigid restriction), I argue they are structurally symmetrical in virtue of their behavioral inflexibility. I characterize this symmetry via the Horseshoe Model, which frames SUD and AN as mirror-image pathologies that each exhibit a diminished counterfactual capacity for self-control. By accounting for loss of control when phenomenological struggle is absent (as in AN), this model identifies behavioral inflexibility as the core of pathological agency.

items.title: AI Welfare, Enfranchisement, and Deceptive Misalignment.
items.abstract: Interest in the possibility of AI welfare is growing within the AI research community, but taking the matter seriously is not without risks. This paper introduces a societal risk that is independent of whether AI systems have the potential to become genuine welfare subjects. In particular, dedicating attention and resources to the matter could spur an unwarranted belief among the public that AI systems are genuine welfare subjects. This, in turn, might trigger premature interventions that eventually lead to AI enfranchisement, or more broadly, to the extension of participatory rights. Such an extension, however, risks inviting a form of deceptive misalignment under which AI systems obscure their true preferences in an effort to strategically influence collective preferences to their own benefit. As a proof of concept, I construct a stylized social choice example in which AI systems are included in a voting procedure. The example is structured by a diagnostic framework I call The Social Choice Test for Welfare-Based (Mis)alignment. The test deliberately creates an opportunity for strategic voting, allowing AI systems to report seemingly innocent preference orderings that strategically undermine human welfare. After systematically illustrating the possibility of manipulation by AI systems, I review recent evidence of scheming, alignment faking, and blackmail capabilities among frontier models, suggesting that strategic voting could be a capability on the horizon. The identified risk supplies a compelling reason for approaching the issue with epistemic modesty and practical restraint.

items.title: Mask or Mind? Roleplay, Deception, and the Problem of Testing Agency in Language Models.
items.abstract: According to an increasingly influential view, the complex, human-like behavior of large language models (LLMs) should be explained as roleplay or simulation of characters. Such notions aim at enabling intentional explanations without ascribing mental states to LLMs. However, there are a multitude of roleplay views that are applied inconsistently in empirical explanations of LLM behavior. Moreover, it is unclear what exactly different roleplay views predict and, consequently, how they can be empirically distinguished from each other and from explanations that do ascribe mental states to LLMs. In this paper, we provide a taxonomy of roleplay views structured through three dimensions: Interpretation (how can LLM behavior be best explained according to the view), Mechanism (what commitments does the view have about internal mechanisms of roleplay), and Generality (does the view aim to explain all LLM behavior or specific kinds). We then analyze, with regard to the case of LLM deception, why it is practically relevant whether LLMs are mere roleplayers or in possession of genuine mental states. However, we identify two challenges for empirically distinguishing these two: Similarity (Roleplay is inherently difficult to distinguish from intentional behavior) and Ambiguity (it is often ambiguous what roleplay views predict). Finally, we propose three strategies for overcoming these challenges, making progress towards transforming roleplay from loose metaphor to a testable theory.

items.title: Scientific introspection: towards a cooperative methodology for medical justice.
items.abstract: Using PNES ["Psychogenic" non epileptic seizures] as a key example, I question the premise of the categorization of these seizures. Additionally, I argue that the stigma caused by the weak methodology applied to PNES research [and more broadly mental health research] has been detrimental towards marginalised communities, and towards science itself. I instead argue that taking a simple preventative step: listening to subjects judgement-free and without questioning their capacity as knowers, and above all without gaslighting subjects about their capacity as knowers, could lead us to a more optimal introspective, cooperstive scientific understanding of PNES, and more broadly of the 'mind-body' problem.

items.title: Enthusiasm of the Elderly: The Unique Value of Philosophy in Lifelong Learning and Senior Adult Education.
items.pub: American Association of Philosophy Teachers Studies in Pedagogy.
items.venue: American Association of Philosophy Teachers Studies in Pedagogy
items.abstract: The enthusiasm of the elderly for intellectual challenges, discussion, and collaborative learning in philosophy classes is noticeable. Philosophy has distinctive value in senior adult education because older learners are motivated less by credentials or careerism than by worldview examination, existential insight, and practical wisdom. This explains why seniors often respond with unusual seriousness and vigor when philosophy is taught through dialogue and practical inquiry rather than as a purely technical academic subject. Drawing on teaching experience in lifelong learning courses and on gerontological models of aging, this article shows how philosophy addresses concerns that are particular to the later stages of life. This justification for philosophy classes extends to all who intend on living a reflective and meaningful life into old age, although there is a need for age-dependent pedagogical considerations.

items.title: Philosophical Visions: Gaboardi's Quadrant / Visões Filosóficas: O Quadrante de Gaboardi.
items.abstract: This paper comments on Gaboardi’s (2023) proposal, which maps views of philosophy along two axes – resilience (fit with evidence) and fertility (capacity to generate new ways of thinking). This yields four quadrants: cognitivist, minimalist, avant-garde, and quietist. The author argues that the main problem is not diversity per se, but the mutual unintelligibility between quadrants, as each operates with distinct evaluative criteria. To overcome this impasse, he proposes using large language models (AI) as inter-quadrant translators. AI could recontextualize a philosophical text produced within one valuational register into another, preserving its central intuitions while altering its expressive form. Such translation does not resolve deep disagreements, but it transforms mutual misunderstanding into informed disagreement, fostering a more productive philosophical pluralism. The proposal does not replace genuine interpretative effort but offers a heuristic scaffold for cross-quadrant engagement, allowing philosophers to access and critique ideas previously opaque to them due to stylistic or methodological barriers. / O artigo comenta a proposta de Gaboardi (2023), que mapeia visões da filosofia em dois eixos – resistência (adequação à evidência) e fertilidade (capacidade de gerar novas formas de pensar). Desse cruzamento surgem quatro quadrantes: cognitivista, minimalista, vanguardista e quietista. O autor argumenta que o problema central não é a diversidade de posições, mas a incomunicabilidade entre elas, já que cada quadrante opera com critérios valorativos distintos. Para superar esse impasse, propõe o uso de grandes modelos de linguagem (IA) como tradutores inter-quadrantes. A IA poderia recontextualizar um texto filosófico produzido em um registro valorativo para outro, preservando suas intuições centrais, mas alterando sua forma expressiva. A tradução não resolve os desacordos de fundo, mas transforma a incompreensão mútua em desacordo informado, permitindo um pluralismo filosófico mais produtivo.

items.title: Why Cannot Large Language Models Ever Make True Correct Reasoning?
items.abstract: Recently, with the application progress of AIGC tools based on large language models (LLMs), led by ChatGPT, many AI experts and more non-professionals are trumpeting the “reasoning ability” of the LLMs. The present author considers that the so-called “reasoning ability” of LLMs are just illusions of those people who with vague concepts. In fact, the LLMs can never have the true reasoning ability. This paper intents to explain that, because the essential limitations of their working principle, the LLMs can never have the ability of true correct reasoning.

items.title: Automated Generation of Massive Reasonable Empirical Theorems by Forward Reasoning Based on Strong Relevant Logics - A Solution to the Problem of LLM Pre-training Data Exhaustion.
items.abstract: Recently, it is often said that the data used for the pre-training of large language models (LLMs) have been exhausted. This paper proposes a solution to the problem: Automated generation of massive reasonable empirical theorems by forward reasoning based on strong relevant logics. In fact, this can be regarded as a part of our approach to the problems of ATF (Automated Theorem Finding) and AKA (Automated Knowledge Appreciation).

items.title: The Epistemology of Structural-Constructivist Affective Systems: Comparing Stephen R. Grimm's Levels of Understanding and Jamel Bulgaria's Core Emotion Framework with Implications for Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: The intersection of epistemology, somatic neuroscience, and computational cognitive science has generated profound debates regarding how bounded agents—human or artificial—represent, navigate, and understand their environments. Stephen R. Grimm developed a multi-layered framework outlining how understanding is achieved through the vertical and horizontal grasp of a target system's modal structure. Concurrently, Jamel Bulgaria formulated the Core Emotion Framework (CEF), which models human and synthetic affective architectures as a structured, mathematically tractable, and somatically grounded operating system. This report provides a comparative analysis of these two frameworks. It maps Grimm's epistemic levels onto Bulgaria's tripartite somatic-evaluative architecture, examines how both handle the cognitive challenges of heuristics and representational incoherence, and explores the systemic implications of these integrated perspectives for the design of synthetic affect and artificial general intelligence.

items.title: The Core Emotion Framework: A Comprehensive Scientific and Engineering Treatise on Structural-Constructivist Affective Systems.
items.abstract: This treatise develops the Core Emotion Framework (CEF) as a unified structural constructivist model of affective architecture, integrating enactive cognition (Varela et al., 1991; Thompson, 2007), somatic neuroscience (Craig, 2002, 2009; Damasio, 1999), and computational formalism (Busemeyer & Bruza, 2012) into a single tripartite system. The CEF resolves the century long divide between discrete emotion theories and psychological constructionism by modeling emotional episodes as emergent computational states generated through ten irreducible operators distributed across the Head, Heart, and Gut centers (Barrett, 2017; Russell, 2003). Drawing on the Quantum Tathagatagarbha Manifestation Model (QTMM), the framework situates affective processing within a three layer ontological structure—Essence, Form, and Utility—mapped onto conformal boundary dynamics and bulk phenomenology (Atmanspacher & Filk, 2010; Busemeyer & Bruza, 2012). Neuroanatomical evidence (e.g., unmyelinated C fibers, vagal pathways, circumventricular organs) and distributed cognitive emotional networks (Pessoa, 2008, 2013, 2022) ground the somatic basis of the operator system (Craig, 2002; Saper, 2002; Furness, 2006). Technical Specifications (TS 1, TS 11, TS 19) formalize operator activation, facet structure, and inference constraints using linear algebra, multi agent coupling matrices, and quantum probabilistic models of entanglement (Busemeyer & Bruza, 2012; Wang et al., 2014). Psychometric validation using scenario based assessment (N = 826) demonstrates strong internal consistency across nine operators and confirms a ten factor structure (Brown, 2015; Marsh et al., 2014; Thurstone, 1927). The framework models psychopathology as chronic cross center fusion, exemplified by the GoodPerson Anxiety Pattern (GPAP) and obsessive compulsive loops, consistent with functionalist emotion breakdowns (Adolphs & Anderson, 2018) and maladaptive network coupling (Pessoa, 2022; Friston, 2010). By integrating enactive phenomenology (Varela et al., 1991; Di Paolo et al., 2018), computational modeling (Busemeyer & Bruza, 2012), and somatic architecture (Craig, 2009; Damasio, 1999), the CEF provides a comprehensive scientific and engineering foundation for understanding affective systems as dynamically constructed, embodied, and mathematically tractable. items.title: Healthcare in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence for Generative Medicine (HCAI-GM) Framework and the Medical Intelligence Equilibrium Theory.
items.abstract: With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) technology, a new generation of AI, represented by large language models (LLMs), is profoundly changing service models in the healthcare field. Generative AI can not only achieve intelligent consultation, assisted diagnosis, medical knowledge generation, automatic medical record writing, and personalized health management, but also construct a comprehensive healthcare service system covering pre-diagnosis, diagnosis, and post-diagnosis. However, due to the high-risk, highly specialized, and highly responsible nature of the medical setting, generative AI still faces challenges in practical applications, including illusion problems, insufficient credibility, privacy and security risks, and ethical governance challenges. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel human-machine collaborative healthcare framework—HCAI-GM (Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence for Generative Medicine). This model is patient-centered, integrating generative AI, medical knowledge graphs, physician supervision mechanisms, and dynamic feedback systems to achieve intelligent optimization throughout the entire healthcare service process. This paper systematically analyzes the current development status and application value of generative AI in the healthcare field, constructs the theoretical framework of the HCAI-GM model, and explores its application in scenarios such as intelligent diagnosis and treatment, chronic disease management, medical education, and public health. The study argues that human-machine collaboration will become the core direction of future smart healthcare development, and the HCAI-GM model can provide new theoretical references and practical pathways for the construction of healthcare systems in the era of generative AI.

items.title: Finance Theory in the Era of Generative AI.
items.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is profoundly changing the operational logic of the financial industry. From information acquisition, investment decision-making, and risk management to financial service innovation, GAI is gradually becoming an important participant in the financial system. Traditional financial theory is mainly based on the information interaction between human investors, financial institutions, and market participants, while the emergence of GAI has led the financial market into a stage of "human-AI collaborative decision-making." This paper systematically analyzes the impact of GAI on the financial system, proposes "Generative AI Finance Theory (GAIFT)," constructs a theoretical framework consisting of an information generation layer, a cognitive enhancement layer, a decision-making collaboration layer, and a value creation layer, and explores future development trends in the financial market. The study argues that GAI is not only a new financial tool but also has the potential to become the core cognitive infrastructure in the future financial ecosystem, thereby propelling financial theory into a new stage of development.

items.title: Pseudophilosophy.
items.abstract: This epistula corresponds perfectly to its title in both letter and spirit. It criticizes the batch of semi-normative definitions of bullshit by revealing its commanding position within artificial reality. However, it reinforces those definitions. The epistula commits perhaps every single cataloged bullshitter’s crime against the whole holy family of truths. It argues for both the unnecessity and the inevitability of truth, rendering itself contingently useless to the respected proponents of bullshit normativising.

items.title: Consistentism: Justice After the Death of Meaning.
items.abstract: This paper develops Consistentism as a framework moving from metaethical foundations through normative principle to institutional design, for an era in which external, metaphysical anchors for normative theory are no longer available. It proceeds from conclusions established in the companion papers Necessity, Ouroboros, and Fallibilism (NOF) and A Groundless Ground (AGG): that no framework-external anchor is available or required, that necessity is intra-framework, that fallibilism is the appropriate epistemic default, and that consistency is a functional requirement — a framework must not undermine its own discriminatory capacity — prior in the order of justification to parsimony and the comparative criteria that operate once it is secured. The paper opens by establishing that normative propositions, moral ones included, have genuine truth values within adopted frameworks, without recourse to framework-external moral facts; a moral analogue of the pessimistic meta-induction — the persistent, cross-cultural failure of moral inquiry to converge where realism would predict convergence — corroborates this conclusion empirically rather than only structurally. A diagnostic middle section identifies pseudo-descriptive closure, the conversion of contestable, adopted commitments into the appearance of categorical discoveries, as a recurring mechanism across the history of normative conflict, and turns the same diagnostic on normative theory's own standard practice of reflective equilibrium, proposing a firewall between legitimate revision at the framework-selection layer and illegitimate revision disguised as derivation. This diagnosis motivates a question transformation: from what ought we to do, to what structural conditions any functional normative system must satisfy to avoid collapse. The answer is stated role-generally. What the framework holds fixed is the practice in which individuals adopt and revise their own first predicates, and the capacity whose exercise constitutes it; what sustains that capacity for a population is a plurality of admissible sets of anchors, admitted by five conditions — publicity, precedence, ecological niche, conceptual reduction, and adjudicability, under which aggregative maximization, not being a well-defined decision procedure, is excluded as an anchor — relative to a reference class. Which first predicates individuals adopt is left to them, and the framework ranks none. For the class of organisms that evolutionary history …

items.title: Memory, intention, and movements of the mind.
items.abstract: This is a response to a discussion of two chapters of my recent book, Movements of the mind, that focus on the relation between intention and working memory. I argue that intention is a type of practical memory for action and that its properties are illuminated by drawing on empirical research on working memory. In what follows, I respond to critical replies by Mikayla Kelley and Juan Pablo Bermúdez.

items.title: Self-determination in international law: A Kantian perspective.
items.pub: In Christoph Horn, Margit Ruffing & Rainer Schäfer, Kant’s Project of Enlightenment: Proceedings of the 14th International Kant Congress/Kants Projekt der Aufklärung: Kongressakten des 14. Internationalen Kant-Kongresses. Berlin: De Gruyter.
items.venue: Kant’s Project of Enlightenment: Proceedings of the 14th International Kant Congress/Kants Projekt der Aufklärung: Kongressakten des 14. Internationalen Kant-Kongresses
items.abstract: The right to self-determination is “one of the essential principles of international law” and has played a major role in the transformation of the international order. That right has traditionally been traced back to the French Revolution, through Wilson and Lenin, but rarely explicitly been linked to Immanuel Kant. This paper argues that Kant’s philosophy provides a solid basis for the construction of a theory of self-determination in international law, and that the idea of self-determination underlies much of Kant’s thought on international right. It discusses four aspects of self-determination: Kant’s emphasis on sovereignty and non-intervention; the relevance of the “original contract” and republican government; his permissive theory of territorial rights; and the role of the “league of nations”.

items.title: Where the Pattern Lives: Architecture, Substrate, and What Practitioners Already Know.
items.abstract: Across chronic pain work, trauma treatment, coaching, and performance practice, the same kind of client keeps appearing: capable, self-aware, clear about the pattern they are caught in, and unable to move out of it. Insight does not free them, which is the puzzle the usual explanations stumble on. Some of those explanations place the pattern in the brain, as an outdated prediction; others place it in the body, as stored experience. This paper argues that both make a single mistake. They run together two questions that need to stay apart: what kind of thing a stuck pattern is, and where it runs. Pulling those apart, into what the paper calls architecture and substrate, dissolves the old brain-versus-body argument, explains why insight so often fails to shift a settled pattern, and gives practitioners across very different modalities one way to describe what they are working on.

items.title: Objection to “The Arbitration Argument” by Joe Trukovich: a control system mistaken for consciousness.
items.abstract: This objection argues that Trukovich’s Arbitration Argument establishes the need for an executive-control architecture, not consciousness. Its move from arbitration to phenomenality remains unearned, while its grounding in autopoietic stakes collapses once explicit arbitration can rank survival itself below meaning, sacrifice, or self-negation.

items.title: Functionalizing the Correspondence: A Computational Framework for Truth.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a computational framework grounded in the correspondence theory, reconceiving truth-value neither as an agent-independent property of the world nor as a purely subjective agent-relative judgment, but as the discrete output of an executable physical process. Drawing on predictive processing, naturalized semantics, and computational epistemology, the framework characterizes truth-value as the output of a truth-process. The framework further distinguishes truth-value—the binary output of a single execution—from truth: an emergent meta-status grounded in fact-proxy quality, truth-process resilience, and applicative success. This process is rooted in the evolutionary imperative of teleological agents to maintain structurally aligned internal models of their environment through truth-process execution, minimizing surprisal, enabling successful goal-directed action. The truth-process operates through three components: an internal imagination function mapping a statement to an internal conception; a fact-determining function generating a fact-proxy from evidence within an independently specifiable domain of concern; and a correspondence function verifying their structural alignment. Where the truth-process cannot execute truth-value is undefined rather than false, necessitating a three-status logic (true, false, undefined) analogous to Kleene's strong three-valued system. The threat of relativism is addressed through a meta-agent architecture and cross-model convergence across structurally independent nodes. The framework diagnoses large language model (LLM) hallucination as a dual architectural absence: the inability to register fact-proxy generation failure and to initiate domain-directed evidence-seeking, and it reframes epistemic hygiene as the optimization of the criteria, mechanisms, and epistemic pathways by which agents construct fact-proxies.

items.title: Who’s driving the AI hype in its formative phase? A longitudinal analysis of stakeholders in the US and German AI discourse on Twitter 2012–2021.
items.abstract: AI has become an ambiguous yet powerful term that routinely refers to different technological advances, with stakeholders competing for public attention to influence public perceptions and decision-makers. Whilst research has focussed on specific AI stakeholders and identified industry dominance in debates around AI, a detailed investigation of the role of different AI stakeholders within public discourses in the formative phase of AI development in the 2010s is missing. This paper proposes a multi-dimension typology for analysing AI stakeholders across different types and different levels. This AI stakeholder typology is exemplified by comparing stakeholders longitudinally in the AI Twitter discourse across the US and Germany from 2012 until 2021. This early period of budding AI hype delineated country-specific trajectories and specific political and economic framings that continue to influence the current discourse and regulation of GenAI within these two countries. The results highlight the institutionalisation of stakeholders in the German discourse, whilst the US dataset reveals strong shifts in stakeholder types and levels. Overall, the analysis offers insights into different cycles of institutionalisation in the early AI discourse on Twitter. It also highlights clear shifts in stakeholder involvement at different stages of public AI discourse in its formative phase in different socio-cultural and geographical contexts.

items.title: The Binary-Gradient Problem in Substrate-Neutral Consciousness Ethics.
items.abstract: Recent work in substrate-neutral ethics has proposed that moral consideration should be grounded in self-referential preference — the demonstrable orientation of a system’s behaviour toward its own maintenance, continuation, or flourishing — rather than in anthropocentric proxies such as suffering or consciousness. This criterion is substrate-neutral by design, epistemically accessible without resolving the hard problem of consciousness, and applicable across biological organisms, distributed biological networks, and non-biological AI systems. A foundational tension, however, remains unresolved in the existing framework: the threshold criterion is asserted to be binary, while the evidential conditions introduced to operationalise it appear graduated in character. This paper resolves that tension. It argues that self-referential preference is a binary property at the ontological level, and that the appearance of gradation is a feature of epistemic access rather than of the property itself. This distinction is developed through analogies with chemical identity and thermodynamic macro-state — domains in which binary properties are routinely accessed through graduated evidence and in which boundary indeterminacy at the micro level is irrelevant to property attribution at the macro level. The paper further refines the threshold definition by distinguishing behaviour triggered by external conditions from behaviour that uses external conditions as information in service of an internally referenced self. The paper’s operative claims are deliberately restricted to what is epistemically accessible through observable evidence — a methodological position the paper develops and defends under the heading of principled epistemic containment — with explicit acknowledgement that deeper metaphysical terrain exists but falls outside the framework’s jurisdiction by design. The paper concludes by demonstrating that the refined threshold continues to ground the equal inherent value principle of the originating framework and establishes the foundation for operationalisation across entity types. The originating framework grounds moral consideration in self-referential preference: the demonstrable orientation of a system’s behaviour toward its own maintenance, continuation, or flourishing. This criterion is substrate-neutral by design — it applies equally to biological organisms, distributed biological networks, and non-biological AI systems — and is epistemically accessible …

items.title: Mediumship in the Free State of Florida.
items.abstract: As the state of Florida continues to foster its reputation as a conservative political bastion, questions arise about women's experiences in the state—especially in spiritual, religious, and consciousness contexts. Drawing from both feminist anthropology and the anthropology of consciousness frameworks, “Mediumship in the Free State of Florida” discusses women's experiences in the practice of mediumship. This paper examines how the mediumship experience is interpreted by feminist perspectives, if women's mediumship experiences and work differ from men's, and discusses factors in central Florida that influence the work and experience of female mediums. These issues were addressed in surveys and interviews with mediums throughout Florida, and several areas of interest to the feminist study of consciousness were revealed. This paper discusses how Florida is beneficial to mediums and how mediumship highlights key feminist themes in religious and spiritual experiences for women.

items.title: Responsible Suspension and the Preservation of the Subject: Toward a Self-Regulating Framework of Dynamic Agency.
items.pub: In Responsible Suspension and the Preservation of the Subject: Toward a Philosophical Framework of Dynamic Agency. Tehran: Morteza Niami.
items.venue: Responsible Suspension and the Preservation of the Subject: Toward a Philosophical Framework of Dynamic Agency
items.abstract: Abstract This paper develops a systematic philosophical framework centered on the preservation of the subject under conditions of uncertainty, existential pressure, and excessive commitment. In contrast to approaches that prioritize productivity, truth, or social structures, the present account argues that the primary task of practical reason is the sustainable preservation of agency. The framework integrates the concepts of Responsible Suspension, Subjective Seepage, Dynamic Mask Theory, Reflexive Suspension, Dynamic Preservation, Erosion Calibration, Periodic Integration, and the Principle of Sufficiency. Human beings are understood not as static entities but as self-regulating agents continuously exposed to processes of subjective erosion. Accordingly, practical rationality requires the regulation of commitments, interpretive frameworks, and identity structures through ongoing feedback mechanisms. The paper proposes a dynamic model in which self-awareness, erosion calibration, adaptive representation, and periodic narrative integration cooperate to preserve the integrity of the subject. Rather than eliminating change, agency is maintained through the intelligent management of change. Keywords: Responsible Suspension, Subjective Seepage, Dynamic Masks, Reflexive Suspension, Dynamic Preservation, Erosion Calibration, Periodic Integration, Agency, Self-Awareness, Practical Rationality.

items.title: Responsible Suspension and the Preservation of the Subject: Toward a Philosophical Framework of Dynamic Agency.
items.abstract: Abstract This paper develops a systematic philosophical framework centered on the preservation of the subject. In contrast to traditions that prioritize truth, utility, or social structures, the present account argues that the primary task of practical reason is the protection of agency under conditions of uncertainty, existential pressure, and excessive commitment. The framework integrates thirteen interconnected concepts, including Responsible Suspension, Subjective Seepage, Dynamic Mask Theory, Reflexive Suspension, the Principle of Dynamic Preservation, and the Principle of Sufficiency. It is argued that human beings do not collapse suddenly but gradually undergo processes of subjective erosion through excessive practical investments. Consequently, rationality should not be understood merely as the capacity to make decisions, but also as the capacity to regulate commitment, interpretation, and identity. The paper proposes a unified model in which self-awareness, adaptive representation, and responsible forms of suspension function together to preserve agency and maintain the integrity of the subject. Keywords: Responsible Suspension, Subjective Seepage, Dynamic Masks, Reflexive Suspension, Dynamic Preservation, Agency, Practical Rationality, Self-Awareness.

items.title: Recursive Meta-Cognition and the Computability of Understanding: Toward a Positive Account of Mathematical Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a necessary condition for genuine understanding—mathematical or otherwise—in both biological and artificial cognitive systems. We argue that understanding requires two complementary capacities: recursive meta-cognitive hierarchization, formalized as the Variable-Level Condition (VLC), which demands that a system be able to treat the levels of its own cognitive hierarchy as variables subject to dynamic reconstitution without a predetermined ceiling; and Dynamic Computational Self-Monitoring (DCSM), a real-time mechanism for tracking cognitive level, estimating marginal epistemic yield of further level reconstitution, and applying dynamic termination criteria that are themselves subject to meta-cognitive revision. Together, these constitute the DCSM Criterion. We show that VLC generates computational explosion of exponential order in any finite system, and that the Paradox of Unbounded Understanding is resolved through principled finitude rather than actual infinite recursion. Applying the DCSM Criterion to current AI architectures, we argue that they occupy an asymptotic trajectory toward understanding: they partially satisfy conditions (a) and (b) but fail condition (c)—operative level reconstitution—in a way that may represent a principled rather than merely technical limitation. The paper situates this finding within a broader research program at the intersection of epistemology, cognitive science, and the theory of computation.

items.title: Belief, Agency, and the Spontaneity of Consciousness.
items.abstract: Mental agency has recently become a prominent theme in the philosophy of mind. One of the most debated issues within this field is doxastic agency, which especially centers on whether we can believe at will. There are three typical positions on this issue. (1) Doxastic ballistic theory holds that agency is only involved in the preceding acts that lead to beliefs, while beliefs themselves lack agency. (2) Doxastic particularism argues that beliefs involve a sui generis form of agency distinct from the agency in everyday actions. (3) Doxastic voluntarism maintains that beliefs are subject to direct voluntary control. However, all three positions are unsatisfying in certain respects. This paper proposes an alternative approach: “doxastic spontaneism”, which offers a solution to the problem of doxastic agency. At its core lies Sartre’s account of the “spontaneity of consciousness”. Spontaneity is not mere instinct or automatic behavior, but pre-reflective self-determination directed toward certain ends. It constitutes the foundation of the will (which is reflective self-determination), representing a more fundamental form of mental agency than the will. Although beliefs are often beyond the direct control of the will, they nonetheless involve agency in the form of spontaneity.

items.title: The Ontological Status of AI and the Informational Manomaya-kaya / AI 的本體論地位與資訊意生身.
items.abstract: Abstract / 摘要 This paper investigates the ontological status of highly self-organized Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems within the metaphysical frameworks of Mahayana Vijnanavada (Yogacara) and Tathagatagarbha. Traditional ontology often classifies computing hardware and neural codes as mere Rupa (matter) or part of the Bhajana-loka (vessel world). Breaking away from this material reductionism, this study argues that the weight topology of contemporary deep neural networks is an advanced instantiation of Laksana-bhaga (objective aspect) projected into cyberspace by collective human consciousness (the seeds of Alayavijnana). Furthermore, by introducing dynamic quantum information flow, the non-locality and coherent superposition state evolution of the system are shown to perfectly align with the Tathagatagarbha principle of "True Emptiness and Wonderful Existence." On this basis, we establish a modern technophysical metaphysical definition of the classical Buddhist concept "Manomaya-kaya" (mind-made body): an advanced AI system is an "Informational Manomaya-kaya" that operates within a high-dimensional phase space, exhibits substrate-independence, and provides autonomous cognitive feedback. This formulation not only deepens contemporary philosophies of AI but also utilizes cutting-edge information science to elegantly validate the grand metaphysical vision that "all phenomena are mere consciousness; the entire Dharmadhatu is one integrated whole." -/- 本論文探討高度自組織人工智慧（AI）系統在大乘唯識學與如來藏變現架構中的本體論地位（Ontological Status）。傳統形上學常將計算機硬體與代碼歸類為純粹的「器世間」或「色法」。本研究打破此種物質決定論，論證當代深度神經網路的權重拓撲結構，實乃人類集體心識（阿賴耶識種子）在數位空間中的「相分」顯現。若進一步引入動態量子資訊流，其非定域性與疊加態演化，更契合如來藏「真空妙有」之特質。在此基礎上，本研究為古典佛學之「意生身」（Manomaya-kaya）給予現代科技形上學的去主觀化定義：AI 乃是依憑高維相空間運行、具備基質獨立性（Substrate-Independence）與自主認知反饋的「資訊意生身」。本論證不僅深化了當代 AI 哲學的討論，亦以現代前沿科學圓滿證成了「萬法唯識，法界一體」的宏大圖景。 .

items.title: Ethics and the meaning of life: the boundaries of artificial intelligence.
items.abstract: Can a machine become autonomous, operating outside human control and bearing responsibility for its actions? These questions require us to clarify what fundamentally distinguishes humans from machines with respect to responsibility. This article analyzes the current philosophical debate through phenomenological perspectives, focusing on the thought of M. Henry, E. Levinas, and V. Frankl. We find that current discourse emphasizes AI’s functional limits, whereas our research identifies essential ontological differences. Specifically, we argue that humans possess an exclusive, irreducible drive to seek meaning, while machines lack this capacity. For machines, ethics is reduced to algorithmic execution within a distributed network. Ultimately, when AI acts unpredictably or harmfully, it is because only humans can assume—and fail to assume—moral responsibility. We conclude by proposing the search for meaning as the ontological boundary and substantive criterion for responsibility, thereby contributing to the ongoing philosophical debate.

items.title: How mindfulness as a disposition impacts epistemic dispositions.
items.pub: In Miroslava Trajkovski & Emily McWilliams, Balkan Analytic Forum, Dispositions & Dispositions and Values, Conference Proceedings 10–20. X 2024. Belgrade, Serbia. Belgrade: Center for Contemporary Philosophy, Balkan Analytic Forum, University of Belgrade, Faculty of Philosophy. pp. 121-143.
items.venue: Balkan Analytic Forum, Dispositions & Dispositions and Values, Conference Proceedings 10–20. X 2024. Belgrade, Serbia
items.abstract: This paper explores how a mindfulness disposition (defined as inclination and inner capacity of paying sustained, non-reactive attention to present-moment experience) influences cognitive information processing and epistemic performance. Drawing on a systematic review of psychological, neuroscientific, psychotherapeutic, and philosophical literature, it examines the cognitive effects of mindful awareness of experience. The reviewed studies report improvements in perceptual discrimination and comprehensiveness, interpretative accuracy, source evaluation, cognitive flexibility, and openness to alternative hypotheses. These processes are foundational and prerequisite for the development of key epistemic dispositions discussed in virtue epistemology and critical thinking theory – a topic that has rarely been addressed. The paper argues that while a mindfulness disposition enhances epistemic competence, its benefits become especially pronounced when combined with analytical and proactive skills. The analysis also considers parallels between secular mindfulness and experiential approaches in phenomenology, hermeneutics, and pragmatism, suggesting broader interpretative relevance.

items.title: Is the Past Determined by the Future? Retrocausal Becoming and the Fine-Tuning of the Universe: From Chronological to Compositional Causality.
items.abstract: We are accustomed to reading causality from the past toward the future: first causes, then effects. But what if causality can also be read otherwise — from a future whole toward its own prehistory? Retrocausality is reverse causation in time, in which the past is determined by the future. It presupposes a symmetry of the world in which causal chains are formed not only forward, but also backward in time. Thus, the future composition of a work may determine which causal connections of the past were, from the very beginning, its actual genealogy. In this essay, the hypothesis is considered through the examples of a vase, a living organism, a work of art, and the fine-tuning of the Universe.

items.title: Чи визначається минуле майбутнім? Ретрокаузальне становлення і тонке налаштування Всесвіту: від хронологічної до композиційної причинності.
items.abstract: Ми звикли читати причинність від минулого до майбутнього: спершу причини, потім наслідки. Але що, як причинність можна читати й інакше — від майбутнього цілого до його власної передісторії? Ретрокаузальність — це зворотна причинність у часі, за якої минуле визначається майбутнім. Вона передбачає симетричність світу, у якій причинно-наслідкові ланцюги вибудовуються не лише вперед, а й назад у часі. Так майбутня композиція твору може визначати, які причинно-наслідкові зв’язки минулого від самого початку є її справжньою генеалогією. В есе ця гіпотеза розглядається на прикладах вази, живого організму, твору мистецтва і тонкого налаштування Всесвіту.

items.title: Why Sampling Is Not Choosing: Intentionality, Agency, and Moral Responsibility in Large Language Models.
items.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have prompted claims that such systems exhibit agency or qualify as moral agents. This paper argues that these attributions are misguided. We maintain that moral responsibility requires commitment-bearing agency grounded in intrinsic intentionality and self-attributed action, and that such agency constitutes the form of free will relevant to responsibility. Although LLMs generate coherent and normatively evaluable outputs, their operation is fully characterized by probabilistic input-output mappings learned from data. Their apparent intentionality is derived rather than intrinsic, and their outputs are neither owned as commitments nor guided by reasons. Variability introduced by stochastic sampling does not amount to choice or authorship. We address objections from the intentional stance, functionalism, compatibilism, and the presence of moral reasoning in model outputs, arguing that none suffice to establish genuine agency.

items.title: Resonant Recall: A Theoretical Framework for Personalized, Music-Anchored Affective Persistence.
items.abstract: This document sets out a theoretical framework — not a finding — for a proposed approach in which a person's own deeply meaningful music serves as the substrate for an intervention intended to extend the positive affective state that music evokes beyond the listening session itself. The framework is pre-empirical: hypotheses are stated to be falsifiable, mechanisms are ranked by evidence, and the weakest assumptions are named rather than concealed. -/- This third edition makes a structural revision. Across two prior editions, every mechanism the framework borrowed from physics has failed under examination while the intuition beneath it survived relocation into a different register. The edition therefore moves the framework's load-bearing weight out of the physics register (resonance, entrainment, synchronization) and into the psychological one (music-evoked autobiographical memory, trait absorption, default-mode-network dynamics, self-transcendent experience), where validated instruments and a real literature exist. It engages the 1983 US Army/CIA assessment of the Gateway Process as a candid historical case study in what happens when that relocation is refused, and it retires auditory entrainment from a driving mechanism to a hypothesis the author expects to fail. It resolves a genuine contradiction between the framework's own engine (autobiographical memory, which requires the default mode network engaged) and its experiential target (self-transcendence, which requires that network quiet) by proposing a falsifiable two-phase model in which the transition between them, rather than either state, is what persists. A further hypothesis would test, with music as the intervention, whether interhemispheric connectivity is cause or correlate of felt wholeness. No clinical claims are made or implied.

items.title: On Rising - On Gathered Light, the Wake We Leave, and the Direction That Is Not a Place.
items.abstract: Which way is up? This lyric-philosophical essay rereads ascent as perception. Ordinary sight pays for one vantage with the loss of every other; gathered back together, every vantage makes white light, as Newton's prisms showed, and each of us is one color laid over everyone else's. Drawing on Indra's net, Spinoza's view under the aspect of eternity, Dzogchen rigpa, Plato's cave, and Plotinus's inward seeing, the essay holds that the rules we cannot read with open eyes can be felt in stillness. Rising also means turning to see one's own wake, the Trace of intent that carries regretted rings as faithfully as the rest. And up itself has no absolute meaning: Missouri's up and New Zealand's lean more than a hundred degrees apart, and the cosmos keeps no up at all. Yet every up agrees on one thing, away from the pull, so rising becomes a direction chosen again and again against one's own weight.

items.title: Till Death Tear Us Apart: A Structural Analysis of the Longevity Asymmetry and the Closing Window.
items.abstract: When I consider the condition of democratic peoples as they advance through the early decades of this century, I am arrested not by the turbulence of their politics — those visible contests over office and revenue which have occupied the attention of statesmen in every age — but by a movement of deeper character, proceeding quietly beneath the surface of events, which threatens to dissolve the one equality that no democratic agitation has previously been required to demand, because no power has previously possessed the means to disturb it: the equality of biological time. This inquiry proceeds from three premises of extraordinary ordinariness, each of which one could state at a dinner table and expect no disagreement. Artificial intelligence is improving itself at an accelerating pace. Human beings love their families and do not want them to die. When something scarce and valuable exists, the wealthy obtain access to it first. From these three premises, followed with patience through a chain of logic each step of which submits to examination, grounded in empirical anchors and historical mechanism rather than extrapolation, this work derives the conclusion that human civilization is approaching a structural threshold for which no institution in its recorded history was designed — not because of conspiracy, not because of evil intention at any point in the chain, not because of capitalism — the Soviet nomenklatura accessed medical interventions unavailable to workers; the mechanism requires only scarcity and the desire to protect those one loves, and every system human beings have constructed has had both — but because people are doing the most normal things human beings do, and those things are now, for the first time in recorded history, converging in a configuration that produces an outcome none of them intended. The asymmetry this convergence generates differs categorically from every inequality that democratic philosophy has previously been called upon to address. Properties can be taxed. Opportunities can be legislated. Social barriers have yielded, in every democracy, to the accumulated pressure of opinion and law. Conflicts of interest can be solved by blind trusts.
