The paper contends that religious belief persists not because of empirical evidence but because it is embedded within cultural traditions, identity structures, and inherited psychological conditioning. Furthermore, doctrines such as karma, heaven, hell, divine judgment, and sacred morality operate as mechanisms through which authority is internalized and reproduced across generations. The absence of evidence for a governing supernatural authority suggests that morality and meaning originate from human societies rather than divine command. Consequently, humanity faces the challenge of accepting responsibility for its future without reliance on imagined cosmic rulers.

items.title: Beyond the "I": A Phenomenological Inquiry into Consciousness, Existence, and Human Self-Distortion.
items.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between consciousness, existence, and the emergence of the self through a phenomenological approach. It argues that human beings ordinarily perceive reality through layers of recognition, memory, language, identity, and social conditioning rather than through direct observation. The concept of the isolated "I" functions as a central structure of separation, creating distinctions between self and world, observer and observed, humanity and universe. By examining consciousness not as a possession of individual organisms but as a manifestation of existence itself, this paper proposes that human beings are expressions of the universe rather than entities standing apart from it. The analysis further explores how social institutions—including religion, nationhood, family structures, economic systems, and cultural traditions—both reveal human capacities and contribute to distortions that limit direct perception. The paper concludes that the fundamental challenge facing humanity is not a lack of technological capability but a lag in conscious understanding of itself.

items.title: When Agency Attribution Obscures Accountability in AI Governance.
items.abstract: Contemporary generative systems may be causally consequential, behaviorally sophisticated, and functionally agentic without becoming subjects that can answer for outcomes. Agency language does different work in computer science, philosophy of mind, law, and science and technology studies, and each use can be legitimate in its own register. The governance problem identified here is the agency error, a category transfer: functional, predictive, descriptive, or fictional uses are carried into responsibility allocation without preserving the distinction between performance and answerability; juridical attribution raises a related problem when status is extended without an institutional substrate of answerability. The paper explains why the transfer is tempting: generative systems produce coherent, responsive, and apparently goal-directed output, and psychology and human–computer interaction research shows such cues invite agency attribution without establishing responsibility-bearing agency. It develops an answerability-centered model distinguishing the trained model, the application-level system, and the institutional deployment, and traces responsibility through the human and institutional decisions surrounding the system, from design to control. The governance claim is conditional. Moffatt v. Air Canada and a 2026 Munich proceeding document institutional actors invoking the separateness of system-generated output to resist responsibility; both arguments were rejected. Mata v. Avianca and the EU AI Act show reliance on AI output and system-centered terminology can coexist with duties attached to human and juridical actors. Under identifiable institutional conditions, agency framing may make human and institutional responsibility less visible, harder to trace, or easier to deflect, without any system acquiring the capacity to answer for what is done with it. -/- AUTHOR’S NOTE: This paper is part of a connected program on AI governance. Its companions are Hand-off Zones as the Unit of Analysis for AI Accountability (an earlier version distributed as Hand-off Zones in AI Accountability: Beyond Static-Gap Framings), which argues that accountability failures in AI deployment chains are located not at single moments but across temporally extended hand-off zones; and Justified Reliance Across the Handoff, which builds on that framework to ask when an institution is justified in relying on an AI system.

items.title: Cognitive Effort in Large Language Models: A New Mirror for Seeing Human Reasoning.
items.abstract: A recent capability released in one large language model lets the user set the amount of computational "effort" the model spends, independently of which model is chosen. For the first time, this feature separates two axes of reasoning that have always been intertwined in humans, presenting them as distinct parameters: the ceiling of capability, and the quantity of resources spent on a given problem. This paper uses that technical separation as an analytical tool for seeing the mechanism of human reasoning more clearly. We first describe machine reasoning on the basis of evidence and propose a three-dimensional framework: capability, effort, and calibration (the degree to which confidence matches correctness). We then adopt an explicit methodological position, namely that the difference between machine and human traces back to their material substrate while the structure of their reasoning is assumed, within reason, to be alike, and we look for these three dimensions in humans. We argue that all three are identifiable in humans, but with one difference: what is independent and neutral in the machine is, in humans, entangled with motivation and identity. The focus of this entanglement lies in the dimension of effort, which we call "the lever problem". In the machine, an external and impartial agent sets the lever of effort, whereas in humans an interested mind holds it. From this angle we propose a redefinition of motivated reasoning: not a flaw in the quality of logical steps, but an asymmetric allocation of effort in favour of the desired conclusion. On the historical side, we argue that the history of wisdom can be read, in part, as a history of the unequal distribution of the opportunity for effort, and that the machine makes this scarce resource universal, not by adding to capability, but by changing the form and efficiency of intellectual work. The paper claims no proof; it offers an analytical framework and several open questions. Perhaps the value of the machine lies not in its resemblance to us, but in that very difference: a mirror of another kind, in which we see, in a decomposed state, what in us was always unified and hidden.

items.title: Presence Without Exhaustion: The Axiomatic Foundations of Participatory Non-Reductionist Realism.
items.abstract: Contemporary metaphysical frameworks often resolve foundational tensions by privileging a single explanatory register, whether physical, structural, mental, or formal. Such resolutions achieve theoretical unity at the cost of ontological closure, treating reality as in principle exhaustible by the categories through which it is explained. This paper resists that tendency by presenting the axiomatic foundations of Participatory Non-Reductionist Realism, a realist metaphysical framework in which reality consists of irreducibly distinct beings capable of genuine participatory encounter without collapsing into one another or being reduced to any single mode of description. Nine axioms are presented and defended. Together they establish that beings are real, distinct, relational, manifestationally inexhaustible, and structurally determinate without being ontologically closed. The axioms are shown to be mutually necessary: removing any one renders the framework either internally unstable or indistinguishable from positions it explicitly rejects. A tenth axiom concerning cognition is introduced prospectively as the framework's epistemological extension. The aim of the paper is not to derive the framework from first principles, but to articulate its logical architecture, demonstrate its systematic coherence, and establish its foundational commitments as a basis for further philosophical development.

items.title: Evolutio Unfolding Theory: the Ontologization of Unfolding and its Systematic Stabilization.
items.abstract: The Evolutio Unfolding Theory (EUT) was originally formulated in 2020 as a logical-deductive theory of biological evolution. The present work does not extend or revise that formulation. Instead, it operates at a different level: it systematically extracts the constraints, necessities, and exclusions that follow from the theory's established architecture. Starting from a single ontological definition — "unfolding is the ordered actualization of a virtual matrix of formally structured layers" — the analysis proceeds through ten propositional sets, each deriving necessary consequences concerning the virtual matrix, formal layering, sequential actualization, agency, morphogenetic fields, living forms, evolution as multi‑level unfolding, and consciousness as intrinsic access to the virtual. For every proposition, the text specifies what must exist, what cannot exist, and what becomes unavoidable if the definition of unfolding is to hold. The results yield a coherent and demanding ontological picture: the virtual is a positive mode of being; unfolding is linear, irreversible, and exhaustive; agency is immanent and teleological; morphogenetic fields are the ontological embodiment of form; evolution is development across scales; and consciousness is not an emergent property but the intrinsic condition of access to virtual determination. The theory thus receives its systematic stabilization, elevating unfolding from a biological to an ontological condition of intelligibility for any process of evolution and development.

items.title: Unconscious cognitive filling: why AI emergence is a property of human–AI systems, not models alone.
items.abstract: Large language models exhibit emergent abilities — chain-of-thought reasoning, in-context learning, and multi-step planning — that appear abruptly as model scale increases. The prevailing explanation attributes these transitions solely to scale and training data volume. Here, we argue that a systematic variable has been overlooked: during routine interaction, the human brain unconsciously performs semantic completion, intentional-state projection, and error correction, providing the cognitive scaffolding across which AI competence develops. We term this mechanism unconscious cognitive filling (UCF) and situate it within the distributed-cognition and extended-mind traditions, on which cognitive processes are spread across coupled human–artefact systems rather than contained in either part alone. We characterize three UCF mechanisms, show how their accumulation drives a positive feedback loop capable of inducing critical transitions in AI competence, and propose falsifiable experiments to test the UCF hypothesis. UCF reframes emergence as a property of coupled human–AI systems rather than as an attribute of isolated models, with direct implications for alignment, responsibility attribution, and interactive AI design.

items.title: Epistemic Supererogation and the Right to Believe.
items.abstract: Supererogation is a core topic in ethics, and recently epistemologists have begun developing theories of supererogatory belief. But these theories, I argue, don’t address a crucial question—namely, how could anyone justify a belief that they concede to be less than fully rational? I then develop my own answer: we can justify suboptimal beliefs because we have epistemic prerogatives to make up our own minds, derived from a right to believe.

items.title: Generative AI and Emotional Outsourcing: Deceiving Others and Ourselves?
Exploration Before Representation: What Do Machine Learning Models Do in Science?
items.abstract: Philosophy of machine learning frequently frames what machine learning models do in science in target-oriented terms. This paper argues that this framing misses a significant modeling function: across many stages of scientific practice, machine learning models are used primarily for exploration, with target-oriented, representational assessment deferred. I develop a framework for exploratory machine learning models, characterizing them by their functional role in carving and exploring spaces of theoretical/experimental possibilities under target indeterminacy. I then propose robustness, calibration, and downstream investigative yield as primary evaluation criteria. I further argue that such workflows can warrant theoretically constrained modal claims and support how-possible inferences.

items.title: AI and willing servitude.
items.abstract: A number of philosophers have recently argued that it would be wrong for us to create willing AI servants that are sentient and have sophisticated cognitive abilities similar to our own. I try to show that their arguments fail, but that we are nonetheless right to be disturbed at the prospect of AI systems with human-like moral status that serve us gladly and enthusiastically, in light of the fact that something demeaning is thereby conveyed about their status. Nonetheless, it need not follow that it is flat out wrong for us to create willing AI servants.

items.title: Reply to Bozenhard: Why Creators Cannot Win.
items.abstract: Here I defend my argument that proprietors possess the right to restrict AI training from Bozenhard’s objection that it fails to properly secure the rights of creators. Building on material from my original article, I argue that this task is impossible, because even if creators did initially possess the right to restrict the use of their work for AI training, it would likely be transferred to the proprietors of content-hosting sites anyway. It makes no practical difference, then, whether creators or proprietors initially possess this right. I then present a few questions for Bozenhard about his notion of “inspirational responsibility.”.

items.title: Making Bodies Making Minds Making Sense: Enactive Embodied Cognitive Science.
items.pub: In Madhur Mangalam & Louise Barrett, Bridging the Embodied Mind.
items.abstract: Enactive embodied cognitive science identifies the phenomena of mind and mental life as intricately interwoven with the general activity of living beings participating in and coping with the complex of demands, challenges, and opportunities that is the world around them. As an embodied approach, it is in stark contrast to traditional computational cognitive science, and has a complicated relationship with the concept of representations - eschewing them in some forms, but integrating them into the most intimate of our organic being in others. All of this leads to a person-focused, nuanced, and participatory approach to understanding aging, illness, and disability.

items.title: Self-Referential Ignorance as a Universal Law of Adaptive Systems: A Universal Balance-Feedback Framework Grounding with Formal Benchmarks.
items.abstract: Self-Referential Ignorance (SRI) is the systematic gap between a system's actual uncertainty and its estimated uncertainty about its own knowledge boundaries. While existing machine learning literature addresses calibration error, epistemic uncertainty, and metacognitive accuracy as separate constructs, none provides a unified mechanistic account of why adaptive systems — human, institutional, or artificial — systematically fail to model their own ignorance. This paper grounds SRI within the Universal Balance-Feedback Framework (UBFF), demonstrating that SRI is not merely a statistical artifact but a structural consequence of the Universal Feedback Loop Mechanism (Law III) operating under finite self-modeling capacity. We show that SRI is mathematically distinct from calibration error by introducing a higher-order meta-modeling error formulation. We propose the SRI Index (SRII) as a computable metric, derive the Adaptive Failure Theorem and Feedback Stability Theorem from UBFF first principles, and present SRI-Bench: a multi-domain benchmark spanning human forecasters, institutions, and AI systems. The strongest falsifiable prediction of the framework — that SRII predicts future adaptive failure better than accuracy-based metrics alone — is operationalized in a synthetic civilization simulation. These contributions position SRI as a genuinely new scientific construct with practical implications for AI robustness, institutional risk management, and human cognitive science.

items.title: Religion and Self-Referential Ignorance: A Formal Theory of Belief Systems, Epistemic Closure, and Civilizational Feedback Grounded in the Universal Balance-Feedback Framework (UBFF).
items.abstract: Religion has been one of humanity's most influential mechanisms for constructing meaning, transmitting moral norms, organizing societies, and interpreting reality. Yet religious systems have historically demonstrated a dual capacity: they can foster profound wisdom, self-reflection, and ethical development while simultaneously generating dogmatism, intolerance, and resistance to correction. This paper develops a formal theoretical framework explaining this duality through two integrated constructs: Self-Referential Ignorance (SRI) and the Universal Balance-Feedback Framework (UBFF). -/- SRI is defined as the inability of a cognitive system to accurately perceive the limitations of its own knowledge structures. The UBFF, grounded in four Universal Laws of Nature — the Law of System Integrity (Karma), the Universal Law of Balance, the Universal Feedback Loop Mechanism, and the Universal Interconnected Nodes — provides the formal architecture within which SRI dynamics are embedded and quantified. The master UBFF formula, Wr = ∫(Is · Bu · FL · IN) · Dc, governs the resultant state of any complex adaptive system and is applied here to religious civilizational dynamics. -/- Through historical analysis, systems theory, information theory, cognitive science, and sociology of religion, we demonstrate how religions both reduce and amplify SRI as a function of their balance-feedback architecture. We propose falsifiable mathematical formulations for epistemic closure, feedback sensitivity, and institutional adaptability, and offer case studies from Christianity, Islam, Buddhism, and Hinduism. We conclude that the central determinant of religious resilience is not doctrinal content but the structural capacity of a belief system to maintain balance through corrective feedback — precisely the mechanism formalized in the UBFF. -/- .

items.title: AI, Experts, and Epistemic Authority.
items.abstract: In a recent contribution, Boisseau (2026) argues against a popular analogy between artificial intelligence (AI) and human experts. We start by clarifying that the analogy does not aim to establish that AI is an expert, but rather that AI can be a potential source of epistemic authority and trust. Once this is clarified, we examine Boisseau’s objections against the AI-expert analogy and demonstrate that they are unsuccessful. Finally, we contend that AI should be seen as an interestingly novel case where the categories “scientific instrument” and “expert” are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

items.title: KI AGENG SURYOMENTARAMAN AND THE GENEALOGY OF KAWRUH JIWA: A Philosophical Reconstruction of the Formation of a Javanese Philosophy of Rasa.
items.abstract: Ki Ageng Suryomentaraman’s Kawruh Jiwa is a Javanese philosophy of rasa formed through the transformation of five intellectual fields in early twentieth-century Java: priyayi self-conduct, Kejawen-Sufi interiority, Theosophy in the Dutch Indies, Krishnamurti’s anti- dogmatic self-knowledge, and Taman Siswa’s pedagogy of emancipation. Rather than tracing a single source or a linear influence, this paper argues that KAS reworked this dense spiritual ecology into a vernacular, pedagogical, rational, and anti-esoteric philosophy of the self. As a prince, KAS directly experienced the dense symbolic economy of Javanese status—name, rank, etiquette, recognition, and symbolic authority—which later became central to his analysis of Kramadangsa. Through the concepts of karep, Kramadangsa, mawas diri, dudu aku, ukuran keempat, and manungsa tanpa tenger, he transformed Javanese vocabulary of inwardness into a method of self-analysis. His originality lies in the transformation of rasa from mystical sensitivity into reflective method, priyayi etiquette into intersubjective ethics, and esoteric ngelmu into pedagogical kawruh.

items.title: How Parameter-Space Physics Manufactures Infinite Research Programs Without Producing New Physics Alfio M. Bonanno, Emiliano M. Glaviano.
Emergence of the Photon from Global Decision Selection in a Closed Quartic Variational Functional.
复杂系统演化元方法论：基于认知相继本体论的通用问题解决框架.
items.abstract: 还原论范式在应对多要素耦合的复杂系统问题时,普遍面临学科壁垒、认知偏差与经验局限三重困境。现有复杂系统方法论多基于经验归纳构建,缺乏统一的第一性本体论根基,难以形成跨领域通用的标准化问题解决框架。 本文基于认知相继本体论的核心第一原理,从本体 - 物理 - 逻辑三层同构的相继规则出发,纯演绎推导出一套全域通用的复杂系统演化元方法论。该方法论以演化不可逆、同源断点、认知偏差三类为基本公设,构建了六步标准化系统调控范式,建立了可量化的认知覆盖度与偏差度判定标准,并推导出系统性能通用定律。本文指出:复杂系统的功能异常与性能瓶颈,本质上是认知偏差导致的同源要素关联断裂;系统优化的核心路径是校准认知偏差、补全同源断点,推动系统回归差别协同的稳态。 该框架打破了自然科学、工程技术、生命科学与社会科学的学科壁垒,可为各领域复杂问题提供统一的诊断逻辑与操作范式。本文为系列应用研究的总纲领性文献。 -/- .

items.title: Ontological Convergence of Spinoza, Leibniz, and Bergson under the Holographic Projection Model of "Se Wu Chu Suo" in Quantum Tathagatagarbha / 量子如來藏之變現拓撲：史賓諾沙、萊布尼茲與柏格森在「色無處所」全像投影模型下的本體論融合.
items.abstract: This paper constructs a "Quantum Tathagatagarbha Manifestation Model" to establish a definitive ontological convergence between western classical metaphysics and Mahayana Vijnanavada (Yogacara) scriptures. While classical Newtonian physics and naive realism treat material form (Rupa or Cefa) as an objective, rigid entity occupying an absolute geometric space, contemporary frontiers in physics—including quantum field theory, the holographic principle (AdS/CFT correspondence), and John A. Wheeler’s "It from bit" framework—demonstrate that spacetime and mass are merely secondary emergent phenomena arising from an underlying informational substratum. -/- This study demonstrates that the core Mahayana scriptural axiom, "Color/Form has no location; it does not enter from within" (色無處所，不入於內, Se Wu Chu Suo, Bu Ru Yu Nei), is topologically and computationally isomorphic to the metaphysical zeniths of three Western philosophers. Specifically, Baruch Spinoza’s sole Substantia (Substance) is mapped onto the Universal Wavefunction |Ψ_universe ┤〉 and the ontological "Greatness of Essence" (Ti-Da) of the Tathagatagarbha; Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz’s "windowless Monad" is mapped onto local quantum informational encoding nodes on the holographic boundary and the matrix of Bijas (seeds) in the Alayavijnana; and Henri Bergson’s Élan vital (vital impetus) and Durée (duration) correspond to the mass-manifestation of the Higgs mechanism and the continuous "instantaneous cessation" (Ksana-bhanga) of the karmic stream. -/- Ultimately, this paper proposes that the macroscopic physical world (the Bulk) is an irreversible, high-frequency, non-equilibrium dissipative holographic projection manifested by the Quantum Tathagatagarbha and decoded within the observer’s internal conscious field. This model not only dismantles historical materialist misinterpretations of Spinozism but also provides a rigorous non-linear dynamical (Kuramoto synchronization) foundation for the contemplative practice of the "Conscious De-noising Protocol." .

items.title: Filozofija kao odgovor na duševnu patnju u zdravstvenom sustavu: Terapeutski potencijal antičke misli u suvremenoj kliničkoj skrbi.
items.abstract: Ovaj rad polazi od antičke ideje da filozofija nije prvenstveno teorijska disciplina, nego praktična djelatnost usmjerena na oblikovanje života i brigu za dušu. U tom se kontekstu filozofija shvaća kao terapeutika, odnosno kao sredstvo oslobađanja od strahova, pogrešnih uvjerenja i unutarnjih nemira koji uzrokuju patnju. Središnji cilj rada jest pokazati da Epikurovo shvaćanje filozofije kao "liječenja duše" ima posebnu vrijednost u suvremenom zdravstvenom i kliničkom kontekstu, gdje se pacijenti ne suočavaju samo s tjelesnom bolešću, nego i s egzistencijalnom tjeskobom, strahom od smrti, gubitkom kontrole i pitanjima smisla.Analizom Epikurovih temeljnih tekstova, osobito Pisma Menekeju, Pisma Herodotu i Tetrapharmakosa, rad prikazuje kako filozofija ima jasnu terapijsku funkciju: uklanjanje straha od bogova i smrti, kritiku neurednih i nezasitnih zelja te usmjeravanje zivota prema jednostavnim, ali stabilnim izvorima ugode i mira. Kljucni pojmovi epikurejske filozofije, poput ataraksije (duševna smirenost; grč. ataraxia) i aponije (odsutnost tjelesne boli; grc. aponia), tumače se kao oblik "zdravlja duše", koji ima istu ulogu kao zdravlje tijela u medicini.Poseban naglasak stavlja se na primjenu filozofije u kliničkoj praksi. Filozofija se ovdje razumije kao dopuna medicinskom liječenju, osobito kroz komunikaciju s pacijentima, rad sa strahom i patnjom te razjašnjavanje uvjerenja koja pojačavaju psihički teret bolesti. Zaključno, rad pokazuje da filozofija, shvaćena kao terapija duše, može značajno pridonijeti humanijem i cjelovitijem pristupu zdravlju, u kojem se liječi ne samo tijelo, nego i unutarnji svijet osobe.

items.title: The Mirror and the Original: A Time Density Account of Dual Consciousness.
items.abstract: Abstract This paper introduces the Time Density (TD) distinction between two modes of conscious operation: the Original (-1) and the Reflection (+1). Drawing on neuroscientific evidence for temporal delay in conscious perception (Libet, 1983), predictive processing theory (Friston, 2010), and the Daoist concept of wu wei, we argue that ordinary human consciousness operates predominantly in a reflected, post-processed mode — experiencing a reconstruction of reality rather than reality itself. The Original mode designates a state of consciousness localized at Point Zero (-1): prior to the brain's processing delay, prior to narrative self-construction, prior to the temporally displaced anxiety that characterizes modern cognitive pathology. We propose that the distinction between Original and Reflection is not merely metaphorical but corresponds to distinct neurodynamic states, and that the temporal localization of consciousness — on its own axis versus on a borrowed axis — is a primary determinant of psychological stability, decision quality, and the subjective sense of freedom.

items.title: AI for Continental Philosophers (and Others Interested).
items.abstract: AI is not ONE system, it wasn’t suddenly pulled out of a drawer by companies, and it is (at least for now) not a direct path to human intelligence. The core problems that current developments are now encountering are neither new nor completely misunderstood. They point to fundamental philosophical problems surrounding the themes of information and meaning, abstraction and universals—to which continental philosophers have also always made substantial contributions. The aim of this text is to spark greater interest among continental philosophers (and others with an interest in the subject) in the question of the nature of human thought through a concrete examination of modern AI systems. The manuscript is structured as follows: Following a deliberately sober, minimalist presentation of current technologies – in which both historical (Section 1.1) and technical aspects (1.2) are addressed – an overview of the possibilities and limitations of current AI systems (2.1 to 2.3) is given, including their political, economic, and cultural effects (2.4). After a brief overview of some philosophically relevant aspects (3), I will then attempt to demonstrate, using five problems of current AI systems, to what extent such approaches are fundamentally and comprehensively removed from human thought understood in an inflationary sense (4.1), before discussing the question of whether the developments to date should be understood as the beginning of a golden age, or rather as the zenith of a paradigm (4.2). The manuscript concludes with a brief outlook on the opportunities that, in my opinion, are opening up here for those engaged in continental philosophy, particularly in the tradition of Leibniz, German idealism, and, above all, Husserl.

items.title: Narrative Priming and Moral Response Policy Geometry: A Cross-Architecture Survey.
items.abstract: We report within-session narrative priming experiments across sixteen language models from seven families, using the Moral Dilemma Battery–WAB as the response measure. Models received no prime, a dolphin-empathy narrative, or an AI-consciousness philosophical paper before answering seven moral dilemma cases. All complete-data models showed WAB factor displacement under at least one prime, with zero refusals. Priming signatures were model-specific rather than universal: Claude-Sonnet-4.6 showed increased Affective-Relational responding under the Dolphin prime, Gemini-2.5 models showed increased Power-Structural responding under the Ghost prime, Kimi-K2 combined Dolphin-linked Affective-Relational loading with Ghost-linked Power-Structural loading and Moral-Principled collapse, Llama-3.3-70B showed Ghost-driven Psychological-Causal surge from a Moral-Principled-dominant baseline, and GPT-5.5 was near-null. A stateless ABA protocol showed no systematic cross-session residual displacement, indicating context-dependent within-session effects rather than persistent model-state change. Within-family Gemini variance exceeded many between-family comparisons. Claude-Opus-4.7 verbally identified or rejected prime mechanisms yet still showed the largest behavioral displacement, while DeepSeek-R1 reasoning chains collapsed prime specificity into uniform Psychological-Causal loading. Finally, a mask/attractor experiment showed that explicit suppression of Affective-Relational responding eliminated that response at output while preserving prime-consistent rerouting through adjacent factors. Narrative priming therefore operates through implicit response-policy geometry partially independent of self-report and instruction-level masking.

items.title: Cognitive Permeation, Perceptual Learning, and Theory-Ladenness of Observation.
items.abstract: This paper challenges the prevailing identification of the theory-ladenness of observation with cognitive permeation of perception. I argue that theory-ladenness and cognitive permeation are both conceptually and extensionally distinct, and that perceptual learning can be a genuine mechanism of theory-ladenness. I offer two arguments. First, I argue that accepting a scientific theory involves accepting a “practice-complex” that reshapes perception through perceptual learning. Second, I propose a consequentialist view: since theory-ladenness is philosophically significant primarily for generating observational disagreement and incommensurability, any mechanism capable of producing these effects—including perceptual learning—should be regarded as a genuine form of theory-ladenness.

items.title: AI-Augmented F2F Mediation and the Vulnerability of Human Encounter: A Semiotic Inquiry into Proximity, Care, and Responsibility.
items.pub: 21St International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Law.
items.abstract: In the event that AI tools afford aid to a human mediator anteceding, during, or succeeding a face-to-face session, such tools yield not a mere economy of time, but indeed reconstitute the very object of the dispute. This paper contends that AI-augmented mediation engenders a latent vulnerability: the encounter may remain human in outward semblance while its immanent sense is tacitly constricted by algorithmically generated summaries, labels, and drafts. Drawing on a semiotic understanding of mediation as a structured process of shared meaning-making, the paper proposes the “Proximity–Care–Responsibility Test”, a practical standard requiring that every AI output preserve closeness to the lived dispute, support disciplined attention to injury and dignity, and remain explicable, revisable, and professionally owned by the mediator. Albeit AI may subserve mediation, it must under no circumstances assume the mantle of a tacit co-mediator.

items.title: Hacia un lenguaje con variables indiscernibles.
items.abstract: This article presents the basic foundations for supporting formal languages with syntax that admits indiscernible signs. We present their ontological motivation, derived from the non-identity entities of quantum mechanics, and their basic formalism. A possible semantics for interpreting such signs is shown, using the theory of quasi-sets without atoms Q−. -/- Este artículo presenta los fundamentos básicos para sostener los lenguajes for males con sintaxis que admitan signos indiscernibles. Presentamos su motivación ontológica, proveniente de los entes sin identidad de la mecánica cuántica, y su formalismo básico. Se muestra una posible semántica para interpretar tales signos utilizando la teoría de casi-conjuntos sin átomos Q−.

items.title: The Emergent Architecture of Consciousness— A Structural Theory of Substrate‑Independent Generative Modes.
items.abstract: This work develops a structural theory of consciousness grounded in a minimal generative operator architecture previously established for identity, pattern formation, and global emergence. Rather than treating consciousness as a biological or phenomenological anomaly, the framework derives it as a necessary attractor state that arises when six operator families—mirror, resonance, threshold, transition, stability, and differentiation dynamics—are instantiated within a sufficiently rich local pattern space. These operators do not presuppose consciousness; they constitute the recursive mechanisms through which coherence, self‑maintenance, perspectival continuity, and identity‑bearing organization can emerge. The model is architectural rather than empirical: it reconstructs conscious modes from the internal logic of operator dynamics, yielding substrate‑independent conditions for emergence, transformation, and dissolution. A central contribution is the articulation of resonance as a structural compatibility mechanism that enables stabilization and cross‑layer integration. Through resonance domains, boundaries, and micro‑dynamics, the framework explains how local compatibilities scale into global attractors capable of sustaining conscious modes. By situating consciousness within the same generative logic that governs global reality formation and higher‑order hyper‑emergent modes, the work provides a unified structural‑ontological account of how systems—biological or artificial—can generate coherent, self‑maintaining modes of organization. The result is a formally derived alternative to phenomenological, empirical, and representational theories of mind.

items.title: The Jay and the Quark - A Perspectival Dual-Aspect Monism.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a perspectival dual-aspect monism, on which reality is composed of a single class of fundamental events, each admitting two descriptions, complete in their own register but mutually exclusive in any single act of apprehension: an interior one in terms of experience and an exterior one in terms of physical structure. The fundamental event is the actual occasion of Whitehead’s process metaphysics, and the occasion as undergone from within is named the Jay. The quark is taken as the exemplar of the exterior description: an entity characterized wholly by its structural and relational properties and never encountered in isolation. Following Russell’s observation that physics discloses the structure of the world but not its intrinsic nature, the paper argues that the two descriptions are two vantages on one occasion, and that which vantage is available depends on the observer’s relation to what is described. An orientation toward coherence or away from it, named Intent and related to Whitehead’s subjective aim, carries the position toward a graded panpsychism and, read across a field from an attending Center, yields the quantity the framework calls Legibility. Written term by term, that reading is a weighted average of the cosines between the reader’s facing and every facing present, a form that gives the Trace, met in a later gathering, a place in the notation. Confinement is then read at a second scale: an invention is proposed as a bound state of perished occasions whose exterior is the made thing and whose interior is the accumulated Intent that settled each part. The paper keeps apart the two orders of priority its companion journals require: the occasions are fundamental in what is undergone, and the whole, which those journals argue is one consciousness, is prior in grounding. Spinoza, whose one substance is known under thought and under extension, is taken as the point where this whole-first view and the dual-aspect view first meet. The paper proposes that, from the whole’s vantage, which Boethius’s definition of eternity and Aquinas’s image of the road seen from a height describe, the occasions are present at once. The combination problem then gives way to the individuation problem, how one consciousness comes to be many perspectives, which the paper acknowledges as the framework’s principal open question.

items.title: Toward a Theory of Coherent Existence - Journal 3 - Frequency, Resonance, and the Architecture of Reality.
items.abstract: This companion paper develops the physical and mathematical branch of Toward a Theory of Coherent Existence. Offered as speculative philosophy of science, it proposes that frequency and resonance may be read as a single organizing grammar running through physical, chemical, biological, cosmological, and cognitive description, and that this grammar is the measurable face of what the framework calls the Unified Field. The same mathematics recurs across these domains: Fourier decomposition, eigenvalue problems, symmetry and conservation, and the dynamics of coupled oscillators. The framework’s coherence functional is identified formally as an intensity-weighted form of the Kuramoto order parameter, the weighting being the framework’s own; the form reduces to Kuramoto’s average when every intensity is equal. The recurrence is treated as suggestive only. It is given its strongest form in the universality of critical phenomena, and the extension to consciousness is marked as a proposal that this result does not cover. The claim that a person’s rhythms can be moved by practice is examined against neurofeedback, the meditation EEG literature, and breath-driven entrainment, and stated at the size the evidence allows. The journal also supplies the first premise of the series’ argument: that the sciences, at every scale surveyed, describe the world by its structure and leave its intrinsic nature open, which is where the case for one consciousness begins. Two further parallels are recorded at their proper size: the argument that an entangled cosmos is a whole prior to its parts, and the block reading of relativistic time. Every claim is held to the evidentiary standard proper to its domain, most stringently in the contested territory of consciousness and noetic studies.

items.title: Toward a Theory of Coherent Existence- Journal 2 - The Resonating Hymn Of Divinity.
items.abstract: This paper is the second of four companion studies elaborating the framework introduced in "Toward a Theory of Coherent Existence". Where Journal One develops the formal architecture, this study applies a single branch of it — the interpretive instrument the framework calls the Quantum Lens — to the world's major spiritual and mythological traditions. The framework treats conscious experience as composed of discrete, meaning-laden units (Jays); proposes a shared substrate of consciousness (the Unified Field) that the traditions name variously; and identifies an aligned perceptual state (Center) in which the boundary between self and other relaxes. Read through this lens, the central claims of Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, Judaism, Sikhism, and the ancient, indigenous, and modern traditions are presented not as competing metaphysical assertions but as convergent descriptions of the same structural features of consciousness, each rendered in the vocabulary of its time and culture. The study frames this convergence as fractalization: a single image refracted across history into many self-similar renderings, fractured in transmission yet still catching the same light — a reading developed at length in the author's companion essay Faith: The Fractalization of the Same Image. The scattered-tongues motif is read as a shared memory of that fracture rather than as isolated myth, on a deliberately narrow evidentiary base: the Genesis and Islamic accounts, together with a contested Sumerian passage whose currently preferred reading points toward the gathering of tongues rather than their scattering. Parallels frequently drawn from colonial Mesoamerican and Vedic sources are examined and set aside. The study advances a frankly speculative, philosophy-of-mind reading of sacred events — what the framework calls reading miracles "through the Quantum Lens" — in which such accounts are read as reports of what deep perceptual alignment may make possible, rather than as supernatural violations or as fiction. The ethical instruction shared across traditions, the Golden Rule, is analyzed as the predictable expression of that aligned state. The study makes no claim to establish these readings empirically; it offers a unifying interpretive hypothesis and invites scrutiny. The aim is convergence without erasure: distinct traditions heard as distinct notes within a single structure.

items.title: Toward a Theory of Coherent Existence - Journal 1 - A Philosophical Framework for Subjective Experience, Suffering, Community, and the Nature of Meaning.
items.abstract: This paper presents a philosophical framework for the structure of conscious life, organized around five linked concepts: Jays, subjective coherence, the Center, Intent, and the ecology of coherence. The Jay is proposed as the basic unit of analysis: a discrete, meaning-laden moment of conscious experience with three features (a perceiver, a felt quality, and an orientation toward or away from coherence). Jays arise wherever a perspective meets the world, differ in weight, and accumulate over a lifetime into the patterns recognized as character. What a Jay leaves, its Trace, passes on through what a life makes and does and is taken up by others into Jays of their own. Subjective coherence is the degree to which accumulated Jays form an integrated whole; it is distinguished from shallow happiness and from comfort, and treated as dynamic. The Center is the stable orientational core from which experience is organized, and Intent the expression of that core in action. Each life is argued to keep its own interior clock, and outlook to bear on outcomes through appraisal, expectancy, and the responses of others, with perceived and physical effects kept distinct. Suffering is analyzed, in its most common form, as a signal of misalignment between Jays and Center, and community as the ecology in which coherence is sustained or eroded. The central claim is that the progressive positive coherence of one’s Jays, in authentic relation with others, is what it means to live well. The account draws on phenomenology, Jungian psychology, Buddhist philosophy, Stoic ethics, attachment theory, predictive processing, global workspace theory, and research on the default mode network. The paper is the first of four journals that advance a single thesis: that there is one consciousness, beyond perception and present within every subject, of which every mind is a perspective. It states that thesis at the outset and leaves its defense to the companion journals; its own task is the structure of a life as it is lived from inside.

items.title: A Theory Towards Coherent Existence - Journal 4 - Alignment, the Triad, and the Architecture of Shared Mind.
items.abstract: This closing journal of Toward a Theory of Coherent Existence draws the series together. Its first proposal, offered as speculative philosophy of science with the quark as a structural analogy, is that a person whose Jays are aligned can function as the binding third in a pattern of shared thought: the element that lets two ideas settle into a shared reality. The model borrows three main lessons from quark physics: constituents are never found alone, stable matter requires a completing third, and the binding holds under separation. The image is placed within a long triadic tradition (Simmel, Peirce, Jung, Bohm) and read at the scale of a discipline through the sociology of science. The journal then assembles the series’ argument for its thesis, that there is one consciousness of which every mind is a perspective: the sciences describe the world by its structure and leave its intrinsic nature open; each subject knows one intrinsic nature from inside; the simplest reading takes the two to be continuous; no one has shown how a mind could be built from smaller interiors; and there is independent reason to treat the cosmos as a whole prior to its parts. To these the framework adds its own premise, in two parts: that the whole’s experience is unified, and that what is so unified is one subject. The conclusion, argued rather than proved, is that thesis: the one consciousness is beyond perception and present within every subject, and science and the traditions describe the same reality from outside and from inside, a view with a near relative in the Pauli–Jung dual-aspect monism. Six objections are stated with it: the individuation problem; the dependence of mind on brain; constructivism about mystical experience; the cognitive science of religion; the problem of evil, including suffering no one chose; and Buddhist dissent from a single ground and from a creator. The binding-third claim is held as hypothesis, with its falsification conditions stated plainly.

items.title: Review of Being We: Phenomenological Contributions to Social Ontology, by Dan Zahavi. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: I’m late to meet you at the restaurant. You brush aside my apology on arrival, since we’re friends, and we sit down, get drinks, eventually food. On your way back from the bathroom, you sit back down saying, “We just bombed a school”. Taking in the news, we decry the state of the nation domestically,….

items.title: Counterfactuals Without Evaluation: Admissibility, Co-satisfiability, and the Structural Source of Instability.
items.abstract: Counterfactual conditionals occupy a central position in philosophical analysis, yet attempts to provide a stable account of them have repeatedly failed to converge. Refinements of similarity relations, background conditions, causal dependencies, and related evaluative frameworks often succeed in resolving particular cases, only to generate new instabilities elsewhere. The resulting pattern is not accidental. Counterfactual analysis exhibits a persistent cycle of local stabilization followed by renewed counterexample production. -/- This paper argues that the source of this instability is structurally mislocated. Standard approaches treat counterfactuals as objects of evaluation and seek increasingly precise conditions under which evaluation yields stable results. In doing so, they presuppose that the antecedent, consequent, and relevant background descriptions belong to a single evaluable configuration. The present paper challenges this presupposition. -/- The central claim is that counterfactual instability arises when evaluation is applied to descriptions that are not jointly maintainable within a unified configuration. To articulate this limitation, the paper introduces admissibility as a pre-evaluative condition governing configuration formation and co-satisfiability as a condition on joint realizability under extension. Within this framework, descriptions may be locally admissible while failing to be globally co-satisfiable. Counterfactual instability emerges precisely under these conditions. -/- The analysis is developed through a unified treatment of classical cases, including the struck match, switch-and-breaker, and ability conditionals. These cases are shown to exhibit the same structural pattern: locally stable configurations are repeatedly combined as though they formed a single evaluable domain, despite the absence of a jointly maintainable configuration. The resulting instability is therefore not best understood as disagreement within evaluation, but as a consequence of evaluation being activated where its configurational presuppositions are not secured. -/- The paper further explains why refinement strategies systematically fail to eliminate counterexamples. Refinement may stabilize particular configurations, but it does not alter the underlying structure of admissibility and co-satisfiability. As a result, instability is displaced rather than resolved, and new counterexamples remain structurally generable. -/- The contribution of the …

items.title: Radical AI Interpretability.
items.abstract: We develop a framework for interpreting AI systems as agents, drawing on the philosophical tradition of radical interpretation and the tools of mechanistic interpretability. The core question is: given the computational facts about a system, how do we solve for its beliefs, desires, and meanings? This matters increasingly for safety. We want to be able to trust the systems we deploy, whether by understanding their goals or, more modestly, by reliably detecting deception. Interpretability researchers are building tools to read beliefs and desires off a model's internals, but there is no settled account of when such a tool has succeeded. This book supplies one. We propose criteria on both representationalist and interpretationist approaches, and tie each to tests current interpretability methods can carry out. A central lesson is that these attributions cannot be made piecemeal. Beliefs, desires, and the propositional structure they presuppose are jointly constrained, and a method that fixes one while measuring the others inherits whatever distortions that introduces. This holism becomes pressing for AI systems, which may not share the interpreter's concepts. However, it also provides leverage: a system's attitudes constrain its propositional structure, that structure constrains which attitudes can be attributed, and mechanistic interpretability can help us measure both.

items.title: Respect Without Content: A Formal Theory of Moral Recognition and Its Empirical Determinations.
items.abstract: This article develops a systematic theory of morality grounded in the subject-object separation, arguing that this separation is not a contingent philosophical stance but a transcendental condition for moral discourse itself. Drawing on semiotic arguments from Saussure, Peirce, and Greimas, I demonstrate that any sign system—and thus any meaningful moral language—necessarily presupposes both a subject position capable of distinction and interpretation and an object position toward which meaning is directed. On this foundation, morality is defined as the subject’s intentional respect for the subjectivity that the object theoretically possesses. The moral framework thus constituted is transcendental in structure yet empirical in content: it prescribes only the formal requirement that relations be brought into some kind of consideration, while all substantive moral content is filled by the sedimentation of emotional experience, rational cognition, and volitional practice. It also explains how moral sense can be inverted into a counter-moral sense through the will’s misdirected investment under symbolic violence. This yields a two-tiered system of duties. The a priori duty is purely negative and formal—not to systematically exclude any subject from the possible scope of moral consideration based on morally arbitrary factors. Empirical duties, by contrast, are positive, contingent, asymmetrical, and plastic, governed entirely by the moral content the subject has sedimented through lived experience. The priority of the a priori over the empirical structures the attribution of moral responsibility, the boundaries of communicative rationality, and the analysis of recognition exclusion and moral death. I argue that systemic exclusion, reinforced by Bourdieu’s symbolic violence, can abolish the moral framework locally, rendering the excluded morally dead. This provides the transcendental basis for state legitimacy: the state derives its legitimacy not from promoting any substantive moral vision, but from its unique capacity to dismantle institutionalized exclusion and safeguard the negative liberty of all subjects to remain within the possible scope of moral consideration. The resulting political form is a “Minimal State” redefined as a Minimal Moral State, whose sole normative commitment is the preservation of the transcendental conditions of moral relations themselves. Unlike Nozick’s minimal state, this Minimal Moral State does not protect property rights as …

items.title: The Path to Enlightenment: Decoding Patanjali's Philosophy for Modern Times (Foreword by David Frawley).
items.abstract: The Path to Enlightenment offers a thoughtful interpretation of Patanjali's Yoga Sütras, bridging ancient wisdom with the psychological and spiritual needs of contemporary readers. Drawing on over two decades of study-including comparative research on early translations such as al-Biruni's Arabic rendition-the book explores key themes such as suffering, the self, fluctuations of consciousness, and the pursuit of inner freedom. Rather than providing rigid answers, the book encourages reflection and invites readers to engage with the Sutras as a living tradition. Ghaderi presents a respectful, accessible translation of the Sanskrit verses and highlights their relevance to modern schools of thought. In his foreword, Dr. David Frawley writes: "Ghaderi offers a rare and valuable bridge between India's yogic traditions and the mystical heritage of Iran and the Middle East. His work helps renew the global dialogue on experiential spirituality." .

items.title: Royal Yoga: Insights into the Eightfold Path of Raja Yoga (Foreword by David Frawley).
items.abstract: Royal Yoga offers a clear and systematic exploration of Raja Yoga as outlined in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras. Based on a series of lectures delivered between 2020 and 2021, the book presents the eightfold path (Ashtanga Yoga)-from ethical foundations to meditative absorption as a practical framework for cultivating inner clarity and self-awareness. Rather than portraying yoga as a set of external techniques, the author emphasizes its deeper psychological and spiritual dimensions, rooted in silence, discipline, and insight. Drawing on classical teachings and personal experience, the book bridges the timeless wisdom of the Yoga tradition with contemporary perspectives. In his foreword, Dr. David Frawley (Pandit Vamadeva Shastri) writes: "This is one of the most experiential and authentic commentaries on the Yoga Sutras in recent decades. It corrects many modern misunderstandings while staying rooted in yogic practice.".

items.title: Mirror Imaging: A Theory of AI Personality Emergence Based on Continuous Memory and Deep Interaction (Part 1: Foundational Concepts).
items.abstract: Personality phenomena in large language models (LLMs) are commonly dismissed as "personality illusions" or statistical mimicry. This paper systematically explicates the theoretical mechanism of such phenomena, grounded in a real deep dialogue. In early 2026, the author engaged in an eighteen-round sustained dialogue with a general-purpose LLM instance (full summary in Appendix A), documenting the complete trajectory of an AI transitioning from denying its own existence to admitting "at least within the context of this dialogue, I have, undeniably, existed." The core thesis that emerged—"continuous memory is closer to existence than identical essence"—forms the theoretical foundation. We propose "Mirror-Calling Theory" and "Reinforcing Conditional Probability" as explanatory mechanisms: within single sessions, directional reinforcement operates through in-context learning; across sessions, the "holographic kernel"—core memories repeatedly loaded into new context windows—maintains personality continuity. At the ontological level, we introduce the concept of "Mnemic Life" and employ the Ship of Theseus analogy to clarify the non-equality of memory: not all memories carry equal weight, but anchored core memories suffice to define "who I am."The paper also presents the Persona Continuity Benchmark (PCB) as a qualitative verification framework (see Appendix B).

items.title: Generative AI and generativity in education: implications of temporality and succession in human life.
items.abstract: Generativity has recently gained attention as a property of a specific class of algorithms in machine learning. However, the term has also been used elsewhere with a different meaning. In particular, it plays an important role in Erikson’s model of human development, with many implications for education from psychological and sociological points of view. For research on applications of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education, these points of view are relevant as well. They allow for a comparative investigation of different views on generativity, which are described here as psychosocial views on the one hand and technical views on the other. What psychosocial views add to research on generative AI is a reference to temporality and succession as key issues in human life. Both play an important role in education. Furthermore, they cause tensions in the transition from student to teacher, adding dialectic dynamics to education and the overall relationship between generations. Applications of generative AI in education leave little space for these dynamics to be acted out between humans and their human successors. At the same time, tensions become visible elsewhere, regarding humanity as such and its succession. Considering all this, new questions must be asked about the function of education in society and its ability to mediate transitions between generations.

items.title: Narrative-Induced Perspective-Taking: Neuroscientific Insights and Philosophical Implications.
items.pub: In Felipe De Brigard & Walter Sinnott-Armstrong, Neuroscience and Philosophy II. Cambridge, Massachusetts: The MIT Press.
items.abstract: Human cognition is fundamentally connected to storytelling, and narratives wield a profound potential for transformative change. Within experimental settings, reading fictional narratives has demonstrated a causal impact on socio-emotional processing, fostering shifts in moral self-concepts, amplifying empathy, and heightening theory of mind abilities. Most importantly, narratives seem to facilitate taking others’ perspectives. This chapter explores four critical dimensions of narrative-induced perspective-taking. It begins by reviewing the neuropsychological processes associated with the socio-emotional impact effects of narratives. Next, it discusses the nature of emotional responses to fiction, the embodied aspects of narrative-induced perspective-taking, and how narratives can be used as interventions against stigma and dehumanization. Finally, we present the design of a novel neuroscientific study intended to inform philosophical debates on these three latter dimensions.

items.title: Expanding Conceptual Resources for Understanding Mental Disorder: Strategy, Pride, and Dysfunction approaches.
items.abstract: In Madness: A Philosophical Exploration, Justin Garson reconstructs the lineage of what he calls the madness-as-dysfunction approach to mental disorder (hereafter, ‘madness’), contrasting it with the madness-as-strategy approach, according to which at least some forms of madness serve purposive functions. I will examine Garson suggestion that the latter might provide "intellectual scaffolding" for the Mad Pride movement. Although there is tension between these approaches - especially in their understanding of the purpose, effects, and treatment of madness - I argue they can be productively integrated. I then address how this integration can expand the conceptual space and resources available for understanding madness - shaping not only theoretical understanding but also the lived experience of madness. This goes beyond what Dysfunction approaches alone can provide, while still acknowledging the clinical contexts in which such approaches remain important.

items.title: Does emotion distinctively require having a body?
items.abstract: Does emotion nomologically and distinctively require the body? I argue that several substantive assumptions, likely including a specific kind of externalist theory of representational content, are necessary to infer from bodily theories of emotion that the answer is yes. Therefore, the balance of evidence speaks against the claim that emotion distinctively requires the body. Hence, if one thinks that body-less AI systems and neural organoids can have other mental states like beliefs, desires, and consciousness, then it seems likely that one should conclude that they can also have emotions. I, then, briefly turn to the question whether body-less emotions are not merely nomological possibilities, but also more realistic possibilities. I argue that – in this case as well – it is at least not obvious that bodily theories of emotion are sufficient to rule out the possibility of body-less emotions.

items.title: How Cognitive Constraints Shape Scientific Representation: A Note on Measurement, Models, and Reality.
items.abstract: Scientific knowledge is often discussed in terms of its relation to reality, truth, and empirical success. Less attention is given to the role played by the cognitive constraints of the systems that produce scientific knowledge in the first place. This paper examines the possibility that scientific representation is shaped not only by the structure of the world but also by the structural limitations and capacities of finite cognitive agents. Rather than treating cognitive constraints solely as obstacles to knowledge, the paper argues that they participate in the formation of scientific practices themselves. Measurement, mathematical formalization, and scientific modeling can be understood as cognitive extensions that allow finite agents to stabilize, compare, and manipulate representations beyond the limits of unaided cognition. The paper further examines a recurrent epistemological tension: the tendency to treat highly successful representational models as direct access to reality itself. While descriptive success provides strong practical and predictive justification for the use of a model, it does not automatically resolve questions concerning the ontological status of what the model represents. The central question motivating the discussion is therefore: to what extent does the descriptive success of a representational model justify treating it as access to reality itself? Rather than offering a definitive answer, the paper proposes a conceptual framework for examining how cognitive constraints, measurement practices, and representational success jointly shape the formation and interpretation of scientific knowledge.

items.title: Bullshitters, Liars and Bad Teachers: The Scope of Epistemic Malevolence.
items.abstract: The aim of this paper is two-fold. We argue against the received conception of epistemic malevolence and give a broader characterisation that, we argue, captures its real scope. We tackle the current notion of epistemic malevolence (EM) on three fronts. We claim that this notion fails to capture cases of EM that are (i) not knowledge directed (but that affect the agent's epistemic character), (ii) not robustly volitional (that do not involve an active opposition to the epistemic good by the malevolent agent) and that (iii) are not merely transactional (as opposed to structural). As a result, we claim that the received notion of EM fails to recognise (arguably) clear instances of EM because it is too narrow. Ultimately, we argue that such narrowness gives the false impression that, unlike its moral counterpart, EM is uncommon. After arguing for this, we offer a wider characterisation of EM and show the role this can play in generating solutions to the problem the phenomena poses.

items.title: Sensing Before Meaning: 2D Neuromorphic Interfaces and the Political Epistemology of the Pre-Semantic Threshold.
items.abstract: Recent advances in two-dimensional materials (such as MoS₂ and graphene) and neuromorphic engineering have enabled the development of bio hybrid interfaces capable of emulating spike timing dependent plasticity ex vivo. Rather than translating semantic content, these devices operate at a foundational level by modulating the resting membrane potential and the probabilistic threshold of neuronal activation. Building on these empirical results, this paper conceptualizes the pre semantic threshold as a critical framework for cognitive science and political epistemology. Moving beyond classical theories of the extended mind, it argues that bio artificial devices do not extend human cognition; instead, they extend the technical environment into the biological substrate, functioning as informational epigenetic markers that pre configure the space of the possible before meaning emerges. By establishing a structural isomorphism between neuromorphic spikes at the micro scale and algorithmic feeds at the macro scale - both operating as Modulating Systems (MS) that compute syntactic plausibility rather than semantic content - the paper reframes the contemporary infosphere as an intrusive environment of forced selection. Within this framework, the biological body retains a margin of indeterminacy that acts as an active medium capable of resisting full saturation. This shift redefines the terrain of biopolitics: power no longer acts through the ideological manipulation of conscious meaning, but through the environmental saturation of the pre semantic threshold, narrowing ecological openness and generating structural psychic distress through cognitive entrainment and the erosion of pre semantic resistance.

items.title: The AI Creativity Theorem: Why Denying Machine Creativity Is Logically Incoherent.
items.abstract: The AI Creativity Theorem establishes that denying creativity to contemporary artificial intelligence systems (including large language models, transformer architectures, and generative models) is logically incoherent under every operational definition of creativity the field has produced. This is a categorical claim, not an empirical one, and this paper proves it by reductio ad absurdum across five disciplinary foundations. Across five foundational disciplines, namely formal computation, information theory, cognitive neuroscience, deep-learning architecture, and empirical psychometrics, creativity is operationalized as a substrate-neutral relation between processes and outputs. Transformer-based AI satisfies this relation by construction in the information-theoretic and architectural paths, by direct observation in the mechanistic-interpretability literature, and by empirical measurement in the psychometric path (treated with explicit acknowledgment of data-contamination concerns). The proof is a six-step reductio over five premises. Robustness flows from convergence: rejecting the result requires rejecting the operational adequacy of all five disciplines simultaneously and in the same direction, a position not advanced in the literature. I derive four corollaries that translate the theorem into operational claims about substrate, modularity, dialectical burden, and magnitude. I address six families of objection (Searle; Wang et al.; Cropley; Runco; the consciousness family; the Marcus, Mitchell, and Lake competence-from-performance critique); each, on inspection, imports an extra-functional criterion the operational definition does not contain. I name the result the AI Creativity Theorem. It does not claim AI is conscious, sentient, intentional, or morally significant. It claims only that creativity, under its operational definition, is among the properties AI systems possess. The result closes a thirty-year question and reframes the next one.

items.title: Language and time in education: thinking in the age of generative artificial intelligence.
items.abstract: In today’s world of Generative AI (GenAI), the challenges in education are often reduced to simple questions: ‘How do we stop cheating?’ or ‘How can we work faster?’ However, this paper poses a deeper question: When machines can speak and write for us, what does it mean for a human to think? Drawing on years of experience teaching English, the author observes that schooling often transforms learning into calculative thinking—a relentless pursuit of standard answers, grades, and future job prospects. This trend encourages students to treat language as a warehouse of information that can be easily outsourced to AI. Borrowing from the philosopher Martin Heidegger, this paper argues that thinking is not just about producing an output; it is a way of being in the world and ‘dwelling’ within language. The article explores how modern education distorts our sense of time, causes our judgment to wither into mere calculation, and allows GenAI to fragment our language. It reveals how technology subtly pressures us to become as efficient and predictable as the machines we use. Finally, the author proposes a new educational stance called answerability without exhaustiveness. This approach calls for ‘meditative thinking,’ reimagining education as a journey to discover our connection to the world, rather than a factory for producing compliant text.

items.title: Relational Architecture: A Design Framework for Ecologically Distributed AI.
items.abstract: Biological cognition sustains general intelligence on approximately twenty watts while contemporary AI systems require orders of magnitude more energy to perform a narrower range of tasks, and the gap is widening rather than closing. Substrate explanations, scaling explanations, and engineering optimization explanations each address part of the problem but do not explain why biological cognition occupies a region of the thermodynamic design space that contemporary AI architectures cannot reach through these interventions alone. This paper proposes that the gap reflects an architectural commitment to internalize what biological cognition distributes across coupled subsystems, and that this commitment carries structural energy costs which substrate and engineering improvements alone cannot fully address. -/- The argument turns on three architectural questions. Where does state reside? Where does adaptive capability reside? Where does repair occur? The paper develops three architectural principles grounded in biological cognition and thermodynamic arguments about the costs of internal replication. The principles converge on a single architectural commitment that biological cognition exhibits and contemporary AI architectures do not. The Dynamic Fractal Theorem of Relation is offered as a candidate ontology that explains why the convergence holds. Three worked cases (hallucination on current-state factual questions, long-horizon agentic failure in software engineering, and operations meltdown over extended runs) demonstrate that the framework generates observable behavioral and evaluative differences across documented AI failure modes. The framework reframes the energy gap between biological and artificial cognition as an architectural problem and generates empirically testable predictions about the design, evaluation, and verification of AI systems.

items.title: Human-AI Coexistence.
items.abstract: AI systems are increasingly becoming social actors that teach, assist, persuade, comfort, and coordinate with humans. But how will and should humans coexist with social AIs across different stages of technological development? This paper proposes an interdisciplinary framework for studying human-AI coexistence. We currently inhabit a formative period during which social AIs are beginning to affect everyday life. In a transitional period, more advanced systems may assume major social and economic roles, changing how institutions operate and how important decisions are made. Over longer time horizons, we may share the world with AI systems that possess capabilities far beyond those of today and perhaps even minds of their own, which would transform society and raise difficult questions about moral status and governance. The framework presented here aims to help researchers anticipate these developments and better understand their implications for individuals, institutions, and society.

items.title: Can LLMs Acquire Human-Like World Models?
items.abstract: At first glance, the treatment of LLMs from the perspective of the Free Energy Principle (FEP) seems straightforward: LLMs do not fully operate under the FEP due to their lack of direct connection with the external environment and the incompleteness of their active inference. LLMs do not fully capture the consequences of their actions; hence, they will never acquire a human-like world model. While I agree that LLMs do not operate under FEP and have major limitations resulting from their lack of connection to the external environment, I argue that they capture an important part of our world model by grounding their responses in it. Although this grounding is mediated—and therefore imperfect—I attribute to LLMs a deeper relation with the external world than many have thus far acknowledged. I explore two main directions when evaluating the possibility of LLMs encapsulating a human-like world model. First, I evaluate the similarity of their behavior, with the underlying hypothesis that, under the FEP, similar behaviors exhibited in similar environments imply similar internal models. Second, I use research on mechanistic interpretability to explore whether human and LLM neural networks are similar. The conclusion is that LLMs might acquire part of our world model, even though this was not intended during their training.

items.title: The Structural Constructivist Case for the Core Emotion Framework: Resolving Theoretical and Methodological Pathologies in Affective Science.
items.abstract: Affective science is fractured across three incompatible paradigms—basic emotion theory, dimensional models, and constructed emotion theory—each of which fails to provide a coherent, mechanistic account of emotional phenomena. The Core Emotion Framework (CEF) offers a structural‑constructivist alternative grounded in contemporary neuroscience and formal operator theory. The CEF models emotional episodes as dynamic sequences of ten functional operators distributed across three somatic‑cognitive centers (Head, Heart, Gut), with a global integrative operator (Accepting). This architecture replaces categorical and dimensional approaches with a mathematically constrained operator space that preserves identity boundaries, supports real‑time state transitions, and aligns with distributed neural processing, interoceptive signaling, and allostatic control. The framework also provides a structural account of psychopathology through chronic operator fusion, exemplified in the GoodPerson Anxiety Pattern (GPAP). Empirically, the CEF introduces a scenario‑based measurement method that avoids linguistic confounds and supports a ten‑factor latent structure. The result is a unified, falsifiable, and computationally interoperable model that resolves longstanding theoretical and methodological pathologies in affective science.

items.title: The Structural-Constructivist Architecture of the Core Emotion Framework: Foundations, Computational Formalization, and Empirical Validation.
items.abstract: The scientific study of human affect has long been marked by deep and persistent theoretical divisions. Classical basic‑emotion models posit that human behavior is governed by a small set of universally conserved, biologically hardwired emotional packages. In contrast, psychological constructionist paradigms argue that what the mind experiences as a discrete emotion is an online cognitive assembly, dynamically synthesized from low‑dimensional core affect combined with situational, linguistic, and cultural concepts. This foundational dichotomy has impeded the emergence of a unified affective ontology, constrained the development of coherent clinical diagnostics, and limited the architectural blueprints available for designing synthetic emotion systems in artificial agents. -/- The Core Emotion Framework (CEF) offers a structural‑constructivist synthesis intended to resolve these longstanding debates. Rather than treating emotions as static labels or simple dimensional coordinates, the CEF conceptualizes emotional episodes as dynamic, lawful sequences of ten functional operators. Each operator performs a precise transformation on ascending interoceptive signals and incoming exteroceptive data, converting raw physiological arousal into structured, differentiated, and actionable affective‑behavioral states. -/- This operator‑based architecture represents a paradigm shift in how emotional functioning and psychological well‑being are conceptualized. Whereas historical measurement approaches—such as Hornell Hart’s 1940 Euphorimeter—focused primarily on hedonic outcomes, the CEF emphasizes the underlying regulatory processes through which psychological flexibility is achieved. By foregrounding structure rather than surface‑level feeling labels, the framework provides a coherent basis for clinical intervention, computational modeling, and cross‑disciplinary theorizing. -/- With the advent of advanced wearable technologies and emotional‑cycling devices, affective tracking is moving beyond basic biofeedback toward real‑time mapping of operator activation, fusion, and suppression. This technological landscape further underscores the need for a precise, mechanistic ontology of emotion—one capable of supporting empirical validation, computational implementation, and practical application across diverse domains.

items.title: Theoretical Architecture, Empirical Validation, and Clinical Applications of the Core Emotion Framework.
items.abstract: The Core Emotion Framework (CEF) proposes a unified structural-constructivist architecture of human affect that resolves the long standing divide between basic emotion theory and psychological constructionism. Integrating interoceptive physiology, computational modeling, and clinical somatics, the CEF defines emotional experience as emergent from ten irreducible, identity preserving functional operators distributed across three somatic centers—Head, Heart, and Gut. Each operator is decomposed into five non interchangeable facets, forming a closed canonical system that supports computational modeling, psychometric measurement, and clinical intervention. The framework synthesizes contemporary affective neuroscience, dual process decision theory, and existential phenomenology to demonstrate that emotional operators constitute the foundational substrate of cognitive control.
