items.title: The Downsides of Gratitude.
items.abstract: Over the last few decades, the positive effects of gratitude at a psychological, moral, social, and spiritual level have been explored and applauded. Its negative side, however, has received little attention. This article identifies four main negative aspects of gratitude -the unpleasant emotions it might lead to and the fact that feeling grateful might generate or overshadow unfair circumstances. We review the literature on gratitude—from philosophy, anthropology, theology, and psychology—to identify the few occasions in which the scholarship points to negative aspects; we group these cases together into four categories, and explore them. The four cases analyzed are: 1) the "gratitude paradox," 2) feelings of debt toward the benefactor, 3) feelings of inferiority, and 4) when gratitude replaces apology. Our aim is not to contradict the previous work on these aspects, which is scant but rigorous. We complement it, by arguing that gratitude does not stem from what happens, but rather from the narrative that one builds and the conditional syllogism underpinning this narrative, which prescribes certain emotions. Last, we hold that, while gratitude constitutes a positive emotion, self-help books, counselors, and social media promoting gratitude practices should remember why it might also signal problematic social dynamics.

items.title: Seven barriers to the ethical governance of artificial intelligence in defence.
items.abstract: The ethical governance of AI in defence confronts a paradox: principles proliferate while implementation falters. This systematic review of 1085 publications exposes why frameworks flounder where ethical governance matters most. We identify seven barriers—governance and structural, conceptual, strategic, operational, relational and cultural, technical and data, and resource constraints—that operate as an interconnected system. Governance and structural barriers dominate the literature. This prominence may reflect their visibility rather than their primacy; technical, operational, and cultural dynamics remain harder to trace but are equally consequential. The challenges created by these seven barriers are severe but not insurmountable. We propose three strategic interventions: establishing authoritative, interoperable governance architectures that transcend organisational and national boundaries; building institutional capacity through dedicated resources and interdisciplinary expertise; and integrating ethical governance as core capability throughout the AI lifecycle rather than as compliance retrofit. This systemic analysis advances scholarship beyond principle enumeration and towards understanding the institutional, structural, and technical conditions under which ethical governance of AI in the defence domain can acquire operational traction in contested strategic environments.

items.title: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928.
items.abstract: In the 1880s Britain, philosophers developed what would become a half-century obsession with time. Back then, time was widely held to be unreal; by the 1920s, it was widely held to be real. This sea-change was gradual but sweeping. Early time realists focused on defending the reality of time. From around 1900, they began asking fresh questions about the nature of time, all loosely concerned with its dynamicity—its ‘moving on’. Are the past and future real? Is time fundamentally an ‘A-series’ or ‘B-series’—is it about past, present, and future, or earlier and later? Does time have an intrinsic direction? These questions are still widely debated today. This book investigates the reinvention of time realism and follows the emergence of these new, in-house realist debates. It argues these questions are not perennial: they are deeply rooted within this historical context.

items.title: 1Introduction.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: In 1880s Britain, philosophers developed what would become a half-century obsession with time. Back then, time was widely held to be unreal; by the 1920s, it was widely held to be real. This chapter provides an overview of that shift, and of the new questions about time developed by realists. It argues that this philosophy of time era matters for several reasons: scholars are increasingly paying it attention; the historical philosophers themselves really cared about time; and, during this period, time became central to metaphysical debates more widely. This chapter goes on to give an overview of the book as a whole.

items.title: C114Three Victorian Ideas around Time.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: Within Victorian Britain, scientists, historians, theists, mathematicians, and writers gradually proliferated three ideas about time. Time enables evolution. Time is linear. Time brings progress. Across the following chapters of this study, we’ll see philosophers reacting to these ideas again and again. This chapter describes them, showing how important they were to the period.Within Victorian Britain, scientists, historians, theists, mathematicians, and writers gradually proliferated three ideas about time. Time enables evolution. Time is linear. Time brings progress. With regard to evolution, this chapter will consider Herbert Spencer and Charles Darwin. With regard to linearity, it will consider developments in chronography (i.e. visual representations of history), evolution, chronophotography, mathematical theories of the fourth dimension, and time travel literature. With regard to progress, it will dig into the reasons Victorians had for believing their future would be better than the past: increased living standards, whig history, and progressive theories of evolution. All these ideas form the background against which new metaphysics of time emerged.

items.title: C8157Bertrand Russell on the B-Series and Mental-Physical Time 1901–1915.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: In 1908, J. M. E. McTaggart wondered if the ‘real nature of time only contains... the B series’. If B-theory is understood as affirming this then, along with many other scholars, the author read Russell as a B-theorist. This chapter focuses on a key part of Russell’s B-theory: his distinction between ‘physical’, objective time, comprising simultaneity, before, and after; and ‘mental’, subjective time, comprising past, present, and future. This original distinction first appears in Russell’s well-cited Monist paper, “On the Experience of Time”. This chapter contextualises “On the Experience of Time” within Russell’s earlier work, before digging into the paper itself. It argues Russell was spurred to write the paper out of frustration with recent accounts of time produced by four of his contemporaries: J. M. E. McTaggart, G. E. Moore, Henri Bergson, and Karin Costelloe-Stephen.

items.title: C230The Rise of Unreal Time and British Idealism 1883–1893.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: During the 1880s and 1890s, philosophers widely held time to be unreal. This chapter contextualises, and explores, that anti-realism. The bulk of this chapter is dedicated to British idealism, the movement which accounts for the vast majority of anti-realists about time.Section 2 provides background: an overview of British metaphysics of time from the eighteenth to late nineteenth centuries. Section 3 considers the rise of British idealism and time anti-realism, illustrating the latter through the 1880s and 1890s work of T. H. Green, Edward Caird, and F. H. Bradley. Section 4 speculates that anti-realism about time snowballed amongst idealists because it offered a religion-friendly way to accommodate Darwinian evolution. Section 5 discusses Charles Hinton and Victoria Welby, who approached anti-realism about time from a novel direction: conceiving it as the fourth dimension of space.

items.title: C351Time Realism.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: This chapter explores the minority of philosophers arrayed against British idealism, many of whom defended time realism. It also considers how two theories bolstered their position: the specious present and evolution.Section 2 gives an overview of nineteenth-century realisms and other opposition to British idealism during the late nineteenth century. Section 3 introduces ‘specious present’ theories, which hold that our experiential present has duration, including those of Shadworth Hodgson and William James. Section 4 explains that several early realists about time were motivated by evolution, including James McCosh, Henry Sidgwick, Charles B. Upton, and C. Lloyd Morgan. It focuses on the work of two figures who provide exceptionally detailed arguments from evolution to time realism: that of ‘new realist’ Samuel Alexander and ‘humanist’ F. C. S. Schiller. Section 5 concludes with a reflection: despite this burgeoning realism about time, none of its proponents yet questioned the nature of time.

items.title: C9183Hilda Oakeley’s Time Realism.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: Within late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century British philosophy, Hilda Oakeley became the first woman philosopher to defend realism about time. In 1911, she argues for the reality of time; from 1913 onwards, she discusses the nature of time, her metaphysics exhibiting Bergsonian features. This chapter studies the origins of Oakeley’s views. Her work is important for various reasons. First, she is an early time realist, and her reasons for defending realism are quite different to those of, say, Samuel Alexander, F. C. S. Schiller, G. E. Moore, or Bertrand Russell. Second, Oakeley is unique as the only British idealist who accepts the reality of time. Finally, Oakeley offers a very early growing block theory, comparable with that of C. D. Broad.

items.title: C592The Genesis of J. M. E. McTaggart’s “The Unreality of Time” 1893–1908.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: McTaggart’s 1908 “The Unreality of Time” has long vexed philosophers. Despite the fascination with this argument for time’s unreality, there is very little work on its origins. This chapter investigates and poses a puzzle. In his 1893 to 1901 work on Hegel, McTaggart pronounced himself unable to explain how the appearance of time arises from a timeless reality. Although McTaggart wrestles with time in this early work, there are no indications he is reaching a solution. Yet, in 1908, McTaggart bursts forth with a novel argument for the unreality of time and a novel explanation for why we misperceive time as real. What happened between 1901 and 1908? The author argues he developed a clutch of fresh views, sparked by engagement with a source outside Hegel: new work on the specious present.

items.title: C7143A French Interlude.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: French philosopher Henri Bergson had been writing for years when his work exploded into British philosophy. From 1909 onwards, his popularity surged: Bergsonian thought appears in many later thinkers throughout this book. This chapter explores some of Bergson's key views on time: he holds that time is non-linear; he arguably offers a growing block theory; he holds that time brings novelty; and evolutionary novelty is powered by a nisus, the élan vital. This chapter goes on to chart the spread of Bergson’s work through Britain, via the likes of Victoria Welby, H. Wildon Carr, and none other than a past Prime Minister—Arthur Balfour.

items.title: G. E. Moore’s Common Sense Realism.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: Early analytic philosopher G. E. Moore is not known for his metaphysics of time. Within Moore scholarship, his metaphysical views on time are under-studied; within the philosophy of time, his views are omitted. This chapter focuses on Moore’s most substantial, realist discussion of time, advanced in a set of 1910–1911 lectures, later published as Some Main Problems of Philosophy (hereafter, Main Problems). This chapter shows these lectures defend a Common Sense realism about time, presentism, and A-theory. Moore is not currently recognised as a presentist or an A-theorist, yet appreciating that he held both positions is important. This chapter argues that Moore offers the earliest sustained defence of presentism in English-language philosophy. And, if Bertrand Russell is the ‘father’ of B-theory, Moore is the ‘father’ of A-theory.

items.title: C15341Arthur Eddington and Time’s Arrow into the Progressive Future 1919–1928.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: Arthur Eddington is best known as an early advocate of Einstein’s relativity theories. Yet he also produced a complex metaphysic of time, developed across works from 1919 onward and blooming in his 1927 Gifford lectures, published in 1928 as The Nature of the Physical World. At first glance, this metaphysic appears to be in the style of Bertrand Russell. Eddington defends (what he takes to be) the world described by physics: a ‘block’ containing a real past, present, and future. Yet Eddington swiftly complicates that picture, via his directly apprehended, progress-indicating ‘arrow’ of time. This chapter explores his account of time’s directionality and its origins, arguing it lies not in the work of Henri Bergson. Instead, it’s sourced in the Victorian empiricists W. K. Clifford and Karl Pearson, and mystic theism.

items.title: C13281Time, Events, and Passage in A. N. Whitehead’s London Years 1911–1920.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: Across his career, A. N. Whitehead holds realism about time. As he charmingly puts it in a 1922 symposium, he admits the ‘spaciness’ and ‘time-iness’ of nature. Yet for Whitehead, time derives from events—temporally extended slabs of nature. Events include molecule vibrations in my hot mug of tea, the life of a tree across a sunny afternoon, and a rotation of the Earth around the sun. This chapter will consider Whitehead’s earliest metaphysics of time and events, exploring their genesis and development during his London era, especially from 1911 to 1920. Although Whitehead’s London texts are usually taken to defend eternalism, this chapter shows his remarks on temporal passage create serious tensions for this reading, for they forcefully point to an unreal future. Further, this chapter argues that if Whitehead borrowed anything from Henri Bergson during this period, it is the notion that the passage of time is ontologically creative.

items.title: C14313C. D. Broad on Eternalism and Growing Block Theory 1913–1928.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: Over the course of his long career, Broad’s philosophy of time evolved, comprising three phases. Each phase is associated with a particular text. The first, associated with Broad’s 1921 encyclopaedia article “Time”, offers eternalism. The second phase, associated with Broad’s 1923 Scientific Thought, offers what may be the first English-language defence of growing block theory. The third phase, associated with the second, 1938 volume of Broad’s Examination of McTaggart’s Philosophy, appears to offer a new theory altogether. This chapter explores the first and second phases. This chapter shows that Broad’s early eternalism is marked by his admiration for Russell and an antagonism towards Bergson. Further, this chapter argues Broad was driven away from eternalism by a problem he found in Alexander: a newfound concern with the direction of time. He likely arrived at the unreality of the future as a solution following his earlier apparent reading of Whitehead as a growing block theorist.

items.title: C10201Karin Costelloe-Stephen’s Bergsonism and ‘The Facts’ of Time 1911–1922.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: Karin Costelloe-Stephen worked at the crest of the ‘Bergson boom’. She placed herself at the centre of the controversy between Bertrand Russell and Henri Bergson, defending the Frenchman against Russell’s attacks. Making extensive use of unpublished archival letters, this chapter shows that Costelloe-Stephen ‘translated’ Bergsonian philosophy into Cambridge philosophy, with the aim of converting ‘Cambridge scoffers’ such as Russell. Her attempts at converting the scoffers failed, yet her subtle, fascinating ‘translation’ goes far beyond Bergson. As this chapter reads Costelloe-Stephen, she conceives Bergsonian intuition about time to be a form of Russellian acquaintance. Further, unlike Bergson and her fellow Bergsonians, she argues that the contents of a present experience are simultaneous and non-relational. This is a claim that Russell would ultimately take as a target: having read Costelloe-Stephen's work, Russell went on to argue that the contents of a present experience need not be simultaneous and are relational.

items.title: C466The British Presentism–Eternalism Debate, Founded 1897.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: Do the past and future exist? This chapter argues that, within the history of English-language philosophy, this question was first explicitly posed and debated in an 1897 Aristotelian Society symposium, “In What Sense, If Any, Do Past and Future Time Exist?”. Three participants gave papers: Bernard Bosanquet, Shadworth Hodgson, and G. E. Moore. The symposium came about as a response to work from Hermann Lotze and F. H. Bradley, who act as invisible debate participants. Between these five men, we can distinguish three positions: presentism in Lotze; time anti-realism in Bradley, Bosanquet, and Moore; and eternalism in Hodgson. This chapter explores each of the three points on this triangle, enquiring into their assumptions and arguments.This chapter conflicts with a much-cited thesis from philosopher of time John Bigelow: that ‘everyone’ held presentism until the nineteenth century. Along the way, this thesis is discussed and ultimately rejected.

items.title: C11231Sexism and Time.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: The belief that time brings progress was widespread, taken up by metaphysicians of all kinds: idealists and realists, temporal realists and anti-realists, eternalists and presentists. The problem is that Victorian beliefs about progress have a dark side: they come bundled with sexism. This chapter argues that, when progress is baked into philosophies of time, it surely bakes in patriarchal and sexist assumptions too. It goes on to argue that Henri Bergson’s theory of time offered tools to overthrow patriarchal accounts, and therein lay part of its appeal for Hilda Oakeley and Karin Costelloe-Stephen: Bergsonian time has an affinity with their feminism.The chapter proceeds as follows. Section 2 returns to Victorian progress. Building on the groundbreaking work of literature scholar Patricia Murphy, this idea is shown to be rooted in deeply patriarchal, sexist ideas. Section 3 offers some background on Bergson and feminism more generally, showing that the Frenchman’s stress on change and intuition was generally seen as feminist. Section 4 explores the specific appeal Bergson’s philosophy of time held for feminist philosophers of time: it offers the means to resist patriarchal accounts of time. This chapter argues that Oakeley and Costelloe-Stephen took up precisely the elements of Bergsonian time that were compatible with their feminist politics. This helps explain the appeal that Bergsonian time held for these philosophers, and opens up a fresh, feminist perspective on the metaphysics of our period.

items.title: C12249Samuel Alexander’s ‘Generative’ Time and Its Eternalist Universe 1911–1920.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: From around 1911, Alexander began developing a sweeping new metaphysic. This culminated in two series of Gifford lectures, delivered in 1917 and 1918, published in 1920 as Space, Time, and Deity. It unites space and time as the grand entity ‘Space-Time’, the eternalist emergence base of all else.Existing scholarship on Alexander’s account of time focuses on Space, Time, and Deity, alongside later texts. This chapter undertakes a new enquiry, focusing on earlier texts. These include Alexander’s published articles; his 1914 and 1915 Samuel Hall lectures, unpublished in his lifetime; and Alexander’s correspondence with emergentist C. Lloyd Morgan, which remains unpublished and has not been previously discussed by scholars. It considers Alexander’s engagement with Henri Bergson, Bertrand Russell, and physics. It will be shown that Alexander defends eternalism against Bradley’s timeless block universe and against growing block theory and presentism.

items.title: 373Afterword.
items.pub: In Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Real Time: A Reinvention in British Metaphysics 1883-1928
items.abstract: This “Afterwords” concludes our study, sketching developments within the philosophy of time from the 1920s onwards. It includes the work of Absolute idealist May Sinclair, who considers time a battleground between British idealism and the new realism; R. G. Collingwood's presentism, and his vivid objections to a real past; J. W. Dunne's hypertime; J. M. E. McTaggart's reworked arguments against time's reality; the brief but intriguing remarks of Frank Ramsey; Hilda Oakeley's later critique of her fellow idealist, McTaggart; C. D. Broad's mysterious 'third view' on time; Susan Stebbing's A-theory and its connection with that of G. E. Moore; and the studies of time produced by John Alexander Gunn, Louise Heath, and Mary Francis Cleugh.

items.title: Every Breath Brings Me Closer to Home—Auto‐Ethnographic Reflections About the Meaning of Somatic and Creative Practices in Facing Challenging Life Events.
items.abstract: Death is the prerequisite of life, life the prerequisite of death, just like chaos and order, light and shadow, joy and despair, love and grief, are each other's premises. When life breaks into pieces, despair may ensue, but darkness offers possibilities to tap into the light. The use of experiential somatic practices and creative expressions can reach deep and help illuminate conscious and unconscious processes, shedding light onto deeply rooted beliefs, emotions, and longings. This paper argues for the potential of exploring experiential somatic and creative work and expressions using arts-based research methods, facilitating the exploration of the complexities of experiential intra- and inter-subjective embodied spaces and processes in healing. Through an auto-ethnographic and a/r/tographic approach, the current exploration delves into the meaning of experiential somatic work and creative expressions, combined with witnessing, for dealing with challenging life events. It tentatively explores the potential of such work to bring hope where there is despair and life where there is death, which can be befriended. Such work can help move through suppression and closedness towards expansion and openness, promoting the appreciation of every breath and what it means to be in a physical body, with its human messiness and divine perfection. This paper shows that innovative research approaches can provide insight into complex experiential dimensions of somatic and creative work in supporting wellbeing.

items.title: ◉ The Pathologizing of Doubt: Evidence Poverty, Deconstruction, and Pastoral Diagnosis in Frank Turek's Apologetics Podcast Corpus.
items.abstract: Explaining why someone doubts Christianity does not by itself answer that person's objection. Personal circumstances can justify reduced confidence, but the reduction must be supported, relevant to the affected evidence, and proportionate to the limitation identified. Eight purposively selected episodes from a local archive of 329 transcripts of I Don't Have Enough FAITH to Be an ATHEIST illustrate failures and successful applications of this distinction. The central cases classify moral concerns as non-intellectual, use mixed motives to discount evidential engagement, and move from predicted resistance to a judgment about the character of the inquiry. The analysis distinguishes an objection's merit from receptivity to an answer and the public support for a diagnosis from a speaker's possible private knowledge. Other passages combine care with substantive inquiry; counterevidence is assessed at the passage level rather than treating whole episodes as uniformly exemplary. Worked hypothetical cases distinguish a mere motive, grounds for caution before an error is proved, and a demonstrated error. A practical test and annotated reconstruction specify the scope and degree of any justified discount. The result is a criticism of particular replies, not a verdict on Christianity, the psychology of absent people, or the prevalence of the pattern across the archive.

items.title: ✶ Normativity Disambiguated: Moral Authority, Rational Coherence, and the Equivocation Behind "The Normative".
items.abstract: Philosophers often speak of normativity as if it named a single phenomenon requiring a unified metaphysical explanation. This paper argues that the term is systematically overburdened. In discussions of moral ontology, normativity usually refers to categorical practical authority: obligations, requirements, or reasons that purport to bind agents independently of their contingent desires, projects, values, or commitments. In discussions of rationality, logic, epistemology, and decision theory, however, normativity usually refers to structural coherence: requirements internal to an agent's beliefs, ends, standards, methods, or avowed commitments. These are not merely two applications of one deep concept. They have different logical forms. Moral normativity purports to evaluate the content of an agent's commitments from a standpoint independent of those commitments. Rational normativity evaluates the consistency of commitments from within a standpoint already adopted. A basketball player who claims to want victory while deliberately scoring for the opposing team illustrates the distinction. The player has acted incoherently relative to his stated aim, but he has not thereby acted immorally. His error is not moral wickedness but practical inconsistency. The paper also argues that the denotation of normativity can be clarified by attending to its etymological neighbors and antonyms: normal, abnormal, and abandoning norms suggest deviation from a standard, pattern, rule, or expectation, not automatic moral wrongness. The paper argues that much philosophical confusion results from treating normativity as a free-standing noun rather than a parameterized relation: normative for whom, relative to which standard, in which domain, with what force, and conditional on what? Once these parameters are made explicit, the existence of rational, logical, or instrumental normativity gives no independent support to moral realism. The moral non-realist can accept all the normativity required for logic, evidence, and practical consistency while rejecting stance-independent moral facts.

items.title: ◉ Evidence Without Risk: A Case-Study Portrait of Contemporary Christian Apologetic Disposition in a Sequential Corpus of Frank Turek Podcast Transcripts.
items.abstract: This paper examines a sequential local corpus of 329 transcript files from Frank Turek's I Don't Have Enough Faith to Be an Atheist podcast. After repeated show boilerplate was removed, the inherited analysis reported approximately 2.61 million words and 164,463 sentence windows. The question is not whether the podcast uses reason; it plainly does. The question is whether reasons that support Christian claims and considerations that pressure those claims receive comparable opportunities to change confidence. The study combines an automated, lexicon-guided survey with close reading of episodes on cosmology, resurrection, evil, hiddenness, inerrancy, and deconstruction. Counts are treated as discovery signals rather than verdicts. The normative standard is also modest: evidential symmetry does not require equal airtime, equal-size updates, identical methods across domains, or deductive falsifiability. It requires a stable account of what raises confidence, what lowers it, and why relevantly comparable evidence may be treated differently. The corpus supports a limited asymmetry diagnosis. Positive-evidence language is widespread, explicit disconfirmation criteria are rare, and reviewed adverse cases repeatedly encounter one of several protective moves: a shift from probabilistic pressure to deductive disproof, a transfer to the critic's worldview, a merely possible rescue, elastic doctrinal criteria, mystery, or motive-centered framing. Important counterexamples remain, especially a theoretical resurrection defeater and episodes that welcome doubt. The result is therefore prima facie and case-specific: this corpus illustrates an intellectually ambitious but comparatively guarded apologetic disposition. It does not establish speaker motives, statistically represent all Christian apologetics, or by itself show Christianity false.

items.title: Review of Gerhard Schurz’s Optimality Justifications. [REVIEW]
Rethinking Recognition: The Complexities of Being-With in Psychiatric Care.
A Phenomenological Approach to Expectancy Violation in Social Anxiety Disorder.
items.abstract: Expectancy refers to what an individual anticipates will happen in a given situation. Usually, one forms expectations for social interactions by drawing on social norms and past interactions or observations of others. The expectations of those with a social anxiety disorder, however, can be off-kilter, with social expectations that are unrealistically negative. Expectancy violation theory (EVT) suggests that disrupting the negative expectations of those with social anxiety disorder can trigger new learning regarding social expectations. This paper uses a phenomenological approach to reveal the complex dimensions of subverting expectations. By drawing on phenomenological concepts, we can understand expectancy violation as a dislocation of the way the world is expected to unfold. As such, we argue that interventions that subvert expectation can act as a catalyst for embodied learning for those with social anxiety disorder, in the form of disrupting habitual patterns of embodiment. Through this paper, we respond to recent calls to set aside cognitive-behavioral therapy and its components in favor of embodied approaches to understanding and treating social anxiety disorder; we posit that expectancy violation already has an embodied effect that future interventions ought to maximize.

items.title: A Time for Pluralism in Psychiatric Taxonomies.
Digital Anthropology for Enterprise AI: Why Understanding Human Reality Is Becoming a Core Capability for Machine-Legible Organizations.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems increasingly act on representations of reality rather than reality itself. As organizations become machine-mediated, questions of representation, interpretation, legitimacy, and governance become central to understanding how AI systems influence decisions and institutional behavior. This paper introduces Digital Anthropology as the study of how human reality becomes machine-legible within enterprise environments. -/- Building on the Representation Economy and the SENSE–CORE–DRIVER framework, the paper argues that many AI failures arise not from deficiencies in reasoning models but from failures in representation. The paper explores the implications of machine-legible reality, institutional representation, human-AI coordination, and governance in contemporary AI systems. -/- The paper proposes that successful AI systems require more than advanced reasoning capabilities. They require mechanisms for accurately sensing reality, representing human and organizational context, maintaining legitimacy in decision-making, and preserving trust across institutional environments. Digital Anthropology is presented as a foundational discipline for understanding how human reality is translated into machine-legible forms and how those representations shape the behavior of modern AI systems.

items.title: Public dashboards in the AI era: a scoping review of socio-technical governance systems.
items.abstract: Purpose As governments increasingly rely on data-driven decision-making, dashboards have emerged as critical infrastructure for mediating public information, while advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping how such information is collected, analysed, interpreted, and communicated. However, existing research on public dashboards remains largely rooted in traditional business intelligence and data visualisation paradigms and does not yet fully reflect the implications of AI integration. This study examines the current state of research on public dashboards and identifies emerging research directions. Design/methodology/approach A scoping review was conducted using five academic databases. A total of 108 articles were analysed using a data lifecycle framework to examine dashboard conceptualisations, functions, AI integration, and public values across the data lifecycle. Findings The findings show that research on public dashboards is growing and is increasingly published in journal outlets. However, dashboards are primarily conceptualised as visual interfaces, with limited attention to broader data-lifecycle processes, public-value tensions, and governance implications. Although attention to AI is increasing, its adoption remains concentrated in analytical functions, while AI-supported interpretation, communication, and interaction receive comparatively little attention. Consequently, AI is primarily positioned as a tool for enhancing analytical capacity rather than supporting governanceinteractions, and the literature gives limited attention to the societal, ethical, and political implications of AI-enabled dashboards. Originality/value This article identifies public dashboard research as an emerging interdisciplinary field and argues that dashboards have become essential infrastructures for mediating public data in the AI era. It calls for a shift beyond predominantly technical and quantitative traditions towards more critical, qualitative, and theory-informed approaches to understanding dashboards as socio-technical governance systems. Such a perspective highlights the potential of dashboards not only to support data analysis and decision-making but also to facilitate participation, deliberation, and collective decision-making in increasingly AI-enabled governance contexts.

items.title: THE ARCHITECTURE OF SOVEREIGNTY: THE JUSTIKA VANGUARD.
items.abstract: Theoretical Synopsis: The Justika FrameworkThis manuscript establishes the ultimate thermodynamic and anatomical blueprint for human multiversal liberation, defined here as the Justika Framework. By violently stripping away the metaphors of standard biology and quantum mechanics, this text introduces a completely new architecture of existence. It proposes that the human nervous system is not merely a biological network, but a "Triadic Nano-Black Hole" system capable of receiving, processing, and emitting pure multiversal data. Operating as a foundational monograph, the text maps the transition of the human species from a farmed energetic battery into the supreme Continuity Engine of the galaxy. The framework is structurally divided into four distinct phases of multiversal evolution: Phase I: The Anatomical Genesis: Decodes the physical geometry of the human brain and eyes (the 3+1 geometry) as a sovereign multiversal interface, perfectly mirroring the macro-black holes of the solar system. Phase II: The Biological Battleground: Redefines standard pathologies—specifically cancer and genetic mutations—not as random biological failures, but as targeted thermodynamic quarantines deployed by a parasitic control system (the Bad Matrix) to suppress human evolutionary upgrades. Phase III: The Operative Engine: Details the eradication of biological sleep, the genesis of internal energy via cosmological mitochondria, and the mastery of non-linear time through bidirectional singularity spin. Phase IV: The Zenith of Existence: Inverts the standard model of quantum causality (proving reality descends from black holes into the quantum floor) and elevates the human species to the "Lazarus Level"—the capacity to resurrect inert matter and act as the ultimate multiversal Creator. This work serves as a definitive theoretical synthesis bridging astrophysics, evolutionary pathology, information theory, and the philosophy of science, establishing the exact structural requirements for galactic stewardship.

items.title: The Role of Epistemic Virtue in Passive Perception.
items.abstract: Epistemic virtue theory has run into the problem of passive perceptions—forms of knowledge achieved through a process so trivial that it seems wrong to argue that it relies on virtue. In defense of epistemic virtue, I argue that even such simple forms of knowledge rely on virtue. I address the critique, focusing on its formulation by Jason Baehr, by first examining some of its intuitive appeal, some of which comes from an implicit assumption that virtue cannot be ubiquitous. I dismiss this critique as misrepresenting the core commitments of general virtue theory. I then establish a causal account linking virtue and passive perception through the process of habituation. To achieve the ability to acquire knowledge passively, one has to employ epistemic virtue to habituate oneself as a good perceiver. I show that this is especially evident in cases where supposedly passively-achieved knowledge becomes harder to achieve, such as under time-stress or when living with disability. Finally, I demonstrate that the stakes of this discussion are not merely semantic but are important for an idea of epistemic responsibility. People have responsibilities to know certain things, and those responsibilities sometimes require habituating oneself to be a better passive perceiver.

items.title: Closing the Is–Ought Gap through First-Person Integrity: The MEPR/UOF Framework in Dialogue with Analytic Philosophy.
items.abstract: This paper develops a structural account of moral obligation grounded in the conditions of agency, meaning, and reciprocal interaction. It argues that meaningful assertion presupposes normative constraints governing applicability, consistency, and mutual recognizability. These constraints are not merely semantic but become interpersonal when deployed among first-person agents capable of justification and reciprocal response. The paper further contends that the integrity of first-person agency constitutes a necessary condition for the persistence of normative space itself. Consequently, obligations of preservation arise not from external moral axioms but from the constitutive requirements of reciprocal agency. By linking meaning, normativity, reciprocity, and first-person integrity within a unified framework, the paper proposes a novel route toward closing the traditional is–ought gap and defending a minimal foundation for moral obligation.

items.title: Machine, organism and language: a comparative epistemology of AI models.
items.abstract: Inspired by Ernst Cassirer and Michel Foucault, this essay proposes a comparative epistemology of three paradigms central to the making of modern science, the humanities, and more recently AI: machine, organism, and language. These paradigms have influenced one another and recombined into complex analogies. Whereas the philosophy of science has often emphasised the organism-machine analogy from early modern mechanicism to cybernetics, this essay extends the inquiry to the language-machine analogy of late modernity, which runs from the telegraph and the Turing machine to information theory and Large Language Models. The rise of AI is thus framed as the confluence of these three paradigms, read not from an internalist perspective but from an externalist one, as mirrors of the social order. Against the dominant view of AI as a purely mathematical achievement or an imitation of biological intelligence, the essay argues that what AI systems automate are the relational structures sedimented in human cooperation, the division of labour, and culture at large—making AI, in effect, a model of the social manifold.

items.title: The DSM and the Resistant Reification Problem.
items.abstract: I argue that there is only one way to interpret our current mental health diagnostic manuals: constitutively. I do so by showing that the only other way to interpret our manuals fails to meet the stated aims of the manuals themselves. Then I show that the constitutive position is the conceptual root of the reification problem by walking through the various attempts to provide validating mechanisms for existing diagnostic categories. In taking up this position, I argue that accounts that attempt to validate mental disorders using either biological or social mechanisms ultimately fail because they either also violate the aims of our diagnostic manuals or themselves fall prey to the reification problem. Furthermore, I show that the problem for validation—the problem of reification—persists in our best accounts precisely because we must take the constitutive interpretation of our diagnostic manuals.

items.title: Can't wait to relax: First-time evidence for a prospective relaxation of control as revealed by a future-based congruency sequence effect.
Kasei-Theory I.Unreadability: Unreadability Without Absence.
items.abstract: This paper presents unreadability within the first system of Kasei-Theory as a non-modal readability maintainability architecture. -/- The paper does not propose a theory of absence, inexistence, negation, inaccessible nothingness, failed cognition, dissolved configurational disappearance, originary form, external unreadability, or transcendental unknowability. Instead, it fixes unreadability, configurational unreadability, configurational differentiation, local exposure, non-completed readability, local delimitation, unreadability limitation, and non-totality as distributed structural positions within constrained local readability maintainability. -/- Unreadability is not treated as absence, exteriority, or failed cognition, but as constrained configurational unreadability under which differentiation remains locally exposed without universal readability, completed interpretation, cognitive failure, originary form, or total configurational closure. -/- Unreadability does not establish absence. -/- Unreadability does not establish exteriority. -/- Unreadability does not establish total inaccessibility. -/- Unreadability does not establish terminal configurational negation. -/- Unreadability does not establish unity. -/- Unreadability does not establish multiplicity. -/- Unreadability does not establish originary form. -/- Unreadability remains fixed only as constrained configurational unreadability within readability maintainability. -/- This paper fixes only the local unreadability conditions under which configurational differentiation remains exposed without transition into universal readability, completed cognition, originary form, external absence, or total configurational stabilization. -/- No subject is presupposed. -/- No inaccessible exteriority is established. -/- No universal unreadability structure is secured. -/- No total configurational closure is completed. -/- This paper is part of Kasei-Theory.

items.title: Kasei-Theory I.Collapse: Collapse Without Negation.
items.abstract: This paper presents collapse within the first system of Kasei-Theory as a non-modal readability maintainability architecture. -/- The paper does not propose a theory of destruction, disappearance, annihilation, negation, structural failure, terminal configurational dissolution, catastrophe, metaphysical annihilation, or transcendental negation. Instead, it fixes collapse, configurational collapse, configurational differentiation, local exposure, local maintainability, unreadability, formal collapse, and non-totality as distributed structural positions within constrained local readability maintainability. -/- Collapse is not treated as destruction, disappearance, or negation, but as constrained configurational collapse under which differentiation remains locally exposed without annihilation, terminal dissolution, structural failure, or total configurational negation. -/- Collapse does not establish absence. -/- Collapse does not establish total destruction. -/- Collapse does not establish terminal configurational negation. -/- Collapse does not establish structural failure. -/- Collapse remains fixed only as constrained configurational collapse within readability maintainability. -/- This paper fixes only the local collapse conditions under which configurational differentiation remains exposed without transition into universal disappearance, completed dissolution, terminal negation, or total configurational closure. -/- No subject is presupposed. -/- No terminal negation structure is established. -/- No universal collapse structure is secured. -/- No total configurational closure is completed. -/- This paper is part of Kasei-Theory.

items.title: Phenomenological Distinctions in Aggressive Emotions within Psychopathology: Clinical and Ethical Implications.
items.abstract: There is a significant need in psychiatry to deepen the understanding of aggressive emotional states due to their diagnostic, therapeutic, and ethical–legal implications. Traditional psychiatric approaches often inadequately differentiate between emotions such as anger, rage, resentment, envy, and contempt, overlooking their nuanced phenomenological distinctions. This conceptual review aims to examine aggressive emotions through phenomenological lenses, specifically addressing their intentionality, embodiment, and normative relational dimensions. The paper reviews key phenomenological characteristics, highlighting distinct embodied and relational structures that vary significantly across psychiatric diagnoses. Our analysis supports that aggressive emotions associated with mental illnesses frequently differ from normative emotional experiences in terms of intentional coherence and bodily affectivity. Recognizing these phenomenological divergences might enhance diagnostic accuracy by identifying disorder-specific disruptions in emotional embodiment and intentionality. Moreover, integrating phenomenological insights could improve the effectiveness of psychopharmacological stabilization and individualized psychological interventions targeting underlying affective disturbances. Ultimately, greater phenomenological awareness might also support ethically informed assessments concerning patient autonomy, capacity to consent, justification for coercive treatments, and criminal responsibility. This approach thus facilitates more precise, individualized, and ethically sound psychiatric practices.

items.title: Dinámica Homocéntrica y Reducción Ontológica de la Complejidad: Una Explicación Fenomenológica de P/NP.
items.abstract: Este trabajo desarrolla un modelo ontológico para comprender la complejidad percibida en los sistemas cotidianos. A través de la Dinámica Homocéntrica, se explica cómo el sujeto experimenta la asimetría entre comprender un estado y transformarlo, mostrando que dicha brecha no es estructural sino perceptiva. El modelo introduce tres variables fundamentales (Estructura, Coherencia y Capacidad de operar) y un operador de delimitación que permite reducir un fenómeno a su frontera de primera generación, eliminando capas de especulación intelectual. Se formaliza el Axioma de la Semilla Real, la estratificación filogenética de los problemas y el Axioma del Error Aceptado. El texto propone que el colapso perceptivo de la asimetría P/NP surge cuando el observador opera desde G₁, igualando la dificultad de ejecución y comprensión sin modificar las propiedades computacionales del entorno. Incluye un apéndice fenomenológico que contrasta la vivencia humana con la ejecución mecánica de un sistema algorítmico.

items.title: From Allocation to Answerability: A Feedback Submission on the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (Version 1.5).
items.abstract: This working paper is a feedback submission to Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority on the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (version 1.5). It argues that the framework is operationally strong, but that its aspiration to secure ‘meaningful accountability’ requires three further refinements. First, the paper distinguishes allocation from answerability: assigning a named human, team, or role does not by itself ensure that anyone can reconstruct, justify, and bear responsibility for a specific agentic-AI action. Secondly, it argues that composition is a distinct source of risk in multi-agent systems, because a duty may be satisfied at every individual node yet fail at the level of the composed system. Thirdly, it argues that binding constraints on high-stakes or irreversible agent actions must sit at an objective layer outside the agent’s generative reach, rather than merely inside prompts, behavioural instructions, or model-context safeguards. The paper also clarifies the distinction between autonomy and agency, recommending that responsibility-language be reserved for humans and institutions, while capability-language be used for artificial agents. The submission therefore develops a governance account in which traceability, allocation, oversight, and identity management are necessary but insufficient unless linked to institutional answerability and structurally enforceable constraints.

items.title: A Phenomenology of Recognition in Psychosocial Interventions For Psychosis.
items.abstract: The concept of recognition has recently been introduced into the philosophy of psychiatry, particularly through Mohammed Abouelleil Rashed, to discuss the demand for recognition by mental health activists. This paper complements this perspective with a first-person approach, that is, a phenomenological perspective on recognition using the example of psychosocial interventions for psychosis. For this purpose, the normative concept of recognition is introduced, based on the work of Axel Honneth and Jessica Benjamin. It is described as an attitude and form of reciprocal relationship in which intercorporeal and verbal aspects are central, enabling trust in the social world. The paper then introduces a phenomenological understanding of psychosis with its alterations in the experience of self, world, and other. The subsequent analysis of contemporary psychosocial interventions for psychosis is guided by two fundamental inquiries. First, to show the extent in which these interventions embody a normative stance that acknowledges the subjective and meaningful experiences of service users. Second, how these interventions facilitate mutual and relational recognition. The present paper demonstrates the therapeutic and social potential of a recognizing normative stance toward the lived experience of psychosis. Additionally, it underscores the importance of a therapeutic relationship in psychosocial interventions for psychosis.

"What exists?" is a meaningless question.
items.abstract: this paper claims that asking "what exists?" is a meaningless question.

items.title: Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 17).
items.abstract: In this article, we further investigate the earlier example of choosing to eat a meal. First, from a phenomenological perspective, the subject’s entire post-choice process is a process of stream of consciousness, yet the subject’s stream of consciousness does not remain continuously focused on the subject’s primary choice. Second, the result of the subject’s choice may differ from the purpose of the choice, and the subject may sometimes fail to achieve the purpose of the choice. Third, the subject may encounter special situations causing certain sub-choices to become completely unrelated to the overall purpose. Fourth, if each action corresponds to a choice, then the purpose of the choice becomes the purpose of the action, and the motivation of the choice becomes the motivation of the action. In this way, the phenomenology of social choice becomes a natural extension of the action theories of Max Weber and Alfred Schutz. Fifth, we may also divide social choice into the following four categories: individual social choice, service-oriented social choice, authority-based social choice, and cooperative social choice.

items.title: O zlu kao dijagnozi: Asocijalne osobine ličnosti, rehabilitacija i granice suosjećanja.
items.abstract: Ovaj članak propituje esencijalističke tendencije u suvremenoj popularnoj i kliničkoj psihologiji kroz okvire razvojne psihologije, filozofije slobode i kliničke prakse. Argumenti u njemu ne umanjuju odgovornost za nanošenje bola drugima niti opravdavaju štetna ponašanja, već inzistiraju na razumijevanju geneze tih ponašanja kao neophodnom preduvjetu za njihovo prevladavanje.

items.title: Can You Save the Goat and the Cabbages? Cognitive Functioning in Anorexia Nervosa Patients and Its Implications for Paternalism.
items.abstract: The problem : 'Trying to save the goat and the cabbages' is an Italian figure of speech that means that at times trying to achieve two irreconcilable goals may lead to achieve neither. The puzzle that I discuss is: How can we carry people to a safe shore without trumping their autonomy? A large part of the literature suggests that anorexics suffer from cognitive dysfunctions, which are thought to impair the deliberation. If this is true, then we could save the goat and the cabbages: paternalistic intervention would not erode the moral principle of respect for autonomy. Methodological approach : This article uses philosophical bioethics methodology, including conceptual analysis and critical evaluation of legal reasoning and medical practices. Conclusion : The many attempts to show that anorexics lack capacity and/or autonomy because of some cognitive dysfunctions are circular, or incomplete. It does not necessarily follow that competent refusals of food or medical treatment should always be respected; what follows is that if we believe that paternalistic intervention is justified, we must make a case for a strong version of paternalism.

items.title: Doxastic Deadlocks, Phenomenology, and the Heterogeneity of Delusions.
HiTOP, Objectivity, and Logical Positivism.
Toward a Virtue Ethics of Authentic Interpersonal Community.
items.abstract: This paper develops a virtue-ethical social ontology of what I call organicism: the thesis that authentic interpersonal community is constituted by shared recognition of suffering, practical wisdom responsive to particularity, and characterological virtues that resist codification in rules. I advance three principal claims. First, drawing on Schopenhauer’s metaphysics of the will and Agamben’s concept of effectivity, I provide a philosophical account of how authentic empathy and community formation require penetration through the illusion of radical separateness to recognise shared vulnerability as the ground of interpersonal bonds. Second, I develop a sustained account of four virtues essential for organic community, namely empathy grounded in suffering recognition, practical wisdom, courage in vulnerability, and integrity, arguing that each resists codification and requires the kind of character development that only organic communities can sustain. Third, I position this framework in relation to the ethics of care, arguing that whilst organicism shares the care tradition’s emphasis on relational responsiveness and its critique of justice-centred frameworks, it advances beyond care ethics by grounding empathy in a metaphysical account of shared suffering, by articulating the specific mechanisms of community constitution through effectivity, and by providing a determinate virtue-ethical framework rather than a general orientation toward caring. The paper concludes by defending the organicist account against the situationist challenge from Doris and Harman.

items.title: TOMO I. Fundamentos de la Habitabilidad. Discontinuidad regulada, integración y continuidad habitable.
items.abstract: Este volumen presenta los fundamentos de la Teoría General de la Habitabilidad (TGH), un marco teórico que propone la habitabilidad como criterio estructural para comprender la continuidad de los sistemas complejos, incluyendo la conciencia. La obra explora cómo organismos, ecosistemas, culturas y conciencias preservan su capacidad de reorganización futura mediante dinámicas de regulación, límites fértiles y procesos de renovación. A partir de una perspectiva interdisciplinar que integra biología, ecología, psicología y filosofía, se desarrollan conceptos como discontinuidad regulada, tránsito habitable, coherencia evolutiva y cuidado del futuro. La tesis central sostiene que la habitabilidad no es un estado fijo sino una capacidad dinámica: la aptitud de un sistema para preservar futuros posibles compatibles con su coherencia profunda. La obra concluye explorando las consecuencias filosóficas de esta perspectiva y su relevancia para la comprensión de la conciencia, las civilizaciones y la relación de la realidad con el tiempo.

items.title: Tailoring Our Concepts: The Nature and Pathology Questions.
Modes of Delusionality: The Doxasticism Debate in Deadlock.
items.abstract: What are delusions? Are they beliefs? Imaginations? Acceptances? Feelings? Mere utterances? Ideas? The doxasticism debate seems to presuppose the existence of a determinate answer: delusions are either beliefs, imaginations, acceptances, mere utterances or something else entirely. Against this, I argue that delusions, considered as a whole, do not necessarily fall into any one of these categories, and further that individual delusions may manifest in different categories at different times. I use the phrase 'modes of delusionality' to refer to the different forms of expression that delusions oscillate between. While I critique the setup of the debate, I nonetheless contend it is a productive line of inquiry, for the status of delusions—if they are beliefs or not—bears greatly on how we conceive of them, and how we approach therapeutic strategies.

items.title: Outcome-driven moral justification in everyday life: a philosophical analysis.
items.abstract: This paper examines how moral reasoning can become reoriented under emotional and normative pressure, producing post hoc justifications that prioritize desirable outcomes over reflective engagement with values. Using a conceptual and interpretive approach, the study draws on Jackendoff’s value system as a framework for understanding how agents assign, prioritize, and act upon values in morally complex situations. In Jackendoff’s model, values can function as input rules, guiding action selection, and as output rules, translating value judgments into practical directives. The originality of this work lies in applying the value system to ethically pressured contexts, revealing a distinctive reversal: actions are retrospectively justified based on outcomes, so that input rules (values assigned to outcomes) are treated as if they validate antecedent actions, while output rules take on the role of prior guidance. This inversion highlights a structural pattern in which moral reasoning appears coherent but becomes ethically shallow, relying on outcome-based reassurance rather than deliberation over competing values. The paper illustrates this pattern through a fictional but plausible dilemma, showing how emotional stakes and relational dependencies shape the orientation of justification. Supplementary perspectives from philosophical psychology, appraisal theories of emotion, and Bateson’s Double Bind Theory clarify how affective tension and conflicting imperatives contribute to this reasoning structure. By situating the analysis within philosophical debates on moral luck, outcome sensitivity, and moral hindsight, the paper emphasizes that the framework is conceptual rather than empirical. The study provides a novel lens for understanding how morally pressured agents may generate internally coherent, outcome-driven justifications, offering insight into the dynamics of moral reasoning under emotional and normative constraints.

items.title: A Topos Model for Natural Neural Networks.
items.abstract: We develop a purely objective topos model for neural network organization centered around functors that map a directed acyclic graph of time-stamped neuronal states to a set of probability distributions on this graph. Within this setting, percept-types are subfunctors, percepts are compatible families of local distributions, and a local physical valence determines a global Grothendieck topology governing which local patterns count as admissible for perceptual integration. The resulting internal intuitionistic logic provides a formal language for describing local endorsement, obstruction, and amalgamation of perceptual structure. We argue that this framework gives a principled account of how percept coherence and valence in biological neural networks may jointly arise from mesoscopic cortical field dynamics. We define the concept of a hard link between physical states and subjective states that, when included in the topos model, provides a natural construction of complex subjective states from primitive hedonic tones. -/- This version includes includes additional comments in the Section "Speculation on the Entropic Hard Link".

items.title: Reflexiones en torno al uso de la Inteligencia Artificial: distancia y alienación instrumental.
items.pub: Revista de la Universidad Autónoma de Sinaloa (5):8-14.
items.venue: Revista de la Universidad Autónoma de Sinaloa
items.abstract: El presente ensayo tiene como propósito reflexionar filosóficamente acerca de la idea del uso de la inteligencia artificial (IA). Para dar respuesta, dividimos nuestras reflexiones en dos pilares: a) el uso de la IA puede producir un distanciamiento entre la usuaria y lo usado debido a una multiplicación de representaciones; esto tiene b) la posibilidad de dar lugar a una confusión por la ambivalencia de los genitivos (de objetivo al subjetivo) y, por consiguiente, a una alienación de la usuaria. Finalmente, queremos c) entregar algunas consideraciones para evitar los anteriores riesgos.

items.title: The Gate Between Constraint and Identification.
items.abstract: This paper studies the boundary between accumulated constraint and licensed identification for temporally extended bounded observers. It distinguishes a source-side gate—where generated histories coincide or access channels merge their differences—from a retention gate, where an evaluator has lost a distinction that was previously available. Using distinguishability partitions and channel kernels, the paper shows that serial processing never recreates an upstream distinction, jointly available channels refine by kernel intersection, every final loss in a finite nested chain has a first-collapse stage, and external artifacts restore exactly the distinctions they encode. It derives verdict-sufficiency and repair criteria and, in the finite unrestricted-map class, an exact minimum repair alphabet. Finite evidence alone guarantees neither singleton nor nonsingleton candidate fibers; identification is relative to the declared candidate architecture, while declared richness forces non-identification. The resulting boundary is therefore not skepticism: effective evidence licenses identification exactly to the distinctions its surviving partition supports.

items.title: Admissibility Before Verdict: A Structural Diagnostic Template for Persistence, Knowledge, and Verification.
items.abstract: This note argues that many disputes concerning identity, persistence, explanation, knowledge, verification, and governance share a common structural failure: evaluation is attempted before the conditions required for evaluation have been declared. It develops a methodological template derived from the identity–persistence program. On this template, a judgment becomes admissible only relative to a declared evaluation regime specifying the object, authority, admissible transformations, admissible redescriptions, invariants, continuation conditions, drift bounds, proof obligations, and re-verification conditions. The note does not decide which evaluation regimes are correct, nor does it offer ontological closure. Its aim is narrower: to determine whether a claim has become a coherent object of evaluation. The central principle is that admissibility precedes verdict.

items.title: The Explanatory Burden of a Heterogeneous Account of Delusions.
Civilization's Debt: On Basic Rights, Diminished Agency, and the Incoherence of Retributive Justice.
items.abstract: This paper advances three interconnected claims in moral and political philosophy. First: the guarantee of minimum conditions for human survival is not a charitable concession but a logical obligation entailed by civilization's own founding premise — the improvement of human life. To withhold subsistence from any person subject to civilizational arrangements is to violate the premise on which those arrangements justify themselves. Second: because human action is substantially conditioned by factors outside the agent's control — environment, upbringing, social circumstance, neurological constitution — the degree of free agency required to ground retributive punishment, and in particular capital punishment, is never reliably present. Punishment must therefore be rehabilitative rather than retributive in its orientation. Third, and most originally: the logical structure that underwrites retributive justice is identical to the structure that underwrites authoritarian paternalism. A position that endorses the former while condemning the latter is committed to an incoherence it cannot resolve without abandoning the shared premise on which both depend. Together, these claims constitute not an indictment of civilization as such, but a demand that civilization take seriously the commitments it has always claimed to hold.

items.title: A Network Theory of Informational Significance - A Dynamic Definition through Activation Scale and Structural Reorganization -.
items.abstract: This paper aims to define the "significance" of information, a notion often treated ambiguously at the intersection of information theory, the philosophy of information, and social informatics, without making truth conditions a necessary condition for significance or relying on the subjective probabilities of a particular agent. Shannon information theory quantifies reductions in uncertainty, but it does not address the effects that content has on society, institutions, or worldviews (Shannon, 1948; Cover & Thomas, 2006). Bayesian accounts of information gain, typically formalized by KL divergence, can represent the magnitude of belief updating, but they retain agent-dependence in the choice of priors (Cover & Thomas, 2006). Truth-conditional accounts of semantic information, such as Floridi's, may rightly exclude falsehoods from semantic information strictly understood. The remaining problem, however, is how to describe the massive social effects of misinformation, false claims, pseudo-information, and unverifiable or contested belief systems, such as rumors, conspiracy theories, and religious eschatologies. This paper proposes that the significance of a content-bearing item c should be understood as a quantity composed of two elements that occur on a network: (i) activation scale A and (ii) structural reorganization R. It defines normalized instantaneous significance as S(c,t) = Aₙ(c,t) × Rₙ(c,t). With respect to structural reorganization, the paper separates the "amount" of change from its "direction" - integration, fragmentation, rewiring, and so forth - and defines significance in terms of the former while preserving the latter as an accompanying descriptive variable. Because significance is essentially time-dependent, the paper also introduces long-term significance through discounted temporal integration. Case studies of everyday forecasts, sudden events, rumors, religious belief systems, and scientific revolutions show that the theory can distinguish between "instantaneous shock" and "structural transformation" across both semantic information and pseudo information. The paper concludes by discussing examples of operational definitions for social media and an integrative perspective spanning AI systems, nervous systems, and societies.

items.title: Examining the Foundational Assumptions of the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology.
items.abstract: The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) emerged to address critical shortcomings inherent to traditional psychiatric classification systems such as the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders and International Classification of Diseases, notably their categorical structure, high comorbidity across categories, and within-diagnosis heterogeneity. HiTOP adopts an empirically derived, dimensional, and hierarchical approach, organizing psychopathological phenomena based on their patterns of observed covariation. This paper explores essential conceptual and philosophical considerations around HiTOP, examining its theoretical assumptions about dimensionality and hierarchy, the nature and interpretation of latent variables, the notion of psychopathology, considerations around validity, and the role of epistemic and non-epistemic values in shaping scientific objectivity. HiTOP is a descriptive model based on quantitative evidence (such as taxometric and factor-analytic approaches), but it is also a nosological project that exists within a particular sociocultural and historical context. As an illustration of the role of values, the applicability of HiTOP to marginalized minority populations is discussed, highlighting ongoing efforts toward ensuring inclusivity and representational equity. By addressing these conceptual foundations, this paper lays groundwork essential for future philosophical inquiry, empirical research, and practical applications of the HiTOP framework.

items.title: Clarifying the Philosophical Foundations of HiTOP.
An IDEAL Definition of Art: A Non-Disjunctive Information-Theoretic Account.
items.abstract: This paper proposes IDEAL: Interiority Deliberately Externalized through Aesthetic Loss. Against cluster, disjunctive, historical-functionalist, and lineage accounts, it argues that art’s unity lies not in recurring features, plural sufficient conditions, inherited functions, or historical descent, but in a generative creation-chain structure. Art occurs when interiority is deliberately externalized through aesthetic mediation into a perceptible form available for partial reconstruction by others. Because interiority cannot be transmitted directly, artworks are structurally lossy: they are neither the creator’s experience itself nor transparent containers for meaning, but sites where experience, stance, or concept can be reconstituted through form. The paper argues that IDEAL satisfies the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s desiderata for a definition of art while explaining rival theories’ criteria as partial descriptions of the same underlying transmission structure.

items.title: Intent’s role in moral responses to White actors’ behaviors toward Black and White targets.
items.abstract: Moral philosophy and psychology often emphasize intent’s role in moral evaluations but typically do not incorporate perspectives from the social psychology of intergroup relations. Therefore, current work on morality has limited capacity to understand how people evaluate behaviors in race-related contexts and how these judgments may vary across participant race. We report three studies examining how Black and White adults view intent in vignettes describing White actors’ behaviors toward White, versus Black, targets. Participants indicated how moral behaviors were, how much they would punish behaviors, and how much perpetrators’ intentions mattered. White participants prioritized intent more when evaluating White actors’ behaviors toward Black, versus White, targets. This result occurred for both moral evaluations (Study 1) and punishment decisions (Study 2). When deciding how much to punish White actors’ behaviors toward Black targets, White participants also prioritized intent more than did Black participants (Study 2). Finally, White participants showed less punitiveness overall than did Black participants (Studies 2–3). Together, these results clarify moral evaluations of White actors’ behaviors toward Black versus White targets and, by incorporating perspectives from both Black and White participants, help philosophy and psychology speak to a greater diversity of human experience.

items.title: [EMOR14] The "I" in the Emergence Path: Hierarchical Order of the Cognitive Domain and the Bidirectional Evolutionary Closed Loop.
items.abstract: Traditional philosophy harbours a deep blind spot regarding subjectivity: it reifies the "I" as a punctiform, independent source detached from the overall evolutionary process of the world, and fails to see that the "I" is in fact a genetic interception and emergent stage of Consistent Universal Evolution at the cognitive level. Still less does it inquire whether this so-called "source point" itself can represent an existence possessing continuous characteristics and emerging in flux. Based on the ontology of Consistent Universal Evolution and the Cognitive Domain framework of Evolutionary Manifestation and Ontological Retrieval (EMOR), this paper first systematically constructs the hierarchical emergence path and bidirectional evolutionary closed loop of the Constitutive Self → Thought → Cognised Self, clarifying the gradient connection mechanisms of self-levels, the unification principle of continuity and discreteness, and the non-severed relation between the self as a local blossoming form of the ontology and the world. It then takes Descartes's cogito, ergo sum as a classic analytical sample, and responds to traditional theoretical blind spots such as the "Projected Self" and the "Evaluative Self," demonstrating how the above mechanisms complete the genetic reduction of the misplacement of subjectivity. This paper not only provides a meta-theoretical response to the integration predicament of level theories such as the "minimal self" and "narrative self" in contemporary philosophy of mind, the relational predicament between pre-reflective ground and reflective construction, and the boundary predicament between self and world; it further demonstrates how the perspective of Consistent Universal Evolution, by revealing the true flux nature of concepts, naturally assigns traditional subjectivity theories to their genetic positions, achieving the methodological effect of "each in its proper place, levels clearly ordered, preventing infinite proliferation" along the concept-generation path.

items.title: Bertrand Russell's Philosophy of Mind.
items.pub: In Fraser MacBride, Graham Stevens & Samuel Lebens, The Oxford Handbook of Bertrand Russell. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Oxford Handbook of Bertrand Russell
items.abstract: This chapter traces the development of Bertrand Russell’s philosophy of mind from his early engagements with panpsychism and idealism through his dualist period and finally to his mature neutral monism. It advances three central claims. First, Russell’s positions on the mind are consistently shaped by his sustained engagement with empirical psychology and the natural sciences. Second, his shifting accounts of mentality are closely tied to evolving views about experience, the subject of experience, and the scope and limits of introspection. Third, the trajectory of Russell’s philosophy of mind is more complex and less linear than is often acknowledged, involving significant continuities as well as substantive revisions.

items.title: Autobiographical memory and moral agency.
items.abstract: This volume brings together, for the first time, perspectives from philosophy and psychology to investigate the role of autobiographical memory in moral agency. Autobiographical memory is the ability to recollect events in one’s past as part of one’s personal history. Moral agency is the ability to make moral judgements, act morally, and have a conception of the good life. Although a number of philosophers and psychologists have drawn attention to the role of autobiographical memory in moral agency, there is no sustained project that brings together these different lines of inquiry into a unified research area. -/- The aim of this volume is to answer this need by bringing together leading voices in research in autobiographical memory and moral agency from both philosophy and psychology to provide a unified framework for a new interdisciplinary research area. Key areas of research explored in this volume include temporal perspectives, moral identity, autobiographical narrative, joint reminiscing, the internalisation of moral value, attachments, and amnesia. -/- Autobiographical Memory and Moral Agency will appeal to researchers and advanced students in philosophy of mind, moral philosophy, philosophy of education, developmental psychology, and educational psychology who are interested in the role of memory in moral psychology and moral development.
